gramatica.titulo: で: where an action happens / with what
よ and ね at the end of a sentence

ve3c627fbdf.frase: 料理に大根を使ったよ。
ve3c627fbdf.frase_furigana: 料理[りょうり]に大根[だいこん]を 使[つか]ったよ。
ve3c627fbdf.tono: ダイコン
ve3c627fbdf.frase_es: I used daikon in my cooking.

gramatica.titulo: よ and ね at the end of a sentence
に: destination, time, where something is

ve3c627fbdf.matiz: A big white radish used all over Japanese cooking: 大根[だいこん]おろし = grated daikon. Slang: 大根役者[だいこんやくしゃ] = a terrible actor, a ham.

v7a852992ee.frase_furigana: このコーヒー、苦[にが]いね。

gramatica.titulo: よ and ね at the end of a sentence

v7a852992ee.matiz: 苦[にが]い顔[かお]をする = to make a sour face. Also 苦[にが]い経験[けいけん] = a bitter experience, just like in English.

v1d486d1858.frase: ニャンの行方がわかりません。
v1d486d1858.frase_furigana: ニャンの行方[ゆくえ]がわかりません。
v1d486d1858.frase_es: We don't know where Nyan is.

gramatica.titulo: が: who or what (the identified subject)

v1d486d1858.matiz: 行方[ゆくえ]がわからない = nobody knows where someone is; 行方不明[ゆくえふめい] (word 2799) = missing. It can also be where things are heading: 試合[しあい]の行方[ゆくえ] = how the match will turn out.

v7f9936860d.furigana: 自己紹介[じこしょうかい]
v7f9936860d.frase: クラスで自己紹介したよ。
v7f9936860d.frase_furigana: クラスで自己[じこ] 紹介[しょうかい]したよ。
v7f9936860d.tono: ジコショウカイ

gramatica.titulo: で: where an action happens / with what
よ and ね at the end of a sentence

v7f9936860d.matiz: 自己紹介[じこしょうかい]する = to introduce yourself. In Japan it's a little ritual that usually ends with よろしくお願[ねが]いします.

v9e6a67d042.frase: 音楽のリズムに合わせて踊りました。
v9e6a67d042.frase_furigana: 音楽[おんがく]のリズムに 合[あ]わせて 踊[おど]りました。
v9e6a67d042.frase_es: I danced to the rhythm of the music.

gramatica.titulo: に: destination, time, where something is

v9e6a67d042.matiz: 音楽[おんがく]のリズムに合[あ]わせる = to move to the beat. Also the rhythm of daily life: 生活[せいかつ]のリズム = your daily routine.

v2591c58fed.frase: 力をフルに出しました。
v2591c58fed.frase_furigana: 力[ちから]をフルに 出[だ]しました。
v2591c58fed.frase_es: I gave it everything I had.
v2591c58fed.matiz: Mostly in compounds or as フルに: フルパワー = full power, フルに使[つか]う = to use something to the fullest.

v5c7a6a1594.frase_furigana: 体[からだ]の 状態[じょうたい]は正常[せいじょう]です。
v5c7a6a1594.tono: セイジョウ

gramatica.titulo: は: the topic of the sentence

v5c7a6a1594.matiz: Normal in the sense of working properly, nothing wrong: said of the body, machines or systems. The opposite is 異常[いじょう], abnormal. For “normal” as in ordinary, use 普通[ふつう] (word 387).

v8116b5ea1b.frase: 果物にはビタミンがあります。
v8116b5ea1b.frase_furigana: 果物[くだもの]にはビタミンがあります。

gramatica.titulo: が: who or what (the identified subject)
Existence: いる (living things) and ある (things)
に: destination, time, where something is

v798f5d7a99.frase: クリスマスにサンタがニャンにプレゼントをくれたよ。
v798f5d7a99.frase_furigana: クリスマスにサンタがニャンにプレゼントをくれたよ。
v798f5d7a99.frase_es: At Christmas, Santa gave Nyan a present.

gramatica.titulo: よ and ね at the end of a sentence
が: who or what (the identified subject)

v647c1cddf7.frase: 庭で野菜を栽培してるよ。
v647c1cddf7.frase_furigana: 庭[にわ]で 野菜[やさい]を栽培[さいばい]してるよ。
v647c1cddf7.tono: サイバイ
v647c1cddf7.frase_es: I grow vegetables in the yard.

gramatica.titulo: 〜ている: ongoing action or resulting state
で: where an action happens / with what
よ and ね at the end of a sentence

v647c1cddf7.matiz: 野菜[やさい]を栽培[さいばい]する = to grow vegetables. More formal than 育[そだ]てる, and used for crops and plants.

v3c67a1afd5.frase_furigana: 箱[はこ]の内側[うちがわ]を 見[み]ました。
v3c67a1afd5.tono: ウチガワ
v3c67a1afd5.frase_es: I looked at the inside of the box.
v3c67a1afd5.matiz: The opposite is 外側[そとがわ], the outside.

va2efae58a3.frase: ロケットが宇宙に飛んでいきました。
va2efae58a3.frase_furigana: ロケットが 宇宙[うちゅう]に 飛[と]んでいきました。
va2efae58a3.frase_es: The rocket flew off into space.

gramatica.titulo: 〜ていく and 〜てくる: direction in time

v8d8d05defd.frase: この料理めっちゃおいしいよ。
v8d8d05defd.frase_furigana: この 料理[りょうり]めっちゃおいしいよ。

gramatica.titulo: よ and ね at the end of a sentence

v8d8d05defd.matiz: Very casual, like とても but street-level. It comes from Kansai dialect and has spread all over Japan.

vbceed47722.frase: 彼女は頑張る決意をしました。
vbceed47722.frase_furigana: 彼女[かのじょ]は 頑張[がんば]る決意[けつい]をしました。
vbceed47722.frase_es: She made up her mind to give it her all.

gramatica.titulo: Relative clauses (a sentence describes a noun)
Verbs: the dictionary form and the two groups

vbceed47722.matiz: Close to 決断[けつだん] (word 2906), but 決意 puts the weight on willpower, the firm resolve to see it through. 決意[けつい]を固[かた]める = to firm up your resolve.

v27c16699e2.frase_furigana: 秘密[ひみつ]が漏[も]れました。

gramatica.titulo: が: who or what (the identified subject)

v27c16699e2.matiz: For liquids, gas, light or information: 水[みず]が漏[も]れる = water leaks; 秘密[ひみつ]が漏[も]れる = a secret leaks out.

v29b0a35df1.frase: ニャンは驚きすぎて、思考が止まった。
v29b0a35df1.frase_furigana: ニャンは 驚[おどろ]きすぎて、思考[しこう]が 止[と]まった。
v29b0a35df1.frase_es: Nyan was so shocked his mind went blank.
v29b0a35df1.matiz: More formal than 考[かんが]え (idea, thought, word 689). Common in compounds: ポジティブ思考[しこう] = positive thinking, 思考力[しこうりょく] = thinking skills.

v9441759fdf.frase: 結婚式でスピーチをしました。
v9441759fdf.frase_furigana: 結婚[けっこん] 式[しき]でスピーチをしました。
v9441759fdf.frase_es: I gave a speech at the wedding.

gramatica.titulo: で: where an action happens / with what

v9441759fdf.matiz: スピーチをする = to give a speech. At Japanese weddings, guests are often asked to give one.

v087de99b7f.frase: 新しいウイルスが出現しました。
v087de99b7f.frase_furigana: 新[あたら]しいウイルスが出現[しゅつげん]しました。
v087de99b7f.tono: シュツゲン

gramatica.titulo: が: who or what (the identified subject)

v087de99b7f.matiz: 出現[しゅつげん]する = to appear, to emerge, more formal than 現[あらわ]れる (word 866). Video games also use it when a monster shows up.

v39f56f649b.frase_furigana: 幕[まく]が 開[ひら]きました。

gramatica.titulo: が: who or what (the identified subject)

v39f56f649b.matiz: 第一幕[だいいちまく] = Act One. Like in English, it's used for beginnings and endings: 幕[まく]を閉[と]じる = to come to a close.

vddbd76bd38.frase: 彼はやめることを宣言しました。
vddbd76bd38.frase_furigana: 彼[かれ]はやめることを宣言[せんげん]しました。
vddbd76bd38.frase_es: He announced that he was quitting.

gramatica.titulo: Generic nouns: こと, ところ, もの
Relative clauses (a sentence describes a noun)

vddbd76bd38.matiz: 宣言[せんげん]する = to declare something officially. Also playful: ダイエット宣言[せんげん] = announcing to everyone that you're going on a diet.

v3f5a3c6575.frase: 星がぱっと光りました。
v3f5a3c6575.frase_furigana: 星[ほし]がぱっと 光[ひか]りました。

gramatica.titulo: と and や: lists of things
が: who or what (the identified subject)

v3f5a3c6575.matiz: Almost always used as ぱっと: 電気[でんき]がぱっとついた = the lights came on all at once.

vb49a200955.frase_furigana: レポート、仕上[しあ]げたよ。
alt: to put the finishing touches on

gramatica.titulo: よ and ね at the end of a sentence

vb49a200955.matiz: More about the final touches than 終[お]わる (to end): the work isn't just over, it's done properly. 仕上[しあ]げ = the finishing touches, the finish.

v28b53f60da.frase: 新しい情報を入手しました。
v28b53f60da.frase_furigana: 新[あたら]しい 情報[じょうほう]を入手[にゅうしゅ]しました。
v28b53f60da.frase_es: I got hold of some new information.
v28b53f60da.matiz: More formal than もらう or 買[か]う: it covers getting something by any means. 入手[にゅうしゅ]困難[こんなん] = hard to come by.

v10a5487017.frase: 駅からのアクセスがいいです。
v10a5487017.frase_furigana: 駅[えき]からのアクセスがいいです。
v10a5487017.frase_es: It's easy to get to from the station.

gramatica.titulo: が: who or what (the identified subject)

v10a5487017.matiz: アクセスする = to access a website or a place. In ads for hotels and apartments, アクセス means how to get there: 駅[えき]から徒歩[とほ]五分[ごふん] = a five-minute walk from the station.

v1c5b3f5a71.frase: 今日はとんでもなく忙しいです。
v1c5b3f5a71.frase_furigana: 今日[きょう]はとんでもなく 忙[いそが]しいです。
v1c5b3f5a71.tono: トンデモ

gramatica.titulo: は: the topic of the sentence

v1c5b3f5a71.matiz: とんでもなく + adjective = incredibly, ridiculously: とんでもなく高[たか]い = outrageously expensive. The most common form is とんでもない (word 2232), which is also a humble “not at all!” when someone thanks or praises you.

vaeaf21c7cf.frase: 「飯、食べよう。」とニャンが言いました。
vaeaf21c7cf.frase_furigana: 「飯[めし]、 食[た]べよう。」とニャンが 言[い]いました。
vaeaf21c7cf.matiz: Rougher than ご飯[はん]; mostly used by men in casual speech. 飯[めし]行[い]こう = let's go grab a bite.

vd96521e6ef.frase: 昔はワープロを使っていました。
vd96521e6ef.frase_furigana: 昔[むかし]はワープロを 使[つか]っていました。
vd96521e6ef.tono: ワープロ
vd96521e6ef.frase_es: We used to use word processors.

gramatica.titulo: 〜ている: ongoing action or resulting state

vd96521e6ef.matiz: Short for ワードプロセッサー. Before ordinary computers took over, Japanese offices and homes used dedicated machines that did nothing but write documents.

vf2ae71e78c.frase: その意見には根拠がありません。
vf2ae71e78c.frase_furigana: その 意見[いけん]には根拠[こんきょ]がありません。
vf2ae71e78c.frase_es: There's no basis for that opinion.

gramatica.titulo: が: who or what (the identified subject)
Existence: いる (living things) and ある (things)
に: destination, time, where something is

vf2ae71e78c.matiz: 根拠[こんきょ]がない = groundless, with nothing to back it up. 根拠[こんきょ]は？ = what's that based on?

vb9fbbf77d1.frase: その仕事を引き受けました。
vb9fbbf77d1.frase_furigana: その 仕事[しごと]を引[ひ]き 受[う]けました。
vb9fbbf77d1.tono: ヒキウケル
vb9fbbf77d1.matiz: 頼[たの]まれた仕事[しごと]を引[ひ]き受[う]ける = to take on a job someone asked you to do, along with the responsibility that comes with it.

ve850bbe2d4.frase: 危険なものを取り除きました。
ve850bbe2d4.frase_furigana: 危険[きけん]なものを取[と]り 除[のぞ]きました。
ve850bbe2d4.tono: トリノゾク

gramatica.titulo: Generic nouns: こと, ところ, もの

ve850bbe2d4.matiz: More formal than just 取[と]る, and it suggests getting rid of something unwanted: 不安[ふあん]を取[と]り除[のぞ]く = to put someone's worries to rest.

v2a2c6f6f06.frase: 国語のテストがありました。
v2a2c6f6f06.frase_furigana: 国語[こくご]のテストがありました。

gramatica.titulo: が: who or what (the identified subject)
Existence: いる (living things) and ある (things)

v2a2c6f6f06.matiz: In Japanese schools, 国語[こくご] is the Japanese class for native speakers, like “English” or “language arts” at an American school. Japanese taught as a foreign language is 日本語[にほんご].

v62597eaa24.frase: 毎月、家賃を払ってるよ。
v62597eaa24.frase_furigana: 毎月[まいつき]、家賃[やちん]を 払[はら]ってるよ。

gramatica.titulo: 〜ている: ongoing action or resulting state
よ and ね at the end of a sentence

v62597eaa24.matiz: 家賃[やちん]を払[はら]う = to pay the rent. Renting in Japan often means extra fees up front too, like 礼金[れいきん], “key money”.

v5c3cfefaef.frase: ニャンは成績が悪くて落ち込んだよ。
v5c3cfefaef.frase_furigana: ニャンは 成績[せいせき]が 悪[わる]くて落[お]ち 込[こ]んだよ。
v5c3cfefaef.tono: オチコム
v5c3cfefaef.frase_es: Nyan got bad grades and felt really down.
v5c3cfefaef.matiz: テストの成績[せいせき]が悪[わる]くて落[お]ち込[こ]む = to feel down about bad test results. It can also describe sales or the economy slumping.

v75e1b66d61.frase_furigana: 服[ふく]を 外[そと]に干[ほ]したよ。
v75e1b66d61.frase_es: I hung the laundry outside to dry.

gramatica.titulo: よ and ね at the end of a sentence
に: destination, time, where something is

v75e1b66d61.matiz: Drying by hanging something up in the sun or air: 布団[ふとん]を干[ほ]す = to air out the futon. 乾[かわ]かす is the general “to dry” by any means, like with a hair dryer.

v291643395f.frase_furigana: アンケートに 答[こた]えました。

gramatica.titulo: に: destination, time, where something is

v291643395f.matiz: From French enquête. アンケートに答[こた]える = to fill out a survey.

v69bbc6e6e5.frase: ニャンと勝負しました。
v69bbc6e6e5.frase_furigana: ニャンと勝負[しょうぶ]しました。
v69bbc6e6e5.frase_es: Nyan and I went head to head.

gramatica.titulo: と and や: lists of things

v69bbc6e6e5.matiz: 勝負[しょうぶ]する = to compete to see who wins. 勝負[しょうぶ]！ = Let's settle this! 真剣[しんけん]勝負[しょうぶ] = a serious contest, no holding back.

vfa98a9b529.frase: この路線は駅がたくさんあります。
vfa98a9b529.frase_furigana: この路線[ろせん]は 駅[えき]がたくさんあります。
vfa98a9b529.frase_es: This line has a lot of stations.

gramatica.titulo: が: who or what (the identified subject)
Existence: いる (living things) and ある (things)

vfa98a9b529.matiz: 電車[でんしゃ]の路線[ろせん] = a train line; 路線図[ろせんず] = a route map. It can also be a course of action: 路線[ろせん]を変[か]える = to change course.

v1c503b42b2.frase: 飛行機が高度を下げ始めた。
v1c503b42b2.frase_furigana: 飛行[ひこう] 機[き]が高度[こうど]を 下[さ]げ 始[はじ]めた。
v1c503b42b2.frase_es: The plane started to lose altitude.
v1c503b42b2.matiz: Also a な-adjective: 高度[こうど]な技術[ぎじゅつ] = advanced technology. For how high a mountain is, 標高[ひょうこう] is the usual word; 高度 is more for planes and things in the air.

va79b3483c9.frase_furigana: 彼[かれ]は 会社[かいしゃ]の会長[かいちょう]です。
va79b3483c9.tono: カイチョウ
va79b3483c9.frase_es: He's the chairman of the company.

gramatica.titulo: は: the topic of the sentence

va79b3483c9.matiz: Close to 社長[しゃちょう] (company president, word 812): in a company, the 会長[かいちょう] is the chair, the position above the 社長. It's also the head of an association or club, like a student council president, 生徒会長[せいとかいちょう].

ve20699971a.frase: この曲の節を覚えました。
ve20699971a.frase_furigana: この 曲[きょく]の節[ふし]を 覚[おぼ]えました。
ve20699971a.frase_es: I learned the tune of this song.
ve20699971a.matiz: 曲[きょく]の節[ふし] = the tune of a song. It's also a joint or a knot: 竹[たけ]の節[ふし] = the joints of bamboo, 指[ゆび]の節[ふし] = knuckles.

v48500d0994.frase: これが標準の大きさだよ。
v48500d0994.frase_furigana: これが標準[ひょうじゅん]の 大[おお]きさだよ。
v48500d0994.tono: ヒョウジュン

gramatica.titulo: よ and ね at the end of a sentence

v48500d0994.matiz: 標準的[ひょうじゅんてき]な = standard, typical. 標準語[ひょうじゅんご] = standard Japanese, as opposed to regional dialects.

v4582a9d0da.frase: 店のカウンターに座りました。
v4582a9d0da.frase_furigana: 店[みせ]のカウンターに 座[すわ]りました。
v4582a9d0da.tono: カウンター

gramatica.titulo: に: destination, time, where something is

v4582a9d0da.matiz: 銀行[ぎんこう]のカウンター = a bank counter. At sushi bars and ramen shops, sitting at the カウンター means sitting right in front of the chef.

v21e0100ca1.frase: ニャンは朝ランなんて絶対しないよ。
v21e0100ca1.frase_furigana: ニャンは 朝[あさ]ランなんて 絶対[ぜったい]しないよ。
v21e0100ca1.frase_es: Nyan would never go for a morning run.

gramatica.titulo: よ and ね at the end of a sentence

v21e0100ca1.matiz: From English “run”: 朝[あさ]のラン = a morning run. In everyday speech, ランニング or ジョギング is more common.

v62104b926d.frase: 学校の制服を着てるよ。

v62104b926d.matiz: 学校[がっこう]の制服[せいふく] = a school uniform. Most Japanese junior high and high schools have one.

v7880a6bb0c.frase: こんな天気はまれだよ。

v0ccce82aff.frase: ニャンは真夜中に起きて、遊んでいました。

lecciones.titulo: Hiragana: the sounds of Japanese
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to read any word written in hiragana, from ねこ to おばあさん, and you'll know why は sometimes sounds like «wa».

secciones.titulo: Three scripts in one sentence

bloques.md: Japanese isn't written with a single alphabet. It uses **three systems at once**, mixed together in the same sentence. Look at this one:

items.jp: ニャンは ケーキを 食[た]べます。
items.es: Nyan eats cake.
items.nota: ニャン and ケーキ are in katakana; 食[た] is a kanji; は, を and べます are in hiragana.

bloques.md:
Each system has its own job:
• **Hiragana** (ひらがな): soft, rounded characters. They can spell **any sound** in Japanese, and they're mostly used for grammar: particles and verb endings.
• **Katakana** (カタカナ): angular characters, hiragana's cousins. They're mainly used for words borrowed from other languages, like ケーキ (from «cake»). They're the next lesson.
• **Kanji**, written 漢字[かんじ] in Japanese: characters that came from China and stand for ideas and whole words, like 食[た] (to eat). They get their own lesson, the third one.

We start with hiragana because it's **the foundation of everything**. Japanese children learn to read with it, picture books are written almost entirely in it, and when a kanji is difficult, its reading is written in tiny hiragana on top. That's called **furigana**, and you'll see it all through this guide: 食[た].

One important idea before we begin: hiragana **isn't an alphabet** like ours. Each character isn't a single letter but **a whole syllable**: か isn't «k», it's «ka». That's why 46 basic characters (plus a few tweaks we'll see) are enough to write the whole language.

It's tempting to study with rōmaji, that is, with Latin letters («neko» instead of ねこ). It looks like a shortcut, but it's a trap, for two reasons. First, rōmaji makes you read with English habits, and many syllables don't sound the way you'd read them (you'll see this soon with the vowels and with «r»). Second, nobody in Japan uses it: signs, menus and messages are all in kana and kanji. Hiragana takes a week or two of light practice to learn, so it's the best investment you can make. In this guide, rōmaji only appears to explain how something sounds.

secciones.titulo: The vowels and the table of 46

bloques.md: Japanese has five vowels, recited in this order: a, i, u, e, o. They're **short and pure**, much like the vowels of Spanish or Italian: «a» as in «father», «i» as in «machine», «u» as in «food», «e» as in «get», «o» as in «note» but without the «w» glide at the end. With just these you can already read your first words:

items.jp: あい
items.es: love

items.jp: いえ
items.es: house

items.jp: うえ
items.es: up, on top

items.jp: あお
items.es: blue

items.jp: いいえ
items.es: no
items.nota: The i is stretched to last two beats. You'll see this in the section on long vowels.

bloques.md:
The one tricky vowel is う: it's said with the lips **barely rounded**, more relaxed than the English «oo». And here's a detail you'll pick up by ear: between certain consonants, i and u sometimes almost disappear. です sounds more like «des», and すき (I like it) like «ski». Don't force it; it's enough to know it happens.

The rest of the table works like a construction kit: **one consonant + one vowel**. Japanese people recite it row by row (かきくけこ, さしすせそ…), and that's the best way to learn it. Here it is in full, with approximate sounds:
Notice the gaps: the y row only has three syllables and the w row only two. There used to be a few more characters, but they fell out of use long ago, so nothing is missing.

bloques.titulo: What doesn't sound the way you'd read it
bloques.md:
• し is «shi», as in «she». Traditional Japanese has no «si» sound.
• ち is «chi», as in «cheese».
• つ is «tsu», a t and an s glued together, like the end of «cats». It can start a word, as in つなみ (tsunami, a Japanese word).
• ふ sits between f and h: blow gently, as if cooling soup, without your lip touching your teeth.
• The r row (ら, り, る, れ, ろ) uses a quick tap of the tongue, like the «tt» in an American «better». It's not the English r, and to your ears it may sound almost like an l or a d. That's normal.
• Don't stretch or reduce vowels the English way: さかな (fish) is three even beats, sa-ka-na, not «suh-KAH-nuh».
• を sounds «o» these days, exactly like お. It's used almost only as a particle, and it gets its explanation in the last section.

Which leaves the last one, ん, which is special: it's **the only consonant that stands alone**, with no vowel, and it almost never starts a word. It's an n that adapts to whatever follows, just as English does without you noticing: before p, b or m it sounds almost like an m (さんぽ, a walk, sounds like «sampo»), and before k or g it sounds like the n in «sing».

On top of that, ん **counts as a full syllable**. In Japanese, each character takes up one beat, like the notes in a song: にほん (Japan) has three beats, に・ほ・ん. This idea of beats is key, and it'll come back several times in this lesson.

ん doesn't merge with the vowel after it. きんえん (no smoking) is said «kin-en», with a tiny break between the two parts, while きねん (anniversary) is «ki-nen». Since ん is a beat of its own, running it into the next vowel turns it into a different word.

secciones.titulo: How to write them, and which ones get mixed up

bloques.md: You don't need to obsess over calligraphy, but it's worth writing each character **with its strokes in the right order**. It isn't a teacher's whim: the order keeps the shape balanced, keeps your handwriting readable when you write fast, and helps you recognise other people's quick handwriting, which relies on that same order.

• Top to bottom, and left to right.
• Horizontal lines go left to right; vertical lines go top to bottom.
• When a horizontal and a vertical cross, the horizontal almost always comes first. In あ, for example: first the top line, then the one going down, and the loop last.
• Pay attention to how each stroke ends: it can stop dead, flick up in a little hook (like the end of the first line of い), or taper off to nothing.

One thing that confuses beginners: printed characters don't always match handwritten ones. In many fonts, き and さ have their bottom curve joined on, and り looks like a single stroke; by hand, that curve in き and さ is written separately, and り is two separate lines. If you see differences between your screen and your notebook, don't worry: it's the same character, just like a printed «a» and a handwritten one.

These pairs trip everyone up at first. The key is almost always **how the stroke ends**:
• ぬ and め: nearly identical, but ぬ ends in a little loop and め doesn't.
• ね, れ and わ: they start the same way; ね ends in a loop (like a cat's curled tail, ね for ねこ), れ in a little kick outwards, and わ in a closed curve.
• る and ろ: る has a loop at the bottom; ろ doesn't.
• は and ほ: ほ has an extra line on top.
• さ and ち: they're mirror images. The belly of さ bulges to the left, like a c; the belly of ち bulges to the right, like the bottom of a 5.
• あ and お: お has a little separate dot at the top right.
• い and こ: い is two vertical lines; こ is two horizontal ones.

secciones.titulo: Two dots and a circle: dakuten and handakuten

bloques.md:
46 characters aren't enough for every sound. For the missing ones, Japanese doesn't invent new characters: it adds **a mark** to one that already exists.

• **Dakuten** (゛): two little strokes, like quotation marks; Japanese people call it «tenten». It makes the consonant **voiced**. Put your fingers on your throat and say «ssss», then «zzzz»: on the second one you feel a buzz. That buzz is voicing. So か (ka) becomes が (ga), さ (sa) becomes ざ (za), た (ta) becomes だ (da), and は (ha) becomes ば (ba).
• **Handakuten** (゜): a little circle, called «maru». It only goes on the h row and turns it into p: は (ha) becomes ぱ (pa).

• が, ぎ, ぐ, げ, ご: the g is **always hard**, as in «get» or «give». げ is never like «gem», and ぎ is never like «giant».
• ざ, ず, ぜ, ぞ: a buzzing z, as in «zoo».
• じ sounds like the j in «jeep».

You'll have noticed that じ and ぢ sound the same, and so do ず and づ. In modern Japanese there's **no difference in sound**, so you almost always write じ and ず. ぢ and づ appear in just a few words, mostly when two words join and a ち or つ becomes voiced: はな (nose) and ち (blood) make はなぢ (nosebleed), and みか (third day) and つき (moon) make みかづき (crescent moon). They also show up when a syllable repeats, as in つづく (to continue).

items.jp: かき → かぎ
items.es: persimmon → key
items.nota: Two tiny strokes, and the whole word changes.

items.jp: さる → ざる
items.es: monkey → bamboo strainer

items.jp: てんき → でんき
items.es: the weather → electricity, the lights

items.jp: ふた → ぶた
items.es: lid → pig

items.jp: さんぽ
items.es: a walk, a stroll
items.nota: ぽ has the little circle, and the ん before it sounds almost like an m: «sampo».

items.jp: ぴかぴか
items.es: sparkling clean
items.nota: An onomatopoeia: this is how something shiny «sounds» in Japanese.

secciones.titulo: Small characters: ゃ, ゅ, ょ and っ

bloques.md:
Some characters are written **small**, and then they change jobs. The first case is や, ゆ and よ. If a syllable from the i column (き, し, ち, に, ひ, み, り and their marked versions) is followed by a small ゃ, ゅ or ょ, the two merge into **one single syllable**: き plus ゃ gives きゃ, «kya», said in one go. It's the same thing that happens at the end of «Tokyo», which in Japanese is a single «kyo», not «kee-oh».

This will ring a bell: Nyan's name, written in katakana as ニャン, uses exactly this, a に with a small ゃ. And a Japanese cat's meow is にゃあ.

items.jp: きょう
items.es: today

items.jp: おちゃ
items.es: tea

items.jp: しゃしん
items.es: photo

items.jp: りょこう
items.es: trip, travel

items.jp: じゅう
items.es: ten
items.nota: The う stretches the u: «juu», two beats.

bloques.md: Size matters, a lot. びょういん (hospital) and びよういん (hair salon) differ only in a small or a big よ. With the small one, び and ょ are one syllable, «byo»; with the big one they're two, «bi-yo». Write the big one and instead of seeing a doctor you'll be getting a haircut.

The second case is the **small っ**, a miniature つ. It doesn't sound like «tsu»: in fact, **it makes no sound at all**. It's a tiny pause that holds the consonant coming next, like the break in «bookkeeper» or in Italian «pizza». And that pause **counts as a beat**: きって (postage stamp) has three, き・っ・て.

items.jp: きて → きって
items.es: come! → postage stamp

items.jp: さか → さっか
items.es: slope → writer

items.jp: おと → おっと
items.es: sound → husband (and also «oops!»)

items.jp: がっこう
items.es: school

items.jp: ちょっと
items.es: a little

bloques.md: っ almost always comes before k, s, t or p (がっこう, ざっし, きって, いっぱい). At the end of a word, especially in manga, it marks a **sudden stop**, like a startled gasp: あっ！

English doesn't write its double consonants this way, so it's very easy to skip the pause. But きて means «come!» and きって means «stamp»: without the pause, you've changed the word. A trick: clap once per beat. き (clap), っ (silent clap), て (clap).

secciones.titulo: Long vowels: stretching changes the word

bloques.md: In Japanese a vowel can last **one beat or two**, and that completely changes the meaning. In English it doesn't matter if you drag out a vowel («hellooo!»), but in Japanese おばさん means «aunt» or «middle-aged lady» and おばあさん means «grandma». To write a long vowel in hiragana, you add another vowel after it. It's usually the same one, with two important exceptions:

filas: おにいさん (older brother), おいしい (tasty)
い after it (usually) or え (a few words)
せんせい (teacher), とけい (clock); おねえさん (older sister)
う after it (usually) or お (a few words)
おとうさん (father), ありがとう (thanks); おおきい (big), とおい (far)

bloques.md: Why is せんせい written with い if it sounds like «sensee»? Because the spelling keeps an older pronunciation. When someone speaks very slowly or sings, you may hear «ei», but in normal conversation it's a long e. Same with おう: ありがとう sounds like «arigatoo». Words spelled with ええ and おお are few and are learned one by one; the vast majority use い and う.

items.jp: おばさん → おばあさん
items.es: aunt, lady → grandma, old lady

items.jp: ゆき → ゆうき
items.es: snow → courage

items.jp: ここ → こうこう
items.es: here → high school

items.jp: とり → とおり
items.es: bird → street

items.jp: え → ええ
items.es: picture → yes

bloques.md: English speakers tend to squash vowel length, and the result shows: mix up おばさん and おばあさん and you've just turned a forty-year-old woman into a grandmother. Count the beats, just like with っ: お・ば・あ・さ・ん is five; お・ば・さ・ん is four.

secciones.titulo: は, へ and を: three characters with a double life

bloques.md:
One last piece. Three characters are read in a special way **when they work as particles**. Particles are little words that go after other words to mark the role they play in the sentence; you'll start using them very soon. For now, you just need to know how they're read:
• は, normally «ha», sounds **«wa»**.
• へ, normally «he», sounds **«e»**.
• を sounds **«o»**, and it exists almost only as a particle.

items.jp: わたしは ねこです。
items.es: I'm a cat.
items.nota: This は is a particle: it sounds «wa», but it's written with は, not わ.

items.jp: はな
items.es: flower
items.nota: Here は is part of the word: «hana».

items.jp: がっこうへ いきます。
items.es: I'm going to school.
items.nota: へ as a particle: «e».

items.jp: へや
items.es: room
items.nota: Part of the word: «heya».

items.jp: おちゃを のみます。
items.es: I drink tea.

bloques.md:
Why the mess? Because centuries ago these particles were pronounced differently. When Japanese spelling was modernised after the Second World War, so that words would be written the way they sound, these three were left as they were: they're so frequent that changing them would have caused chaos, and this way you can spot a particle at a glance.

For the same reason, the greetings こんにちは (hello, good afternoon) and こんばんは (good evening) end in a は that sounds «wa». They were originally the start of a sentence, something like «As for today…», and that は was a particle.
In casual messages you'll sometimes see こんにちわ, with わ. It's a slip (or a joke), and in Japan it stands out the way «definately» does in English. The correct spelling is こんにちは.

And now, how to learn all this painlessly. Go **row by row**, five characters at a time. Read them in real words as soon as you can (あお, いえ, ここ…). Write each new character a few times while saying its sound out loud. And make up your own visual hooks: if ね looks to you like a curled-up cat, perfect; that hook is yours and you won't forget it. In a few days you'll be reading slowly; in a couple of weeks, without thinking.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does し sound like?
ejercicios.explica: し is «shi», as in «she». Traditional Japanese has no «si» syllable: before i, the s turns into «sh». «chi» is a different character, ち.

ejercicios.pregunta: Find «ne», as in ねこ (cat):
ejercicios.explica: All three start the same way; what changes is the ending. ね ends in a loop (the cat's curled tail), れ in a little kick outwards, and わ in a closed curve.

ejercicios.pregunta: How do you read かぎ (key)?
ejercicios.explica: The two little strokes on ぎ voice the k: き (ki) becomes ぎ (gi). And the Japanese g is always hard, as in «give», never as in «giant». Without the strokes, かき is «persimmon».

ejercicios.pregunta: Add the dakuten (゛) to か. What syllable do you get? Type it.
ejercicios.explica: The dakuten voices the consonant, and a voiced k is a g: か (ka) becomes が (ga). The whole row works the same way: き→ぎ, く→ぐ, け→げ, こ→ご.

ejercicios.pregunta: Now add the little circle (゜) to は. What do you get?
ejercicios.explica: The little circle only goes on the h row, and it turns it into p: は becomes ぱ. With the two strokes instead, you'd get ば (ba).

ejercicios.pregunta: Which one means «postage stamp»?
ejercicios.explica: The small っ is a pause that lasts one beat: き・っ・て. Without it, きて means «come!»; and with a stretched i, きいて means «listen!». Three different words over one detail.

ejercicios.pregunta: You've got a terrible stomach ache. Where do you go?
ejercicios.explica: びょういん, with a small ょ, is the hospital: び and ょ merge into one syllable, «byo». With a big よ they're two syllables, «bi-yo», and びよういん is the hair salon. びよいん isn't a word.

ejercicios.es: grandma
ejercicios.explica: Five beats: お・ば・あ・さ・ん. The あ stretches the ば; without it you'd have おばさん, «aunt» or «middle-aged lady».

ejercicios.pregunta: How does せんせい (teacher) sound in normal conversation?
ejercicios.explica: The combination えい usually sounds like a long e, two beats long. It's written with い because the spelling keeps an older pronunciation. And the e can't be short: you'd lose a beat.

ejercicios.pregunta: Write the word that sounds like «sensee» (teacher) in hiragana.
ejercicios.explica: A long e is almost always written with い after it: せんせい. Only a handful of words, like おねえさん, use え instead.

ejercicios.es: school
ejercicios.explica: がっこう sounds like «gakkoo»: が, the pause of っ (holding the k), こ, and a う that stretches the o. Four beats.

ejercicios.pregunta: In this sentence, how does は sound?
ejercicios.jp: わたしは ねこです。
ejercicios.explica: Here は is a particle, and as a particle it sounds «wa». It's still written は because, when the spelling was modernised, these particles were kept as they had always been.

ejercicios.pregunta: Type the missing particle; it sounds «o»: おちゃ＿ のみます (I drink tea).
ejercicios.explica: As a particle, the sound «o» is written を, not お. It's one of the three characters with a double life (along with は and へ). On a keyboard you type it as «wo».

lecciones.titulo: Katakana: words from abroad
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to read words like コーヒー, パン and ビール, tell シ from ツ without hesitating, and write your own name in Japanese.

secciones.titulo: Hiragana's angular cousin

bloques.md:
Katakana has **exactly the same sounds as hiragana**, one for one, just with different shapes: where hiragana is round and flowing, katakana is all straight lines and corners. あ and ア both sound «a»; か and カ both sound «ka». If you already know hiragana, there are no new sounds to learn here (well, almost: we'll see a handful at the end), only new shapes.

It was born over a thousand years ago, when Buddhist monks began jotting down pronunciations in the margins of the Chinese texts they studied. To save time, instead of writing out a whole kanji, they copied just a little piece of it. That's why katakana looks like «bits of kanji»: very often, that's exactly what it is.

So what is it used for today, if hiragana can already write every sound? Katakana has its own territory:
• **Words borrowed from other languages**, mostly English: コーヒー (coffee), テレビ (TV), パン (bread).
• **Foreign names** of people, countries and cities: ロンドン (London), アメリカ (America).
• **Sound effects**, especially in manga: ニャー (meow), ワンワン (woof woof), ドキドキ (a pounding heart).
• **Emphasis**, the way we use italics or capitals. An ordinary Japanese word written in katakana jumps out: ダメ！ (No! No way!).
• It's also very common for **pet and character names**. That's why our heroes are written ニャン, タマ and カゲ.

items.jp: コーヒー
items.es: coffee
items.nota: The dash stretches the vowel: ko-o-hi-i.

items.jp: テレビ
items.es: television
items.nota: From «television», trimmed down.

items.jp: パン
items.es: bread
items.nota: This one isn't from English but from Portuguese «pão»: the Portuguese reached Japan in the sixteenth century.

items.jp: ニャー
items.es: meow!

items.jp: ダメ！
items.es: No! No way!
items.nota: だめ is a native Japanese word; in katakana it sounds more forceful.

bloques.md: So when you're reading Japanese and a cluster of straight-lined characters appears, you already have a clue: it's probably a foreign word, a foreign name, a sound effect, or something the writer wants to highlight.

secciones.titulo: The table

bloques.md: Here's the complete table. It's organised exactly like the hiragana one, so you can go row by row comparing it with what you already know:

And the good news: **every trick from the last lesson works the same way**. The two strokes and the little circle do the same job (カ→ガ, ハ→パ). Small ャ, ュ, ョ merge with the syllable before them (キャ, シュ, チョ). And the small ッ is still a pause that doubles the next consonant. ヲ exists, but you'll hardly ever see it: for the particle, Japanese uses hiragana を.

items.jp: ギター
items.es: guitar

items.jp: シャツ
items.es: shirt
items.nota: シャ is a single syllable, just like しゃ in hiragana.

items.jp: チョコレート
items.es: chocolate

items.jp: ベッド
items.es: bed
items.nota: The ッ makes the pause before the final d.

items.jp: キッチン
items.es: kitchen

bloques.md: A study tip: don't try to learn katakana at the same time as hiragana. Get one solid first, then move on to the other, or the shapes will get tangled. And once you start, practise on words you already know from English; it's the most rewarding script there is, because as soon as you decode a word, you usually know what it means.

secciones.titulo: Look-alikes

bloques.md: Since katakana is built from simple strokes, some characters look extremely alike. The most famous pair is **シ (shi) and ツ (tsu)**, and right next to them are **ン (n) and ソ (so)**. They seem designed to trip you up, but all four follow the same logic, and once you see it you'll never hesitate again.

bloques.titulo: The trick for シ, ツ, ン and ソ
bloques.md:
Look at **which way the long stroke goes**; it's the last one written:
• In シ and ン, the long stroke **goes up**: it starts at the bottom left and sweeps up to the top right. Their short marks lie more flat and sit on the left.
• In ツ and ソ, the long stroke **comes down**: it starts at the top right and falls to the bottom left. Their short marks stand more upright and sit along the top.

In short: if it goes up, it's シ or ン; if it comes down, it's ツ or ソ. And within each pair, the one with two short marks is シ or ツ, and the one with just one is ン or ソ.

Other pairs worth a second look:
• ク, ケ and タ: ケ has a horizontal line sticking out to the right; タ is a ク with an extra little stroke inside.
• ウ, ワ and フ: ウ has a little tick on top and another on the left; ワ has only the one on the left; フ has neither.
• ス and ヌ: ヌ has a line crossing its long stroke; ス just has a little leg at the bottom.
• コ and ユ: in ユ the bottom line sticks out, like a foot.
• マ and ア: ア has a stroke dropping down to the left; マ has a little stroke tucked inside at the bottom.

And some katakana are almost identical to simple kanji: カ and 力[ちから] (strength), エ and 工[こう] (craft), ニ and 二[に] (two), ハ and 八[はち] (eight), ロ and 口[くち] (mouth). That's no coincidence: they really are related, because katakana was born by clipping pieces off kanji. In practice, context settles it: if it's surrounded by katakana, it's katakana.

secciones.titulo: The dash ー: long vowels

bloques.md:
In hiragana, a long vowel is written by adding another vowel (おかあさん). Katakana makes it simpler: you add **a dash, ー**, which means «hold the previous vowel for one more beat». So コーヒー is read ko-o-hi-i: the ー after コ stretches the o, and the one after ヒ stretches the i.

When text runs vertically, as in many books and manga, the dash turns vertical too, following the direction of the writing.

items.jp: ケーキ
items.es: cake

items.jp: スーパー
items.es: supermarket
items.nota: From «supermarket», trimmed: Japanese loves shortening long words.

items.jp: ルール
items.es: rule

items.jp: ビル → ビール
items.es: building → beer
items.nota: ビル comes from «building», cut short; ビール comes from Dutch «bier». One dash is all that separates an office block from a bar.

bloques.md: The dash isn't decoration: it counts as a full beat, just like hiragana long vowels. Ask for a ビル instead of a ビール and you're asking for a building. Also, don't confuse it with the kanji 一[いち] (one), which is also a horizontal line: the katakana dash only ever appears attached to a syllable, stretching it.

secciones.titulo: New sounds with small vowels

bloques.md: Traditional Japanese has no syllables like «fa», «ti», «di» or «we». But with so many foreign words coming in, they were needed, and the solution was clever: use **small vowels** (ァ, ィ, ゥ, ェ, ォ) attached to another syllable. The first syllable supplies the consonant, and the small vowel replaces its own:

filas: ファ, フィ, フェ, フォ
ソファ (sofa), カフェ (café), フォーク (fork)
パーティー (party), ティッシュ (tissue)
ウィ, ウェ, ウォ
ウェブ (web), ウォーキング (walking for exercise)
シェ, ジェ, チェ
ヴァイオリン or バイオリン (violin)

bloques.md: This explains something curious: words that arrived long ago were adapted more heavily, while recent ones stay closer to the original. «Team» came in as チーム, with «chi», because back then there was no other way; «party», a newer arrival, kept パーティー. Same with v: the usual way is to write it with the b row (テレビ, バイオリン), and ヴ appears mostly when someone wants to be more faithful to the original. You'll see both; neither is a mistake.
The small vowel doesn't form a syllable of its own: it merges with the one before it, just like ャ, ュ, ョ. ファ is a single beat, «fa», not «fu-a». Read it as a big フア and you're saying two syllables.

secciones.titulo: How a word becomes Japanese (your name too)

bloques.md: When a word enters Japanese, it's reshaped to fit Japanese sounds. It isn't random: a few rules cover most cases, and knowing them helps you guess new words and write your own name.

• **No consonant stands alone** (except ン): it gets a vowel. Usually that's u (desk → デスク), but after t and d it's o (test → テスト, bed → ベッド), and after «ch» and «j» it's usually i (match → マッチ, orange → オレンジ).
• **L and r** both become the r row: ラジオ (radio), ホテル (hotel).
• **V** moves to the b row (or to ヴ).
• **Th** becomes s or z: サンキュー (thank you).
• After a short, stressed vowel, the final consonant is often doubled with ッ: カップ (cup), ベッド (bed).
• Long words get chopped without mercy: パソコン (personal computer), コンビニ (convenience store), エアコン (air conditioner).
• English vowels are respelled by how they sound, not how they're written: «Michael» becomes マイケル, «cake» becomes ケーキ.

items.jp: ロンドン
items.es: London
items.nota: The d gets its o, and the final n is ン.

items.jp: マイケル
items.es: Michael
items.nota: Written the way it sounds: «my-kel». The l takes the r row, and a u so it isn't left alone.

items.jp: エミリー
items.es: Emily
items.nota: The final «y» sound becomes a long i.

items.jp: クリス
items.es: Chris
items.nota: The «ch» here sounds like k, so it's ク.

items.jp: マドリード
items.es: Madrid
items.nota: Words from Spanish follow the same rules: the stressed i is lengthened, and the final d gets its o.

items.jp: パブロ・ピカソ
items.es: Pablo Picasso
items.nota: The dot ・ separates first and last names, since katakana doesn't use spaces.

items.jp: パエリア
items.es: paella

items.jp: チュロス
items.es: churros

bloques.md: And a nice story to finish: the sponge cake カステラ, a speciality of Nagasaki, also came with the Portuguese, and its name is usually traced back to Castile, the Spanish kingdom. So a little piece of Spain has been eaten in Japan for centuries.

Many katakana words sound English but **don't mean what you'd expect**, because Japanese has used them its own way:
• マンション isn't a mansion: it's a flat in an apartment block.
• アルバイト (from German «Arbeit», work) is a part-time job.
• コンセント is a wall socket.
• カンニング (from «cunning») means cheating in an exam.
It isn't that Japanese speakers got them wrong: these words are Japanese now and have a life of their own, just as English says «déjà vu» or «karaoke» in ways the original speakers wouldn't quite recognise.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which one is «tsu»?
ejercicios.explica: In ツ the two short marks sit side by side along the top, and the long stroke comes down from the right. In シ the long stroke goes up, and ソ has only one short mark.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which one is «n»?
ejercicios.explica: ン has a single short mark on the left, and its long stroke goes up. ソ also has one short mark, but its long stroke comes down. And シ has two.

ejercicios.pregunta: How do you read コーヒー (coffee)?
ejercicios.explica: Each ー holds the previous vowel for one more beat: コー is «koo» and ヒー is «hii». Without the dashes it would shrink to «kohi», two beats instead of four.

ejercicios.pregunta: You're thirsty and want a beer. What do you order?
ejercicios.explica: ビール, with a long i, is beer. ビル, with no dash, is a building (from «building», cut short), and ベル is a bell. The ー counts as a full beat and changes the word.

ejercicios.pregunta: Read this word and type how it sounds: ロンドン
ejercicios.explica: ロ・ン・ド・ン: «rondon». It's London: the l becomes the r row, the d gets an o so it isn't left alone, and each n is ン.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does マンション mean?
opciones: a flat in an apartment block
ejercicios.explica: It comes from English «mansion», but in Japanese it's used for flats in modern apartment buildings. It's a false friend: the word is Japanese now and means what Japanese speakers use it for.

ejercicios.pregunta: Why is «Michael» written マイケル and not ミカエル?
opciones: Because loanwords follow the sound, not the spelling
Because every i in English becomes マイ
Because names always end in ル
ejercicios.explica: Katakana copies what the ear hears. «Michael» sounds like «my-kel», so it becomes マイケル. The final l takes the r row plus a u, since a consonant can't stand alone.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Party» is a fairly modern loanword. How is it written?
ejercicios.explica: ティ, with a small ィ, creates the syllable «ti», which traditional Japanese didn't have. Older loans used チ instead (チーム, from «team»), but newer ones stay closer to the original.

ejercicios.es: chocolate
ejercicios.explica: チョ・コ・レー・ト. The small ョ merges with チ into one syllable, the ー stretches the e, and the final t gets an o so it isn't left alone.

ejercicios.es: ice cream
ejercicios.explica: ア・イ・ス・ク・リー・ム. The s and the c each need a vowel (ス, ク), the long «ee» becomes リー, and the final m gets its u.

ejercicios.pregunta: How do you say «Madrid» in Japanese? Type how it sounds.
ejercicios.explica: マドリード: the final d can't stand alone, so it gets an o (ド), and the stressed i is stretched with ー. It's the same rule that turns «bed» into ベッド.

ejercicios.pregunta: A sign says ダメ！ Why is it in katakana, when だめ is a Japanese word?
opciones: To make it punchier, like writing it in capitals
ejercicios.explica: Katakana is also used for emphasis. An ordinary Japanese word written in these straight-lined characters jumps out at you, like a «NO!» in capitals.

lecciones.titulo: Kanji: how they work and how they're read
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll know why Japanese uses thousands of Chinese characters, why a single one can be read in several ways, and how to guess which reading a word needs.

secciones.titulo: Pictures that became ideas

bloques.md:
**Kanji** are characters that were born in China and reached Japan about 1,500 years ago. Their name says as much: 漢[かん] is the old Han China, and 字[じ] means «character». Unlike hiragana and katakana, which stand for sounds, **each kanji stands for a meaning**: an idea, a thing, an action.

Many of them started out as drawings. With a little imagination, you can still see it:

items.jp: 山[やま]
items.es: mountain
items.nota: Three peaks.

items.jp: 川[かわ]
items.es: river
items.nota: Three lines of flowing water.

items.jp: 木[き]
items.es: tree
items.nota: A trunk, with branches above and roots below.

items.jp: 日[ひ]
items.es: sun, day
items.nota: It was a circle with a dot inside; over time it turned square.

items.jp: 人[ひと]
items.es: person
items.nota: A human figure reduced to the bare minimum: two legs.

items.jp: 口[くち]
items.es: mouth

bloques.md: But drawings only get you so far, so most kanji **are built by combining others**. This is where they get fun, because the combination usually makes sense:

items.jp: 林[はやし]
items.es: grove
items.nota: Two trees.

items.jp: 森[もり]
items.es: forest
items.nota: Three trees: more trees, more forest.

items.jp: 休[やす]む
items.es: to rest
items.nota: A person (亻, the narrow form of 人[ひと]) leaning against a tree. Exactly what Nyan does after lunch.

items.jp: 明[あか]るい
items.es: bright
items.nota: The sun and the moon together: all the light there is.

bloques.md: How many are there? A great many, but you don't need them all. Japan has an official list of **2,136 kanji in common use**, which is what's taught at school and what newspapers and signs use. And the good news is that you don't learn them all at once: with a few hundred you already recognise a huge share of what you read, because the most frequent ones turn up again and again.

secciones.titulo: Why not write everything in hiragana?

bloques.md:
Everyone asks this: if hiragana can already write every sound, why bother with thousands of characters? There are three good reasons.

**First: Japanese has few sounds**, so a great many words sound the same. In conversation, context helps, but in writing the kanji tells you instantly which word is meant:

filas: 紙[かみ] / 髪[かみ] / 神[かみ]
橋[はし] / 箸[はし] / 端[はし]
機械[きかい] / 機会[きかい]
公園[こうえん] / 講演[こうえん]

bloques.md: **Second: Japanese doesn't put spaces between words.** Kanji act as signposts: they almost always mark where a content word begins, and the hiragana around them is the grammar. There's a famous tongue twister that proves it. Written only in hiragana, it's a puzzle:

items.jp: にわにはにわにわとりがいる。
items.es: No kanji: where does each word end?
items.nota: All run together, it's very hard to tell where one word stops and the next begins.

items.jp: 庭[にわ]には 二羽[にわ] 鶏[にわとり]が いる。
items.es: In the garden there are two chickens.
items.nota: With kanji it reads at a glance: 庭[にわ] (garden), 二羽[にわ] (two, counting birds) and 鶏[にわとり] (chicken).

bloques.md:
By the way: in this guide you'll see sentences split up with spaces. That's a help for beginners, the way Japanese picture books do it (they're written in hiragana, with spaces); ordinary texts for adults don't have them.

**Third: you can see the meaning even if you can't read the word.** If you know the kanji 雪[ゆき] (snow), any sign in Sapporo that contains it tells you it's about snow, even if you don't know how the whole word is pronounced. Over time, this makes reading Japanese incredibly fast.

secciones.titulo: Two ways of reading: on and kun

bloques.md:
Here's what baffles everyone at first: **the same kanji can be read in several ways**. Why? Because of its history. When the Japanese adopted Chinese characters, they did two things at once:
• They took **the Chinese pronunciation** of each character, adapted to Japanese sounds. That's the **on** reading; in Japanese, 音読[おんよ]み, «sound reading».
• And they also used the character to write **their own Japanese word** with that meaning. That's the **kun** reading; in Japanese, 訓読[くんよ]み, «meaning reading».

So the kanji for mountain is read やま when it's the everyday Japanese word, and サン when it carries its Chinese-derived pronunciation, as in 富士山[ふじさん], Mount Fuji. Dictionaries usually print on readings in katakana and kun readings in hiragana, precisely to tell them apart.

columnas: A word with the on reading
filas: 日本人[にほんじん] (Japanese person)
食堂[しょくどう] (canteen, dining hall)

bloques.md: Notice that 人 has two on readings. That happens with quite a few kanji, because they were borrowed at different times and from different parts of China, and each borrowing brought its own pronunciation.

• **A kanji on its own, or with hiragana attached after it** → usually **kun**: 山[やま], 水[みず], 食[た]べる.
• **Two or more kanji together forming a word** → usually **on**: 食堂[しょくどう], 火山[かざん] (volcano), 日本人[にほんじん].

It's a tendency, not a law. There are two-kanji words read in kun, like 手紙[てがみ] (letter), mixtures like 毎朝[まいあさ] (every morning), and nearly all family names and place names use kun: 山田[やまだ].

And there's one last group: words that are **read as a single block**, where the individual kanji don't keep their normal readings. They're few but very common, so you'll pick them up quickly: 今日[きょう] (today), 明日[あした] (tomorrow), 大人[おとな] (adult), 一人[ひとり] (one person, alone).

The classic mistake is memorising lists of readings for each kanji: 山, やま, サン, 水, みず, スイ… It's exhausting and barely helps, because a reading on its own doesn't tell you when to use it. What works is **learning words**. Once you know that Mount Fuji is 富士山[ふじさん], you know 山 is read サン in compounds; the word leads you to the reading, not the other way round.

secciones.titulo: Okurigana: the hiragana tail

bloques.md: Japanese verbs and adjectives change shape: «eat», «don't eat», «ate»… But a kanji can't change. The solution is to split the work: **the kanji carries the meaning, and the hiragana after it carries the part that changes**. That hiragana is called **okurigana**; in Japanese, 送[おく]り 仮名[がな], roughly «accompanying kana».

items.jp: 食[た]べる / 食[た]べます / 食[た]べない
items.es: to eat / I eat (polite) / I don't eat
items.nota: 食 stays put; everything that changes is in hiragana. You'll meet these forms lesson by lesson.

items.jp: 高[たか]い / 高[たか]くない
items.es: it's expensive / it isn't expensive

bloques.md: Okurigana has a second, very handy job: **it tells you which reading to use**. The same kanji with a different tail is a different word:

items.jp: 上[うえ]
items.es: above, on top

items.jp: 上[あ]がる
items.es: to go up

items.jp: 上[あ]げる
items.es: to raise; to give (something to someone)

items.jp: 生[なま]
items.es: raw

items.jp: 生[い]きる
items.es: to live

items.jp: 生[う]まれる
items.es: to be born

bloques.md: Which part goes in kanji and which in hiragana is fixed by convention, so pay attention the first time you see a word. 少[すく]ない (few, scarce) and 少[すこ]し (a little) share a kanji, but the tail marks where it ends and tells you which of the two words it is. If you invent your own split, a Japanese reader stumbles, just as you would at an English word broken in the wrong place.

secciones.titulo: When they join: sound changes and 々

bloques.md: When two pieces join into one word, the sound sometimes adjusts to make it easier to say. There are three things to know, and all three are **tendencies**, not fixed rules: when you learn a word, learn it with its real sound.

The first consonant of the second part gains the two little strokes: k→g, s→z, t→d, h→b.
• 花[はな] (flower) + 火[ひ] (fire) → 花火[はなび] (fireworks)
• 手[て] (hand) + 紙[かみ] (paper) → 手紙[てがみ] (letter)
• 折[お]り (folding) + 紙[かみ] → 折[お]り 紙[がみ] (origami)

When the first part ends in く, つ, ち or き and the second starts with a similar sound, they merge into a pause:
• 学[がく] + 校[こう] → 学校[がっこう] (school)
• 日[にち] + 記[き] → 日記[にっき] (diary)
• 北[ほく] + 海[かい] + 道[どう] → 北海道[ほっかいどう], Nyan's favourite region

Sometimes the h also turns into p: 日[にち] + 本[ほん] → 日本[にっぽん], one way of saying «Japan» (the other, more common in conversation, is にほん).

々 isn't a kanji: it's a mark that **repeats the previous kanji**, a bit like ditto marks in a list. And since it joins two pieces, it often brings rendaku with it:
• 人々[ひとびと]: people
• 時々[ときどき]: sometimes
• 色々[いろいろ]: all sorts, various
• 山々[やまやま]: the mountains, a mountain range

A note on Hokkaido while we're here: many of its place names come from the language of the Ainu, the island's indigenous people, and their kanji were chosen for how they sound, not for what they mean. 札幌[さっぽろ] (Sapporo) is one of them. That's why some names there have readings you'd never expect: don't try to work them out; learn them as proper names.

secciones.titulo: How to write them and how to learn them

bloques.md: Kanji follow the same stroke habits as hiragana (top to bottom, left to right) and add a few of their own. They're worth knowing, because once they become second nature, any new kanji practically writes itself.

• Horizontal before vertical when they cross: in 十[じゅう], the flat line first.
• Centre before sides when there's symmetry: in 小[ちい]さい and 水[みず], the middle stroke first.
• Frame before contents, but **the bottom lid last**: in 国[くに] (country), you draw the frame, then what's inside, and close the box at the end.
• A stroke that cuts through everything goes last: in 中[なか] (inside), the long vertical line comes last.

And now the secret to not drowning: **kanji are made of recurring pieces**. We call those pieces **elements**. Once you know them, a new kanji stops being a drawing with twelve strokes and becomes «this piece plus that one». Some elements also hint at meaning:
• 氵, water: 海[うみ] (sea), 池[いけ] (pond), 泳[およ]ぐ (to swim).
• 木, tree: 林[はやし], 森[もり], 村[むら] (village).
• 亻, person: 休[やす]む, 体[からだ] (body), 作[つく]る (to make).

Other elements give **sound hints**. 青[あお] (blue) has the on reading セイ, and you'll find it inside 晴[は]れ (clear weather), 清[きよ]い (pure) and 静[しず]か (quiet): all three have the on reading セイ. The element beside it changes the meaning (sun, water…), and 青 supplies the sound.

That's how you'll learn them in Nyango. First, the **elements**, the loose pieces. Then each kanji with its own sheet: **which pieces make it up**, **a short story** tying them together (休 is «a person leaning on a tree», and you'll never forget it), and **the real words** you'll find it in, which is where you truly learn its readings. A few each day, reviewed at just the right moment: that's how you reach two thousand without noticing.

Two tips to keep your spirits up. One: **recognising matters more than writing**. In daily life you'll read kanji constantly, but you'll type almost everything, and the keyboard offers you the right kanji. Writing some by hand helps fix their shape, but don't obsess over writing them all. Two: **don't wait until you know kanji to learn grammar**. It all happens together, and in this guide every kanji comes with furigana so you never get stuck.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does 山[やま] mean?
ejercicios.explica: 山 is one of the kanji that began as a drawing: three mountain peaks. River is 川[かわ] and tree is 木[き].

ejercicios.pregunta: Hint: a person (亻) leaning against a tree (木). What does 休[やす]む mean?
ejercicios.explica: Compound kanji usually make sense: someone leaning against a tree is resting. Lots of kanji can be understood (and remembered) like this, through their pieces.

ejercicios.pregunta: 紙, 髪 and 神 are all read かみ. Why are they written differently?
opciones: Because they're different words that sound alike, and the kanji shows which one
Because they're actually pronounced very differently
No reason at all, just tradition
ejercicios.explica: Japanese has few sounds and many words that sound alike. The kanji makes it clear whether you mean paper (紙), hair (髪) or a god (神). It's one of the main reasons kanji are still used.

ejercicios.pregunta: The kanji for mountain stands alone, with nothing next to it. Which reading do you expect?
ejercicios.explica: A kanji on its own is usually the everyday Japanese word, which means the kun reading: やま. The on reading, サン, appears in compounds, as in 富士山[ふじさん].

ejercicios.pregunta: 食堂 (dining hall) is two kanji together. How is it read?
ejercicios.explica: Two kanji forming a word usually take on readings: 食 is ショク and 堂 is ドウ, giving 食堂[しょくどう]. The kun reading た only appears with its hiragana tail, 食[た]べる.

ejercicios.pregunta: 花[はな] (flower) + 火[ひ] (fire) make the word for «fireworks». How does it sound?
ejercicios.explica: That's rendaku: when they join, the second piece becomes voiced and the h turns into b. 花火[はなび] is one of the loveliest words of the Japanese summer.

ejercicios.pregunta: In 高[たか]い (it's expensive) and 高[たか]くない (it isn't expensive), which part never changes?
ejercicios.explica: The kanji carries the meaning and stays put; what changes when you conjugate is the okurigana, the hiragana tail. That's why verb and adjective forms are written half in kanji, half in hiragana.

ejercicios.pregunta: 学 is read がく and 校 is read こう. How do you read 学校 (school)?
ejercicios.explica: がく and こう merge: the final く and the following こ turn into a pause, っ. That gives 学校[がっこう], not «gakukou». It's the same thing that happens in 北海道[ほっかいどう].

ejercicios.pregunta: 々 repeats the kanji before it. How do you read 人々 (people)? 人 alone is ひと.
ejercicios.explica: 々 copies 人, and as the two pieces join, the second becomes voiced (rendaku): 人々[ひとびと]. The same happens in 時々[ときどき] (sometimes).

ejercicios.es: Hokkaido
ejercicios.explica: 北 (north), 海 (sea) and 道 (road, region). Their on readings are ホク, カイ and ドウ, but the ク of ホク merges with the following カ into a っ: 北海道[ほっかいどう].

ejercicios.es: Japanese (the language)
ejercicios.explica: 日本[にほん] is Japan (literally, «origin of the sun»), and 語[ご] means «language». Many language names are built this way: the country, followed by 語[ご].

ejercicios.pregunta: 晴 (clear), 清 (pure) and 静 (quiet) all contain the piece 青, read セイ. How would you expect 晴天 (clear sky) to be read?
ejercicios.explica: A compound takes on readings, and the piece 青 gives you the clue: 晴 is read セイ. 晴天[せいてん]. The sound hints hidden in elements will save you a huge amount of work.

lecciones.titulo: To be or not to be: だ and じゃない
lecciones.resumen: Your first grammar: saying that something is (or isn't, or was, or wasn't) whatever it is. «It's a cat», «it wasn't a dream»… and why the だ is sometimes better left out.

secciones.titulo: A one-word sentence

bloques.md: We'll start with something that's surprisingly simple in Japanese: saying **what something is**. Imagine Tama points at a furry thing asleep on the sofa and asks you what it is. You answer:

items.jp: 猫[ねこ]だ。
items.es: It's a cat.
items.nota: 猫[ねこ] is «cat», and だ plays the part of «is».

bloques.md:
And that's it. That's a complete, correct sentence. Notice everything you **don't** need:
• **No subject.** English insists on «it» in «it's a cat»; Japanese doesn't. If it's clear what you're talking about, you don't name it. Depending on context, 猫[ねこ]だ can mean «it's a cat», «they're cats» or even «I'm a cat», if Nyan says it.
• **No articles.** There's no «a» or «the». 猫[ねこ] is «cat», «a cat», «the cat»…
• **No plural.** 猫[ねこ] works for one cat or fifty.
• **だ doesn't change with the person.** No «am, are, is»: always だ.

It looks like information is missing, but it isn't: the information is in the context, and Japanese trusts context far more than English does. When something isn't clear, you add it; when it is, repeating it is just clutter.

A noun, followed by だ.
猫[ねこ] → 猫[ねこ]だ (it's a cat)
学生[がくせい] → 学生[がくせい]だ (I'm / she's a student)
ニャン → ニャンだ (it's Nyan)

items.jp: 学生[がくせい]だ。
items.es: I'm a student. / He's a student.
items.nota: Who? The context tells you.

items.jp: ニャンだ。
items.es: It's Nyan.
items.nota: For example, when you spot him coming in the distance.

items.jp: 本[ほん]だ。
items.es: It's a book.

items.jp: 友達[ともだち]だ。
items.es: We're friends.
items.nota: If Tama says it about Nyan and herself. In another context, the same sentence could mean «he's a friend» or «they're friends».

items.jp: 雪[ゆき]だ！
items.es: Snow! / It's snowing!
items.nota: What you cry out when you open the window in Sapporo and everything's white. Literally, «it's snow!».

bloques.md: だ is like English «to be», but only part of it. It says **what something is or who someone is**: a cat, a student, snow. To say that **there is** something or someone somewhere («there's a cat in the garden»), Japanese has verbs of its own, which you'll meet in the lesson «Existence: いる (living things) and ある (things)». And for states like «I'm tired» or «it's tasty», it uses adjectives, which have their own lesson. So don't translate every «is» as だ on autopilot.

secciones.titulo: The だ that disappears, and the だ that sounds blunt

bloques.md: Now for a detail that textbooks often skip, and that makes a big difference to how you sound. In casual conversation between friends, **the final だ often disappears**, and the sentence is still perfect:

items.jp: 猫[ねこ]。
items.es: A cat. (It's a cat.)
items.nota: Same meaning as 猫[ねこ]だ; softer and more natural in a chat.

items.jp: 学生[がくせい]。
items.es: Student. (I'm a student.)

bloques.md:
Why drop it? Because だ, alone at the end of a sentence, is **a flat, firm assertion** with nothing to soften it. It's like saying a full stop out loud: «It's a cat. Period.» Among friends that can sound curt, as if you were closing the subject or delivering a verdict. So it's often left out, or accompanied by particles like よ or ね, which soften it (they have their own lesson later on).

That doesn't mean だ is forbidden, far from it. It sounds perfectly natural:
• **In exclamations of discovery**: 雪[ゆき]だ！ (snow!), ニャンだ！ (it's Nyan!).
• **In writing**: in a diary, a novel or some notes, だ is the ordinary neutral ending and doesn't sound blunt at all.
• **When you want to sound firm** on purpose: 俺[おれ]の 勝[か]ちだ (I win!), as Kage would say.

Then there's register. だ belongs to **plain speech**, the kind you use with friends, family and people you're close to. With older people, strangers or your teacher, you use the polite version, です. If you say 学生[がくせい]だ to Fukuro-sensei, it's not badly built: it's just that you sound as if you were talking to a classmate, and that comes across as blunt, almost rude. With her you'd say:

items.jp: 学生[がくせい]です。
items.es: I'm a student. (said politely)
items.nota: です has its own lesson, «です with adjectives, and politeness». For now, it's enough to know it exists and when it's needed.

bloques.md: A very common beginner's mistake is using だ with everyone because it's «the basic form». Basic, yes, but not neutral: it's the form for people you're close to. When you're not sure which register to use with someone, choose です; being too polite hardly ever offends, but being too casual can.

secciones.titulo: Saying no: じゃない

bloques.md: To say that something **isn't** whatever it is, swap だ for **じゃない**:

A noun, followed by じゃない.
猫[ねこ]だ (it's a cat) → 猫[ねこ]じゃない (it isn't a cat)
魚[さかな]だ (it's fish) → 魚[さかな]じゃない (it isn't fish)

items.jp: 猫[ねこ]じゃない。
items.es: It isn't a cat.

items.jp: 魚[さかな]じゃない。
items.es: It isn't fish.
items.nota: What Nyan discovers, to his great disappointment, on opening a parcel.

items.jp: カゲじゃない。
items.es: It isn't Kage.

items.jp: 夢[ゆめ]じゃない。
items.es: It isn't a dream.

items.jp: イギリス 人[じん]だ。 日本人[にほんじん]じゃない。
items.es: I'm British. I'm not Japanese.
items.nota: A country followed by 人[じん] (person) gives the nationality: イギリス 人[じん], 日本人[にほんじん], アメリカ 人[じん].

bloques.md:
There's also **ではない**, which means exactly the same. In fact, じゃ is a contraction of では, just as English says «gonna» for «going to». The difference is one of style:
• **じゃない**: the one for everyday conversation.
• **ではない**: more careful; you'll see it in writing, on the news, in speeches, or when someone is speaking with care.

items.jp: 夢[ゆめ]ではない。
items.es: It isn't a dream.
items.nota: Same meaning; it sounds written, or solemn.

bloques.md: Don't say 猫[ねこ]だじゃない. It looks logical («is» + «isn't»), but だ **is already inside** じゃない: じゃ comes from では, and that で is a form of だ itself. In other words, じゃない isn't just «not», it's the whole «isn't». Add だ and you're saying «is isn't».

A heads-up for when you start listening to Japanese: said with your voice rising at the end, **じゃない？** changes meaning and becomes a question that invites the other person to agree: 猫[ねこ]じゃない？ is «isn't it a cat?», that is, «I'd say it's a cat, right?». It's the same trick as English «isn't it great?», which actually claims it is. Questions have their own lesson, right after the one on particles.

secciones.titulo: The past: だった and じゃなかった

bloques.md:
To talk about the past, each of the two forms has its own version:
• だ becomes **だった**: was.
• じゃない becomes **じゃなかった**: wasn't.

じゃなかった has its own logic: じゃない ends in ない, and ない conjugates like an adjective, swapping its final い for かった. You'll see this work the same way with adjectives ending in い, in their lesson, so this form is good practice.

items.jp: 子猫[こねこ]だった。
items.es: It was a kitten.
items.nota: That noise in the garden… was a kitten.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]、 雨[あめ]だった。
items.es: It rained yesterday. (Yesterday was a rainy day.)
items.nota: In Japanese it doesn't «rain»: the day «is rain».

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]だった。
items.es: It was the teacher.
items.nota: The one knocking at the door.

items.jp: カゲじゃなかった。
items.es: It wasn't Kage.

items.jp: 夢[ゆめ]じゃなかった！
items.es: It wasn't a dream!
items.nota: What you say when you wake up and the cake is still there.

bloques.md: The present-tense だ can be dropped in conversation, but **だった can't**. The reason is simple: drop it and you take the past tense with it. 猫[ねこ]。 means «a cat», and nobody would guess you meant «it was a cat». Whatever carries no information can go; whatever does carry information stays.
A note on tenses: Japanese only distinguishes **past** and **non-past**. The non-past form covers both present and future, and context makes it clear which:

items.jp: 明日[あした]、 休[やす]みだ！
items.es: Tomorrow's a day off!
items.nota: Future, but with plain だ: 明日[あした] (tomorrow) already says when.

secciones.titulo: All four forms at a glance

bloques.md: And that's the whole picture of the Japanese «to be» in plain speech. Just four forms, and they work with any noun:

filas:
猫[ねこ]だ
it's a cat

猫[ねこ]じゃない
it isn't a cat

猫[ねこ]だった
it was a cat

猫[ねこ]じゃなかった
it wasn't a cat

bloques.md: Plus their more careful versions with では, which you'll mostly see in writing: ではない and ではなかった. In conversation, it's almost always じゃ.

lineas.jp: あっ、 カゲだ！
lineas.es: Oh, it's Kage!

lineas.jp: カゲじゃない。 ゴミ 袋[ぶくろ]だ。
lineas.es: It isn't Kage. It's a rubbish bag.

lineas.jp: え？ ゴミ 袋[ぶくろ]？
lineas.es: Huh? A rubbish bag?

lineas.jp: うん…… あれ？ ゴミ 袋[ぶくろ]じゃない。
lineas.es: Yeah… Huh? It isn't a rubbish bag.

lineas.jp: 俺[おれ]だ。
lineas.es: It's me.

lineas.jp: カゲだった……
lineas.es: It was Kage…

bloques.md: Notice how each line is just a noun with its form of «to be»: you don't need anything else to hold a conversation. And notice Kage: his 俺[おれ]だ, with a good firm だ, is exactly the solid (and slightly theatrical) tone that suits his character.

You may be wondering how to say «Tama **is** a cat», with the subject up front. For that you need one more piece: the particle は, which marks what you're talking about. It's the very first thing in the next lesson, and with it, everything you've learned here becomes much more powerful: タマは 猫[ねこ]だ.

ejercicios.pregunta: Between friends: «It's a cat».
ejercicios.jp: 猫[ねこ]＿。
ejercicios.explica: だ is the «is» of plain speech. じゃない would be «isn't», and だった, «was».

ejercicios.pregunta: «It isn't fish.»
ejercicios.jp: 魚[さかな]＿。
ejercicios.explica: じゃない negates the present: «isn't». じゃなかった would be the past, «wasn't».

ejercicios.pregunta: «It was a dream.»
ejercicios.jp: 夢[ゆめ]＿。
ejercicios.explica: だった is the past affirmative of だ. じゃなかった would say the opposite: «it wasn't a dream».

ejercicios.pregunta: «It wasn't Kage.»
ejercicios.jp: カゲ＿。
ejercicios.explica: Negative and past at once: じゃない swaps its final い for かった, just like an adjective, giving じゃなかった.
Swap だ for じゃない (or ではない, the more careful version): 学生[がくせい]じゃない, «isn't a student». だ disappears because it's already built into じゃない.
だ becomes だった: 雨[あめ]だった, «it was (a day of) rain», that is, «it rained». This だった can't be dropped, because it's the part that says it's past.

respuestas: せんせいじゃなかった
せんせいではなかった
ejercicios.explica: First the negative, じゃない, then into the past by swapping い for かった: 先生[せんせい]じゃなかった, «it wasn't the teacher».

ejercicios.pregunta: You open the window in Sapporo and everything's white. What do you cry out?
ejercicios.explica: An exclamation of discovery is the perfect place for だ: «it's snow!». With じゃない you'd be saying it isn't, and with だった you'd be talking about the past.

ejercicios.pregunta: You're talking to Fukuro-sensei. How do you say «I'm a student»?
ejercicios.explica: With your teacher you use です, the polite form. だ, or the bare noun, are for people you're close to: grammatically fine, but with her you'd sound blunt, as if you were talking to a classmate.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which sentence is incorrect?
ejercicios.explica: じゃない already contains だ (じゃ comes from では, and that で is a form of だ). Adding another だ would be like saying «is isn't». The other two are correct: じゃない for speaking, ではない for more careful language.

ejercicios.es: It wasn't a dream.
ejercicios.explica: First the noun, then the form of «to be», which always comes last: 夢[ゆめ]じゃなかった.

ejercicios.es: Tomorrow isn't a day off.
ejercicios.explica: First when, 明日[あした] (tomorrow); then what, 休[やす]み (day off); and じゃない at the end. The non-past form covers the future too: the word 明日[あした] already says when.

lecciones.titulo: Your first particles: は, も and が
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to say who you're talking about (は), add «too» and «not… either» (も), and point out exactly who (が). And the eternal は-or-が question will start to make sense.

secciones.titulo: Labels stuck on behind

bloques.md:
In English, the role of each word is shown mostly by **word order** and by **prepositions**, which come before the word: «**to** school», «**with** Tama». That's why «the dog bites the cat» and «the cat bites the dog» are very different stories.

Japanese does it another way: after each important word it attaches **a particle**, a tiny word that works like a label and says what role that word plays in the sentence. It's like labelling boxes when you move house: it doesn't matter what order they go into the van, because each one says where it belongs.

Three ideas to start with:
• A particle always goes **after** the word it marks, never before. Read them together, as a block: タマは, ニャンも.
• Since the labels show each word's role, sentence order is fairly flexible. What doesn't move is **the end**: the form of «to be», or the verb, always closes the sentence.
• Particles don't translate word for word. You need to understand **what they do**, not hunt for an exact English equivalent.

In this lesson you'll meet the first three, which are also the most frequent in the language: **は** (what we're talking about), **も** (also) and **が** (exactly who or what). With them and what you already know about だ, you can build your first complete sentences.

secciones.titulo: は: «speaking of…»

bloques.md:
は marks **the topic** of the sentence: what you're going to talk about. Remember that, as a particle, it's pronounced **«wa»**, even though it's written は.

The best way to understand it is to translate it in your head as **«speaking of…»** or **«as for…»**. First you announce the topic, then you say something about it:

〔topic〕は 〔what you say about it〕だ
タマは 猫[ねこ]だ。 → Speaking of Tama: she's a cat. In other words, «Tama is a cat».

items.jp: タマは 猫[ねこ]だ。
items.es: Tama is a cat.

items.jp: わたしは ニャンです。
items.es: I'm Nyan.
items.nota: This is how Nyan introduces himself in class, with です because the teacher is there.

items.jp: ポンさんは 店長[てんちょう]だ。
items.es: Pon is the shop manager.
items.nota: さん after a name is a respectful title, a bit like «Mr» or «Ms». It gets its own lesson later.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 雨[あめ]だ。
items.es: It's raining today.
items.nota: Literally, «speaking of today: rain». The topic doesn't have to be a person: it can be a day, a place, anything.

items.jp: 俺[おれ]は 友達[ともだち]じゃない。 ライバルだ。
items.es: I'm not your friend. I'm your rival.
items.nota: Kage's words. Notice that the second sentence doesn't repeat 俺[おれ]は: the topic is still the same.

bloques.md:
That last example shows something important: **the topic lasts**. Once you've said what you're talking about, you don't need to repeat it in every sentence; it stays in force until you change the subject. That's why Japanese leaves out subjects so often: they aren't missing, they've already been said.

And here's a very handy conversational use: a topic on its own, with rising intonation, means **«what about…?»**. It's how you bounce a question back:

items.jp: わたしは 学生[がくせい]。 タマは？
items.es: I'm a student. What about you, Tama?
items.nota: Where English says «what about you?», Japanese usually uses the person's name. You'll see why in the lesson «How to address people».

items.jp: カゲは？
items.es: What about Kage? / Where's Kage?
items.nota: «And speaking of Kage…?» Context fills in the rest.

bloques.md: は isn't exactly «the subject», although it often coincides with it. It's the **topic**, and the difference matters. In 今日[きょう]は 雨[あめ]だ, the topic is «today», but nobody would call «today» the subject of «it's raining». If you think of は as «speaking of…», you'll never misread it.

secciones.titulo: も: too (and not… either)

bloques.md: も means **«too, also»**. You use it instead of は when what you're saying about something has already been said about something else:

items.jp: タマは 猫[ねこ]だ。 ニャンも 猫[ねこ]だ。
items.es: Tama is a cat. Nyan is a cat too.

items.jp: わたしも 学生[がくせい]です。
items.es: I'm a student too.

items.jp: わたしも！
items.es: Me too!
items.nota: The most useful reply in the world, no extras needed.

bloques.md: English switches from «too» to «either» in negative sentences («me neither»). Japanese doesn't bother: **it's the same も**. Whether it means «too» or «not… either» depends only on whether the sentence is positive or negative:

items.jp: コタローは 猫[ねこ]じゃない。 犬[いぬ]だ。
items.es: Kotarō isn't a cat. He's a dog.
items.nota: A shiba, to be precise.

items.jp: ポンさんも 猫[ねこ]じゃない。
items.es: Pon isn't a cat either.
items.nota: He's a tanuki. Same も as in «too»; the じゃない turns it into «not… either».

items.jp: 俺[おれ]も。
items.es: Me neither. / Me too.
items.nota: Only context tells you which: it depends on what was said before.

bloques.md: Use も with two things and it means **«both… and…»**; in the negative, **«neither… nor…»**:

items.jp: ニャンも タマも 猫[ねこ]だ。
items.es: Both Nyan and Tama are cats.

items.jp: ニャンも タマも 犬[いぬ]じゃない。
items.es: Neither Nyan nor Tama is a dog.

bloques.md: With a negative, も can also sound like **«not even»**, because it stresses that not even that one escapes. You'll see this at full strength in the lesson on questions, when it teams up with words like 何[なに] («what»): 何[なに]も means «nothing, not a single thing».

も **replaces** は; it isn't added to it. タマはも and タマもは don't exist. That's because both do the same job, marking what you're talking about, and も just adds the idea of «too». Using both would be like saying «speaking of Tama, also speaking of Tama». The same goes for が: も replaces it too.

secciones.titulo: が: exactly who

bloques.md: And now が. If は announces what we're talking about, が **points at someone or something specific**: «this one, and no other». Picture this: a cake has gone missing from Pon's shop, and everyone is looking at each other. Pon asks:

items.jp: 誰[だれ]が 犯人[はんにん]？
items.es: Who's the culprit?
items.nota: 誰[だれ] is «who» and 犯人[はんにん] is «culprit». He's looking for ONE specific person, so it's が.

items.jp: ……わたしが 犯人[はんにん]です。
items.es: …I'm the culprit. / …It was me.
items.nota: Nyan confesses. With が he says «it's ME, nobody else».

bloques.md:
Look at the translation: «It was ME». In English, to single someone out like this, we stress the word with our voice or use a special structure: «It was HIM», «Nyan is the one who did it». Japanese doesn't need to raise its voice or rearrange anything: が is enough.

Compare these two ways of introducing yourself:

items.jp: わたしは ニャンです。
items.es: I'm Nyan.
items.nota: A normal introduction: «speaking of me, I'm Nyan».

items.jp: わたしが ニャンです。
items.es: I'm Nyan. (I'm the one you're looking for.)
items.nota: The answer when someone is looking for Nyan: «the Nyan you want is me».

bloques.md:
Question words like 誰[だれ] (who) or 何[なに] (what) **take が, never は**. And the answer to those questions takes が as well.
誰[だれ]が 犯人[はんにん]？ → ニャンが 犯人[はんにん]だ。

Why? Because は presents something **already known** in order to talk about it, and a question word is exactly the opposite: the thing you don't know. You can't say «speaking of who…», because you don't yet know who you're speaking of.

That doesn't mean you can't ask questions with は; it only means the question word can't be the topic. See the difference:
• 誰[だれ]が 犯人[はんにん]？ → Who's the culprit? (the unknown is 誰[だれ], and it takes が)
• 犯人[はんにん]は 誰[だれ]？ → The culprit: who is it? (the topic is «the culprit», and the unknown sits in the comment)

Both questions are correct and ask for the same thing; the only thing that doesn't exist is 誰[だれ]は.

が has many more jobs, and you'll meet them lesson by lesson: it marks the subject of the verbs of existence («there's a cat»), what you like or are good at, and much more. But the underlying idea is always this: **が points, は announces**.

secciones.titulo: は or が: the difference in practice

bloques.md:
Here's a simple way to see it that works in about 90 % of cases: **は spotlights what comes after it; が spotlights what comes before it.**
• With は, the known thing is the topic, and the interesting part, the new information, comes **afterwards**.
• With が, the interesting part is **the very word that carries が**.

filas:
ニャンは 何[なに]？
What's Nyan?

ニャンは 猫[ねこ]だ。
Nyan is a cat.
猫[ねこ], what comes after は

誰[だれ]が 猫[ねこ]？
Which one is the cat?

ニャンが 猫[ねこ]だ。
Nyan is the cat.
ニャン, what comes before が

bloques.md: And one use of は you'll see all the time: **contrast**. When you set two topics side by side, は weighs them against each other: «this one, like this; that one, differently»:

items.jp: タマは 猫[ねこ]だ。 コタローは 犬[いぬ]だ。
items.es: Tama is a cat; Kotarō, on the other hand, is a dog.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 休[やす]みじゃない。 明日[あした]は 休[やす]みだ。
items.es: Today isn't a day off. Tomorrow is.
items.nota: The second は carries a hint of «tomorrow, on the other hand…».

bloques.md: A trick for deciding: try the sentence in English with «as for…». If it works («as for Tama, she's a cat»), it's は. If what you mean is «it's X, and nobody else», or you're answering a «who?» or «what?», it's が. And don't worry if you hesitate at first: most Japanese people couldn't explain the difference either, but they feel it because they've heard it millions of times.
