You'll come to feel it the same way, one example at a time.

lineas.jp: あれ？ ケーキは？
lineas.es: Huh? Where's the cake?

lineas.jp: 誰[だれ]が 犯人[はんにん]？ コタロー？
lineas.es: Who did it? Kotarō?

lineas.jp: ちがう！ 犯人[はんにん]じゃない！
lineas.es: No! It wasn't me!

lineas.jp: 俺[おれ]も 犯人[はんにん]じゃない。
lineas.es: Wasn't me either.

lineas.jp: ……わたしが 犯人[はんにん]。
lineas.es: …It was me.

lineas.jp: やっぱり！
lineas.es: I knew it!

bloques.md: Go back over the dialogue with what you now know: ケーキは？ uses は to ask about the topic («what about the cake?»); 誰[だれ]が hunts for one specific culprit; 俺[おれ]も means «not me either» because the sentence is negative; and わたしが points at the real culprit. Four particles, four different jobs.

ejercicios.pregunta: You're telling someone about your friend: «Tama is a cat».
ejercicios.jp: タマ＿ 猫[ねこ]だ。
ejercicios.explica: You present Tama as the topic («speaking of Tama…») and then say something about her: that's は. が would mean «the cat is Tama, nobody else», which answers a different question.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama is a cat, and Nyan…
ejercicios.jp: ニャン＿ 猫[ねこ]だ。
ejercicios.explica: What you're saying about Nyan has already been said about Tama, so it's も, «too».

ejercicios.pregunta: Pon isn't a cat, and Kotarō…
ejercicios.jp: コタロー＿ 猫[ねこ]じゃない。
ejercicios.explica: In Japanese, «not… either» is the same も as «too»: the negative sentence turns it into «either». With は you'd just be saying «Kotarō isn't a cat», without the idea of «him neither».

ejercicios.pregunta: You're looking for Nyan among a crowd of cats. «Which one is Nyan?»
ejercicios.jp: 誰[だれ]＿ ニャン？
ejercicios.explica: Question words take が. は presents something known, and 誰[だれ] is exactly what you don't know: you can't say «speaking of who…».

ejercicios.pregunta: You answer the previous question: «I'M Nyan».
ejercicios.jp: わたし＿ ニャンです。
ejercicios.explica: The answer to a «who?» also takes が: it points at one specific person, «it's me, nobody else».

ejercicios.pregunta: Now you're introducing yourself in class, and nobody is looking for you: «I'm Nyan».
ejercicios.jp: わたし＿ ニャンです。
ejercicios.explica: In a normal introduction, «I» is the topic and the new part is your name: は. With が it would sound like «the Nyan you're all looking for is me».

ejercicios.pregunta: You've said you're a student and want to bounce the question back to Tama: «What about you, Tama?»
ejercicios.jp: タマ＿？
ejercicios.explica: A topic on its own, with rising intonation, means «what about…?»: タマは？ is «and speaking of Tama…?», that is, «what about you?».

ejercicios.es: Tama is a student too.
ejercicios.explica: も goes right after whatever is «too» (Tama), and だ closes the sentence.

ejercicios.es: Kage isn't a friend.
ejercicios.explica: Topic with は, what you say about it, and じゃない at the end. The negative always comes last, because it's part of «to be».

ejercicios.es: Nyan is the culprit (him and nobody else).
ejercicios.explica: To single out the culprit, が goes after Nyan: what matters is what comes before が.

ejercicios.base: カゲは 友達[ともだち]だ
respuestas: カゲはともだちじゃない
カゲはともだちではない
ejercicios.explica: The particle doesn't change: only the ending does. だ becomes じゃない: カゲは 友達[ともだち]じゃない.

ejercicios.base: わたしも 犬[いぬ]だ
respuestas: わたしもいぬじゃない
わたしもいぬではない
ejercicios.explica: When you make the sentence negative, も switches from «too» to «either» without being touched: わたしも 犬[いぬ]じゃない, «I'm not a dog either».

ejercicios.pregunta: Which sentence is incorrect?
opciones: 誰[だれ]は 先生[せんせい]？
誰[だれ]が 先生[せんせい]？
先生[せんせい]は 誰[だれ]？
ejercicios.explica: 誰[だれ] can't be the topic, because は presents something known and 誰[だれ] is the unknown. The other two are correct: in one the unknown takes が, and in the other the topic is «the teacher» and the question sits in the comment.

lecciones.titulo: Asking questions: か and question words
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to ask questions politely and among friends, use what, who, where and when, say «something», «nothing» and «anything», and even tuck a question inside another sentence: «I don't know who did it».

secciones.titulo: か: a question mark you can hear

bloques.md:
In English, you turn a statement into a question by rearranging words («it is» → «is it?») or adding «do» («you like» → «do you like?»). Japanese has something much simpler: **a particle at the end, か**, which turns any sentence into a question. It's like a question mark that you actually pronounce.

And the best part: **nothing else changes**. Not the word order, not the verb form. Take a polite statement, add か, and you have your question:

〔polite sentence〕か
学生[がくせい]です (I'm a student) → 学生[がくせい]ですか (are you a student?)

items.jp: 学生[がくせい]ですか。
items.es: Are you a student?

items.jp: フクロウ 先生[せんせい]ですか。
items.es: Are you Fukuro-sensei?

items.jp: はい、 学生[がくせい]です。
items.es: Yes, I'm a student.
items.nota: はい is the polite «yes».

items.jp: いいえ、 先生[せんせい]です。
items.es: No, I'm a teacher.
items.nota: いいえ is the polite «no».

bloques.md: Notice the punctuation: in writing, a question with か often ends in an ordinary full stop, 。, because か already does the question mark's job. In informal texts and messages you'll also see ？. When speaking, you can let your voice rise a little at the end, but with か it isn't required: the question is already clear.

secciones.titulo: Asking among friends

bloques.md: With friends, things change. In plain speech, the usual thing is to **drop the だ and leave out か**: the question is carried by intonation alone, with your voice rising at the end, just like English «Student?».

items.jp: 学生[がくせい]？
items.es: Are you a student?
items.nota: With your voice going up. In writing, with ？.

items.jp: カゲ？
items.es: Kage? (Is that you, Kage?)

items.jp: 犯人[はんにん]じゃない？
items.es: Isn't he the culprit? / Couldn't he be the culprit?
items.nota: Remember: じゃない？ with rising intonation invites the other person to agree.

bloques.md:
Why does だ disappear? Because だ is a firm assertion, like a full stop said out loud, and **you can't assert and ask at the same time**. That's why 学生[がくせい]だ？ sounds odd, and 学生[がくせい]だか？ simply isn't said.

And why leave out か? You can use it, but in plain speech か sounds **blunt**, like an interrogation: 学生[がくせい]か？ is roughly «you a student, or what?». Traditionally it's a more masculine tone, and not a very friendly one even then. And said to yourself, か sounds like thinking aloud: そうか is «oh, I see», not a question.

There's a third very common way: ending with **の**. It sounds softer and shows interest in the other person, as if you were asking them to explain. After a noun, you add な: 学生[がくせい]なの？ («oh, so you're a student?»). And you'll hear it constantly in set phrases:

items.jp: どうしたの？
items.es: What's wrong? / What happened?
items.nota: What Tama asks Nyan every time she sees his hungry face.

items.jp: 本当[ほんとう]なの？
items.es: Really? / Seriously?

bloques.md:
This の has a lot going on (it's used to ask for and give explanations), and you'll see it in depth in the lesson «〜んです: explaining or asking for an explanation». For now, knowing it exists and sounds soft is enough.

And when answering among friends, «yes» and «no» relax too: **うん** is «yes» and **ううん** is «no». Mind the difference: うん is short and falling; ううん has two beats, almost «uh-uh». はい and いいえ are kept for polite speech.

Don't mix registers within the same question: 学生[がくせい]ですか is polite and 学生[がくせい]？ is casual; both are fine, each in its place. What doesn't work is 学生[がくせい]だか, which mixes a firm assertion with a question and ends up sounding like neither.

secciones.titulo: Question words

bloques.md:
To ask what, who, where or when, you use a **question word**. And here's the golden rule: **the question word goes exactly where the answer would go**. It doesn't jump to the front as it does in English. Think of the answer and replace the piece you don't know:
• カゲは 公園[こうえん]だ。 (Kage is at the park.) → カゲは どこ？ (Where's Kage?)

filas: これは 何[なん]ですか。 What is this?
あの 人[ひと]は 誰[だれ]？ Who's that person?
トイレは どこですか。 Where's the toilet?
誕生日[たんじょうび]は いつ？ When's your birthday?
日本語[にほんご]は どう？ How's your Japanese going?
どれが タマ？ Which one is Tama? (in a photo)
どっちが カゲ？ Which of the two is Kage?
これは いくらですか。 How much is this?

bloques.md:
A few notes on the table:
• 何 is read **なん** before d, n and t sounds (as in 何[なん]ですか, 何[なん]だ or 何[なん]の) and before counters; everywhere else, including when it stands alone at the end, it's **なに** (as in 何[なに]が, 何[なに]も or それ、 何[なに]？). If in doubt, think about what's easier to say: なん blends more smoothly into what follows.
• どちら is the polite version of どっち, and with です it also works as an elegant «where»: お 国[くに]は どちらですか (where are you from?).
• なんで is more colloquial than どうして; both ask for a reason.

You'll have noticed that many of these words start with ど. That's no accident: Japanese has a neatly organised family of pointing words, **こ・そ・あ・ど**, which works like «this» and «that» plus a question at the end. Unlike English, it has three distances, not two:

filas: この 本[ほん] this book
その 本[ほん] that book
あの 本[ほん] that book over there
どの 本[ほん] which book?

bloques.md: By the way, the earlier table hid a grammar clue: どれ, like 誰[だれ] and 何[なに], takes **が** when it's the subject (どれが タマ？), never は. You already know why: は announces something known, and the question word is precisely what you don't know.

The classic English-speaker's mistake is putting the question word first, as in English: 何[なに]は これ？ It fails for two reasons: Japanese word order doesn't change for questions, and 何[なに] can't take は anyway. The right way is これは 何[なに]？: «this, what is it?». Always think of the answer (これは 本[ほん]だ) and swap out just the gap.

secciones.titulo: Something, nothing, anything: か, も and でも

bloques.md:
Here's one of the loveliest mechanisms in Japanese. Attach a particle to a question word and you get new words **without learning anything else**:
• With **か**, the question turns into **«some-»**: something, someone, somewhere. It's a question left unanswered. 何[なに]か is «something»: a thing, I don't know which.
• With **も**, you cover **everything** («always», «all of them») or, with a negative, **nothing** («nobody», «nowhere»). It's the same も as «too» and «either»: «this one too, that one too…» until it covers the lot.
• With **でも**, you get **«any-»**: it doesn't matter which.

filas: どれでも any of them

bloques.md:
With も you need to pay a little attention, because **it depends on the word**. 何[なに]も and 誰[だれ]も nearly always go with a negative sentence: «nothing», «nobody». On the other hand, いつも means «always» and goes with positive sentences, and どれも and どこも work both ways: in positive sentences, «all of them» or «everywhere»; in negative ones, «none of them» or «nowhere». For «everything» and «everyone», Japanese prefers other words: 全部[ぜんぶ] and みんな.

Some of the examples use verbs in their polite form (ending in ます or ません); you'll study those properly in the next lesson. Here, just focus on the question word and what happens to it:

items.jp: 何[なに]か 食[た]べますか。
items.es: Will you have something to eat?

items.jp: 誰[だれ]か いますか。
items.es: Is anybody there?
items.nota: What you say at an open door, or when you walk into Pon's shop and can't see him.

items.jp: いつか 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]きます。
items.es: Someday I'll go to Hokkaido.

items.jp: 何[なに]も 食[た]べません。
items.es: I don't eat anything.
items.nota: A sentence Nyan has never once said.

items.jp: 誰[だれ]も いません。
items.es: There's nobody here.

items.jp: タマは いつも 一番[いちばん]だ。
items.es: Tama always comes first.

items.jp: どれも 百円[ひゃくえん]です。
items.es: They're all a hundred yen.

items.jp: 何[なん]でも いいです。
items.es: Anything's fine.
items.nota: Kotarō's answer whenever someone asks what he wants to eat.

items.jp: いつでも どうぞ。
items.es: Anytime you like.

bloques.md: Watch the reading: 何[なに]か and 何[なに]も are read with なに, but 何[なん]でも is read with なん, because the で after it calls for the short form, just as in 何[なん]ですか. And beware the false friend in 何[なに]も: it isn't «what, too», it's «nothing». Here も doesn't add anything: it shuts every door.

secciones.titulo: Questions inside a sentence: か and かどうか

bloques.md: Sometimes a question isn't asked directly but sits **inside another sentence**: «I don't know **who did it**», «I don't know **whether it's Kage**». Japanese handles this with the same か, which now acts as «a question packed in a box». After it comes what you say about that question, usually 分[わ]からない (I don't know, I'm not sure) or 知[し]らない (I don't know, no idea).

With a question word: 〔question〕か 分[わ]からない
誰[だれ]が 犯人[はんにん]か 分[わ]からない。 → I don't know who the culprit is.

Without a question word (yes-or-no questions): 〔question〕かどうか 分[わ]からない
ニャンが 犯人[はんにん]かどうか 分[わ]からない。 → I don't know whether Nyan is the culprit.

With nouns, **だ disappears** before か: 犯人[はんにん]だか ✗ → 犯人[はんにん]か ✓.

items.jp: 誰[だれ]が 犯人[はんにん]か 分[わ]からない。
items.es: I don't know who the culprit is.

items.jp: それが 何[なに]か 分[わ]からない。
items.es: I don't know what that is.

items.jp: 駅[えき]が どこか 分[わ]からない。
items.es: I don't know where the station is.
items.nota: Here どこか doesn't mean «somewhere»: it's どこ plus the か of the tucked-in question. The rest of the sentence makes that clear.

items.jp: ニャンが 犯人[はんにん]かどうか 分[わ]からない。
items.es: I don't know whether Nyan is the culprit (or not).

items.jp: 明日[あした]、 雨[あめ]かどうか 分[わ]かりません。
items.es: I don't know whether it'll rain tomorrow.
items.nota: 分[わ]かりません is the polite version of 分[わ]からない.

bloques.md:
Why does だ disappear? For the same reason as in casual questions: だ asserts, and here you're saying precisely that **you don't know** whether it's so. Asserting something and doubting it in the same breath doesn't fit.

And why かどうか? どう comes from «how»: かどうか is something like «whether it's so, or how it is». It's for questions answered with yes or no, just like «whether» in «I don't know whether she's coming». In conversation it's sometimes shortened to just か, but かどうか is the clear, complete form.

Don't mix up the two kinds of か. In 誰[だれ]か いますか, 誰[だれ]か means «someone». In 誰[だれ]が 犯人[はんにん]か 分[わ]からない, the か closes the question «who's the culprit?». What comes next tells you which: if, after the か, the sentence goes on to talk about that question (with 分[わ]からない, 知[し]らない…), it's a question tucked inside the sentence.

secciones.titulo: At Pon's shop

bloques.md: To finish, a scene with everything together. Nyan walks into Pon's shop. Since Pon is older and the shopkeeper, Nyan speaks to him with です and か; Pon, as a good shopkeeper, is polite with his customer too:

lineas.jp: すみません。 誰[だれ]か いますか。
lineas.es: Excuse me. Is anybody here?

lineas.jp: はい、 いらっしゃい！
lineas.es: Yes, welcome!

lineas.jp: これは 何[なん]ですか。
lineas.es: What's this?

lineas.jp: どら 焼[や]きです。
lineas.es: It's a dorayaki.

lineas.jp: いくらですか。
lineas.es: How much is it?

lineas.jp: どれも 百円[ひゃくえん]です。
lineas.es: They're all a hundred yen.

lineas.jp: じゃあ…… 全部[ぜんぶ]！
lineas.es: In that case… all of them!

bloques.md: And now the version among friends, when Tama bumps into Nyan leaving the shop with an enormous bag:

lineas.jp: ニャン！ それ、 何[なに]？
lineas.es: Nyan! What's that?

lineas.jp: どら 焼[や]き。
lineas.es: Dorayaki.

lineas.jp: 全部[ぜんぶ]？ どうして？
lineas.es: All of those? Why?

lineas.jp: 何[なん]でも いい。
lineas.es: Never mind why.

lineas.jp: 本当[ほんとう]に 一人[ひとり]で？
lineas.es: Seriously, all by yourself?

lineas.jp: ……タマも 一[ひと]つ？
lineas.es: …Want one too, Tama?

bloques.md: Compare the two dialogues: with Pon, か and です; with Tama, intonation, no だ and no か. The question words, however, are the same in both: 何[なに], どうして, いくら. What changes with register is the end of the sentence, not the heart of the question.

ejercicios.pregunta: You ask your teacher whether she's Fukuro-sensei.
ejercicios.jp: フクロウ 先生[せんせい]です＿。
ejercicios.explica: か at the end turns the polite sentence into a question, without changing anything else.

ejercicios.pregunta: Among friends: «Are you a student?»
ejercicios.explica: In plain speech you drop だ and ask with intonation. だ asserts, and you can't assert and ask at the same time; that's why だか doesn't exist. 学生[がくせい]だ。 is a statement, not a question.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Where's the toilet?»
ejercicios.jp: トイレは ＿ですか。
ejercicios.explica: どこ is «where», and it goes exactly where the answer would go (トイレは あそこです, the toilet's over there).

ejercicios.pregunta: «When's the festival?»
ejercicios.jp: お 祭[まつ]りは ＿？
ejercicios.explica: いつ is «when». Among friends: no だ, and your voice rising.

ejercicios.pregunta: In the sentence これは 何ですか, how is 何 read?
ejercicios.explica: Before d, n and t sounds (here, the で of です), 何 is read なん, which blends better into what follows. なに is for cases like 何[なに]が or 何[なに]も.

ejercicios.pregunta: You call through an open door: «Is anybody there?»
ejercicios.jp: ＿ いますか。
ejercicios.explica: Question word plus か = «someone», a person you can't identify. 誰[だれ]も would be «nobody» and 誰[だれ]でも, «anyone».

ejercicios.pregunta: You go in and find the house empty: «There's nobody here».
ejercicios.jp: ＿ いません。
ejercicios.explica: 誰[だれ]も in a negative sentence is «nobody»: も covers everyone («not this one, not that one…»), and the negative empties it.

ejercicios.pregunta: Pon asks which dorayaki you want, and you don't mind: «Any of them is fine».
ejercicios.jp: ＿ いいです。
ejercicios.explica: With でも, the question word becomes «any». どれも would be «all of them» (or «none» with a negative), and どれか, «one of them».

ejercicios.pregunta: «Tama always comes first.»
ejercicios.jp: タマは ＿ 一番[いちばん]だ。
ejercicios.explica: いつ + も = «always», on every occasion. いつか is «someday» and いつでも, «anytime».

ejercicios.es: What's this?
ejercicios.explica: Word order doesn't change in questions: first the topic (これは), and 何[なん] right where the answer would go (これは 本[ほん]です).

ejercicios.es: Where's Kage?
ejercicios.explica: Topic with は, and the question word in the answer's slot. どこ can't take は, so there's only one possible order.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I don't know who the culprit is.»
ejercicios.jp: 誰[だれ]が 犯人[はんにん]＿ 分[わ]からない。
ejercicios.explica: With a question word, か is enough. だ disappears, because you aren't asserting anything: you're saying you don't know. かどうか isn't needed because there's already a question word, 誰[だれ].

ejercicios.pregunta: «I don't know whether Nyan is the culprit.»
ejercicios.jp: ニャンが 犯人[はんにん]＿ 分[わ]からない。
ejercicios.explica: It's a yes-or-no question tucked into the sentence, so it takes かどうか. And だ disappears before か: asserting and doubting at the same time doesn't fit.
Just add か: 学生[がくせい]ですか. Neither the word order nor the form of です changes.

lecciones.titulo: Speaking politely: です and ます
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to talk to your teacher, a shopkeeper or any stranger without sounding blunt: verbs with ます in all four forms, です with nouns and adjectives, and why おいしいでした is a mistake.

secciones.titulo: Two ways of speaking

bloques.md:
English marks politeness mostly through word choice and tone: «Could you possibly…?» instead of «Give me…», «Mr Smith» instead of «Dave». Japanese builds it right into the grammar, at **the end of the sentence**. The same sentence comes in two versions:
• **Plain**: for friends, family and people you're close to. It's the one you've seen with だ.
• **Polite**: for people you keep some distance from or show respect to. It ends in **です** or **ます**.

This isn't stiff, ceremonial Japanese: it's the ordinary polite Japanese of everyday life, the kind used in shops, in class, with neighbours or with a colleague. There are much higher levels of respect too (keigo), which you'll meet in the lesson «Honorific and humble language (keigo)», but for living in Japan, this is what you'll use most with people you don't know.

Who gets which? The key isn't only age but **the circle**: if the person is in your inner circle, plain; if they're outside it, polite.
• With Tama, with Kage, with your brothers and sisters: **plain**.
• With Fukuro-sensei, with Pon when you're buying something, with someone who stops you in the street, with an older person you've just met: **polite**.
• And the other way round, a shopkeeper speaks politely to customers, even children, because in the shop the customer is outside their circle.

Over time, two people who know each other may switch from polite to plain: it's a sign the relationship has grown closer, and sometimes the older person suggests it. And if someone suddenly switches back to polite with a friend, it's usually a bad sign: it signals distance, like a sudden, icy «Sir».

English speakers are used to being casual and friendly with almost everyone: first names, «hey», «cheers». That habit can backfire in Japanese. There, polite speech is **the normal way to talk to anyone who isn't close**, including a slightly older colleague or the neighbour next door. Using plain speech with a stranger doesn't come across as friendly; it comes across as rude. So when in doubt, go polite: being too polite hardly ever bothers anyone, but being too casual can.

secciones.titulo: ます: attached to the verb stem

bloques.md:
Japanese verbs are listed in the dictionary in their **dictionary form**, which is their plain form: 食[た]べる (to eat), 飲[の]む (to drink), 行[い]く (to go). To make them polite, you remove the ending and add **ます**. What's left after removing the ending is called the **stem**, and it's a piece you'll use constantly throughout this guide.

How do you get the stem? It depends on the type of verb. Japanese has two big families of verbs plus two irregulars, and the next lesson, «Verbs: the dictionary form and the two groups», will teach you to tell them apart without fail. Here's a preview so you can start right away:

• Many verbs ending in -iru or -eru: **drop る**. 食[た]べる → 食[た]べ → 食[た]べます.
• All the others: **the final u becomes i**. 飲[の]む (nomu) → 飲[の]み (nomi) → 飲[の]みます.
• The two irregulars: する (to do) → します; 来[く]る (to come) → 来[き]ます.

filas: 帰[かえ]る to go home

bloques.md: Look at 帰[かえ]る: it ends in -eru, and yet it doesn't drop its る; it turns it into り instead. It belongs to the second family, however well it hides it. There are a handful of tricky verbs like this, and the next lesson tells you which ones and how to spot them. Look at 来[く]る too: when it becomes polite, even the reading of its kanji changes, く → き. That's why it's irregular.

ます doesn't change with the person: 食[た]べます is «I eat», «you eat», «she eats», «we eat»… Who's eating is shown by context, or by the topic with は. Nor do you need a separate future tense: the non-past form covers present, habits and future. 明日[あした] 行[い]きます is «I'm going tomorrow» or «I'll go tomorrow», and Japanese doesn't distinguish between the two.

secciones.titulo: The four forms of ます

bloques.md: Just as だ had four forms, so does ます: positive and negative, non-past and past. And the good news is that **all four are formed the same way for every verb**, because they all attach to the same stem:

filas:
食[た]べます
I eat, I'll eat

食[た]べません
I don't eat, I won't eat

食[た]べました
I ate

食[た]べませんでした
I didn't eat

bloques.md: Some examples use を, a particle that marks what you eat, drink or watch. It has its own lesson («を: the direct object»), but you'll get the idea straight away:

items.jp: ニャンは よく 寝[ね]ます。
items.es: Nyan sleeps a lot.
items.nota: よく means «often, a lot». Habits also go in the non-past.

items.jp: 明日[あした]、 学校[がっこう]に 行[い]きます。
items.es: I'll go to school tomorrow.
items.nota: に marks where you're going; you'll also see it in the lesson on particles with verbs.

items.jp: コタローは 野菜[やさい]を 食[た]べません。
items.es: Kotarō doesn't eat vegetables.
items.nota: Greedy as he is, vegetables are the one thing he leaves alone.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]、 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]りました。
items.es: It snowed yesterday.
items.nota: 降[ふ]る (to fall, of rain or snow) → 降[ふ]ります → 降[ふ]りました.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]は 勉強[べんきょう]しませんでした。
items.es: I didn't study yesterday.
items.nota: 勉強[べんきょう]する (to study) conjugates like する: 勉強[べんきょう]します, 勉強[べんきょう]しませんでした…

items.jp: コーヒーを 飲[の]みますか。
items.es: Do you drink coffee? / Would you like a coffee?
items.nota: A question with か, just like with です.

bloques.md: Look at how they're built, because there's logic to it: ます → **ません** (the n of negation); ます → **ました** (the た of the past, which you'll see everywhere); and the past negative, **ませんでした**, is ません plus でした, the polite past of «to be». It's like saying «I don't eat, that's how it was».

A very common slip: 食[た]べませんでした is long, and at first people blurt out 食[た]べませんだった or 食[た]べなかったです. The first doesn't exist: でした is the polite partner of ません, and だった is plain, so mixing them is like saying «Didn't eat it, mate» to your teacher. The second does get heard in conversation, but it's less careful; to begin with, stick to ませんでした.

secciones.titulo: です with nouns: だ in its Sunday best

bloques.md: With nouns, です does exactly the same job as だ, only politely. So here's another four-form table, running parallel to the one you already know:

filas: 学生[がくせい]じゃない

学生[がくせい]じゃないです
学生[がくせい]じゃありません
学生[がくせい]じゃなかった

学生[がくせい]じゃなかったです
学生[がくせい]じゃありませんでした

bloques.md:
You'll see there are **two polite negatives**, and both are correct. Where does each one come from?
• **じゃないです**: take the plain negative, じゃない, and stick です on it to make it polite. This is the most common form in conversation.
• **じゃありません**: comes from another construction, では + ありません (ありません is the polite negative of ある, a verb of existence you'll meet soon). It sounds a little more formal and careful, and it's the one textbooks tend to teach.

And the most formal of all, for speeches and written texts, is **ではありません**, with the full では instead of じゃ.

items.jp: わたしは 学生[がくせい]です。
items.es: I'm a student.

items.jp: カゲさんは 友達[ともだち]じゃないです。
items.es: Kage isn't my friend.
items.nota: Said to someone you need to be polite with; to Tama it would be 友達[ともだち]じゃない.

items.jp: それは 宿題[しゅくだい]じゃありません。
items.es: That isn't your homework.
items.nota: A typical Fukuro-sensei line: she speaks carefully.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]は 休[やす]みでした。
items.es: Yesterday was a day off.

bloques.md: じゃないです versus じゃありません is a difference of tone, not of correctness. Talking to your teacher or in an interview, じゃありません sounds more polished; in ordinary conversation with someone you treat respectfully, じゃないです is perfectly polite and sounds less like a textbook. What you mustn't do is drop the です: bare 学生[がくせい]じゃない is back in plain speech.

secciones.titulo: です with adjectives: not a polite だ

bloques.md:
Adjectives get their own lesson later, but to speak politely you need to know one thing now. Japanese has **two kinds of adjectives**:
• Those ending in **い**: 高[たか]い (expensive, tall), おいしい (tasty), 寒[さむ]い (cold).
• Those that behave almost like nouns, called **な-adjectives**: 静[しず]か (quiet), 元気[げんき] (lively, well), きれい (pretty, clean).

With な-adjectives, です works just as it does with a noun: 静[しず]かです, 静[しず]かじゃないです, 静[しず]かでした. Nothing new.

With い-adjectives, though, there's something important to understand.

bloques.titulo: Why you can't say たかいだ
bloques.md:
An い-adjective **is already a complete sentence on its own**: 高[たか]い doesn't mean «expensive», it means «it's expensive». The final い already includes the «is». That's why in plain speech you just say 高[たか]い, and 高[たか]いだ is wrong: it would be «it's expensive is».

So what does です do in 高[たか]いです? **It doesn't mean «is»**: it's simply a politeness sticker added to the end to soften the sentence. It adds no tense and no meaning.

How can you prove that this です isn't «to be»? With the past tense. If です were the verb «to be», the past of 高[たか]いです would be 高[たか]いでした. But it isn't: the past goes **inside the adjective**, which swaps its い for かった, while です stays as it is, a sticker:

filas:
高[たか]くないです
高[たか]くありません

高[たか]くなかったです
高[たか]くありませんでした

bloques.md: How くない and かった are formed you'll see in the lesson «い-adjectives». Here, focus on the essential point: in the polite column, **the adjective does all the work and です is just tacked on at the end**.

items.jp: この ケーキは おいしいです。
items.es: This cake is delicious.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]は 寒[さむ]かったです。
items.es: It was cold yesterday.
items.nota: In Sapporo in January, a sentence you hear a lot.

items.jp: 公園[こうえん]は 静[しず]かでした。
items.es: The park was quiet.
items.nota: 静[しず]か is a な-adjective: its polite past is でした, like a noun's.

bloques.md: The star mistake: おいしいでした. It looks logical (でした is the past of です), but you now know why it fails: that です isn't «to be», so it has no past of its own. The right form is おいしかったです: the adjective goes into the past, and the politeness sticker comes after it. If it's hard at first, think of the plain version (おいしかった) and add です.

secciones.titulo: In class with Fukuro-sensei

bloques.md: To finish, a scene in class. Nyan speaks to his teacher politely, of course. Fukuro-sensei also uses です and ます with her students: in class, many teachers speak like this, with a touch of kindly distance.

lineas.jp: ニャンさん、 宿題[しゅくだい]は？
lineas.es: Nyan, where's your homework?

lineas.jp: すみません。 昨日[きのう]は 寝[ね]ました。
lineas.es: I'm sorry. Yesterday I slept.

lineas.jp: 一日中[いちにちじゅう]ですか。
lineas.es: All day?

lineas.jp: はい。 でも、 夢[ゆめ]で 勉強[べんきょう]しました。
lineas.es: Yes. But I studied in my dreams.

lineas.jp: それは 宿題[しゅくだい]じゃありません。
lineas.es: That isn't homework.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 明日[あした] します。
lineas.es: Then I'll do it tomorrow.

lineas.jp: いいえ、 今日[きょう] しましょう。
lineas.es: No: let's do it today.

bloques.md: And here's the same idea in plain and polite speech, so you can see the contrast at a glance. The information is identical; the only thing that changes is who you're saying it to:

filas: 猫[ねこ]じゃないです。 / 猫[ねこ]じゃありません。

bloques.md: You already know the plain form of verbs, 食[た]べる: it's the dictionary form. You'll learn its other plain forms (negative, past…) over the coming lessons, starting with the negative in «Negative verbs». And the teacher's しましょう («let's do it») has its place in the lesson «Volitional: let's…».

ejercicios.pregunta: To your teacher: «I'm going tomorrow».
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした] 行[い]き＿。
ejercicios.explica: ます is the non-past positive, which also covers the future: 明日[あした] already says when.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I don't drink coffee.»
ejercicios.jp: コーヒーは 飲[の]み＿。
ejercicios.explica: ません is the polite negative. ませんでした would be the past, «I didn't drink».

ejercicios.pregunta: «It snowed yesterday.»
ejercicios.jp: 昨日[きのう]、 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]り＿。
ejercicios.explica: It's past and positive: ました. That た is the past-tense marker you'll keep seeing everywhere.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I didn't study yesterday.»
ejercicios.jp: 昨日[きのう]は 勉強[べんきょう]し＿。
ejercicios.explica: Past negative: ません plus でした. Without でした it would be present («I don't study»).
食[た]べる belongs to the family that drops る: the stem is 食[た]べ, and ます is attached to it.
飲[の]む belongs to the other family: the final u becomes i (む → み), followed by ます: 飲[の]みます.
Stem 行[い]き (く → き), plus the polite past negative, ませんでした: «I didn't go».
来[く]る is irregular: when it becomes polite, the reading of its kanji changes, giving 来[き]ます. That's why you have to learn it separately.

respuestas: がくせいじゃないです
がくせいじゃありません
がくせいではありません
がくせいではないです
ejercicios.explica: Two valid forms: じゃないです (the plain negative plus the です sticker, very conversational) and じゃありません (a little more careful). With では instead of じゃ, more formal still.

ejercicios.pregunta: Politely: «It was delicious».
ejercicios.explica: With an い-adjective, the past goes inside the adjective (おいしかった) and です is added afterwards purely for politeness. おいしいでした is the star mistake: that です isn't «to be» and has no past of its own.

ejercicios.pregunta: «The park was quiet.» Hint: 静[しず]か is a な-adjective.
ejercicios.jp: 公園[こうえん]は 静[しず]か＿。
ejercicios.explica: な-adjectives behave like nouns: their polite past is でした, just like 学生[がくせい]でした. かった is only for い-adjectives.

ejercicios.pregunta: You're talking to Tama, your best friend: «Are you coming tomorrow?»
opciones: 明日[あした]、 来[く]る？
明日[あした]、 来[き]ますか。
明日[あした]、 来[く]るか。
ejercicios.explica: With your best friend: plain, with rising intonation. 来[き]ますか is well built, but with her it would sound distant and stiff. And 来[く]るか, with か in plain speech, sounds blunt.

ejercicios.es: Nyan doesn't eat vegetables.
ejercicios.explica: Topic with は, what he eats with を, and the verb in the polite negative at the end. The verb always closes the sentence.

ejercicios.es: It was cold yesterday. (politely)
ejercicios.explica: The adjective carries the past, 寒[さむ]かった, and です comes after it purely as politeness. Never 寒[さむ]いでした.

lecciones.titulo: Verbs: the dictionary form and its two families
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll know what the dictionary form is, which of the two families any verb belongs to (including sneaky ones like 帰[かえ]る), and why that decides how everything else is conjugated.

secciones.titulo: The verb rules from the end

bloques.md:
In Japanese, the verb **always comes at the end of the sentence**. Everything before it (who, what, where, when) sets the scene, and the verb arrives last to close the sentence and decide what it means. That's why Japanese listeners wait until the end: negation, tense and politeness all live there, attached to the verb. Until the very last syllable, you don't know whether Nyan 食[た]べます (eats) or 食[た]べません (doesn't eat).

And Japanese verbs work very differently from English ones:
• **They don't change with the person.** 食[た]べる covers «I eat», «you eat», «she eats», «we eat» and «they eat». Not even the little «-s» of «eats».
• **They change for lots of other things**: whether it's negative, past, polite, a wish, a possibility… All of that is added as pieces at the end of the verb, one after another.
• **A verb on its own is a complete sentence.** No subject, nothing else: 食[た]べる。 is «I'll eat (it)», and 行[い]く？ is «are you going?».

items.jp: 食[た]べる。
items.es: I'll eat it. / I eat.
items.nota: A complete sentence: context tells you who and what.

items.jp: 行[い]く？
items.es: Are you going? / Coming?
items.nota: A question between friends, with rising intonation.

items.jp: ニャンは 寝[ね]る。
items.es: Nyan's going to bed. / Nyan sleeps.

secciones.titulo: The dictionary form

bloques.md:
The form in which a verb appears in the dictionary is called, naturally, the **dictionary form**. It has two features worth memorising:
• **It always ends in a u sound**: う, く, ぐ, す, つ, ぬ, ぶ, む or る. Those nine endings are the only possibilities.
• **It isn't an infinitive.** An English dictionary lists «to eat», which you don't use on its own as a sentence. In Japanese, 食[た]べる is a living form, used just as it is: it's the **non-past, positive, plain** form. In other words, the casual version of 食[た]べます.

filas: 食[た]べる, 帰[かえ]る

bloques.md: Since it's the plain form, you'll use it with friends. But not only then: later you'll see that **inside a sentence** (for instance, when a verb describes a noun) the plain form is always used, even when you're talking to your teacher. The end of the sentence carries the politeness; what's inside stays plain. So the dictionary form isn't «the informal one»; it's **the basic form**, and all the others grow out of it.

items.jp: 明日[あした]、 タマが 来[く]る。
items.es: Tama's coming tomorrow.
items.nota: Non-past: it covers the future, just like 来[き]ます.

items.jp: カゲは 毎朝[まいあさ] 走[はし]る。
items.es: Kage goes running every morning.
items.nota: Habits go in the non-past too.

items.jp: コタローは 何[なん]でも 食[た]べる。
items.es: Kotarō will eat anything.

secciones.titulo: Two families: る-verbs and う-verbs

bloques.md:
Almost every Japanese verb belongs to one of **two families**, and the family decides how the verb conjugates. You saw it with ます: 食[た]べる drops its る, giving 食[た]べます, while 飲[の]む turns む into み: 飲[の]みます. That difference repeats in every form you're going to learn.

**Family 1: る-verbs.** They end in る and, when conjugated, simply **drop the る** and attach whatever comes next. Their stem never moves. Textbooks call them ichidan, «one-step» verbs, precisely because everything is built on the same base: 食[た]べ + ます, 食[た]べ + ない, 食[た]べ + た…

**Family 2: う-verbs.** Their last syllable **changes its vowel** depending on the form, running through all five vowels: a, i, u, e, o. That's why they're called godan, «five-step» verbs. Look at what happens to 飲[の]む, which is «nomu»:

You don't need to learn all those forms now: each has its own lesson. What matters is the idea: **in う-verbs, the last syllable moves along its consonant's row** (ま, み, む, め, も), while in る-verbs the stem stays put and the る disappears. So the first thing you need to know about a new verb is which family it belongs to.

secciones.titulo: How to tell which family

bloques.md: The good news is that you can nearly always tell from the dictionary form. Ask yourself two questions:

**1. Does it end in る?**
If it doesn't, like 飲[の]む, 行[い]く, 話[はな]す, 待[ま]つ or 買[か]う, it's a **う-verb**. Always, no exceptions.

**2. If it ends in る, what vowel comes right before it?**
• If it's **a, u or o**, as in 分[わ]かる (wakaru), 作[つく]る (tsukuru) or 乗[の]る (noru), it's a **う-verb**. Always.
• If it's **i or e**, as in 見[み]る (miru), 食[た]べる (taberu) or 起[お]きる (okiru), it's **almost always** a **る-verb**… apart from a handful of exceptions.

Watch out for kanji, which hide the vowel. 帰[かえ]る doesn't look like it ends in -eru until you check the reading: かえる, kaeru. That's why you should always look at the furigana, not just the kanji.

And now, the exceptions. These are verbs that end in -iru or -eru and look like る-verbs, but **are actually う-verbs**. There aren't many, and the most common ones stick quickly because they're used all the time:

filas: 知[し]ります (in practice you'll use 知[し]っています, which you'll meet later)

bloques.md: The trickiest cases are pairs that are **spelled the same in hiragana** but belong to different families. Only the kanji, and the ます form, give them away:

items.jp: 着[き]る → 着[き]ます
items.es: to put on (clothes) → る-verb

items.jp: 切[き]る → 切[き]ります
items.es: to cut → う-verb

items.jp: いる → います
items.es: to be, to exist (living things) → る-verb

items.jp: 要[い]る → 要[い]ります
items.es: to need → う-verb

items.jp: 変[か]える → 変[か]えます
items.es: to change (something) → る-verb

items.jp: 帰[かえ]る → 帰[かえ]ります
items.es: to go home → う-verb

bloques.md: How do you avoid mistakes? With one simple habit: **learn every new verb together with its ます form**. If you know it's 帰[かえ]ります, you know 帰[かえ]る is a う-verb, because the る turned into り instead of disappearing. Dictionaries mark the family too, but the ます form is the handiest clue, since it's the one you'll hear most. And if you're ever unsure about an -iru or -eru verb, bet on the る family: you'll be right the vast majority of the time.

secciones.titulo: The two irregulars: する and 来る

bloques.md:
Only two verbs break out of the families, and they're two of the most used in the language, so you'll learn them just by seeing them so often.

**する (to do).** It's the all-purpose verb of Japanese. As well as «to do», it attaches to lots of nouns to turn them into verbs. Imagine if English said «do study» for «study», «do cooking» for «cook», and it were completely normal:

items.jp: 勉強[べんきょう]する
items.es: to study (do study)

items.jp: 料理[りょうり]する
items.es: to cook (do cooking)

items.jp: 散歩[さんぽ]する
items.es: to go for a walk

items.jp: 電話[でんわ]する
items.es: to phone

items.jp: コピーする
items.es: to photocopy
items.nota: It even works with foreign words: take the word in katakana and attach する.

bloques.md:
All these verbs conjugate exactly like する: 勉強[べんきょう]します, 勉強[べんきょう]しません… Learn する once and it covers hundreds of verbs.

**来[く]る (to come).** Its quirk is that **the vowel of its first syllable changes**, and with it the reading of the kanji: 来[く]る, 来[き]ます, 来[こ]ない. The kanji is always the same, but it's read く, き or こ depending on the form. That's why this guide always gives it furigana, and why it's worth paying attention to.

Besides these two, a couple of verbs have one isolated quirk in a single form, such as ある (to exist, for things) or 行[い]く (to go). They aren't fully irregular: they conjugate like normal う-verbs except at that one point, and you'll meet each quirk exactly when it comes up, in the lesson for that form.

secciones.titulo: Coming and going

bloques.md: To finish, a plain-speech conversation between Tama and Nyan, using only dictionary forms. Notice how every sentence ends with the verb:

lineas.jp: ニャン、 明日[あした] うちに 来[く]る？
lineas.es: Nyan, are you coming to my place tomorrow?

lineas.jp: 行[い]く！ 何[なに]か 食[た]べる？
lineas.es: I'm coming! Shall we eat something?

lineas.jp: うん。 カゲも 来[く]る。
lineas.es: Yeah. Kage's coming too.

lineas.jp: ……カゲも？
lineas.es: …Kage too?

lineas.jp: コタローも 来[く]る。
lineas.es: And Kotarō's coming too.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 早[はや]く 行[い]く！
lineas.es: Then I'm coming early!

bloques.md:
Nyan has his reasons for arriving early: with Kotarō at the party, the food won't last.

And look closely at one detail: Tama asks 来[く]る？ (are you coming?), and Nyan answers 行[い]く, which literally means «I'll go». In Japanese, 来[く]る means moving **towards the speaker**, and 行[い]く means moving **away from the speaker**. Nyan is heading to Tama's house, away from where he is, so from his point of view he «goes». English says «I'm coming!» here, because it takes the listener's point of view, but Japanese sticks to the speaker's: 行[い]く.

This is a real trap for English speakers: answering 来[く]る！ to mean «I'm coming!» sounds as if you expect Tama to come to you. Whenever you're the one moving towards someone else, it's 行[い]く. And one more thing from the first line: うち means «home», and also «my home, my family». うちに 来[く]る is «come to my place». The に that marks the destination has its own lesson, coming next: «に: destination, time, where something is».

ejercicios.pregunta: Which family does 飲[の]む (to drink) belong to?
ejercicios.explica: It doesn't end in る, so it's a う-verb, no exceptions possible. That's why its stem turns む into み: 飲[の]みます.

ejercicios.pregunta: What about 食[た]べる (to eat)?
ejercicios.explica: It ends in る with an e before it (taberu): it's a る-verb, one of those that simply drop their る: 食[た]べます.

ejercicios.pregunta: What about 分[わ]かる (to understand)?
ejercicios.explica: It ends in る, but the vowel before it is a (wakaru). With a, u or o before る, it's always a う-verb: 分[わ]かります.

ejercicios.pregunta: What about 帰[かえ]る (to go home)?
opciones: う-verb, though it hides it well
ejercicios.explica: It ends in -eru and looks like a る-verb, but it's one of the exceptions: it's a う-verb. That's why its ます form is 帰[かえ]ります, with り.

ejercicios.pregunta: What about する (to do)?
ejercicios.explica: する is one of the two irregulars, along with 来[く]る. It conjugates its own way (します, しない), and so do all the verbs built on it, like 勉強[べんきょう]する.
見[み]る (miru) is a る-verb: drop the る and attach ます. 見[み]ます.
It doesn't end in る: a う-verb. The last syllable moves up to the i step: つ → ち. 待[ま]ちます.
The most famous exception: it looks like a る-verb but it's a う-verb, so the る doesn't disappear but turns into り. 帰[かえ]ります.
Another exception: hairu ends in -iru, but it's a う-verb. The る becomes り: 入[はい]ります.
Noun plus する: only する conjugates, becoming します. 勉強[べんきょう]します.

ejercicios.pregunta: 着[き]る (to put on clothes) and 切[き]る (to cut) sound the same. What's the ます form of 切[き]る?
ejercicios.explica: 切[き]る is a う-verb (one of the exceptions), so its る becomes り: 切[き]ります. 着[き]る, on the other hand, is an ordinary る-verb: 着[き]ます. Only the kanji and the ます form tell them apart.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama asks you 「 来[く]る？」 (are you coming?). How do you answer «I'm coming!»?
ejercicios.explica: 来[く]る is moving towards the speaker; 行[い]く is moving away. You're heading to where Tama is, away from yourself, so from your point of view you «go»: 行[い]く. English says «I'm coming», but Japanese keeps the speaker's point of view.

ejercicios.es: Nyan sleeps a lot.
ejercicios.explica: Topic with は, the adverb, and the verb at the end, in the dictionary form because this is plain speech.

ejercicios.es: Kage goes running every morning.
ejercicios.explica: The verb closes the sentence. 走[はし]る, by the way, is another of the exceptions: its ます form is 走[はし]ります.

lecciones.titulo: Particles with verbs: を, に, へ, で, から and まで
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to say who does what, where, when, with what, and from where to where, and say that something or someone is somewhere with いる and ある. With this, you can build real sentences.

secciones.titulo: Labels around the verb

bloques.md:
You already know that the verb closes the sentence and that particles go **after** each word, like labels saying what role it plays. With は, も and が you marked what you're talking about and who's who. Now for the rest of the cast: **what** gets eaten, **where** you're going, **where** something happens, **with what** it's done, **from when** and **up to where**.

Look at this sentence and how each piece wears its label:

items.jp: ニャンは 日曜日[にちようび]に 公園[こうえん]で おにぎりを 食[た]べます。
items.es: Nyan eats onigiri in the park on Sundays.
items.nota: ニャンは: who we're talking about. 日曜日[にちようび]に: when. 公園[こうえん]で: where it happens. おにぎりを: what he eats. 食[た]べます: the action, at the end.

bloques.md: Since each piece carries its label, you can **shuffle the chunks** without losing the meaning: 公園[こうえん]で 日曜日[にちようび]に… is perfectly understandable too. The only fixed point is the verb at the end. Still, there's an order that sounds most natural and that you should stick to at first: **topic, when, where, what, verb**.

secciones.titulo: を: what receives the action

bloques.md: を marks **the direct object**: the thing the action lands on. What you eat, what you drink, what you watch, what you buy. Remember it's pronounced «o», even though it's written を.

items.jp: お 茶[ちゃ]を 飲[の]みます。
items.es: I drink tea.

items.jp: タマは 本[ほん]を 読[よ]みます。
items.es: Tama reads a book.

items.jp: テレビを 見[み]る。
items.es: I watch TV.

items.jp: ポンさんの 店[みせ]で パンを 買[か]います。
items.es: I buy bread at Pon's shop.
items.nota: ポンさんの 店[みせ] is «Pon's shop»: の works like English «'s», and it has its own lesson, «の: possession and description».

bloques.md: を has a second use that surprises people at first: with verbs of movement it marks **the space you move through** or **the place you leave**. The street isn't «receiving» the action; you're crossing it from one side to the other:

items.jp: 道[みち]を 渡[わた]ります。
items.es: I cross the street.

items.jp: 公園[こうえん]を 散歩[さんぽ]します。
items.es: I take a walk through the park.
items.nota: Going across it, from end to end.

items.jp: 七時[しちじ]に 家[いえ]を 出[で]ます。
items.es: I leave home at seven.
items.nota: を marks the place you leave behind.

bloques.md: Not everything that's a direct object in English takes を in Japanese. With some verbs and adjectives, the thing you understand or like takes が, because Japanese treats them more as states than as actions: 日本語[にほんご]が 分[わ]かります (I understand Japanese). You'll see this in detail with adjectives, in «Liking and being good at: が with adjectives». So don't slap を on everything that follows a verb in English.

secciones.titulo: に and へ: the exact point and the direction

bloques.md: に is the hardest-working particle in Japanese, but all its uses share something: **it pins down a specific point**, like a drawing pin on a map or a calendar. Here are the main ones.

The point you arrive at.
学校[がっこう]に 行[い]きます。 → I go to school.
うちに 帰[かえ]る。 → I go home.
お 風呂[ふろ]に 入[はい]ります。 → I get into the bath (I have a bath).

The point on the clock or calendar.
七時[しちじ]に 起[お]きます。 → I get up at seven.
冬[ふゆ]に 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]きます。 → In winter I go to Hokkaido.
日曜日[にちようび](に) 映画[えいが]を 見[み]ます。 → On Sunday I watch a film. (With days of the week, に is optional.)

bloques.titulo: 3. Where something is: the place of existence
bloques.md:
The point where something or someone **is**. It goes with the verbs of existence いる and ある, which you'll meet later in this lesson.
タマは 部屋[へや]に います。 → Tama is in her room.

The person the action is aimed at.
タマに 電話[でんわ]します。 → I call Tama.
先生[せんせい]に 聞[き]きます。 → I ask the teacher.

に only goes with moments you can pin on a calendar: a time, a day of the week, a month, a season. It does **not** go with words calculated from today, like 今日[きょう] (today), 明日[あした] (tomorrow), 昨日[きのう] (yesterday), 毎日[まいにち] (every day) or 今[いま] (now). Why? Because those words already say when on their own, relative to the moment you're speaking, so they don't need a pin. English works the same way: «at seven», «on Sunday», but never «on tomorrow». 明日[あした]に 行[い]きます sounds just as odd.

And **へ** is the particle of **direction**: «towards». As a particle it's pronounced «e». With verbs of going, coming and returning, へ and に are almost interchangeable: 学校[がっこう]へ 行[い]きます and 学校[がっこう]に 行[い]きます mean the same thing. The difference is a nuance: に focuses on the **point of arrival**, and へ on **the way there**, the direction you're heading in.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]へ 行[い]きます。
items.es: I'm off to Hokkaido. (I'm heading that way.)

items.jp: タマへ
items.es: To Tama
items.nota: How you head a card or label a present: «towards Tama». Here へ can't be swapped for に.

bloques.md: へ is only for movement. You can't use it for a time, as in 七時[しちじ]へ ✗; or for where something is, as in 部屋[へや]へ いる ✗; or for the person you're phoning. Why? Because へ is a heading, and neither a time nor «being somewhere» has a heading. When in doubt, use に: it works for the destination and everything else.

secciones.titulo: で: where it happens and with what

bloques.md: で has two main jobs. The first: it marks **the place where an action happens**, the stage on which something takes place.

items.jp: 公園[こうえん]で 遊[あそ]びます。
items.es: I play in the park.

items.jp: 図書館[としょかん]で 勉強[べんきょう]します。
items.es: I study at the library.

items.jp: ニャンは 家[いえ]で 寝[ね]る。
items.es: Nyan sleeps at home.

bloques.md: The second: it marks **the means or tool**, what you do something with. English uses «with», «by» or «in» depending on the case; Japanese always uses で:

items.jp: 箸[はし]で 食[た]べます。
items.es: I eat with chopsticks.

items.jp: バスで 行[い]きます。
items.es: I go by bus.

items.jp: 日本語[にほんご]で 話[はな]します。
items.es: I speak in Japanese.

items.jp: 手[て]で 食[た]べる。
items.es: You eat it with your hands.
items.nota: That's how you eat onigiri, for example.

bloques.titulo: に or で: the great «in/at» dilemma
bloques.md:
English uses «in» or «at» for both: «I'm in the park», «I play in the park». Japanese uses two different particles, and the key is **the verb**:
• If the verb says something **is** somewhere (いる, ある, 住[す]む…), the place takes **に**.
• If the verb is **an action happening** there (eating, playing, studying, working…), the place takes **で**.

公園[こうえん]に いる → is in the park.
公園[こうえん]で 遊[あそ]ぶ → plays in the park.

items.jp: 札幌[さっぽろ]に 住[す]んでいます。
items.es: I live in Sapporo.
items.nota: 住[す]む (to live somewhere) is a verb of being, so it takes に. The form 住[す]んでいます comes up in «〜ている: ongoing action or resulting state».

items.jp: 札幌[さっぽろ]で 働[はたら]きます。
items.es: I work in Sapporo.
items.nota: Working is an action that happens there: で.

bloques.md: The two mirror-image mistakes are 公園[こうえん]で いる and 公園[こうえん]に 遊[あそ]ぶ. If you catch yourself, ask: is the verb about being or about doing? Being, に; doing, で. Another way to see it: に is a pin (a point where something stays) and で is a stage (a place where things happen).

secciones.titulo: から and まで: from and until

bloques.md: These two are easy: **から** is «from» and **まで** is «until» or «as far as». They work for time and for space alike, and they often go together:

items.jp: 九時[くじ]から 五時[ごじ]まで 勉強[べんきょう]します。
items.es: I study from nine to five.

items.jp: 家[いえ]から 学校[がっこう]まで 歩[ある]きます。
items.es: I walk from home to school.

items.jp: 札幌[さっぽろ]から 小樽[おたる]まで 電車[でんしゃ]で 行[い]きます。
items.es: I go by train from Sapporo to Otaru.
items.nota: A classic day trip from Sapporo: Otaru is on the coast, with its canal and old warehouses.

items.jp: タマから 手紙[てがみ]が 来[き]ました。
items.es: I got a letter from Tama.
items.nota: から also marks who something comes from.

bloques.md: Notice that まで marks the end of the journey but doesn't say you «arrive» the way に does: 学校[がっこう]まで 歩[ある]く is «walk as far as the school», with the focus on the whole route. And から has a second, very common meaning, «because», when it comes after a whole sentence. Don't mix them up: that から has its own lesson, «から and ので: because».

You don't have to use them as a pair. 九時[くじ]から 勉強[べんきょう]します (I study from nine) and 駅[えき]まで 歩[ある]きます (I walk to the station) are complete sentences. What you mustn't do is swap まで for に when you mean «until»: 五時[ごじ]に 勉強[べんきょう]します means «I study at five», not «until five».

secciones.titulo: いる and ある: there is, and being somewhere

bloques.md:
To say that **there is** something, or that something **is** somewhere, Japanese has two verbs, and choosing between them depends on something English never asks: whether the thing that exists **is alive and moves by itself**.
• **いる**: people and animals. Tama, a cat, a fish, a bird, Fukuro-sensei.
• **ある**: things, plants, and also events. A cake, a tree, a party, an exam.

いる is a る-verb (います); ある is a う-verb (あります).

**There's an X somewhere** (introducing something new): 〔place〕に 〔X〕が いる / ある
公園[こうえん]に 猫[ねこ]が います。 → There's a cat in the park.

**X is somewhere** (you already know what you're talking about): 〔X〕は 〔place〕に いる / ある
タマは 部屋[へや]に います。 → Tama is in her room.

See the difference? With が, the thing that exists is the **new information**: «there's a cat!». With は, the thing is already known, and the new part is **where it is**. It's the same logic as in the lesson on は and が: が points, は announces.

items.jp: 冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に ケーキが あります。
items.es: There's cake in the fridge.
items.nota: Nyan's favourite sentence in the world.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]は 教室[きょうしつ]に います。
items.es: The teacher is in the classroom.

items.jp: 庭[にわ]に 木[き]が あります。
items.es: There's a tree in the garden.
items.nota: Alive, yes, but a tree doesn't walk about: ある.

items.jp: 明日[あした]、 テストが あります。
items.es: There's a test tomorrow.
items.nota: Events (exams, parties, meetings) also «exist» with ある.

items.jp: 時間[じかん]が ありません。
items.es: I don't have time.
items.nota: A false friend: English «have» is often «there is» in Japanese. Literally, «there's no time».

items.jp: 誰[だれ]も いません。
items.es: There's nobody here.

bloques.md: The polite negatives are **いません** and **ありません**. You'll see the plain ones in the next lesson, where a surprise awaits: the plain negative of ある isn't «あらない» but simply **ない**. It's one of those isolated quirks we warned you about in the lesson on verbs.

The line between いる and ある is «does it move on its own?», not «is it alive?». That's why a tree or a flower takes ある, while a fish or an insect takes いる. And don't confuse these verbs with だ: 猫[ねこ]だ is «it's a cat» (what it is); 猫[ねこ]が いる is «there's a cat» (that it exists, that it's there).

secciones.titulo: When the place is the topic: には, では, にも

bloques.md: You know that は and も mark the topic. So what happens if the topic is a place or time that already carries に or で? They **stack**: には, では, にも, でも. The place particle stays, because it says what role the place plays, and は or も is added after it to make it the topic, or to add «too».

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]には 熊[くま]が います。
items.es: In Hokkaido there are bears.
items.nota: には: «speaking of Hokkaido, there are…». There's a hint of contrast: elsewhere, maybe not.

items.jp: 日本[にほん]では 車[くるま]は 左[ひだり]を 走[はし]ります。
items.es: In Japan, cars drive on the left.
items.nota: では: «as for what happens in Japan…».

items.jp: 小樽[おたる]にも 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]ります。
items.es: It snows in Otaru too.
items.nota: にも: «in Otaru as well».

items.jp: 家[いえ]でも 勉強[べんきょう]します。
items.es: I study at home too.

bloques.titulo: When do they stack, and when do they replace?
bloques.md:
• が and を **disappear** when は or も arrives: 猫[ねこ]が → 猫[ねこ]は; ケーキを → ケーキは, ケーキも.
• に, で, へ, から and まで **stay**, with は or も after them: には, では, へは, からも…

The reason: the role of が and を can be worked out from the verb (if someone eats something, it's obvious what got eaten), so nothing is lost by dropping them. に and で, on the other hand, carry information the verb doesn't give (was it there, or did it happen there?), and dropping them would lose it.
To finish, a scene at Pon's shop. Nyan is a customer, so they both speak politely:

lineas.jp: ポンさん、 どら 焼[や]きは ありますか。
lineas.es: Pon, do you have any dorayaki?

lineas.jp: すみません、 今日[きょう]は ありません。
lineas.es: Sorry, not today.

lineas.jp: え…… どこに ありますか。
lineas.es: Oh… Where can I find some?

lineas.jp: 駅前[えきまえ]に パン 屋[や]が あります。
lineas.es: There's a bakery in front of the station.

lineas.jp: 駅前[えきまえ]まで 歩[ある]きますか。
lineas.es: Do I walk to the station?

lineas.jp: バスで 十分[じゅっぷん]です。
lineas.es: It's ten minutes by bus.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 バスで 行[い]きます！
lineas.es: Then I'll go by bus!

lineas.jp: あ、 でも 今日[きょう]は 日曜日[にちようび]です。 パン 屋[や]は 休[やす]みです。
lineas.es: Ah, but today's Sunday. The bakery's closed on Sundays.

bloques.md: Go over the particles in the dialogue: どこに and 駅前[えきまえ]に, with ある, mark where things are; まで marks how far you go; バスで, the means; and 今日[きょう]は, a time turned into the topic («today, specifically…»). With just these few labels, you can already describe almost anything that happens around you.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I drink tea.»
ejercicios.jp: お 茶[ちゃ]＿ 飲[の]みます。
ejercicios.explica: The tea is what receives the action of drinking: direct object, を.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I go to school.»
ejercicios.jp: 学校[がっこう]＿ 行[い]きます。
ejercicios.explica: に marks the destination, the point you arrive at. (へ would also work, focusing on the direction.) で would be the place where an action happens, but here the school is where you're going.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I get up at seven.»
ejercicios.jp: 七時[しちじ]＿ 起[お]きます。
ejercicios.explica: A clock time is an exact point: に, the pin for time.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I'm going to Sapporo tomorrow.» What goes after 明日[あした]?
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした]＿ 札幌[さっぽろ]に 行[い]きます。
ejercicios.explica: 明日[あした] is calculated from today, so it already says when by itself and takes no に. The same goes for 今日[きょう], 昨日[きのう] and 毎日[まいにち], just as English never says «on tomorrow».

ejercicios.pregunta: «I play in the park.»
ejercicios.jp: 公園[こうえん]＿ 遊[あそ]びます。
ejercicios.explica: Playing is an action that happens in the park: で, the stage. に would be for saying something or someone is there.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Tama is in her room.»
ejercicios.jp: タマは 部屋[へや]＿ います。
ejercicios.explica: With いる (to be, to exist), the place takes に: it's the point where someone is, not a stage where an action happens.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I eat with chopsticks.»
ejercicios.jp: 箸[はし]＿ 食[た]べます。
ejercicios.explica: で marks the means or tool: what you do something with. With を you'd be eating the chopsticks.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I cross the street.»
ejercicios.jp: 道[みち]＿ 渡[わた]ります。
ejercicios.explica: With verbs of movement, を marks the space you pass through from one side to the other. Crossing the street means going across it.

ejercicios.pregunta: «There's cake in the fridge.»
ejercicios.jp: 冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に ケーキが ＿。
ejercicios.explica: Cake is a thing that doesn't move by itself: ある. いる is for people and animals. And です would mean «is», not «there is».

ejercicios.pregunta: «In Hokkaido there are bears.» (Hokkaido as the topic)
ejercicios.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]＿ 熊[くま]が います。
ejercicios.explica: With いる, the place takes に, and to make it the topic you add は: には. では would be for the place of an action, and をは doesn't exist: when は arrives, を disappears.
ある is a う-verb: stem あり, followed by ません. ありません: «there isn't». In plain speech, as you'll see next lesson, it's simply ない.
いる is a る-verb: drop る and add ませんでした. いませんでした: «wasn't there», «there was nobody».

ejercicios.es: Nyan eats onigiri in the park.
ejercicios.explica: Topic, where it happens (で), what (を), and the verb at the end. The middle chunks could swap places, but the verb never moves.

ejercicios.es: I go by train from Sapporo to Otaru.
ejercicios.explica: から (from), まで (to) and で for the means of transport. Each chunk wears its label, and the verb comes last.

lecciones.titulo: Saying no: the ない form
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to make any verb negative in plain speech: 食[た]べない, 行[い]かない, しない… and even use it to invite someone, one of the most Japanese tricks there is.

secciones.titulo: The «no» you use with friends

bloques.md: With ます you can already say no politely: 食[た]べません, «I don't eat». But with Tama, with Kage or with your family, ません sounds distant and stiff. Among friends you use the **plain negative**, which ends in **ない**:

items.jp: 食[た]べない。
items.es: I don't eat it. / I won't eat it.

items.jp: 行[い]かない。
items.es: I'm not going.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 勉強[べんきょう]しない。
items.es: I'm not studying today.
items.nota: Nyan's words, almost every day.

bloques.md:
Here's a detail you'll find useful very soon: **ない behaves like an い-adjective**. In fact, ない also exists as a word on its own, meaning «there isn't, non-existent». So when you later want to put the negative into the past, you'll do what you do with adjectives: い becomes かった, 食[た]べない → 食[た]べなかった. You'll see it in the lesson «Negative past».

Now, how it's formed. This is where the lesson on the two verb families starts to pay off.

secciones.titulo: る-verbs: off with the る

bloques.md: With る-verbs there's no mystery: just as with ます, **drop the る and add ない**. The stem is the same one you already know.

filas: 起[お]きる to get up

items.jp: カゲは 野菜[やさい]を 見[み]ない。
items.es: Kage won't even look at vegetables.

items.jp: 日曜日[にちようび]は 早[はや]く 起[お]きない。
items.es: I don't get up early on Sundays.

items.jp: 教室[きょうしつ]に 誰[だれ]も いない。
items.es: There's nobody in the classroom.

secciones.titulo: う-verbs: down to the a step

bloques.md:
Remember the five steps of う-verbs? For ます, the last syllable moved up to the i step: 飲[の]む → 飲[の]みます. For the negative it **moves down to the a step**, and ない follows:
飲[の]む (nomu) → 飲[の]ま (noma) → 飲[の]まない.

filas: 帰[かえ]る to go home

bloques.md: Look at the つ row: the a step of つ is た, so 待[ま]つ becomes 待[ま]たない. And in う-verbs ending in る, like 帰[かえ]る, 入[はい]る or 分[わ]かる, the る **doesn't disappear**: it drops to ら. That's exactly the difference from る-verbs, and why knowing each verb's family matters so much. 帰[かえ]る → 帰[かえ]らない; 変[か]える (to change, a る-verb) → 変[か]えない.

bloques.titulo: The exception: う turns into わ
bloques.md:
Verbs ending in う don't go to あ, but to **わ**:
買[か]う → 買[か]わない (I don't buy)
言[い]う → 言[い]わない (I don't say)
会[あ]う → 会[あ]わない (I don't meet someone)

Why? Because centuries ago these verbs ended in another consonant, something like an f or a w, which gradually vanished from the dictionary form. In the negative, though, it survived as わ. Besides, 買[か]あない would be a stumble to pronounce, with two a's colliding.

items.jp: コーヒーは 飲[の]まない。
items.es: Coffee, I don't drink.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 帰[かえ]らない。
items.es: I'm not going home today.

items.jp: ニャンは 泳[およ]がない。
items.es: Nyan doesn't swim.
items.nota: He's a cat: water is best admired from a distance.

items.jp: それは 買[か]わない。
items.es: I'm not buying that.

items.jp: カゲは 何[なに]も 言[い]わない。
items.es: Kage doesn't say anything.
items.nota: 何[なに]も with a negative: «nothing», as in the lesson on questions.

bloques.md: The most typical mistake is treating a う-verb ending in る as if it were a る-verb: 帰[かえ]ない ✗, 入[はい]ない ✗, 走[はし]ない ✗. They sound almost right, which is why they slip out. The cure is the same as in the last lesson: if you know it's 帰[かえ]ります (with り), you know it's a う-verb, and that its negative is 帰[かえ]らない (with ら).

secciones.titulo: The odd ones: する, 来る and ある

bloques.md: Three verbs break the pattern, and all three are among the most used, so you'll master them quickly:

filas: Irregular: its stem is し, and ない attaches to that.
Irregular: the kanji changes its reading, く → こ.
There's no «あらない»: its negative is just ない.

bloques.md:
The ある one makes sense. We said that ない is also a word on its own meaning «there isn't». So to say something doesn't exist, Japanese keeps it simple: instead of conjugating ある, it uses ない directly. 時間[じかん]が ある (there's time) → 時間[じかん]が ない (there's no time).

And every verb built with する follows する: 勉強[べんきょう]する → 勉強[べんきょう]しない, 電話[でんわ]する → 電話[でんわ]しない.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 宿題[しゅくだい]を しない。
items.es: I'm not doing my homework today.

items.jp: タマは 明日[あした] 来[こ]ない。
items.es: Tama isn't coming tomorrow.

items.jp: 冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に ケーキが ない！
items.es: There's no cake in the fridge!
items.nota: A tragedy for Nyan. And you know who the suspect is.

items.jp: お 金[かね]が ない。
items.es: I don't have any money.
items.nota: Literally, «there's no money»: English «have» is often ある in Japanese.

bloques.md: Don't confuse 来[こ]ない (doesn't come) with 来[く]ない, which doesn't exist. The kanji 来 is the same, but in the negative it's read こ. Say it aloud as くない and a Japanese listener will be puzzled, because くない sounds like the end of a negative adjective, as in 高[たか]くない. Always check the furigana on 来.

secciones.titulo: All together, and a detail with は

bloques.md: With this lesson you now have three forms of every verb: the dictionary form, the polite form with ます, and the plain negative with ない. Look at them side by side and you'll see the logic of the two families repeat every time: る-verbs keep their stem still, and う-verbs change step.

Does that ない ring a bell? It's the same one you saw in じゃない, the negative of だ. じゃない comes from では + ない: the Japanese «not» is always this same piece, attached to whatever needs it. That's why, from here on, every plain negative conjugates the same way.

And a detail of usage you'll notice as soon as you listen to real Japanese. Compare these two sentences:

items.jp: コーヒーを 飲[の]む。
items.es: I drink coffee.

items.jp: コーヒーは 飲[の]まない。
items.es: Coffee, I don't drink.
items.nota: When negating, を usually switches to は.

bloques.md: In negative sentences, the thing you're negating is usually marked with **は** instead of を. Why? Because negating something is nearly always **contrasting** it with something else: «not coffee (but tea, yes)». And contrast, as you saw in the lesson on は and が, is は's territory. It isn't compulsory, and コーヒーを 飲[の]まない is correct too, but with は it sounds more natural and hints at «not this, something else though».

For the same reason, when someone offers you something you don't want, 野菜[やさい]は 食[た]べない (vegetables, I don't eat) sounds more natural than with を, because you're setting the vegetables apart from the rest of the food. Kotarō, who eats everything else, says it a lot.

secciones.titulo: ない or ません? Plus a trick for inviting

bloques.md:
The choice is the same as with だ and です: **ない with people you're close to, ません with people you should treat respectfully**. Say 分[わ]からない to Fukuro-sensei and it sounds like a teenager with folded arms; the polite answer is 分[わ]かりません.

While we're here, a useful nuance: both 分[わ]からない and 知[し]らない translate as «I don't know», but they don't sound the same. 分[わ]からない is «I don't know, I'm not sure»: it admits something is missing. 知[し]らない is «I don't have that information», and said flatly it can sound like «no idea, and I don't care». So to say you don't know something without sounding curt, 分[わ]からない is usually the better choice.

items.jp: 分[わ]からない。
items.es: I don't know. (to a friend)

items.jp: 分[わ]かりません。
items.es: I don't know. (to the teacher)

items.jp: 知[し]らない！
items.es: How should I know!
items.nota: Said crossly or in a hurry, that's exactly how it sounds.

bloques.md: And now the promised trick. In Japanese, **a negative question is a way of inviting**. Instead of «shall we go to the park?», you say «won't we go to the park?». It sounds gentler, because it leaves the other person room to say no without awkwardness. In plain speech, the negative with rising intonation is enough:

items.jp: 公園[こうえん]に 行[い]かない？
items.es: Want to go to the park? / Shall we go to the park?
items.nota: Not «aren't you going to the park?», but an invitation.

items.jp: 一緒[いっしょ]に 食[た]べない？
items.es: Shall we eat together?

bloques.md: How do you tell an invitation from a real question? By context and intonation. If Tama sees you with your backpack at the park gate and says 行[い]かない？, she's inviting you. If you've just said you're staying home and she says 行[い]かないの？, with の, she's asking «so you're not going?». In polite speech, the invitation is 行[い]きませんか, which you'll see again in the lesson «Volitional: let's…».

lineas.jp: ニャン、 公園[こうえん]に 行[い]かない？
lineas.es: Nyan, want to go to the park?

lineas.jp: 行[い]かない。 寒[さむ]い。
lineas.es: No. It's cold.

lineas.jp: カゲも 来[く]る。
lineas.es: Kage's coming too.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 なおさら 行[い]かない。
lineas.es: Then all the more reason not to go.

lineas.jp: 焼[や]き 芋[いも]も ある。
lineas.es: There'll be roasted sweet potatoes too.

lineas.jp: ……うん、 行[い]く。
lineas.es: …Fine, I'm going.

bloques.md: Notice that Tama's first line and Nyan's first line use the same verb, 行[い]かない, and mean different things: with rising intonation it's an invitation, with falling intonation it's a refusal. And notice who wins the argument: the 焼[や]き 芋[いも], roasted sweet potatoes sold in autumn and winter from stalls and little vans on Japanese streets.

ejercicios.pregunta: What's the plain negative of 見[み]る (to see)?
ejercicios.explica: 見[み]る is a る-verb: drop the る and add ない. 見[み]らない would treat it as a う-verb, which it isn't.
る-verb: off with the る, and ない after it. 食[た]べない.
う-verb: the last syllable drops to the a step, む → ま, then ない. 飲[の]まない.
The a step of つ is た: 待[ま]つ → 待[ま]たない.
Verbs in う don't go to あ but to わ: 買[か]わない. It's the trace of an old consonant that survives only in this form.

ejercicios.pregunta: What about the plain negative of 入[はい]る (to enter)?
ejercicios.explica: 入[はい]る looks like a る-verb, but it's one of the exceptions: it's a う-verb. Its る drops to ら: 入[はい]らない. The giveaway is its ます form: 入[はい]ります.
帰[かえ]る is a う-verb in disguise: the る doesn't disappear, it drops to ら. 帰[かえ]らない.
する is irregular: stem し, then ない. しない. Likewise 勉強[べんきょう]する → 勉強[べんきょう]しない.
来[く]る is irregular: in the negative the kanji is read こ. 来[こ]ない, never «くない».
The negative of ある is simply ない, which already means «there isn't». «あらない» doesn't exist.

ejercicios.pregunta: You want to invite Tama to the festival. What do you say?
opciones: お 祭[まつ]り、 行[い]かない？
お 祭[まつ]り、 行[い]きません。
お 祭[まつ]り、 行[い]かない。
ejercicios.explica: A negative question with rising intonation is a gentle invitation: «shall we go to the festival?». 行[い]きません。 is a polite refusal, and 行[い]かない。 without the question means «I'm not going».

ejercicios.pregunta: Fukuro-sensei asks you something and you don't know the answer. What do you say?
ejercicios.explica: With your teacher, ません. Besides, 分[わ]かる admits something is missing; bare, plain 知[し]らない can sound like «no idea, and I don't care».

ejercicios.es: Tama isn't coming tomorrow.
ejercicios.explica: Topic, when, and the negative verb at the end. Remember that in the negative the kanji of 来[く]る is read こ: 来[こ]ない.

ejercicios.es: There's no class today.
ejercicios.explica: With ある, the thing that exists takes が; and in the negative, ある simply becomes ない.

lecciones.titulo: Adjectives: い and な
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to describe things and people (a tall mountain, a quiet park), conjugate any adjective in the present, past and negative, and say what you like and what you're good at.

secciones.titulo: Two kinds of adjectives

bloques.md:
We gave you a preview in the lesson on politeness: Japanese has **two kinds of adjectives**, and each works in its own way.
• **い-adjectives**: they end in い and **conjugate by themselves**, almost like verbs. 高[たか]い (tall, expensive), 安[やす]い (cheap), 寒[さむ]い (cold), おいしい (tasty), 楽[たの]しい (fun), 眠[ねむ]い (sleepy).
• **な-adjectives**: they behave **like nouns**, leaning on だ and です. 静[しず]か (quiet), 元気[げんき] (lively, well), 有名[ゆうめい] (famous), 便利[べんり] (handy), きれい (pretty, clean), 好[す]き (liked).

They're called «な-adjectives» because of the な that pops up in front of a noun, as you'll see in a moment. And why two kinds? い-adjectives are native Japanese words with conjugation built in. Many な-adjectives, on the other hand, are words that came from Chinese or other languages, like 有名[ゆうめい], 便利[べんり] or ハンサム, and Japanese fitted them in by treating them as nouns.

On word order, good news: just as in English, **adjectives always go before the noun**: «tall mountain», 高[たか]い 山[やま]. And as usual, adjectives don't change for number: 高[たか]い 山[やま] works for one tall mountain or ten.

secciones.titulo: In front of a noun

bloques.md:
• **い-adjective**: as it is, right before the noun.
高[たか]い 山[やま] → a tall mountain
• **な-adjective**: with な between the two.
静[しず]かな 公園[こうえん] → a quiet park

items.jp: おいしい ケーキ
items.es: a tasty cake

items.jp: 寒[さむ]い 朝[あさ]
items.es: a cold morning

items.jp: 大[おお]きい 雪[ゆき]だるま
items.es: a big snowman
items.nota: There are giant ones at the Sapporo Snow Festival in February.

items.jp: 元気[げんき]な 猫[ねこ]
items.es: an energetic cat
items.nota: What people call Nyan when he smells food, and only then.

items.jp: きれいな 雪[ゆき]
items.es: beautiful snow

items.jp: 有名[ゆうめい]な 店[みせ]
items.es: a famous shop

bloques.md: That な is actually the shape だ takes in front of a noun. That's why な-adjectives need it and い-adjectives don't: an い-adjective carries its own «is» inside, whereas a な-adjective, like a noun, needs something to supply the «is». Think of it that way and you'll never put な after an い-adjective.

secciones.titulo: As the predicate: saying something is so

bloques.md:
When the adjective comes at the end, saying what something is like, each kind does its own thing again:
• **An い-adjective stands alone**: 山[やま]は 高[たか]い, «the mountain is tall». Nothing after it. In polite speech, add the です sticker: 高[たか]いです.
• **A な-adjective takes だ**, like a noun: 公園[こうえん]は 静[しず]かだ. The な disappears, because it only appears in front of nouns. In polite speech, です: 静[しず]かです.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]は 寒[さむ]い。
items.es: Hokkaido is cold.

items.jp: この ラーメンは おいしい！
items.es: This ramen is amazing!
items.nota: Sapporo's miso ramen is famous all over Japan.

items.jp: ニャンは 今日[きょう]も 眠[ねむ]い。
items.es: Nyan is sleepy today too.

items.jp: タマは 元気[げんき]だ。
items.es: Tama is full of energy.

items.jp: この 町[まち]は 静[しず]かです。
items.es: This town is quiet.

bloques.md: The two mirror-image mistakes: 高[たか]いだ and 静[しず]かな だ. The first is wrong because the い-adjective already includes «is» (it would be «is tall is»). The second, because な only exists in front of a noun: at the end of a sentence, a な-adjective acts like a noun and takes plain だ. English «is» + adjective maps onto a bare い-adjective in Japanese: «it's cold» is just 寒[さむ]い. Don't go looking for an «is» to add.

secciones.titulo: Conjugating い-adjectives

bloques.md: い-adjectives conjugate by changing their final い. There are only three new endings, and you've glimpsed them already: **くない** (negative), **かった** (past) and **くなかった** (past negative).

filas:
高[たか]くない
it isn't expensive

高[たか]かった
it was expensive

高[たか]くなかった
it wasn't expensive

bloques.md: There's logic to it: く is the form an adjective takes to hook onto other things, and ない is the same old «not», which itself behaves like an い-adjective. That's why the past negative is くなかった: first the «not» (くない), then the past of that «not» (なかった). And for the polite version, you know the drill: add です to the end of any of the four, 高[たか]かったです, 高[たか]くないです.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 寒[さむ]くない。
items.es: It isn't cold today.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]の 映画[えいが]は 楽[たの]しかった。
items.es: Yesterday's film was fun.
items.nota: 昨日[きのう]の 映画[えいが] is «yesterday's film»: の working like «'s» again.

items.jp: テストは 難[むずか]しくなかった。
items.es: The test wasn't hard.

items.jp: ケーキ、 おいしかった！
items.es: The cake was delicious!
items.nota: What Nyan says, always in the past tense, because cake never lasts.

bloques.md:
いい (good, fine) is the most useful adjective in the language, and it has a catch: when it conjugates, **it turns into よ**.
いい → よくない (it's not good)
いい → よかった (it was good; phew!)
いい → よくなかった (it wasn't good)

The reason is that いい is a colloquial form of an older adjective, **よい**, which is still in use. All the conjugations come from よい, not from いい. The same goes for compounds built on いい, like かっこいい (cool, good-looking): かっこよくない, かっこよかった.

いくない and いかった are among the most common beginner mistakes, precisely because they follow the rule. But いい is the exception: よくない, よかった. And よかった deserves to be learned right now as a phrase in its own right: it's the Japanese «phew!» or «that's great!», and you'll hear it constantly.

secciones.titulo: Conjugating な-adjectives

bloques.md: Nothing new here: な-adjectives **conjugate exactly like nouns**, with the four forms of だ you learned in the lesson «The state-of-being».

filas:
静[しず]かじゃない
it isn't quiet

静[しず]かだった
it was quiet

静[しず]かじゃなかった
it wasn't quiet

bloques.md:
And in polite speech, just as with nouns: 静[しず]かです, 静[しず]かじゃないです or 静[しず]かじゃありません, 静[しず]かでした…

There is, however, a trap everyone falls into: some な-adjectives **end in い** and look like い-adjectives. The two most famous are **きれい** (pretty, clean) and **嫌[きら]い** (disliked, hated). Since that い isn't an ending but part of the word, you leave it alone:

items.jp: 雪[ゆき]は きれいだ。
items.es: Snow is beautiful.

items.jp: 部屋[へや]は きれいじゃない。
items.es: The room isn't clean.
items.nota: Never «きれくない»: the い of きれい doesn't change.

items.jp: 昔[むかし]は 野菜[やさい]が 嫌[きら]いだった。
items.es: I used to hate vegetables.

bloques.md: How can you tell that きれい is a な-adjective? Write it in kanji: 綺麗[きれい]. That い is part of the reading of the second kanji, 麗[れい], not an ending. And 嫌[きら]い comes from the verb 嫌[きら]う (to hate): it's the verb's stem, not an い-adjective. The clincher is to put it in front of a noun: you say きれいな 花[はな] (a pretty flower), with な. If it takes な, it's a な-adjective.

secciones.titulo: Liking and being good at: が with adjectives

bloques.md: To say you like something, Japanese doesn't use a verb but a な-adjective: **好[す]き**. And the thing you like doesn't take を, but **が**:

〔who〕は 〔what they like〕が 好[す]きだ
ニャンは 魚[さかな]が 好[す]きだ。 → Nyan likes fish.

Why が? Because 好[す]き isn't an action Nyan performs on the fish; it's a quality of the fish from Nyan's point of view: «speaking of Nyan, fish is likeable». English puts the fish in object position («I like fish»), but older English had it the Japanese way round: «fish pleases me», with the fish as the subject. Japanese marks that subject with が, and the person with は.

Three other very common adjectives work the same way:
• **嫌[きら]い**: to dislike, to hate. It's strong, and people often prefer 好[す]きじゃない, «I don't like it», which sounds gentler.
• **上手[じょうず]**: skilful, good at. Used about other people.
• **下手[へた]**: clumsy, bad at.
And to turn it up: 大好[だいす]き (to love) and 大嫌[だいきら]い (to loathe).

items.jp: ニャンは 魚[さかな]が 大好[だいす]きだ。
items.es: Nyan loves fish.

items.jp: タマは 歌[うた]が 上手[じょうず]だ。
items.es: Tama is a great singer.
items.nota: Literally, «speaking of Tama, singing is skilful».

items.jp: カゲは 野菜[やさい]が 嫌[きら]いだ。
items.es: Kage hates vegetables.

items.jp: わたしは 料理[りょうり]が 下手[へた]です。
items.es: I'm bad at cooking.
items.nota: Nyan admits it: his thing is eating, not cooking.

items.jp: 好[す]きな 季節[きせつ]は 冬[ふゆ]です。
items.es: My favourite season is winter.
items.nota: In front of a noun, with な: 好[す]きな 季節[きせつ], «the season I like».

bloques.md: Two important cultural points. First: 上手[じょうず] about yourself sounds like bragging, because it's a compliment, and in Japan you don't compliment yourself. To say something is your strong point, the normal word is **得意[とくい]**: 料理[りょうり]が 得意[とくい]です. And if someone tells you 日本語[にほんご]が 上手[じょうず]ですね, the natural reply isn't «thank you» but playing it down: いえいえ, まだまだです (oh no, I've still got a long way to go).
