Notice the difference: 勉強[べんきょう]したけど、 だめだった (I studied, but it went badly) is a simple contrast. 勉強[べんきょう]したのに、 だめだった (I studied and everything, and it still went badly!) is a complaint.

**Plain form + のに**. Nouns and な-adjectives with **な**のに, just like in んです (because there's a の in there too).

勉強[べんきょう]したのに · 高[たか]いのに · 日曜日[にちようび]なのに · 静[しず]かなのに

items.jp: せっかく 作[つく]ったのに、 コタローが 全部[ぜんぶ] 食[た]べた！
items.es: After all the trouble I went to making it, Kotarō ate the lot!
items.nota: せっかく (after all that effort) goes hand in hand with のに.

items.jp: 日曜日[にちようび]なのに、 学校[がっこう]に 行[い]く。
items.es: It's Sunday, and I still have to go to school.

items.jp: 春[はる]なのに、 札幌[さっぽろ]は まだ 雪[ゆき]だ。
items.es: It's spring, and it's still snowing in Sapporo.

bloques.md: Don't follow のに with a plan or a request of your own («even though it's raining, let's go»). のに is for noting something that **is happening or has happened** and lets you down; not for deciding what to do. For «even if it rains, I'll go», Japanese has a different structure, 〜ても, which you'll see later on. And use it carefully with someone above you: since it's a complaint, it can sound like a reproach.

secciones.titulo: Things like… and…: たり〜たり

bloques.md: Remember や, the open list of nouns («bread, milk and that sort of thing»)? **たり** is the same thing for actions: you give a couple of examples of what you do and it's understood there's more. «On Sundays I read, have a nap… that kind of thing».

**Plain past + り** for each action, and **する** at the end (which carries the tense and politeness).

読[よ]んだ → 読[よ]んだり · 寝[ね]た → 寝[ね]たり
本[ほん]を 読[よ]んだり、 昼寝[ひるね]を したり する。 (I read, have a nap, that sort of thing)

items.jp: 休[やす]みの 日[ひ]は、 本[ほん]を 読[よ]んだり、 昼寝[ひるね]を したり します。
items.es: On my days off I read, have a nap, stuff like that.

items.jp: 祭[まつ]りで たこ焼き[たこやき]を 食[た]べたり、 金魚[きんぎょ]すくいを したり した。
items.es: At the festival we ate takoyaki, scooped goldfish and so on.

items.jp: 週末[しゅうまつ]は 掃除[そうじ]を したり する。
items.es: At weekends I do things like cleaning.
items.nota: With a single たり it means «among other things».

bloques.md: Don't forget the final する: a bare 「 読[よ]んだり、 寝[ね]たり」 is left without a verb to close the sentence, and the listener is left hanging. And don't use たり when you want to tell a sequence in order («I got up, had breakfast and went out»): that's what the て-form is for. たり doesn't say what order things happen in, only that they're examples.

secciones.titulo: All together: Nyan's Sunday

lineas.jp: ニャン、 日曜日[にちようび]は 何[なに]を した？
lineas.es: Nyan, what did you do on Sunday?

lineas.jp: 朝[あさ] 起[お]きて、 ご 飯[はん]を 食[た]べて、 また 寝[ね]た。
lineas.es: I got up, had breakfast and went back to sleep.

lineas.jp: えー、 天気[てんき]が よかったのに！
lineas.es: What? It was such a lovely day!

lineas.jp: だって、 眠[ねむ]かったし、 寒[さむ]かったし…
lineas.es: Well, I was sleepy, it was cold…

lineas.jp: わたしは カゲと 公園[こうえん]で 走[はし]ったり、 ポンさんの お 店[みせ]に 行[い]ったり したよ。
lineas.es: I went running in the park with Kage, went to Pon's shop, that kind of thing.

lineas.jp: ポンさんの お 店[みせ]？ いいなあ。 あそこの パンは 安[やす]くて おいしいから…
lineas.es: Pon's shop? Lucky you. His bread's cheap and delicious, so…

lineas.jp: 来週[らいしゅう]は 一緒[いっしょ]に 行[い]こうね。 寝[ね]ないで！
lineas.es: Let's go together next week, OK? And don't fall asleep!

bloques.md: Go back over it: Nyan chains his morning with て, 起[お]きて、 食[た]べて、 寝[ね]た; Tama complains with のに because the day looked so promising; Nyan makes excuses with two し; Tama sums up her day with たり〜たり; and Nyan gives his reason with から and leaves the sentence hanging, because the rest is obvious. At the end Tama uses two forms that are coming soon: 行[い]こう (let's go), the volitional, and 寝[ね]ないで (don't fall asleep), which you'll see in the lesson on asking for things.

ejercicios.explica: る-verb: drop る and add て, just as the past added た.
Like the past 書[か]いた, but with て: 書[か]いて.
む/ぶ/ぬ family: the past is 読[よ]んだ, so the て-form is 読[よ]んで.
The usual exception: since the past is 行[い]った, the て-form is 行[い]って.
い-adjectives change い into くて to link up with another quality.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Otaru is a quiet, pretty town.»
ejercicios.jp: 小樽[おたる]は 静[しず]か＿ きれいな 町[まち]です。
ejercicios.explica: 静[しず]か is a な-adjective: to link it uses で, the て-form of だ. くて is only for い-adjectives.

ejercicios.pregunta: «It's raining, so I'm staying in.»
ejercicios.jp: 雨[あめ]＿、 家[いえ]に いる。
ejercicios.explica: With a noun, から needs だ in front; a bare 雨[あめ]から would be «from the rain». けど would mean «but».

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan makes an excuse to the teacher: «As I have a headache, I won't come in today».
ejercicios.jp: 頭[あたま]が 痛[いた]い＿、 今日[きょう]は 休[やす]みます。
ejercicios.explica: ので gives a reason in a soft, objective way, ideal with someone above you. のに would be a complaint and し would pile up reasons.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I studied so much, and the test still went terribly!»
ejercicios.jp: たくさん 勉強[べんきょう]した＿、 テストは だめだった。
ejercicios.explica: The result goes against what you expected and annoys you: that's のに. から and ので would say you failed BECAUSE you studied.

ejercicios.pregunta: On Sundays Nyan reads, has a nap and so on.
ejercicios.jp: 本[ほん]を 読[よ]んだり、 昼寝[ひるね]を ＿。
ejercicios.explica: Each action takes たり and you need する at the end to close the sentence.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan has several reasons for loving Furano.
ejercicios.jp: ラベンダーが きれいだし、 メロンも おいしい＿、 大好[だいす]き！
ejercicios.explica: し piles up reasons one after another. けど and のに would set ideas against each other, and here they all point the same way.

ejercicios.es: I went to Tama's house and we did our homework.
ejercicios.explica: The actions go in order: first going (in the て-form) and then doing the homework, with the final verb in the past.

ejercicios.es: This cake is expensive, but it's delicious.
ejercicios.explica: けど goes after the first idea and opens the contrasting one; the order follows the ideas.

lecciones.titulo: Asking, telling and forbidding: from ください to «Freeze!»
lecciones.resumen: You'll ask for things at Pon's shop, ask the teacher to say it again, understand why your mum says 寝[ね]なさい… and learn to recognise the imperatives anime characters bark at each other, without ever using them on anyone.

secciones.titulo: Asking for a thing: ください

bloques.md:
The simplest way to ask for something is to name it, mark it with を and add **ください**: 水[みず]を ください (water, please). It's what you'll say in a shop, in a restaurant, or when someone offers you something and you want to accept.

ください comes from a respectful verb meaning «to give (to me)», so literally you're saying «give me water»: polite, but direct. If you want a certain number, put the number with its counter just before it: りんごを 三[みっ]つ ください.

items.jp: ポンさん、 おにぎりを 二[ふた]つ ください。
items.es: Pon, two onigiri, please.

items.jp: これを ください。
items.es: I'll take this one, please.
items.nota: Pointing at something in a shop: the most useful sentence of any trip.

items.jp: すみません、 お 水[みず]を ください。
items.es: Excuse me, could I have some water, please?

bloques.md: In restaurants and shops you'll also hear **お 願[ねが]いします** instead of ください: コーヒーを お 願[ねが]いします (a coffee, please). It sounds a little softer, because instead of «give me» it says «I request it of you». Both are correct and very common; お 願[ねが]いします has the advantage of working for services too (タクシーで 駅[えき]まで お 願[ねが]いします, to the station, please).

secciones.titulo: Asking someone to do something: 〜てください

bloques.md: To ask for an **action**, put the verb in the て-form and add ください: 待[ま]って ください (please wait). Literally, «give me the waiting». It's the normal way to make a request or give instructions politely: the teacher to the class, a shop assistant to a customer, you to a stranger.

**て-form + ください**

待[ま]つ → 待[ま]って ください · 見[み]る → 見[み]て ください · 書[か]く → 書[か]いて ください · する → して ください

**Among friends**: just the て-form, no ください: 待[ま]って！ (wait!), 見[み]て！ (look!). With ね it's softer: ちょっと 待[ま]ってね.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]、 もう 一度[いちど] 言[い]って ください。
items.es: Sensei, could you say that again, please?

items.jp: ここに 名前[なまえ]を 書[か]いて ください。
items.es: Please write your name here.

items.jp: タマ、 見[み]て！ 雪[ゆき]だよ！
items.es: Tama, look! It's snowing!

items.jp: ちょっと 待[ま]って、 すぐ 行[い]くから。
items.es: Hang on a sec, I'm coming.

bloques.md: Polite as it is, 〜てください is still a request that assumes the other person will comply. For instructions or in a shop it's perfect, but for asking **a favour** of someone above you («could you lend me your book?») it sounds a bit stiff, almost like a polite order. For that there are softer forms, like 〜て くれませんか or 〜て いただけませんか, which you'll see in the lesson on giving and receiving favours.

secciones.titulo: Asking someone not to: 〜ないでください

bloques.md: To ask someone **not** to do something, take the plain negative and add **で ください**. That で is the て-form of ない, so the logic is the same as before: «give me the not-doing». Among friends, just like before, drop ください and you're left with **〜ないで**.

**Plain negative + で ください**

食[た]べない → 食[た]べないで ください · 触[さわ]らない → 触[さわ]らないで ください · 行[い]かない → 行[い]かないで

You'll read it on countless signs: 写真[しゃしん]を 撮[と]らないで ください (no photos, please), 触[さわ]らないで ください (please do not touch).

items.jp: わたしの ケーキを 食[た]べないで ください。
items.es: Please don't eat my cake.
items.nota: Nyan, very seriously, to Kotarō.

items.jp: 心配[しんぱい]しないで ください。
items.es: Please don't worry.

items.jp: 行[い]かないで！
items.es: Don't go!

secciones.titulo: ちょうだい: asking at home

bloques.md:
**ちょうだい** does the same job as ください, with things and with the て-form, but it sounds **affectionate and homely**. Children use it a lot with their parents, mothers with their kids and, generally, people who are very close. It has a childish or tender touch, so it doesn't suit strangers or anyone above you at all.

それ ちょうだい (give me that) · ちょっと 見[み]せて ちょうだい (let me see, go on)

items.jp: お 母[かあ]さん、 お 菓子[かし] ちょうだい！
items.es: Mum, can I have a sweet?

items.jp: コタロー、 その パン、 半分[はんぶん] ちょうだい。
items.es: Kotarō, give us half that bread, go on.

secciones.titulo: 〜なさい: what mums and teachers say

bloques.md: **なさい** attaches to the verb stem (the same one as ます) and gives an **order**, though not a harsh one: it's the voice of someone with authority over you using it matter-of-factly. A mother to her child, a teacher to her pupils. It also appears in exam instructions: 次[つぎ]の 質問[しつもん]に 答[こた]えなさい (answer the following question).

**Verb stem + なさい** (drop ます and add なさい)

食[た]べます → 食[た]べなさい · 寝[ね]ます → 寝[ね]なさい · 勉強[べんきょう]します → 勉強[べんきょう]しなさい · 来[き]ます → 来[き]なさい

items.jp: もう 十一時[じゅういちじ]ですよ。 早[はや]く 寝[ね]なさい。
items.es: It's eleven o'clock already. Off to bed.

items.jp: ニャンさん、 ちゃんと 宿題[しゅくだい]を しなさい。
items.es: Nyan, do your homework properly.
items.nota: Fukuro-sensei, patient but leaving no room for doubt.

bloques.md: Don't use なさい with your friends or, above all, with anyone above you. なさい assumes **you're the one in charge**; saying it to the teacher would be like giving your boss an order. Among friends it would sound as if you were playing mum or teacher, and sometimes it's used exactly like that, as a joke.

secciones.titulo: The imperative: eat!, go!

bloques.md: And now for the raw, bare order, the **imperative**: no ください, no なさい, nothing to soften it. Here's how it's formed:

filas: 食[た]べる → 食[た]べろ · 見[み]る → 見[み]ろ · 起[お]きる → 起[お]きろ
行[い]く → 行[い]け · 飲[の]む → 飲[の]め · 待[ま]つ → 待[ま]て · 帰[かえ]る → 帰[かえ]れ · 買[か]う → 買[か]え

bloques.md:
Notice that う-verbs change their last vowel to **e**: く → け, む → め, つ → て, る → れ, う → え. It's the same row of the syllabary you'll meet again later in the potential form and the conditional, so hang on to it.

And **forbidding**? Even easier: dictionary form + **な**. 行[い]くな (don't go!), 食[た]べるな (don't eat!), 触[さわ]るな (don't touch!). Don't confuse this な with the な people put at the end of a sentence when thinking aloud, which you'll see in another lesson: this one is curt and said as an order, the other is soft and reflective.

items.jp: 逃[に]げろ！
items.es: Run!
items.nota: An emergency: no time for ください here.

items.jp: 待[ま]て、 ニャン！
items.es: Wait, Nyan!
items.nota: Kage chasing Nyan in a race.

items.jp: 負[ま]けて 泣[な]くなよ。
items.es: And don't cry when you lose, yeah?
items.nota: Kage showing off: a prohibition with な, plus よ to needle him.

secciones.titulo: Where you'll hear imperatives (and why you shouldn't use them)

bloques.md:
The Japanese imperative is much stronger than the English one. In English we say «pass me the salt» or «come here» and nobody bats an eyelid; in Japanese, 塩[しお]を 取[と]れ or こっちに 来[こ]い sound like a drill sergeant or the start of a fight. The reason is that Japanese politeness is all about softening requests: asking, going round the houses, leaving room. The imperative strips all that away in one go, and said to a person it sounds as if you're putting yourself above them.

So where does it show up?

- **Signs**, where brevity is needed: the Japanese stop sign says **止[と]まれ** (stop!).
- **Sport and cheering**: 走[はし]れ！ (run!), 行[い]け！ (go!). And above all **頑張[がんば]れ！** (come on!, you can do it!), the most affectionate imperative in the language: you shout it to encourage someone, and nobody takes it as an order.
- **Emergencies**: 逃[に]げろ！ (run for it!).
- **Anime, manga and video games**, especially from tough characters or in action scenes.
- **Between very close guys**, sometimes, and always with a rough tone.

Learn to recognise imperatives, but don't use them on anyone. Even if you hear them all the time in anime, in real life saying 食[た]べろ to a friend sounds as though you're bossing them about. To ask for something, go up a level: among friends, the て-form, 食[た]べて; with anyone else, 〜てください or one of the softer forms you'll see later. The one safe exception is 頑張[がんば]れ for cheering someone on.

filas: 待[ま]って ください
待[ま]たないで ください

secciones.titulo: All together: the race in the park

lineas.jp: みなさん、 ここに 並[なら]んで ください。
lineas.es: Everyone, line up here, please.

lineas.jp: ポンさん、 おにぎり ちょうだい！ お 腹[なか]が 空[す]いた…
lineas.es: Pon, can I have an onigiri? I'm starving…

lineas.jp: 走[はし]る 前[まえ]は たくさん 食[た]べないでね。
lineas.es: Don't eat too much before you run, OK?

lineas.jp: コタローくん、 早[はや]く 来[き]なさい。
lineas.es: Kotarō, come here now.

lineas.jp: ニャン、 負[ま]けて 泣[な]くなよ。
lineas.es: Nyan, don't start crying when you lose.

lineas.jp: ニャン、 頑張[がんば]れ！ 走[はし]れ！
lineas.es: Come on, Nyan! Run!

lineas.jp: 待[ま]って〜！ 置[お]いて 行[い]かないで〜！
lineas.es: Wait! Don't leave me behind!

bloques.md: Here's the whole scale: Fukuro-sensei gives an instruction with 〜てください and a teacher's order with なさい; Kotarō asks with ちょうだい, like a child with someone he trusts; Pon asks him not to with 〜ないで, softened with ね; Kage uses the blunt prohibition 〜な, because he wants to needle Nyan; Tama shouts imperatives to cheer, 頑張[がんば]れ and 走[はし]れ, which in a race are the most natural thing in the world; and Nyan pleads with the bare て-form and 〜ないで, between friends.

ejercicios.explica: て-form, 待[ま]って, plus ください. 待[ま]つ is in the う/つ/る family, which gives って.
Plain negative, 食[た]べない, plus で ください: «please don't eat».
なさい goes on the stem, the same one as ます: 寝[ね]ます → 寝[ね]なさい.
With う-verbs, the final u becomes e: く → け.
る-verb: change る to ろ.
来[く]る is irregular: its imperative is 来[こ]い, read こ.
Dictionary form + な: a flat prohibition, the kind you see on signs or hear in anger.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan didn't catch it and asks the teacher to say it again.
ejercicios.jp: 先生[せんせい]、 もう 一度[いちど] 言[い]って ＿。
ejercicios.explica: With the teacher, 〜てください. なさい is an order from someone in authority, and ちょうだい sounds homely, far too familiar.

ejercicios.pregunta: A mother sends her child to bed.
ejercicios.jp: もう 遅[おそ]いから、 早[はや]く 寝[ね]＿。
ejercicios.explica: なさい is the normal order from someone with authority over you, like a mother: firm but not harsh.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama cheers Nyan on in the race: «Come on!».
ejercicios.jp: ニャン、 ＿！
ejercicios.explica: 頑張[がんば]れ is the affectionate imperative par excellence: you shout it to cheer someone on. なさい would sound like a lecture and ないで would mean «don't try».

ejercicios.pregunta: In the museum, a sign asks people not to take photos.
ejercicios.jp: 写真[しゃしん]を 撮[と]ら＿ ください。
ejercicios.explica: To ask someone not to do something: negative + で ください. なくて is a different form that isn't used for requests, and な goes only with the dictionary form, without ください.

ejercicios.es: Please don't eat my cake.
ejercicios.explica: What you don't want eaten, with を; then the negative with で, and ください closing the request.

ejercicios.es: Please write your name here.
ejercicios.explica: The verb's て-form plus ください: the polite way to ask for an action.

lecciones.titulo: The て-form at work: ている, てある, ておく, ていく and てくる
lecciones.resumen: You'll say what's happening right now, what's already been done, what you're getting ready for the festival and how things change over time… and you'll see why «I'm married» isn't said with 結婚[けっこん]する.

secciones.titulo: 〜ている: doing it… or done

bloques.md:
You already know how to make the て-form. Now you'll see that, with a helper verb stuck on the end, it turns into a Swiss army knife. The most important helper is **いる**: て-form + いる, **〜ている**.

The core idea is simple: ている describes **a state that holds**. «Being in the situation of…». And depending on the verb, that state can be two different things:

1. **An action in progress**: 読[よ]んで いる, is reading. Reading lasts, and right now you're in the middle of it.
2. **The result of a change**: 結婚[けっこん]して いる, is married. Getting married is a moment; what lasts afterwards is the state of being married.

**て-form + いる**, and いる conjugates as usual:

読[よ]んで いる (is reading) · 読[よ]んで いない (isn't reading) · 読[よ]んで いた (was reading) · 読[よ]んで います (polite)

items.jp: タマは 本[ほん]を 読[よ]んで いる。
items.es: Tama is reading a book.

items.jp: ニャンは まだ 寝[ね]て います。
items.es: Nyan is still asleep.

items.jp: 外[そと]で 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]って いる。
items.es: It's snowing outside.

items.jp: 毎朝[まいあさ]、 公園[こうえん]を 走[はし]って いる。
items.es: I go running in the park every morning.
items.nota: It also works for ongoing habits: a routine is a state that lasts.

secciones.titulo: Verbs of change: where English leads you astray

bloques.md:
Here's the trap. Some Japanese verbs express **an instant change**, a moment when something switches from one state to another: getting married, arriving, leaving, finding out, putting clothes on… With these, ている does **not** mean «in the middle of doing it» (you can't spend years in the act of getting married), but **the state left afterwards**.

And many of those states are said in English with a simple present or «be» + adjective, so translating word for word goes wrong:

filas: 結婚[けっこん]する (get married)
結婚[けっこん]して いる

items.jp: フクロウ 先生[せんせい]は 結婚[けっこん]して いますか。
items.es: Is Fukuro-sensei married?
items.nota: 結婚[けっこん]しますか would be «is she getting married?».

items.jp: カゲを 知[し]って いる？
items.es: Do you know Kage?

items.jp: カゲは 公園[こうえん]の 近[ちか]くに 住[す]んで いる。
items.es: Kage lives near the park.

items.jp: タマは もう 来[き]て いるよ。
items.es: Tama's already here.
items.nota: She came and is still here: a resulting state.

items.jp: カゲは 黒[くろ]い マフラーを して いる。
items.es: Kage is wearing a black scarf.
items.nota: Accessories like scarves or watches usually take する: the state is «having it on».

bloques.md: The negative of 知[し]って いる is **知[し]らない**, not 「 知[し]って いない」. The reason is Japanese logic: 知[し]る is the moment of finding out, and 知[し]って いる the state of knowing. If you don't know, you never found out: there's no state you ever entered, so you use the verb's simple negative. 知[し]って いますか ―― いいえ、 知[し]りません (do you know? — No, I don't).

secciones.titulo: Everyday forms: てる and まだ〜ていない

bloques.md:
In speech, the い of ている almost always drops out: **ている → てる**, ていた → てた, ていない → てない. 何[なに] してる？ (what are you doing?), 知[し]ってる (I know), 寝[ね]てた (I was asleep). Among friends it's the norm; in an exam or in writing, use the full form.

And at last the full answer to «have you eaten yet?» when you haven't: **まだ 食[た]べて いない** (I haven't eaten yet; politely, まだ 食[た]べて いません). It makes sense: you haven't yet entered the state of «having eaten». That's why 食[た]べなかった, which reports that you didn't eat at some closed moment, doesn't work here.

items.jp: ニャン、 何[なに] してる？ ―― 寝[ね]てる…
items.es: Nyan, what are you doing? — Sleeping…

items.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]、 もう した？ ―― ううん、 まだ して ない。
items.es: Have you done your homework yet? — No, not yet.

secciones.titulo: 〜てある: someone left it done

bloques.md:
If you use **ある** instead of いる, the focus shifts: you're no longer looking at whoever acted, but **at the object, which has been left that way because someone did it on purpose**. 窓[まど]が 開[あ]けて ある: the window is open, and it's open because someone opened it deliberately (to air the room, say).

Since what matters now is the object and not who did it, the object drops を and takes **が**: it's the star of the state. And it's used with verbs where someone does something to a thing: open, write, put, prepare, buy…

**[object] が + て-form + ある**

窓[まど]を 開[あ]ける (open the window) → 窓[まど]が 開[あ]けて ある (the window is open, someone has left it that way)
名前[なまえ]を 書[か]く → 名前[なまえ]が 書[か]いて ある (the name is written)

items.jp: 黒板[こくばん]に 今日[きょう]の 宿題[しゅくだい]が 書[か]いて ある。
items.es: Today's homework is written on the blackboard.

items.jp: 飲み物[のみもの]は もう 冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に 入[い]れて ある。
items.es: The drinks are already in the fridge.

items.jp: テーブルに お 皿[さら]が 並[なら]べて あります。
items.es: The plates have been laid out on the table.

bloques.md: Don't confuse 窓[まど]が 開[あ]けて ある with 窓[まど]が 開[あ]いて いる. Both translate as «the window is open», but they tell different stories. The first uses 開[あ]ける (to open something, someone does it) and makes it clear there was a person with an intention. The second uses 開[あ]く (to open, it happens by itself) with ている, and just describes how the window is, without saying why. You'll see these verb pairs in depth in the lesson on transitive and intransitive verbs.

secciones.titulo: 〜ておく: doing it in advance, or leaving it as it is

bloques.md: **おく** means «to put, to leave». Attached to the て-form, it adds the idea of **doing something with later in mind**: getting it ready in good time, or leaving it as it is so it stays that way. It's the verb of people who plan ahead.

**て-form + おく** (conjugates like an う-verb: おいた, おかない, おきます…)

買[か]って おく (buy in advance) · 読[よ]んで おく (read it beforehand) · 開[あ]けて おく (leave it open)

**In speech**: ておく → **とく**, でおく → **どく**. 買[か]っとく, 読[よ]んどく, 開[あ]けといて (leave it open).

items.jp: お 祭[まつ]りの 前[まえ]に、 銀行[ぎんこう]で お 金[かね]を 下[お]ろして おく。
items.es: Before the festival I'll get some cash out of the bank (so I've got it ready).

items.jp: 明日[あした] テストだから、 今夜[こんや] 教科書[きょうかしょ]を 読[よ]んで おきます。
items.es: There's a test tomorrow, so I'll read the textbook tonight.

items.jp: 暑[あつ]いから、 窓[まど]を 開[あ]けといて。
items.es: It's hot, leave the window open.

items.jp: ケーキは 冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に 入[い]れて おいたよ。
items.es: I've put the cake in the fridge, just so you know.

secciones.titulo: 〜ていく and 〜てくる: over there, over here

bloques.md:
With **いく** (go) and **くる** (come) after it, the て-form gains a **direction**. In space it's very intuitive: 〜ていく is doing something and moving away (over there), and 〜てくる is doing something and coming closer (over here, towards the speaker).

- 傘[かさ]を 持[も]って いく: take the umbrella (I pick it up and go off with it).
- 傘[かさ]を 持[も]って くる: bring the umbrella (I pick it up and come with it).
- ジュースを 買[か]って くる: go and buy a juice and come back.

This gives us one of the most Japanese phrases there is: **行[い]って きます**, «I'll go and come back», what you say when you leave home. And whoever stays behind answers 行[い]って らっしゃい (go and come back).

items.jp: 雨[あめ]だから、 傘[かさ]を 持[も]って いって。
items.es: It's raining, take an umbrella.

items.jp: お 祭[まつ]りには コタローも 連[つ]れて いく。
items.es: I'm taking Kotarō to the festival too.
items.nota: With people and animals, 連[つ]れて いく / 連[つ]れて くる.

items.jp: ちょっと 飲み物[のみもの]を 買[か]って くるね。
items.es: I'm just popping out to get a drink.

bloques.md:
And now the lovely part: the same idea applies **to time**. Picture yourself standing in the present. **〜てくる** is a change coming **towards you, up to now**: something that has been happening and can now be felt. **〜ていく** is a change heading **from now into the future**: something that will keep on happening.

- 寒[さむ]く なって きた: it's got cold (the cold has been creeping up until today).
- これから 寒[さむ]く なって いく: from now on it'll get colder and colder.

That 寒[さむ]く なる means «to become cold»; you'll see it in depth in the lesson on なる and する. With verbs like 降[ふ]る, 〜てくる marks a beginning you notice: 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]って きた, it's started raining.

items.jp: 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]って きた！
items.es: It's started snowing!

items.jp: 日本語[にほんご]が 少[すこ]し 分[わ]かって きた。
items.es: I'm starting to understand a bit of Japanese.

items.jp: これからも 日本語[にほんご]を 勉強[べんきょう]して いきます。
items.es: I'll keep on studying Japanese from here on.

secciones.titulo: All together: getting ready for the festival

lineas.jp: ニャン、 何[なに] してるの？
lineas.es: Nyan, what are you doing?

lineas.jp: おにぎりを 作[つく]ってる。 お 祭[まつ]りに 持[も]って いくんだ。
lineas.es: Making onigiri. I'm taking them to the festival.

lineas.jp: えらい！ 飲み物[のみもの]は？
lineas.es: Good for you! What about drinks?

lineas.jp: もう 冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に 入[い]れて あるよ。
lineas.es: They're already in the fridge.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 わたしは 提灯[ちょうちん]を 飾[かざ]って おくね。
lineas.es: Then I'll put the lanterns up ready.

lineas.jp: おい、 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]って きたぞ。
lineas.es: Hey, it's started raining.

lineas.jp: えっ！ カゲ、 傘[かさ]、 持[も]って きた？
lineas.es: What?! Kage, did you bring an umbrella?

lineas.jp: 当然[とうぜん]だ。 俺[おれ]は いつも 持[も]って いる。
lineas.es: Obviously. I always have one.

lineas.jp: あっ、 コタロー！ もう おにぎりを 食[た]べてる！
lineas.es: Oh no, Kotarō! He's already eating the onigiri!

bloques.md: All in one afternoon: 作[つく]ってる and 食[た]べてる, actions in progress in the contracted form; 持[も]って いく, taking something along; 入[い]れて ある, drinks that someone already put in the fridge; 飾[かざ]って おく, getting the lanterns ready for later; 降[ふ]って きた, rain that's starting; 持[も]って きた, what Kage has brought; and 持[も]って いる, the state of having, which is Kage's habit.

ejercicios.explica: て-form, 読[よ]んで, plus いる: reading, in progress.
In speech, the い of ている drops out: 食[た]べてる.
て-form, 買[か]って, plus おく: buy it in advance. In speech, 買[か]っとく.
て-form, 持[も]って, plus いく: pick it up and take it away with you.
The state of knowing is 知[し]って いる, but its negative is 知[し]らない: if you never found out, you never entered that state.

ejercicios.pregunta: «My older brother is married.»
ejercicios.jp: 兄[あに]は 結婚[けっこん] ＿。
ejercicios.explica: 結婚[けっこん]する is the moment of getting married; the state that lasts afterwards is 結婚[けっこん]して いる. します would be «is getting married».

ejercicios.pregunta: «I live in Sapporo.»
ejercicios.jp: 札幌[さっぽろ]に ＿。
ejercicios.explica: 住[す]む is settling somewhere; living there is the resulting state, 住[す]んで いる.

ejercicios.pregunta: The window is open because someone opened it to air the room.
ejercicios.jp: 窓[まど]が 開[あ]けて ＿。
ejercicios.explica: With a verb like 開[あ]ける and the object with が, 〜てある says someone left it that way on purpose.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan looks out of the window: «It's started raining!».
ejercicios.jp: 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]って ＿！
ejercicios.explica: 〜てくる marks a change reaching up to now, up to you: the rain starts and you notice it.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan is leaving home. What does he say?
opciones: 行[い]って いきます
ejercicios.explica: 行[い]って きます, «I'll go and come back», is the set phrase for leaving home. The idea is that you'll be back.

ejercicios.pregunta: — Have you read the book? — Not yet.
ejercicios.jp: 本[ほん]、 読[よ]んだ？ ―― まだ 読[よ]んで ＿。
ejercicios.explica: You haven't yet entered the state of «having read it»: まだ + 〜ていない.

ejercicios.es: Tama is reading a book.
ejercicios.explica: The て-form followed by いる, which closes the sentence: an action in progress.

ejercicios.es: I've already bought the drinks (for later).
ejercicios.explica: The drinks are the topic; もう, «already»; and 買[か]って おいた, bought in advance, at the end.

lecciones.titulo: Wanting, inviting and giving advice
lecciones.resumen: You'll say what you want to do and what you want to have, ask others to do things for you, invite your friends with ましょう and give advice without sounding bossy… and find out why in Japanese you can't just say that Tama wants a cake.

secciones.titulo: 〜たい: wanting to do something

bloques.md: To say you want to **do** something, take the verb stem (the ます one) and stick **たい** on it: 食[た]べます → 食[た]べ**たい** (I want to eat). It's one of the most useful forms you'll ever learn, and it's dead easy too, because the result **behaves like an い-adjective**. Everything you learnt about い-adjectives applies as it is.

filas: 食[た]べたい (I want to eat)
食[た]べたくない (I don't want to eat)
食[た]べたかった (I wanted to eat)
食[た]べたくなかった (I didn't want to eat)

bloques.md: What you want to do can take **を**, as usual, or **が**: 水[みず]を 飲[の]みたい and 水[みず]が 飲[の]みたい are both correct. The difference is one of focus: with が, the object becomes the centre of the desire, as in 猫[ねこ]が 好[す]き; it sounds like «what I fancy is water». With longer verbs or busier sentences, を is the usual choice.

items.jp: 冬[ふゆ]に 北海道[ほっかいどう]へ 行[い]きたい。
items.es: I want to go to Hokkaido in winter.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 何[なに]も したくない…
items.es: I don't want to do anything today…
items.nota: Nyan, any given Monday.

items.jp: 子供[こども]の 時[とき]、 パン 屋[や]さんに なりたかった。
items.es: When I was little, I wanted to be a baker.

items.jp: 冷[つめ]たい ジュースが 飲[の]みたいです。
items.es: I fancy a nice cold juice.

secciones.titulo: Why you don't just say «Tama wants…»

bloques.md:
Here comes something very Japanese. **たい expresses a desire from the inside**, and in Japanese you only have direct access to what goes on inside you. Saying 「 タマは ケーキを 食[た]べたい」 sounds as if you were reading Tama's mind, as if you knew for certain what she feels. The same goes for other words of inner sensation, like 痛[いた]い (it hurts) or 嬉[うれ]しい (I'm happy).

So with someone else's wishes, Japanese describes them **from the outside**, by what can be seen or what has been said:

- **〜たがる**: «shows signs of wanting». It's the stem + たがる, which conjugates like an う-verb, and it almost always appears as 〜たがって いる: タマは ケーキを 食[た]べたがって いる (Tama's dying for some cake, you can tell).
- **〜たいと 言[い]って いる**: «says she wants to», with the quoting と you'll see in its own lesson.
- **Asking** directly: 食[た]べたい？ (do you want to eat?). You can ask the person in front of you about their wishes, because they're the one answering.

items.jp: コタローは いつも 何[なに]か 食[た]べたがって いる。
items.es: Kotarō is always after something to eat.

items.jp: タマも 行[い]きたいと 言[い]って いたよ。
items.es: Tama said she wants to go too.

items.jp: ニャン、 何[なに]が 食[た]べたい？
items.es: Nyan, what do you feel like eating?

bloques.md: Even asking isn't a good idea with someone above you. 「 先生[せんせい]、 コーヒーを 飲[の]みたいですか」 sounds too direct, like prying into her cravings. To offer the teacher something, the natural way is **コーヒーは いかがですか** (would you care for a coffee?), which asks about the thing and not about her appetite.

secciones.titulo: ほしい: wanting a thing

bloques.md:
たい is for actions. For **things** («I want a new bike»), you use **欲[ほ]しい**, a perfectly ordinary い-adjective. What you want takes **が**, just like with 好[す]き: 新[あたら]しい 自転車[じてんしゃ]が 欲[ほ]しい.

And since it's an adjective of inner feeling, it has the same restriction as たい: for other people, **欲[ほ]しがって いる** (you can tell they want it).

items.jp: 新[あたら]しい 手袋[てぶくろ]が 欲[ほ]しい。
items.es: I want some new gloves.

items.jp: 誕生日[たんじょうび]に 何[なに]が 欲[ほ]しい？
items.es: What do you want for your birthday?

items.jp: お 金[かね]は あまり 欲[ほ]しくない。 時間[じかん]が 欲[ほ]しい。
items.es: I don't really want money. What I want is time.

items.jp: カゲは タマの 帽子[ぼうし]を 欲[ほ]しがって いる。
items.es: Kage is desperate to have Tama's hat.
items.nota: You can tell: hence 欲[ほ]しがって いる.

bloques.md: Don't mix 欲[ほ]しい with actions: «I want to eat» isn't 「 食[た]べる 欲[ほ]しい」, it's 食[た]べたい. Think of it like this: 欲[ほ]しい wants to **have** a thing; たい wants to **do** something. If in English you'd say «I want a…», it's 欲[ほ]しい; if you'd say «I want to + verb», it's たい.

secciones.titulo: 〜てほしい: wanting someone else to do something

bloques.md:
What if what you want is for **someone else** to do something? Then you combine the two ideas: the verb's て-form + **ほしい**. The person you want to do it takes **に**.

タマに 来[き]て ほしい = I want Tama to come (literally, «I want from Tama the coming»).

In this use ほしい is usually written in hiragana, because it no longer means «wanting a thing» but works as a grammatical piece. For the opposite, **〜ないで ほしい**: I want them not to.

items.jp: タマに お 祭[まつ]りに 来[き]て ほしい。
items.es: I want Tama to come to the festival.

items.jp: カゲに もっと 優[やさ]しく して ほしい。
items.es: I wish Kage would be a bit nicer to me.

items.jp: わたしの お 菓子[かし]を 食[た]べないで ほしい。
items.es: I'd rather you didn't eat my sweets.
items.nota: Nyan, staring hard at Kotarō.

bloques.md: 〜てほしい expresses what **you** want, and with someone above you it can sound like a demand: 「 先生[せんせい]に 説明[せつめい]して ほしいです」 said to the teacher is uncomfortably close to «I want you to explain it to me». To ask something of her, a soft request is better, like the ones you'll see in the lesson on favours.

secciones.titulo: ましょう: let's…, shall I?

bloques.md:
To **suggest** doing something together, use the verb stem + **ましょう**: 行[い]きましょう (let's go), 食[た]べましょう (let's eat). This is the polite form; the version for friends, 行[い]こう, is in the next lesson.

With **か** at the end, ましょう becomes an offer or a question about plans: **手伝[てつだ]いましょうか** (shall I help?), **何時[なんじ]に 会[あ]いましょうか** (what time shall we meet?). It's very handy for offering to do something without imposing.

And for **inviting**, there's a very Japanese step first: asking in the negative with **〜ませんか** (won't you…?). 一緒[いっしょ]に 行[い]きませんか sounds like «would you like to come?», leaving the other person free to say no. If they accept, they answer with ましょう: いいですね、 行[い]きましょう. Opening straight away with 行[い]きましょう to someone you're inviting can sound a bit as if you've already decided for them.

The negative sounds softer for the same reason English says «wouldn't you like to…?»: it gives the other person an easy way out.

items.jp: もう 遅[おそ]いですね。 帰[かえ]りましょう。
items.es: It's late. Let's head home.

items.jp: 重[おも]そうですね。 持[も]ちましょうか。
items.es: That looks heavy. Shall I carry it?

items.jp: 週末[しゅうまつ]、 一緒[いっしょ]に 映画[えいが]を 見[み]ませんか。
items.es: Would you like to see a film together this weekend?

secciones.titulo: Giving advice: 〜たらどう and 〜ほうがいい

bloques.md:
There are two very common ways to suggest something to someone:

**〜たら どう？** (why don't you…?, how about…?): plain past + ら + どう. 休[やす]んだら どう？ (why don't you have a rest?). Politely: 〜たら どうですか. Among friends it shrinks to 休[やす]んだら？ That たら is a conditional form you'll see properly in the lesson on conditionals; here, just learn the whole phrase.

**〜ほうが いい** (you'd better…, it's best to…): literally «the side of… is better». For specific advice it's almost always used with the **past**: 早[はや]く 寝[ね]た ほうが いい (you'd better go to bed early). To advise **against** something, use the negative: 無理[むり]しない ほうが いい (best not to overdo it).

items.jp: 眠[ねむ]いなら、 少[すこ]し 寝[ね]たら どう？
items.es: If you're sleepy, why not have a little nap?
items.nota: なら, «if that's the case», is covered with the conditionals.

items.jp: 熱[ねつ]が あるから、 今日[きょう]は 休[やす]んだ ほうが いいよ。
items.es: You've got a temperature, so you'd better rest today.

items.jp: 夜[よる]は 一人[ひとり]で 山[やま]に 行[い]かない ほうが いい。
items.es: Best not to go up the mountain alone at night.

bloques.md: Both assume **you know better than the other person** what's good for them, so they aren't used for advising someone above you: 「 先生[せんせい]、 休[やす]んだ ほうが いいですよ」 sounds as if you were correcting her. And ほうが いい with the past is fairly firm advice; said in the wrong tone, it sounds like a warning. Among friends, with よ or ね, it comes across as caring.

secciones.titulo: All together: at the autumn festival

lineas.jp: たこ焼き[たこやき]が 食[た]べたい！ 綿菓子[わたがし]も 欲[ほ]しい！
lineas.es: I want takoyaki! And I want candyfloss!

lineas.jp: コタロー、 さっき 焼きそば[やきそば]を 食[た]べたよね？
lineas.es: Kotarō, didn't you just have some yakisoba?

lineas.jp: みなさん、 あそこで 金魚[きんぎょ]すくいを しませんか。
lineas.es: Everyone, how about some goldfish scooping over there?

lineas.jp: いいですね！ やりましょう！
lineas.es: Great idea! Let's do it!

lineas.jp: カゲも 一緒[いっしょ]に やらない？
lineas.es: Kage, aren't you joining in?

lineas.jp: 俺[おれ]は… いい。
lineas.es: I'm… fine.

lineas.jp: ふふ、 カゲ、 本当[ほんとう]は やりたがって いるでしょう。
lineas.es: Hehe, Kage, you're dying to have a go really.

lineas.jp: カゲ、 もっと 素直[すなお]に なったら どう？
lineas.es: Kage, why don't you just be honest for once?

lineas.jp: …じゃあ、 一回[いっかい] やる。 お 前[まえ]には 負[ま]けたくないからな。
lineas.es: …Fine, one go. Only because I'm not letting you beat me.

bloques.md: Look at who does what: Kotarō says what he wants to do with たい and what he wants to have with 欲[ほ]しい; Fukuro-sensei invites with ませんか, leaving them free; Nyan accepts with ましょう; Tama invites Kage casually, with the plain negative やらない？; since Tama can't know what Kage feels inside, she describes it from the outside with やりたがって いる; Nyan advises him with 〜たら どう; and Kage owns up to his wish in the negative, 負[ま]けたくない, because that one he does feel himself. Tama's でしょう is «isn't that right?», which you'll see in the lesson on probability.

ejercicios.explica: Stem, 食[た]べ, plus たい: «I want to eat».
たい conjugates like an い-adjective: たい → たくない.
Like an い-adjective: たい → たかった, «I wanted to drink».
て-form, 来[き]て, plus ほしい: «I want you to come».
Plain past, 休[やす]んだ, plus ほうが いい: specific advice, «you'd better rest».

ejercicios.pregunta: «I want a new bike.»
ejercicios.jp: 新[あたら]しい 自転車[じてんしゃ]が ＿。
ejercicios.explica: For wanting a thing you use 欲[ほ]しい, with が. したい would be «want to do», and 欲[ほ]しがる describes someone else's desire.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama clearly wants some cake. How do you say so?
ejercicios.jp: タマは ケーキを 食[た]べ＿。
ejercicios.explica: You can't state from the inside what someone else feels; you describe it from the outside with 〜たがって いる.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan sees Pon with a heavy box and offers to carry it.
ejercicios.jp: 重[おも]そうですね。 持[も]ち＿。
ejercicios.explica: ましょうか is for offering to do something: «shall I carry it?». たいです would say he fancies carrying it and なさい would be an order.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan invites Tama to the cinema, leaving her free to say no.
ejercicios.jp: 一緒[いっしょ]に 映画[えいが]を 見[み]＿。
ejercicios.explica: For inviting, the negative question ませんか leaves the other person a way out. ましょう is more for answering, or when it's already decided.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan wants to offer the teacher a coffee.
ejercicios.jp: 先生[せんせい]、 コーヒーは ＿。
ejercicios.explica: Asking someone above you directly about their wants is too direct; いかがですか politely offers the thing itself.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama has a temperature and Nyan advises her to rest.
ejercicios.jp: 熱[ねつ]が あるから、 休[やす]んだ ＿よ。
ejercicios.explica: 〜たほうが いい is the advice: «you'd better rest». Among friends, with よ, it sounds caring.

ejercicios.es: I want to go to Hokkaido in winter.
piezas: 北海道[ほっかいどう]へ
ejercicios.explica: When and where with their particles, and the verb with たい at the end.

ejercicios.es: I want Tama to come to the party.
ejercicios.explica: The person you want to act takes に, and the verb in the て-form + ほしい closes the sentence.

lecciones.titulo: Let's go! and «I'm thinking of…»: the plain volitional
lecciones.resumen: You'll invite your friends the way Japanese people really do, with a good 行[い]こう！, psych yourself up, ask «how about…?» and talk about your plans with 〜ようと 思[おも]う.

secciones.titulo: The friends' version of ましょう

bloques.md: In the previous lesson you saw ましょう, the polite form of «let's…». Among friends nobody says 行[い]きましょう: they say **行[い]こう**. This is the **plain volitional**, the form that expresses will: «let's do it», «I'm going to do it». You'll hear it all the time in conversation, songs, anime and adverts, because it's the voice of wanting to get something done.

filas: 食[た]べる → 食[た]べよう · 見[み]る → 見[み]よう · 寝[ね]る → 寝[ね]よう
the final u becomes o, then add う
行[い]く → 行[い]こう · 飲[の]む → 飲[の]もう · 待[ま]つ → 待[ま]とう · 帰[かえ]る → 帰[かえ]ろう · 買[か]う → 買[か]おう · 話[はな]す → 話[はな]そう · 遊[あそ]ぶ → 遊[あそ]ぼう · 泳[およ]ぐ → 泳[およ]ごう

bloques.md:
Look at the う-verbs: they change their last vowel to **o** and then take an う that lengthens that o. 行[い]こう is pronounced «ikoo», with a long o. It's the same idea of syllabary rows you saw with the imperative (which switched to e): each verb form uses a different row.

And the match is exact: 行[い]こう = 行[い]きましょう, 食[た]べよう = 食[た]べましょう. Same meaning, different register.

secciones.titulo: Inviting your friends

bloques.md:
The most common use is suggesting something to your friends. And as always, the particles at the end set the tone:

- **行[い]こう！**: let's go!, direct and keen.
- **行[い]こうよ**: oh come on, let's go!, nudging a bit (よ pushes the idea towards the other person).
- **行[い]こうね**: let's go, OK?, to confirm a plan you both share (ね looks for agreement).

items.jp: タマ、 一緒[いっしょ]に 帰[かえ]ろう！
items.es: Tama, let's walk home together!

items.jp: 雪[ゆき]だ！ 外[そと]で 遊[あそ]ぼうよ！
items.es: It's snowing! Come on, let's go and play outside!

items.jp: 明日[あした]も また 会[あ]おうね。
items.es: Let's meet up again tomorrow, OK?

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は カレーを 作[つく]ろう。
items.es: Let's make curry today.

bloques.md: With the teacher or anyone above you, no 行[い]こう: it sounds as if you were talking to a mate. Go up to 行[い]きましょう, or better still, invite with 行[い]きませんか, which leaves them free to decline. The plain volitional is for people you're on casual terms with.

secciones.titulo: Volitional + か: how about…?, what shall we do?

bloques.md:
Add **か** and the volitional loses its certainty and becomes a tentative suggestion: **行[い]こうか** (shall we go?, how about going?). It also works for offering: **持[も]とうか** (shall I carry it?). It's the friends' version of ましょうか.

And with question words you get a question you'll ask yourself a thousand times: **どうしようか** (what shall we do?), or without か, alone and stressed: **どうしよう…** (what am I going to do now?). That last one is the panic phrase par excellence.

items.jp: 疲[つか]れたね。 ちょっと 休[やす]もうか。
items.es: We're tired, aren't we? Shall we have a little rest?

items.jp: 重[おも]そうだね。 半分[はんぶん] 持[も]とうか。
items.es: That looks heavy. Shall I take half?

items.jp: お 昼[ひる]、 何[なに]を 食[た]べようか。
items.es: What shall we have for lunch?

items.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]、 忘[わす]れた… どうしよう…
items.es: I forgot my homework… What am I going to do?

secciones.titulo: Talking to yourself: よし、やろう！

bloques.md: The volitional doesn't need anyone else around. When you make a decision on the spot, Japanese speakers say it to themselves in the volitional: **よし、 やろう！** (right, let's do this!), **もう 寝[ね]よう** (OK, time for bed). It's like the «right, here we go» we tell ourselves to get started.

items.jp: よし、 今日[きょう]こそ 早[はや]く 起[お]きよう！
items.es: Right, today I'm definitely getting up early!
items.nota: こそ, «today of all days», comes later on.

items.jp: お 腹[なか]が 空[す]いた。 何[なに]か 食[た]べよう。
items.es: I'm hungry. I'll eat something.

secciones.titulo: 〜ようと おもう: talking about your plans

bloques.md:
To tell someone what you're **planning to do**, Japanese quotes your own will: it uses the volitional, the particle **と** (which marks what's said or thought, and which you'll see properly in the lesson on quoting) and **思[おも]う** (to think). 行[い]こうと 思[おも]う is literally «I think: let's go!», in other words «I think I'll go», «I'm going to go».

There's a subtle difference between two forms:

- **〜ようと 思[おも]う**: an intention that has just occurred to you or that you're deciding now. «I think I'll…».
- **〜ようと 思[おも]って いる**: an intention you've had for a while, a plan in motion. «I've been meaning to…», «I'm planning to…». Since it's a lasting state, it takes ている.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 早[はや]く 寝[ね]ようと 思[おも]う。
items.es: I think I'll go to bed early today.

items.jp: 冬休[ふゆやす]みに 北海道[ほっかいどう]へ 行[い]こうと 思[おも]って います。
items.es: I'm planning to go to Hokkaido over the winter holidays.

items.jp: 来年[らいねん]から ピアノを 習[なら]おうと 思[おも]って いる。
items.es: I've been meaning to take up piano from next year.

items.jp: タマは 留学[りゅうがく]しようと 思[おも]って いる。
items.es: Tama is planning to study abroad.
items.nota: For someone else's plans, 思[おも]って いる: you're describing a state seen from outside.

bloques.md: How is it different from たい? **たい** is a wish: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]きたい (I want to go to Hokkaido) might be a dream you never fulfil. **〜ようと 思[おも]う** is an intention: you've decided to do it, or nearly. So if someone asks about your holiday plans, 行[い]こうと 思[おも]って います sounds like a real plan, and 行[い]きたいです sounds like wishful thinking.

For someone else's plans, use 〜ようと 思[おも]って いる, not 〜ようと 思[おも]う. It's the same as with たい: bare 思[おも]う is a thought coming out of you right now, and you can only state it about yourself. What someone else thinks you only know as a state they've let show or told you about, and that's ている.

secciones.titulo: All together: winter plans

lineas.jp: 冬休[ふゆやす]み、 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]こうと 思[おも]ってるんだ。
lineas.es: I'm planning to go to Hokkaido over the winter holidays.

lineas.jp: いいね！ わたしも 一緒[いっしょ]に 行[い]こうか？
lineas.es: Nice! How about I come with you?

lineas.jp: うん、 行[い]こう！ 札幌[さっぽろ]で ラーメンを 食[た]べよう！
lineas.es: Yes, let's go! Let's eat ramen in Sapporo!

lineas.jp: 小樽[おたる]にも 行[い]こうよ。 ガラスの お 店[みせ]が たくさん あるよ。
lineas.es: Let's go to Otaru too. There are loads of glassware shops.

lineas.jp: 俺[おれ]も… ちょうど 行[い]こうと 思[おも]って いた。
lineas.es: I was… actually thinking of going too.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 みんなで 行[い]こう！ 何[なに]で 行[い]こうか。
lineas.es: Then let's all go! How shall we get there?

lineas.jp: 電車[でんしゃ]と 船[ふね]、 どっちに しよう…
lineas.es: Train or boat… which one shall we pick?

bloques.md: Nyan shares a plan he already has with 行[い]こうと 思[おも]ってる; Tama tentatively offers to come with 行[い]こうか; Nyan invites eagerly with 行[い]こう and 食[た]べよう; Tama nudges with 行[い]こうよ; Kage admits to a plan he already had, in the past, 思[おも]って いた; and at the end 行[い]こうか and しよう help them decide together. That どっちに しよう is «which shall we choose?», with the にする of choosing that you'll see in the lesson on なる and する.

ejercicios.explica: る-verb: drop る and add よう.
う-verb: the final u becomes o and you add う: く → こう.
む → も, lengthened with う: 飲[の]もう.
帰[かえ]る is an う-verb even though it ends in る, so る → ろう, not 「 帰[かえ]よう」.
する is irregular: しよう.
来[く]る is irregular and changes its reading: 来[こ]よう.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan suggests to Tama that they walk home together.
ejercicios.jp: タマ、 一緒[いっしょ]に 帰[かえ]＿！
ejercicios.explica: Among friends, the plain volitional: 帰[かえ]ろう. ましょう would be too formal with Tama, and 帰[かえ]れ is a blunt imperative.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan has forgotten his homework and panics.
ejercicios.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]、 忘[わす]れた… ＿…
ejercicios.explica: どうしよう, the volitional said to yourself, is the stressed «what am I going to do?». どうしろ would be an imperative.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama is planning to study abroad. How do you say so?
ejercicios.jp: タマは 留学[りゅうがく]しようと ＿。
ejercicios.explica: Someone else's plans are described as a state seen from outside: 思[おも]って いる. Bare 思[おも]う only works for yourself.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan is tired and tentatively suggests a short rest.
ejercicios.jp: ちょっと 休[やす]もう＿。
ejercicios.explica: Volitional + か turns the suggestion into a question: «shall we have a little rest?». It lets the other person decide.

ejercicios.es: I think I'll go to Otaru tomorrow.
ejercicios.explica: The volitional with と quotes your intention, and 思[おも]う closes the sentence: «I think I'll go».

ejercicios.es: Let's eat ramen in Sapporo!
ejercicios.explica: Where (with で) and what (with を), then the volitional at the end to invite.

lecciones.titulo: Verbs that stick to other verbs: start, keep on, overdo it…
lecciones.resumen: With one simple trick (stem + another verb) you'll say that you're starting to eat, that you keep on running, that you've overeaten, that you've left a book half-read or that you have to redo your homework. Nyan is a master of one in particular: 食[た]べすぎる.

secciones.titulo: The trick: stem + another verb

bloques.md:
In English, to add nuance to an action we use helper phrases: «**start** eating», «**keep** running», «**finish** reading», «write it **again**». Japanese does something similar, but more compactly: it sticks a second verb straight onto the **stem** of the first (the ます stem, which you already know) and makes a brand-new verb.

食[た]べます → 食[た]べ + 始[はじ]める → **食[た]べ 始[はじ]める** (to start eating)

The first verb says **what** you do; the second says **how** that action is going: whether it's starting, carrying on, finishing, going too far… And the big advantage is that the compound verb conjugates **like the second verb**: if that one is a る-verb, the whole thing conjugates like a る-verb. 食[た]べ 始[はじ]めた, 食[た]べ 始[はじ]めない, 食[た]べ 始[はじ]めて…

secciones.titulo: Starting, continuing and finishing

filas: 食[た]べ 始[はじ]める, 降[ふ]り 始[はじ]める, 習[なら]い 始[はじ]める
走[はし]り 続[つづ]ける, 待[ま]ち 続[つづ]ける
読[よ]み 終[お]わる, 食[た]べ 終[お]わる

bloques.md:
**〜 始[はじ]める** marks the start of an action that's going to last: 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]り 始[はじ]めた (it started snowing), 去年[きょねん]から 日本語[にほんご]を 習[なら]い 始[はじ]めた (I started learning Japanese last year).

**〜 続[つづ]ける** says the action doesn't stop: 三時間[さんじかん] 走[はし]り 続[つづ]けた (I kept running for three hours straight). It often carries a hint of perseverance, or of stubbornness.

**〜 終[お]わる** and **〜 終[お]える** mark the end. In conversation, 〜 終[お]わる is the usual one, even when there's an object with を: 本[ほん]を 読[よ]み 終[お]わった (I've finished reading the book). 〜 終[お]える sounds more formal or deliberate, more like written language.

items.jp: ニャンは いただきますの 前[まえ]に 食[た]べ 始[はじ]めた。
items.es: Nyan started eating before saying いただきます.
items.nota: いただきます is what you say before a meal; skipping it is a breach of manners Tama won't let him forget.

items.jp: 雨[あめ]が 一晩中[ひとばんじゅう] 降[ふ]り 続[つづ]けた。
items.es: It kept raining all night long.

items.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]、 やっと やり 終[お]わった！
items.es: I've finally finished my homework!

items.jp: カゲは 負[ま]けても 練習[れんしゅう]し 続[つづ]けた。
items.es: Even though he lost, Kage kept on training.
items.nota: 負[ま]けても, «even if he loses», is covered in the lesson on 〜ても.

bloques.md: Even when the action starts by itself (rain, snow, a song), the compound uses **始[はじ]める**, not 始[はじ]まる: 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]り 始[はじ]めた, not 「 降[ふ]り 始[はじ]まった」. As a building block, 始[はじ]める has lost its sense of «you start something» and only contributes the idea of beginning. The same goes for 終[お]わる and 終[お]える: what matters here isn't who does what, but where the action has got to.

secciones.titulo: 〜すぎる: overdoing it

bloques.md: **すぎる** means «to pass, to go beyond», and stuck onto another word it says something **goes further than it should**: too much, too… It's one of the most useful, because it works with verbs and with adjectives.

**Verb**: stem + すぎる. 食[た]べすぎる (eat too much), 寝[ね]すぎる (sleep too much), 飲[の]みすぎる (drink too much)
**い-adjective**: drop い + すぎる. 高[たか]い → 高[たか]すぎる, 寒[さむ]い → 寒[さむ]すぎる
**な-adjective**: drop な + すぎる. 静[しず]か → 静[しず]かすぎる
**The exceptions**: いい → **よすぎる**; ない → **なさすぎる**, as in 時間[じかん]が なさすぎる (there's no time at all)

すぎる is a る-verb: すぎた, すぎない, すぎて…

On top of that, stem + すぎ works as a **noun**: 食[た]べすぎ (overeating), 飲[の]みすぎ, 働[はたら]きすぎ. It's very natural for telling someone off: 食[た]べすぎだよ (you're eating way too much!). And the classic morning-after regret: 昨日[きのう]は 食[た]べすぎた (I ate too much yesterday).

items.jp: この 靴[くつ]は 高[たか]すぎて、 買[か]えない。
items.es: These shoes are too expensive; I can't afford them.
items.nota: 買[か]えない is the potential form, coming soon.

items.jp: ニャン、 寝[ね]すぎだよ。 もう お 昼[ひる]だよ。
items.es: Nyan, you've overslept. It's already midday.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 天気[てんき]が よすぎて、 勉強[べんきょう]したくない。
items.es: The weather's far too nice today to study.

items.jp: 図書館[としょかん]は 静[しず]かすぎて、 眠[ねむ]く なる。
items.es: The library is so quiet it makes me sleepy.

bloques.md:
Careful with いい: «too good» is **よすぎる**, never «いすぎる» or «いいすぎる». And watch out, because **言[い]いすぎる** does exist, but it's something else: «to say too much», to go too far with your words. If someone snaps 言[い]いすぎだよ at you, they mean you've crossed a line with what you said.

And a note on nuance: すぎる is almost always negative, because it's about excess. Among young people you'll sometimes hear it as over-the-top praise, かわいすぎる (it's sooo cute!), but that's a casual use; in general, if something is «too» anything, there's a problem.

secciones.titulo: 〜きる: completely, all the way

bloques.md: **切[き]る** means «to cut», and as a building block it brings the idea of **cutting off at the end, leaving nothing**: doing something completely, until it's used up. It's often written in hiragana, 〜きる.

items.jp: この 本[ほん]、 一日[いちにち]で 読[よ]み 切[き]った！
items.es: I read this whole book in one day!

items.jp: 牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]を 使[つか]い 切[き]った。
items.es: We've used up all the milk.

items.jp: マラソンを 最後[さいご]まで 走[はし]り 切[き]った。
items.es: I ran the marathon all the way to the end.

items.jp: こんなに たくさん、 食[た]べきれないよ。
items.es: I can't finish all this.
items.nota: 〜きれない, «can't get to the end of», is a very common form.

bloques.md: That 〜きれない in the last example is the negative potential of きる (not being able to get all the way through), and it's so common that it's worth learning now: 食[た]べきれない (I can't finish it), 数[かぞ]えきれない (countless, too many to count), 待[ま]ちきれない (I can't wait, I'm too impatient).

secciones.titulo: 〜かける: half-done, nearly

bloques.md:
**〜かける** says an action **has started but not finished**: it's been left half-done, or it's about to happen. With actions that take time, it's «half-way»: 読[よ]みかける (start reading and leave it). With sudden changes, it's «nearly»: 死[し]にかける (to nearly die), 忘[わす]れかける (to nearly forget).

Very handy is its noun form, **〜かけ**, with の before another noun: 読[よ]みかけの 本[ほん] (a half-read book), 食[た]べかけの パン (a half-eaten bread roll), 飲[の]みかけの ジュース.

items.jp: 机[つくえ]の 上[うえ]に 読[よ]みかけの 本[ほん]が ある。
items.es: There's a half-read book on the desk.

items.jp: 何[なに]か 言[い]いかけて、 やめた。
items.es: He started to say something and stopped.

items.jp: その 食[た]べかけの お 餅[もち]、 だれの？
items.es: Whose is that half-eaten mochi?
items.nota: A very dangerous question if Kotarō is around.

secciones.titulo: 〜なおす and 〜あう: redoing, and doing together

bloques.md: **直[なお]す** means «to fix, to correct». Stuck onto another verb it means **doing it again so it comes out right**: 書[か]き 直[なお]す (rewrite), やり 直[なお]す (start over), 考[かんが]え 直[なお]す (reconsider), 見直[みなお]す (review, and also «see someone in a better light»). It's English «re-» or «again», but with a flavour of correction: you don't repeat for the sake of it, you repeat because it didn't come out right the first time.

**合[あ]う** means «to fit, to match». Stuck onto another verb it adds **reciprocity**: several people doing it to each other. 話[はな]し 合[あ]う (talk it over, discuss), 助[たす]け 合[あ]う (help each other), 知[し]り 合[あ]う (get to know each other). It's English «each other», but built into the verb.

items.jp: 字[じ]が 汚[きたな]いから、 書[か]き 直[なお]して ください。
items.es: The handwriting's too messy, please write it out again.
items.nota: Fukuro-sensei, handing Nyan's homework back.

items.jp: 失敗[しっぱい]しても、 また やり 直[なお]せば いい。
items.es: Even if you fail, you can always start again.
items.nota: A very Japanese word of encouragement; the 〜ば is a conditional you'll meet later.

items.jp: けんかは やめて、 話[はな]し 合[あ]おう。
items.es: Stop fighting and let's talk it over.

items.jp: ニャンと タマは いつも 助[たす]け 合[あ]って いる。
items.es: Nyan and Tama always help each other out.

bloques.md: Don't use 合[あ]う if the action only goes one way. 「 ニャンが タマを 助[たす]け 合[あ]う」 makes no sense, because 合[あ]う requires both to do the same thing to each other. That's why the participants are normally joined with と and made the subject: ニャンと タマが 助[たす]け 合[あ]う, or ニャンは タマと 助[たす]け 合[あ]う.

secciones.titulo: All together: the festival poster

lineas.jp: さあ、 お 祭[まつ]りの ポスターを 描[か]き 始[はじ]めよう！
lineas.es: Right, let's start drawing the festival poster!

lineas.jp: その 前[まえ]に、 ポンさんの お 餅[もち]を… おいしすぎる！
lineas.es: Before that, Pon's mochi… They're too good!

lineas.jp: ニャン、 食[た]べすぎだよ。 もう 五つ目[いつつめ]でしょう。
lineas.es: Nyan, you're overdoing it. That's your fifth already.

lineas.jp: うう… もう 食[た]べきれない…
lineas.es: Ugh… I can't eat any more…

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 その 食[た]べかけの お 餅[もち]、 ぼくが 食[た]べる！
lineas.es: Then I'll have that half-eaten mochi!

lineas.jp: おい、 この ポスター、 字[じ]が 小[ちい]さすぎる。 書[か]き 直[なお]せ。
lineas.es: Hey, the writing on this poster is too small. Redo it.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 みんなで 話[はな]し 合[あ]って、 もう 一度[いちど] やり 直[なお]そう。
lineas.es: OK, let's talk it over together and do it again.

lineas.jp: …ふん。 やるなら、 最後[さいご]まで やり 切[き]るぞ。
lineas.es: …Hmph. If we're doing it, we're seeing it through to the end.

bloques.md: All in one afternoon: 描[か]き 始[はじ]めよう (starting), おいしすぎる and 食[た]べすぎ (overdoing it, with an adjective and as a noun), 食[た]べきれない (can't finish), 食[た]べかけ (half-eaten), 小[ちい]さすぎる (too small), 書[か]き 直[なお]せ and やり 直[なお]そう (redoing), 話[はな]し 合[あ]って (together) and やり 切[き]る (all the way). Kage's 書[か]き 直[なお]せ is a blunt imperative, very much his style; 五つ目[いつつめ] is «the fifth», with the 目[め] of ordinals.

ejercicios.base: 食[た]べる + 始[はじ]める
ejercicios.explica: Stem of the first verb, 食[た]べ, plus 始[はじ]める: «to start eating».
Stem 読[よ]み + 終[お]わる, and the whole thing conjugates like 終[お]わる: 読[よ]み 終[お]わった.
With verbs, stem + すぎる: 飲[の]みすぎる, to drink too much.
With い-adjectives you drop the い: 高[たか]すぎる.
いい conjugates from よい, so it's よすぎる. 言[い]いすぎる would be «to say too much».
Stem 書[か]き + 直[なお]す: rewrite it so it comes out right.

ejercicios.pregunta: «It's started snowing.»
ejercicios.jp: 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]り＿。
ejercicios.explica: Compounds use 始[はじ]める even when the action starts by itself. 続[つづ]けた would be «it kept snowing».

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan has eaten the whole cake, down to the last crumb.
ejercicios.jp: ケーキを 全部[ぜんぶ] 食[た]べ＿。
ejercicios.explica: 〜 切[き]る is doing it completely, all the way. 〜かけた would mean leaving it half-eaten and 〜 直[なお]した, eating it again.

ejercicios.pregunta: There's a half-read book on the desk.
ejercicios.jp: 机[つくえ]に 読[よ]み＿の 本[ほん]が ある。
ejercicios.explica: 〜かけ, as a noun with の, describes something started and not finished: 読[よ]みかけの 本[ほん].

ejercicios.pregunta: «The weather's too nice to study.»
ejercicios.jp: 天気[てんき]が ＿て、 勉強[べんきょう]したくない。
ejercicios.explica: いい always conjugates from よい: よすぎる. いいすぎ would sound like 言[い]いすぎ, «saying too much».

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan and Tama help each other.
ejercicios.jp: ニャンと タマは いつも 助[たす]け＿ いる。
ejercicios.explica: 〜 合[あ]う adds reciprocity: the two of them help each other.

ejercicios.es: Kotarō always eats too much.
ejercicios.explica: The adverb いつも up front and the compound with すぎる at the end, like any other verb.

ejercicios.es: I read that book all the way to the end.
ejercicios.explica: 〜 切[き]る reinforces the «all the way» already carried by 最後[さいご]まで.

lecciones.titulo: While, right now and every time
lecciones.resumen: You'll learn to place actions on the clock: eating while watching TV, being just about to leave or having just arrived, making the most of the tea while it's still hot, and doing something without fail every time you go to Hokkaido.

secciones.titulo: Two things at once: ながら

bloques.md:
Nyan is an expert at doing two things at once, as long as one of them is eating. To say it, Japanese has **ながら**, which attaches to the verb stem and means “while”, “at the same time as”.

What matters is who plays which role. The action with **ながら** is the backdrop, the background music; the action at the end of the sentence is the star, the thing you're really doing. Japanese always saves the main event for last, and this is no exception.

Verb stem (the ます form without ます) + **ながら**, followed by the main action.
食[た]べます → **食[た]べながら**
聞[き]きます → **聞[き]きながら**
歩[ある]きます → **歩[ある]きながら**
します → **しながら**
Politeness goes on only once, at the end: 飲[の]みながら 話[はな]しましょう. Never ✗ 飲[の]みますながら, because ます only appears where the sentence closes, not halfway through.

items.jp: テレビを 見[み]ながら ご 飯[はん]を 食[た]べる。
items.es: I eat dinner while watching TV.
items.nota: What you're doing is eating; the TV is the background.

items.jp: タマは 歌[うた]を 歌[うた]いながら 歩[ある]く。
items.es: Tama walks along singing.

items.jp: 音楽[おんがく]を 聞[き]きながら 勉強[べんきょう]します。
items.es: I study while listening to music.

items.jp: コーヒーを 飲[の]みながら 話[はな]しましょう。
items.es: Let's talk over a coffee.

items.jp: スマホを 見[み]ながら 歩[ある]かないで。
items.es: Don't walk around staring at your phone.

bloques.md:
Notice that English often renders **ながら** as “while …ing”: “eat while watching TV”, “walk along singing”. That makes a handy detector: if your English sentence has an -ing action running alongside the main one, the Japanese is very likely **ながら**.

What if you flip the sentence around? The grammar still works, but you change who the star is:

items.jp: 音楽[おんがく]を 聞[き]きながら 勉強[べんきょう]する。
items.es: I study with music on in the background.
items.nota: What you're doing is studying.

items.jp: 勉強[べんきょう]しながら 音楽[おんがく]を 聞[き]く。
items.es: I listen to music while I study.
items.nota: Now what you're doing is listening to music, and studying is just filler. Fukuro-sensei would not be pleased.

bloques.md: **ながら** only works when **the same person** does both things. If Tama is sleeping and Nyan is eating, ✗ タマが 寝[ね]ながら、 ニャンが 食[た]べる doesn't work. Why? Because ながら attaches straight to the verb stem, leaving no room for a subject of its own: it's like saying “Nyan, sleeping, eats”, which would make Nyan the sleeper. For two different people you'll use **間[あいだ]** or **うちに**, coming up below.

Both actions have to **last**. ながら wants verbs that stretch out over time, like eating, walking, listening or thinking, because two things can only overlap if they take up a while. With instant verbs such as 着[つ]く (to arrive) or 決[き]める (to decide) it makes no sense: nobody “arrives while” doing something else.

You'll run into **ながら** in a few set phrases with a different meaning, “although”. The most useful is **残念[ざんねん]ながら**, “unfortunately” (literally “though it's a pity”). For now, stick with “while”: that's the everyday use.

secciones.titulo: The exact moment: ところ

bloques.md: **ところ** means “place”, but here it's a place in time: a specific point in the life of an action. Picture the act of eating as a road with three stops: just before you start, halfway along, and just after you finish. The form of the verb you put before ところ tells which of those three stops you mean.

filas: 今[いま] 食[た]べるところ
今[いま] 食[た]べているところ
今[いま] 食[た]べたところ

bloques.md: It almost always takes **だ** or **です** after it, and often **ちょうど** (“just”) or **今[いま]** (“now”) before it, because ところ is about this very moment. It's the textbook answer when someone calls and asks what you're up to.

items.jp: ちょうど 家[いえ]を 出[で]るところです。
items.es: I'm just leaving the house.
items.nota: You haven't left yet: your hand is on the doorknob.

items.jp: 今[いま]、 お 風呂[ふろ]に 入[はい]っているところ。
items.es: I'm in the bath right now.

items.jp: 今[いま]、 駅[えき]に 着[つ]いたところです。
items.es: I've just got to the station.

items.jp: ちょうど 電話[でんわ]しようと 思[おも]っていたところ！
items.es: I was just about to call you!
items.nota: A classic line between friends: I was right in the middle of “thinking of calling you”.

lineas.jp: もしもし、 ニャン？ 今[いま] 何[なに] してる？
lineas.es: Hello? Nyan? What are you doing?

lineas.jp: 今[いま]、 ご 飯[はん]を 食[た]べているところ。
lineas.es: I'm having dinner right now.

lineas.jp: えっ？ 公園[こうえん]で 待[ま]ってるよ！
lineas.es: What? I'm waiting for you at the park!

lineas.jp: あっ、 忘[わす]れてた！ 今[いま] 出[で]るところ！
lineas.es: Oh no, I forgot! I'm just heading out!

lineas.jp: 本当[ほんとう]に？
lineas.es: Really?

lineas.jp: ……まだ 食[た]べているところ。
lineas.es: …Still eating.

bloques.md: **ところ** is about **now**. ✗ 来年[らいねん] 日本[にほん]に 行[い]くところです sounds very odd, because you're telling someone you're at the very instant of leaving… for a trip next year. For plans, plain 行[い]きます will do, or 行[い]こうと 思[おも]っています.
Don't mix it up with **ところで** at the start of a sentence, which means “by the way” and is used to change the subject. They look alike, but that ところで stands alone, with no verb in front.

secciones.titulo: Only just: たばかり

bloques.md: **ばかり** after the た form also says something has just happened, but it looks at it from a different angle. **たところ** is a stopwatch: it marks the instant right after finishing, seconds or minutes ago. **たばかり** is a feeling: “to me, this is recent”. It could be five minutes, three days or a month ago; what counts is that it feels like no time at all to you.

た form + **ばかり**, then です or だ, or の before a noun.
食[た]べた → **食[た]べたばかり**
来[き]た → **来[き]たばかり**
買[か]った → **買[か]ったばかりの 靴[くつ]** (brand-new shoes, just bought)
All you need is the verb in the past; ばかり itself never changes.

items.jp: 先月[せんげつ]、 札幌[さっぽろ]に 来[き]たばかりです。
items.es: I only moved to Sapporo last month.
items.nota: A month is too long for ところ, but fine for ばかり: it still feels recent to you.

items.jp: 日本語[にほんご]を 始[はじ]めたばかりです。
items.es: I've only just started Japanese.

items.jp: 食[た]べたばかりだから、 お 腹[なか]が いっぱい。
items.es: I've just eaten, so I'm full.

items.jp: 買[か]ったばかりの 傘[かさ]を なくした……。
items.es: I lost the umbrella I'd just bought…

bloques.md: That's why **ばかり** is perfect for **excuses** and **complaints**: “I've just eaten (so don't ask me to eat more)”, “I only just bought it (and it's already broken!)”. It leans on how recent something is to say that something else shouldn't be happening. Nyan uses it a lot when it's his turn to do the dishes: 起[お]きたばかりだから…, “but I've only just got up…”.

filas: ✓ 今[いま] 着[つ]いたところ
✓ 今[いま] 着[つ]いたばかり
✗ 先月[せんげつ] 来[き]たところ
✓ 先月[せんげつ] 来[き]たばかり

bloques.md: Don't confuse it with the **ばかり** that means “nothing but” (ケーキばかり 食[た]べる, “eats nothing but cake”), which you'll meet in the lesson on だけ, しか and ばかり. The clue is what comes before it: after a verb in た it means “just did”; after a noun, or in 寝[ね]てばかり いる, it means “nothing but”.

secciones.titulo: While you still can: うちに

bloques.md: **うち** means “inside”, and **うちに** marks a window of time: “while this lasts”. Not just any window, though, but one that's about to close. It's what every Japanese grandmother says: 熱[あつ]いうちに 食[た]べなさい, “eat it while it's hot”. The soup is going to get cold, so you need to act inside that window. Whenever you hear うちに, think “make the most of it”.

い-adjective + **うちに**: 熱[あつ]いうちに, 若[わか]いうちに
な-adjective + な + **うちに**: 元気[げんき]なうちに
Noun + の + **うちに**: 子供[こども]のうちに, 午前中[ごぜんちゅう]のうちに
Verb in ている or ない + **うちに**: 覚[おぼ]えているうちに, 暗[くら]くならないうちに

items.jp: 熱[あつ]いうちに 食[た]べてね。
items.es: Eat it while it's hot.

items.jp: 若[わか]いうちに、 いろいろな 所[ところ]へ 行[い]きたい。
items.es: I want to go to lots of places while I'm young.

items.jp: 明[あか]るいうちに 帰[かえ]ろう。
items.es: Let's head home while it's still light.

items.jp: 忘[わす]れないうちに、 メモして おく。
items.es: I'll jot it down before I forget.

items.jp: 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]らないうちに、 公園[こうえん]に 行[い]こう。
items.es: Let's go to the park before it rains.

bloques.md: Look at the trick in the last two sentences. Where English says “**before** it rains”, Japanese says “**while it's still not** raining”: 降[ふ]らないうちに. It's the same idea seen from inside the window: it isn't raining yet, so go for it. That ない doesn't really negate anything; it just measures how much time you have left.

There's a second, rather lovely use. With a verb that lasts (usually in ている) and a change at the end, **うちに** tells how something changed **without you noticing**, little by little, while you were busy with something else.

items.jp: 何度[なんど]も 聞[き]いているうちに、 覚[おぼ]えた。
items.es: After hearing it over and over, I'd learned it by heart.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 住[す]んでいるうちに、 雪[ゆき]が 好[す]きに なった。
items.es: Living in Hokkaido, I grew to love the snow.

secciones.titulo: During, or at some point: 間 and 間に

bloques.md: **間[あいだ]** means “the space between two things”. In time, it's an interval with a start and an end: while something lasts. Unlike ながら, here the two actions can belong to different people: one can be asleep while the other gets up to mischief. The key question is whether **に** follows it, because that changes the whole picture.

Plain **間[あいだ]**: the main action fills **the whole** interval, from start to finish. It often comes with ずっと or ている.
**間[あいだ]に**: the main action happens **at some point** inside the interval. It's a dot, not a line.
Before it goes anything that can describe a noun: a plain verb (often in ている), an い-adjective, a な-adjective with な, or a noun with の, as in 夏休[なつやす]みの 間[あいだ].

items.jp: タマが 寝[ね]ている 間[あいだ]、 ニャンは ずっと 待[ま]っていた。
items.es: While Tama slept, Nyan waited the whole time.

items.jp: タマが 寝[ね]ている 間[あいだ]に、 ニャンは ケーキを 食[た]べた。
items.es: While Tama was asleep, Nyan ate the cake.
items.nota: Eating the cake is one (glorious) moment inside Tama's nap: hence 間[あいだ]に.

items.jp: 夏休[なつやす]みの 間[あいだ]、 おばあちゃんの 家[いえ]に いた。
items.es: I stayed at Grandma's all summer.

items.jp: 夏休[なつやす]みの 間[あいだ]に、 一度[いちど] 北海道[ほっかいどう]へ 行[い]きたい。
items.es: I want to go to Hokkaido at some point during the summer holidays.

bloques.md: A trick for choosing: if you can add “the whole time” in English, it's **間[あいだ]**; if you can add “at some point”, it's **間[あいだ]に**. That's why ✗ 寝[ね]ている 間[あいだ]に ずっと 待[ま]っていた grates: ずっと (the whole time) clashes with a に that marks a single point.

So how do **間[あいだ]に** and **うちに** differ, if both can be translated “while”? 間[あいだ]に simply places something inside an interval, nothing more. うちに adds the feeling that the window is closing (hurry up!) or that something changed without you noticing. When Grandma says 熱[あつ]いうちに she's hurrying you along; if she said 熱[あつ]い 間[あいだ]に, it would sound like a technical report.

secciones.titulo: Every time: たびに

bloques.md: **たび** means “occasion, time”. **たびに** says something happens **every time** something else does, without exception, like a law of nature. It usually carries a sense of “always, without fail”, sometimes fondly and sometimes with a sigh.

Dictionary-form verb + **たびに**: 会[あ]うたびに, 行[い]くたびに
Noun + の + **たびに**: 旅行[りょこう]のたびに, 試験[しけん]のたびに

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]くたびに、 ソフトクリームを 食[た]べる。
items.es: Every time I go to Hokkaido, I have a soft-serve ice cream.

items.jp: カゲは 会[あ]うたびに 「 勝負[しょうぶ]だ！」と 言[い]う。
items.es: Every time we meet, Kage says: “Duel!”

items.jp: この 歌[うた]を 聞[き]くたびに、 ふるさとを 思[おも]い 出[だ]す。
items.es: Every time I hear this song, I think of my hometown.

items.jp: 旅行[りょこう]のたびに、 お 土産[みやげ]を 買[か]いすぎる。
items.es: On every trip I buy way too many souvenirs.

bloques.md: Before **たびに** the verb stays in the **dictionary form** even when you're talking about the past; the final verb carries the tense: 会[あ]うたびに 喧嘩[けんか]した, “every time we met, we'd argue”. And it doesn't work for a one-off: たびに needs repetition. For “when I went to Hokkaido” you'd say 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]った 時[とき].

secciones.titulo: All together: which one?

filas: I do two things at once (myself)
歩[ある]きながら 話[はな]す
今[いま] 出[で]るところ
I'm right in the middle of…
今[いま] 食[た]べているところ
今[いま] 着[つ]いたところ
先月[せんげつ] 来[き]たばかり
寝[ね]ている 間[あいだ]、 ずっと
寝[ね]ている 間[あいだ]に

lineas.jp: 小樽[おたる]に 来[く]るたびに、 お 腹[なか]が すく。
lineas.es: Every time I come to Otaru, I get hungry.

lineas.jp: さっき お 寿司[すし]を 食[た]べたばかりだよ！
lineas.es: You've only just had sushi!

lineas.jp: でも、 あの お 店[みせ]、 もうすぐ 閉[し]まるよ。 開[あ]いているうちに 行[い]こう！
lineas.es: But that shop's closing soon. Let's go while it's still open!

lineas.jp: もう……。 じゃあ、 歩[ある]きながら 話[はな]そう。
lineas.es: Honestly… Fine, we'll talk on the way.

lineas.jp: やった！ 今[いま]、 お 店[みせ]に 入[はい]るところ！
lineas.es: Yay! I'm going into the shop right now!

ejercicios.pregunta: “I eat dinner while watching TV.”
ejercicios.jp: テレビを ＿ ご 飯[はん]を 食[た]べる。
ejercicios.explica: ながら attaches to the verb stem, which is the ます form without ます: 見[み]ます → 見[み]ながら. Neither the dictionary form nor the て form fits there.
飲[の]む → 飲[の]みます → drop ます and add ながら: 飲[の]みながら.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama calls and your hand is on the doorknob.
ejercicios.jp: ちょうど 家[いえ]を 出[で]る＿です。
ejercicios.explica: Dictionary form + ところ marks the instant just before the action: you're about to leave. ばかり would follow the た form, and うちに would need another action after it.

ejercicios.pregunta: You arrived in Japan last month and it still feels recent.
ejercicios.jp: 先月[せんげつ]、 日本[にほん]に 来[き]た＿です。
ejercicios.explica: A month is too long for たところ, which is a stopwatch for the instant right after. たばかり says it still feels recent to you.
Put the verb in the た form, 食[た]べた, and add ばかり: 食[た]べたばかり, “I've just eaten”.

ejercicios.pregunta: Grandma serves you freshly made soup.
ejercicios.jp: 熱[あつ]い＿ 食[た]べてね。
ejercicios.explica: うちに marks a window that's about to close: the soup will go cold, so eat it now. たびに would mean “every time”, and ながら doesn't attach to adjectives with this meaning.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Let's go home before it rains.”
ejercicios.jp: 雨[あめ]が ＿うちに 帰[かえ]ろう。
ejercicios.explica: Where English says “before it rains”, Japanese says “while it's still not raining”: 降[ふ]らないうちに. The ない just measures the time you have left.

ejercicios.es: Don't walk around staring at your phone.
ejercicios.explica: First the background action with ながら (looking at your phone), then the main one at the end, which is the one being forbidden: 歩[ある]かないで.

ejercicios.pregunta: You want to say: “Nyan cooks while Tama reads.”
opciones: タマが 本[ほん]を 読[よ]んでいる 間[あいだ]、 ニャンは 料理[りょうり]を する。
タマが 本[ほん]を 読[よ]みながら、 ニャンは 料理[りょうり]を する。
タマが 本[ほん]を 読[よ]むたびに、 ニャンは 料理[りょうり]を する。
ejercicios.explica: These are two different people, so ながら won't do: it only works when the same person does both things. 間[あいだ] does allow different subjects. たびに would mean “every time Tama reads”, which is something else.

ejercicios.pregunta: You stayed at Grandma's all summer long, start to finish.
ejercicios.jp: 夏休[なつやす]みの ＿、 ずっと おばあちゃんの 家[いえ]に いた。
ejercicios.explica: The action fills the whole interval (note ずっと, “the whole time”), so it's 間[あいだ] without に. 間[あいだ]に would point to a single moment within the summer.

ejercicios.pregunta: The cake vanished at some point during Tama's nap.
ejercicios.jp: タマが 寝[ね]ている＿、 ニャンは ケーキを 全部[ぜんぶ] 食[た]べた。
ejercicios.explica: Eating the cake is one point inside the interval “while Tama sleeps”: 間[あいだ]に. ながら won't work because the sleeper and the eater aren't the same cat.
たびに follows the dictionary form: 会[あ]うたびに, “every time we meet”.

ejercicios.es: I lost the umbrella I'd just bought.
ejercicios.explica: 買[か]ったばかり behaves like a noun, so it links to 傘[かさ] with の: 買[か]ったばかりの 傘[かさ], “the just-bought umbrella”.

ejercicios.es: Living in Hokkaido, I grew to love the snow.
piezas: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に
ejercicios.explica: Verb in ている + うちに and a change at the end: your love of snow crept up on you, little by little, while you lived there.

lecciones.titulo: Sentences that describe: relative clauses
lecciones.resumen: You'll learn to put a whole sentence in front of a noun to say “the cat that eats fish” or “the shop where I bought the tea”, with no “that”, “who” or “where”: Japanese always describes from the front.

secciones.titulo: An adjective the size of a sentence

bloques.md:
In English, to describe something with an action you use a clause after it: “the cat **that** eats fish”, “the book **which** I bought yesterday”. Japanese has no word for that “that”. Instead, it uses the same trick as with adjectives: it puts the description **in front of** the noun.

You already know 赤[あか]い 猫[ねこ], “a red cat”. Well, a whole sentence can take the place of 赤[あか]い: **魚[さかな]を 食[た]べる 猫[ねこ]**, “a cat that eats fish”. The entire sentence 魚[さかな]を 食[た]べる works like a giant adjective stuck onto the cat.

**Sentence in plain form + noun**
The sentence ends in its verb (or adjective) and the noun it describes comes right after. Nothing goes in between: no “that”, no particle, no pause.

items.jp: 本[ほん]を 読[よ]んでいる 猫[ねこ]
items.es: the cat who's reading a book

items.jp: 昨日[きのう] 買[か]った 本[ほん]
items.es: the book I bought yesterday

items.jp: タマが 作[つく]った ケーキ
items.es: the cake Tama made

items.jp: 日本語[にほんご]を 勉強[べんきょう]する 人[ひと]
items.es: people who study Japanese

bloques.md:
To build one, start from an ordinary sentence: **タマが ケーキを 作[つく]った**, “Tama made a cake”. Pick the noun you want to talk about (ケーキ), take it out of its place and move it to the end. The particle it had (を) disappears, because it's no longer needed: **タマが 作[つく]った ケーキ**.

That whole block is now a noun like any other, so you can put は, を, が or whatever you need after it and drop it into a bigger sentence.

items.jp: タマが 作[つく]った ケーキは おいしい。
items.es: The cake Tama made is delicious.

items.jp: ポンさんが 売[う]っている お 茶[ちゃ]を 買[か]った。
items.es: I bought the tea Pon sells.

items.jp: 赤[あか]い 帽子[ぼうし]を かぶっている 猫[ねこ]が カゲです。
items.es: The cat wearing the red hat is Kage.
items.nota: Everything before 猫[ねこ] describes it; after it come が and the rest of the sentence.

secciones.titulo: No “that”, no “where”, no “with whom”

bloques.md: English changes the linking word depending on the noun's role in the description: “the cat **that** sings”, “the town **where** he was born”, “the day **when** we met”, “the friend I went **with**”. Japanese marks none of that. The particle the noun had in the original sentence (が, を, で, に, と…) simply vanishes, and context supplies the meaning. English does something similar when it drops “that” (“the book I bought”), but Japanese takes it all the way.

filas: 猫[ねこ]が 歌[うた]う
ニャンが ケーキを 食[た]べた
ニャンが 食[た]べた ケーキ
ニャンが その 町[まち]で 生[う]まれた
ニャンが 生[う]まれた 町[まち]
the town where Nyan was born
その 日[ひ]に 初[はじ]めて 会[あ]った
初[はじ]めて 会[あ]った 日[ひ]
友達[ともだち]と 一緒[いっしょ]に 行[い]った
一緒[いっしょ]に 行[い]った 友達[ともだち]

bloques.md:
You'd think that would leave everything terribly vague, but in practice it's perfectly clear, because the verb and the noun already tell most of the story: a town is a place where you're born, not something you eat.

One of these nouns will pop up constantly: **時[とき]**, “time, moment”. It isn't a magic word meaning “when”; it's just another noun, and whatever comes before it describes it: 暇[ひま]な 時[とき] (when I'm free, lit. “free time”), 寝[ね]る 時[とき] (at bedtime), 子供[こども]の 時[とき] (when I was little).

Sometimes Japanese leaves open something English wouldn't. **話[はな]した 人[ひと]** can mean “the person who spoke” or “the person I spoke with”. A Japanese speaker resolves it from context, just as you know whether “a bank” is for money or for fishing by the river. If there's a real risk of confusion, just add the missing piece: わたしが 話[はな]した 人[ひと] (the person I spoke with).

secciones.titulo: Always plain on the inside

bloques.md: The verb in the description goes in the **plain form**, in whatever tense you need: present, past, negative, ongoing… Everything you know about plain forms applies here as is.

filas: 魚[さかな]を 食[た]べる 猫[ねこ]
魚[さかな]を 食[た]べた 猫[ねこ]
the cat that ate the fish
魚[さかな]を 食[た]べない 猫[ねこ]
the cat that doesn't eat fish
魚[さかな]を 食[た]べなかった 猫[ねこ]
the cat that didn't eat the fish
魚[さかな]を 食[た]べている 猫[ねこ]

bloques.md: No ます inside: ✗ 昨日[きのう] 買[か]いました 本[ほん]. Why? Japanese politeness is a tone applied to the whole sentence, and it goes on only once, at the end, because it's how you address the person listening. The description of the book isn't talking to anyone; it just describes. The right version is 昨日[きのう] 買[か]った 本[ほん]です: plain inside, polite at the end. In very ceremonious speeches a ます sometimes slips inside, but that's a special register; you stay plain.

The tense inside is independent: it's about the action being described, not the main sentence. **明日[あした] 着[き]る 服[ふく]を 昨日[きのう] 買[か]った**, “yesterday I bought the clothes I'll wear tomorrow”: inside is 着[き]る, tomorrow's action, and outside is 買[か]った, yesterday's. English works exactly the same way, so you're on home ground here.

secciones.titulo: が or の, but never は

bloques.md: If the description has its own subject, it takes **が**, not は: ニャンが 食[た]べた ケーキ. The reason is that **は** announces the topic of the whole sentence (“as for…”), and a description has no topic of its own: it's just one piece of a noun.
