Put は in and the listener thinks you're starting the main sentence: ニャンは 食[た]べた ケーキ… sounds like “As for Nyan, he ate, the cake…” and the sentence gets tangled.

items.jp: ニャンが 好[す]きな 食[た]べ 物[もの]は 魚[さかな]です。
items.es: The food Nyan likes is fish.
items.nota: The は is outside: the topic of the whole sentence is “the food Nyan likes”. The が is inside.

items.jp: ニャンは タマが 作[つく]った ケーキを 食[た]べた。
items.es: Nyan ate the cake Tama made.
items.nota: Two subjects, two particles: ニャンは for the big sentence, タマが for the description.

bloques.md: What's more, the **が** inside can turn into **の**: タマの 作[つく]った ケーキ means the same as タマが 作[つく]った ケーキ. It's very common in writing, in careful speech and in set phrases like **わたしの 好[す]きな 歌[うた]**, “my favourite song” (lit. “the song I like”). You can always use が yourself, but you need to recognise the の when you see it.

Switching to **の** works well when the description is short and has no object with を. If it does, the の would be read as possession: タマの ケーキを 作[つく]った 店[みせ] would sound like “the shop that made Tama's cake”. With を inside, stick with が: タマが ケーキを 作[つく]った 店[みせ], “the shop where Tama made the cake”.

secciones.titulo: With adjectives and nouns

bloques.md:
The description can also end in an adjective or a noun. You just need to remember how each type attaches to a noun.

**い-adjectives** go on as they are. They give rise to a very Japanese construction, “X が adjective” + noun, which matches our “with an adjective X”: **目[め]が 大[おお]きい 猫[ねこ]**, “a cat with big eyes” (lit. “a cat whose eyes are big”). Likewise: 足[あし]が 速[はや]い 犬[いぬ] (a really fast dog, like Kotarō), 髪[かみ]が 長[なが]い 人[ひと] (someone with long hair).

**な-adjectives** swap their だ for **な**: 魚[さかな]が 好[す]きな 猫[ねこ], “a cat who likes fish”. And **nouns** swap their だ for **の**: 医者[いしゃ]の 父[ちち], “my father, who's a doctor”. In writing you'll also see である in that slot: 医者[いしゃ]である 父[ちち].

filas: 目[め]が 大[おお]きい
目[め]が 大[おお]きい 猫[ねこ]
魚[さかな]が 好[す]きだ
魚[さかな]が 好[す]きな 猫[ねこ]
父[ちち]は 医者[いしゃ]だ
医者[いしゃ]の 父[ちち]
公園[こうえん]が 静[しず]かだった
静[しず]かだった 公園[こうえん]
学生[がくせい]じゃない
学生[がくせい]じゃない 人[ひと]

bloques.md: The な and the の only appear in the **present affirmative**. As soon as the description is past or negative, the usual plain form comes back: 好[す]きだった 歌[うた], 好[す]きじゃない 歌[うた]. And never ✗ 好[す]きだ 歌[うた]. Why? Because だ is the one form that can't sit right before a noun, so it disguises itself as な or の. だった and じゃない have no such problem.

secciones.titulo: Why the verb goes last (and how to read long sentences)

bloques.md:
Japanese has one underlying rule that explains almost everything: **the important part goes last, and whatever describes it goes first**. The verb closes the sentence; the noun follows its adjective; the owner comes before の and the thing owned after it. Relative clauses aren't an exception, just the same rule applied to whole sentences.

That's why a long Japanese sentence is like a Russian doll you open from the end:

items.jp: 昨日[きのう] タマと 行[い]った ポンさんの 店[みせ]で 買[か]った お 茶[ちゃ]は おいしい。
items.es: The tea I bought at Pon's shop, where I went with Tama yesterday, is really good.
items.nota: Open it from the end: お 茶[ちゃ], the tea ← 買[か]った, that I bought ← ポンさんの 店[みせ]で, at Pon's shop ← タマと 行[い]った, where I went with Tama ← 昨日[きのう], yesterday.

bloques.md:
A reading trick: when you see a plain-form verb followed directly by a noun, rather than by the end of the sentence, you've just come out of a description. Find that noun: it's the star, and everything before it is about it.

And a speaking trick: lots of Japanese questions are asked this way, by describing someone and asking who they are.

items.jp: ケーキを 作[つく]った 人[ひと]は 誰[だれ]？
items.es: Who made the cake?
items.nota: Literally, “the person who made the cake is who?”.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]で 行[い]きたい 所[ところ]は どこ？
items.es: Where in Hokkaido do you want to go?

items.jp: 日本語[にほんご]が 話[はな]せる 猫[ねこ]を 知[し]っています。
items.es: I know a cat who can speak Japanese.

lineas.jp: あそこで たこ 焼[や]きを 食[た]べている 猫[ねこ]、 誰[だれ]？
lineas.es: Who's the cat eating takoyaki over there?

lineas.jp: あれは カゲだよ。 去年[きょねん] 転校[てんこう]して 来[き]た 猫[ねこ]。
lineas.es: That's Kage. The cat who transferred to our school last year.

lineas.jp: ああ、 いつも ニャンと 喧嘩[けんか]している 猫[ねこ]？
lineas.es: Oh, the one who's always fighting with you?

lineas.jp: そう。 あっ！ あれは わたしが 買[か]った たこ 焼[や]きだ！
lineas.es: That's him. Hey! That's the takoyaki I bought!

ejercicios.pregunta: “a cat that eats fish”
ejercicios.jp: ＿ 猫[ねこ]
opciones: 魚[さかな]を 食[た]べる
魚[さかな]を 食[た]べます
魚[さかな]を 食[た]べるの
ejercicios.explica: The description goes in plain form and attaches straight to the noun. ます can't go in because politeness only comes at the end of the sentence, and の is extra: nothing goes between the description and the noun.

ejercicios.pregunta: “the cake Tama made”
ejercicios.jp: タマ＿ 作[つく]った ケーキ
ejercicios.explica: The subject of a description takes が. は would announce the topic of the whole sentence, and a description has no topic of its own.

ejercicios.pregunta: “a cat who likes fish”
ejercicios.jp: 魚[さかな]が 好[す]き＿ 猫[ねこ]
ejercicios.explica: 好[す]き is a な-adjective: before a noun, its だ becomes な. だ can't sit right before a noun.

ejercicios.pregunta: “my father, who's a doctor”
ejercicios.jp: 医者[いしゃ]＿ 父[ちち]
ejercicios.explica: With a noun in the present, だ becomes の before another noun: 医者[いしゃ]の 父[ちち].
Inside the description goes the plain form: 読[よ]んだ 本[ほん], “the book I read”.
静[しず]か is a な-adjective, so before a noun it takes な: 静[しず]かな 公園[こうえん].
The past of 行[い]かない is 行[い]かなかった: 行[い]かなかった 人[ひと], “the people who didn't go”.

ejercicios.es: the book I bought yesterday
ejercicios.explica: The whole description, 昨日[きのう] 買[か]った, comes first, and the noun it describes closes it off: 本[ほん].

ejercicios.es: Who's the cat sleeping over there?
ejercicios.explica: あそこで 寝[ね]ている describes the cat; that block becomes the topic with は, and the question closes the sentence.

ejercicios.pregunta: “the shop where I bought the tea”
opciones: お 茶[ちゃ]を 買[か]った 店[みせ]
お 茶[ちゃ]を 買[か]った で 店[みせ]
お 茶[ちゃ]を 買[か]いました 店[みせ]
ejercicios.explica: The で the shop had in the original sentence, 店[みせ]で 買[か]った, disappears when the shop moves to the end. And no ます inside a description.

ejercicios.pregunta: “my favourite song” (lit. “the song I like”)
ejercicios.jp: わたし＿ 好[す]きな 歌[うた]
ejercicios.explica: In a short description, the subject's が can become の: わたしの 好[す]きな 歌[うた]. が would also be fine.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which sentence is correct?
opciones: ニャンが 食[た]べた ケーキは おいしかった。
ニャンが 食[た]べました ケーキは おいしかった。
ニャンを 食[た]べた ケーキは おいしかった。
ejercicios.explica: The second puts ます inside the description, when politeness only goes at the end. The third says the cake ate Nyan.

ejercicios.es: This is the tea I bought at Pon's shop.
ejercicios.explica: The whole description, ポンさんの 店[みせ]で 買[か]った, goes before お 茶[ちゃ], and the final です makes the whole sentence polite.

lecciones.titulo: Giving and receiving: あげる, くれる and もらう
lecciones.resumen: Japanese has three verbs for giving and receiving, and which one you pick depends on which way the gift is travelling. With them you'll thank people for favours without saying “thank you”, and ask for help in just the right tone, from your mate to your teacher.

secciones.titulo: Three verbs for “give”

bloques.md:
In English, “give” works for everything: I give you, you give me, she gives him. In Japanese, **the direction** of the gift matters a lot, and above all whether it's coming **towards you** or moving away from you. Picture a circle around yourself: inside are you and yours (your family, your close group); outside is everyone else.

- If something leaves the circle heading out, or passes between two outsiders, it's **あげる**.
- If something enters your circle from outside, it's **くれる**.
- And if you tell it from the receiver's side (“I received”), it's **もらう**.

filas: From me outwards, or between others
わたしは タマに 本[ほん]を あげた。
From someone else to me (or mine)
タマが わたしに 本[ほん]を くれた。
わたしは タマに 本[ほん]を もらった。
I got a book from Tama.

bloques.md: Why so much fuss over something so simple? Because in Japanese, giving and receiving isn't just moving an object around: it's a relationship. With **くれる** you acknowledge that someone has been generous to you; with **あげる** you describe a gesture of your own. Picking the wrong one isn't just a grammar slip, it says something odd about who did what for whom.

secciones.titulo: あげる: what goes out from you

bloques.md: **あげる** is giving outwards. The giver takes は or が, and the receiver takes **に**. It also works for what other people give each other, because that gift doesn't enter your circle either.

items.jp: わたしは タマに 花[はな]を あげた。
items.es: I gave Tama some flowers.

items.jp: カゲに チョコを あげました。
items.es: I gave Kage a chocolate.

items.jp: タマは コタローに クッキーを あげた。
items.es: Tama gave Kotarō a biscuit.
items.nota: Neither of them is you: the gift passes between two outsiders, so it's あげる.

bloques.md: **あげる** never comes towards you. ✗ タマが わたしに 本[ほん]を あげた is a classic mistake. It's not that nobody understands it, but あげる pictures the gift moving away from the speaker, and when it lands in your hands Japanese makes you use くれる. It's like saying in English “Tama went to my house” instead of “Tama came to my house”: the direction is off.

secciones.titulo: くれる: what comes to you

bloques.md: **くれる** is the verb for gifts you receive. The subject is the giver (with が or は), and the receiver is you or one of yours. Since くれる already means “to me”, you usually leave out わたしに: it goes without saying.

items.jp: タマが マフラーを くれた。
items.es: Tama gave me a scarf.

items.jp: ポンさんが お 菓子[かし]を くれました。
items.es: Pon gave me some sweets.

items.jp: タマが 妹[いもうと]に 本[ほん]を くれた。
items.es: Tama gave my little sister a book.
items.nota: Your sister is inside your circle, so the gift “comes in”: くれる.

bloques.md: The other way round doesn't work either: ✗ わたしは タマに 本[ほん]を くれた. くれる always points towards you or yours, so you can't be the giver. If you're the one giving, it's あげる.

secciones.titulo: もらう: receiving

bloques.md: **もらう** tells the same story from the other side: the subject is the receiver. The giver takes **に** or **から**. に is the norm between people; から (“from”) works better when the giver is an institution, a company or something that isn't a specific person.

items.jp: わたしは タマに マフラーを もらった。
items.es: I got a scarf from Tama.

items.jp: カゲも タマから チョコを もらった。
items.es: Kage got a chocolate from Tama too.

items.jp: 学校[がっこう]から 手紙[てがみ]を もらいました。
items.es: I got a letter from the school.
items.nota: The school isn't a person: から sounds more natural than に.

bloques.md: Notice that **タマが くれた** and **タマに もらった** describe the same event. The difference is where the camera points. With くれた it's on Tama and her generosity (“Tama gave it to me”); with もらった it's on you and what you got (“I was given it, it's mine”). Both are equally correct and both sound grateful: the one thing you'd never do is tell it with あげる.

lineas.jp: 見[み]て！ この マフラー、 タマが くれたんだ。
lineas.es: Look! Tama gave me this scarf.

lineas.jp: ふん。 俺[おれ]も 昨日[きのう]、 タマに チョコを もらった。
lineas.es: Hmph. I got a chocolate from Tama yesterday.

lineas.jp: えっ……。
lineas.es: Huh…?

lineas.jp: 二人[ふたり]とも 友達[ともだち]だから、 あげたの！
lineas.es: I gave you both something because you're my friends!

secciones.titulo: Turning the respect up and down

bloques.md: Each of these verbs has a version for when you're dealing with someone above you (your teacher, a customer), and one has a rougher version too. They're used exactly the same way; only the level of respect changes.

filas: さしあげる when giving to someone of higher rank; やる to plants, animals or, bluntly, to people of lower rank
くださる when someone of higher rank gives you something
いただく when you receive from someone of higher rank

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]が 辞書[じしょ]を くださいました。
items.es: My teacher gave me a dictionary.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]に 辞書[じしょ]を いただきました。
items.es: I received a dictionary from my teacher.

items.jp: 毎朝[まいあさ]、 花[はな]に 水[みず]を やる。
items.es: I water the flowers every morning.
items.nota: Literally “I give water to the flowers”. Many people say あげる here out of affection; you'll hear both.

bloques.md: Two details you'll love. First: **くださる** makes its ます form as くださいます (not くださります), and its command form is… **ください**. So every time you say ください, you're literally saying “kindly give it to me”. Second: the **いただきます** people say before eating is いただく, “to receive humbly”: you're giving thanks for the food you're receiving.

With people, **やる** sounds blunt or condescending, like “here, have this”. You'll hear it among boys who are very close, but don't use it with people yourself. With plants and animals, on the other hand, it's perfectly normal.

secciones.titulo: Doing favours: てあげる, てくれる, てもらう

bloques.md: Now for the best part. In Japanese you don't just give things: you give **actions** too. Put a verb in the て form before あげる, くれる or もらう, and what's being given is that action, in other words a favour. The directions are exactly the same as before.

filas: タマに 傘[かさ]を 貸[か]してあげた。 (I lent Tama my umbrella.)
タマが 宿題[しゅくだい]を 手伝[てつだ]ってくれた。 (Tama helped me with my homework.)
I receive someone's favour (often because I asked)
タマに 宿題[しゅくだい]を 手伝[てつだ]ってもらった。 (I got Tama to help me with my homework.)

bloques.md:
**〜てくれる** is the most important one for you, because it's the Japanese way of being grateful. Japanese speakers mark it all the time: タマが 手伝[てつだ]ってくれた. If you just say タマが 手伝[てつだ]った, the sentence is correct but sounds like a police report, cold, as if you didn't care. With くれた, the thanks come built in.

**〜てもらう** is grateful too, but it puts the focus on you as the receiver, and often implies you asked for it. That's why it's the natural way to talk about services: 髪[かみ]を 切[き]ってもらった (I had my hair cut), 医者[いしゃ]に 診[み]てもらう (to get checked by a doctor). The person doing the favour takes **に**.

items.jp: ポンさんが 安[やす]く してくれた。
items.es: Pon gave me a discount (how kind).

items.jp: ポンさんに 安[やす]く してもらった。
items.es: I got Pon to give me a discount.

items.jp: カゲが 道[みち]を 教[おし]えてくれた。
items.es: Kage showed me the way.
items.nota: Deep down, he's a good sort.

items.jp: コタローの 散歩[さんぽ]に 行[い]ってあげた。
items.es: I took Kotarō for a walk (as a favour).

bloques.md: Be careful with **〜てあげる** in front of the person you're helping, especially someone of higher rank. 先生[せんせい]、 荷物[にもつ]を 持[も]ってあげます sounds like “Sensei, I'll do you the favour of carrying your bag”: you put yourself above them, as if granting a kindness. To offer help, the natural thing is 持[も]ちましょうか, “shall I carry it?”. Even among friends, using てあげる a lot sounds like you're keeping score of what you do for people.

secciones.titulo: Asking favours, step by step

bloques.md: To ask a favour, you turn these verbs into a question. And here Japanese has a whole staircase of politeness: each step is a little softer, more indirect and more respectful than the one before.

filas: 手伝[てつだ]ってくれる？
手伝[てつだ]ってくれない？
手伝[てつだ]ってもらえる？
手伝[てつだ]ってください
Strangers, shops; best for simple things
手伝[てつだ]ってくれませんか
手伝[てつだ]ってもらえませんか
手伝[てつだ]っていただけませんか

bloques.md:
Why does the **negative** sound softer? Because asking “won't you help me?” assumes the other person might say no, and leaves the door open for them. “Will you help me?” pushes a bit harder: it expects a yes. English does something similar with “I don't suppose you could give me a hand?”.

And why does **もらえる** sound softer than **くれる**? くれる asks about the other person's will (“will you give me this?”). もらえる is the potential form of もらう, “to be able to receive”, so the question becomes about you: “could I receive this favour?”. Talking about your own possibility instead of the other person's will is more indirect, and in Japanese, indirect is polite. いただける is the same thing with the respectful verb.

**〜てください** isn't the most polite option, even though it looks it. It's polite in form, but it's still an instruction: “do this”. It's perfect in clear-cut situations (in a shop, giving directions), but to ask your teacher a real favour, 〜ていただけませんか is far more respectful, because you're asking rather than telling.

lineas.jp: 先生[せんせい]、 すみません。 もう 一度[いちど] 説明[せつめい]して いただけませんか。
lineas.es: Excuse me, Sensei. Could you possibly explain that again?

lineas.jp: いいですよ。 よく 聞[き]いてくださいね。
lineas.es: Of course. Listen carefully, now.

lineas.jp: タマ、 あとで ノートを 見[み]せてくれない？
lineas.es: Tama, could you show me your notes later?

lineas.jp: いいよ。 でも、 ケーキを おごってね。
lineas.es: Sure. But you're buying me cake.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama gave you a chocolate.
ejercicios.jp: タマが わたしに チョコを ＿。
ejercicios.explica: The gift comes into your circle, so it's くれる. あげる always goes outwards, and with もらう the subject would have to be the receiver.

ejercicios.pregunta: You gave Kage a book.
ejercicios.jp: わたしは カゲに 本[ほん]を ＿。
ejercicios.explica: You're giving, outwards: あげる. くれる can never have you as the giver.

ejercicios.pregunta: You got a scarf from Tama.
ejercicios.jp: わたしは タマ＿ マフラーを もらった。
ejercicios.explica: With もらう, the giver takes に (or から). The scarf already has を, and が would mark a different subject.
て form, 手伝[てつだ]って, + くれた: 手伝[てつだ]ってくれた, “helped me”, with the thanks built in.

ejercicios.pregunta: You received a book from your teacher (humbly).
ejercicios.jp: 先生[せんせい]に 本[ほん]を ＿。
ejercicios.explica: Receiving respectfully is いただく, the humble version of もらう. くださる would need the teacher as subject, with 先生[せんせい]が, and さしあげる would mean you gave her something.

ejercicios.pregunta: Your teacher gave you a book.
ejercicios.jp: 先生[せんせい]が 本[ほん]を ＿。
ejercicios.explica: The teacher is the subject, 先生[せんせい]が, and the gift comes to you: くれる, in its respectful form くださる.

ejercicios.pregunta: You water the flowers every morning.
ejercicios.jp: 毎朝[まいあさ]、 花[はな]に 水[みず]を ＿。
ejercicios.explica: With plants and animals, やる is the traditional choice (あげる is common too). くれる and くださる would mean the flowers were giving something to you.

ejercicios.pregunta: Your friend helped you without being asked. How kind!
opciones: 友達[ともだち]が 手伝[てつだ]ってくれた。
友達[ともだち]が 手伝[てつだ]ってあげた。
友達[ともだち]が 手伝[てつだ]った。
ejercicios.explica: てくれた captures the favour coming your way and has the gratitude built in. てあげた would say they helped someone else, and plain 手伝[てつだ]った is correct but cold.

ejercicios.es: Could you lend me your umbrella? (polite)
ejercicios.explica: て form of the favour, 貸[か]して, + もらえませんか: you ask whether you could receive the favour, which is gentler than asking for it outright.
て form, 貸[か]して, + くれない: 貸[か]してくれない？, the soft casual request, perfect with friends.

ejercicios.pregunta: You ask Fukuro-sensei to explain it again.
ejercicios.jp: 先生[せんせい]、 もう 一度[いちど] 説明[せつめい]して＿。
ejercicios.explica: With your teacher, go for the top step: いただけませんか, a negative question with the humble verb. くれない is for friends, and あげませんか would get the direction of the favour backwards.

ejercicios.es: I got Pon to give me a discount.
ejercicios.explica: With てもらう, the person doing the favour takes に, ポンさんに, and you're the one receiving it: 安[やす]く してもらった.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which is the better way to offer to carry your teacher's bag?
opciones: 先生[せんせい]、 荷物[にもつ]を 持[も]ちましょうか。
先生[せんせい]、 荷物[にもつ]を 持[も]ってあげます。
先生[せんせい]、 荷物[にもつ]を 持[も]ってくれます。
ejercicios.explica: てあげる in front of the person you're helping, especially someone of higher rank, sounds like you're granting a kindness. ましょうか offers without putting yourself above them. てくれます would mean she carries something for you.

lecciones.titulo: Open it or it opens: transitive and intransitive verbs
lecciones.resumen: Japanese has pairs of verbs: one for when someone does something, like ドアを 開[あ]ける, and one for when something just happens, like ドアが 開[あ]く. You'll learn the most useful pairs, how to pick the right particle, and how to apologise properly when a cup gets broken.

secciones.titulo: One scene, two verbs

bloques.md:
Look at these two sentences: “Nyan opens the door” and “the door opens”. In the first, someone is acting; in the second, the door opens and that's that, we don't know (or care) who did it. English uses the very same verb for both. Japanese, on the other hand, uses **two different verbs**:

- **開[あ]ける**: someone opens something. It's **transitive**: the action passes from someone to a thing, which takes **を**.
- **開[あ]く**: something opens. It's **intransitive**: nobody is acting on the thing; the thing is the subject and takes **が**.

items.jp: ニャンが ドアを 開[あ]けた。
items.es: Nyan opened the door.
items.nota: There's someone acting (Nyan) and something being acted on (the door, with を).

items.jp: ドアが 開[あ]いた。
items.es: The door opened.
items.nota: There's only the door, with が. Maybe the wind opened it, or a ghost.

items.jp: タマが 電気[でんき]を つけた。
items.es: Tama switched on the light.

items.jp: 電気[でんき]が ついた。
items.es: The light came on.

bloques.md: Think of them as a pair of actors sharing the same scene. The transitive is the version with a culprit: someone made it happen. The intransitive is the version without one: it happened. Japanese leans heavily on the second, as you'll see at the end of the lesson, because it often prefers to describe what happens rather than point at who did it.

secciones.titulo: The pairs you'll use most

bloques.md: Not every verb has a partner (eating or going don't need one), but a huge number of everyday verbs do. These are the ones you'll meet every day. Learn them two at a time, like socks: a transitive on its own isn't much use if you don't know its partner.

filas: switch off, erase / go out, disappear

bloques.md: Notice that English sometimes uses two different verbs where Japanese has a pair (put in / go in, drop / fall), and sometimes one verb for both (open, close, change). So don't rely on the translation to choose: always ask yourself **whether someone is acting on the thing or not**.

A note on **終[お]わる**: although it's the intransitive of its pair, in conversation plenty of people also use it transitively, as in 仕事[しごと]を 終[お]わる. 終[お]える sounds more formal. So if you hear it with を, it's not that you got it wrong: spoken Japanese is just flexible with this verb.

secciones.titulo: Clues for spotting them

bloques.md: There's no rule that always works, but there are a few shape clues that are right almost every time **within a pair**:

**1. The one ending in -aru is the intransitive.** 閉[し]まる, 始[はじ]まる, 止[と]まる, 決[き]まる, 変[か]わる, 見[み]つかる, 集[あつ]まる, 終[お]わる. Its partner usually ends in -eru: 閉[し]める, 始[はじ]める…
**2. The one ending in -su is the transitive.** 出[だ]す, 消[け]す, 落[お]とす, 起[お]こす, 壊[こわ]す, 直[なお]す. Their partners happen by themselves: 出[で]る, 消[き]える, 落[お]ちる…
**3. The one ending in -reru is usually intransitive.** 壊[こわ]れる, 割[わ]れる: things that break on their own.

A plain -eru ending tells you **nothing**, and it's the most common trap: in 開[あ]ける, つける or 入[い]れる it's the transitive, but in 壊[こわ]れる or 割[わ]れる it's the intransitive. When in doubt, remember one example with its particle for each pair: ドアを 開[あ]ける, ドアが 開[あ]く. The particle will bring the rest back.

And a fun fact: the biggest pair of all is **する** (to do) and **なる** (to become), which work on exactly the same logic: one is what you do, the other is what happens. They have their own lesson, a little further on.

secciones.titulo: The particle gives the verb away

bloques.md: Since each verb in a pair comes with its own particle, the most typical mistake isn't the verb itself but the mix: a transitive with が, or an intransitive with を. To a Japanese ear they sound about as odd as “Nyan fell the cup” sounds to yours.

items.jp: ✗ ドアを 開[あ]いた。
items.es: Wrong: an object with a verb where nobody acts.
items.nota: 開[あ]く has no one acting, so it can't have an object. Correct: ドアが 開[あ]いた, or ドアを 開[あ]けた.

items.jp: ✗ 電気[でんき]が 消[け]した。
items.es: Wrong: the light can't switch anything off.
items.nota: 消[け]す needs someone to do the switching off. Correct: 電気[でんき]が 消[き]えた, or 電気[でんき]を 消[け]した.

items.jp: 授業[じゅぎょう]が 始[はじ]まる。
items.es: The lesson starts.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]が 授業[じゅぎょう]を 始[はじ]める。
items.es: The teacher starts the lesson.

bloques.md: A trap: some intransitive verbs of movement take **を**, like **家[いえ]を 出[で]る** (to leave the house) or **公園[こうえん]を 歩[ある]く** (to walk through the park). It's not a mistake or an object: that を marks the place you leave or pass through. The house isn't having anything done to it; you're leaving it. **入[はい]る**, on the other hand, takes **に** for the place you enter: 部屋[へや]に 入[はい]る.

secciones.titulo: Is it open, or has someone opened it?: ている and てある

bloques.md:
Pairs really shine when you describe how things are. With **ている**, an intransitive tells you the state something has ended up in: 窓[まど]が 開[あ]いている, “the window is open”. It's a snapshot: that's how the window is, no more information.

With **てある**, a transitive tells you someone left it that way **on purpose**: 窓[まど]が 開[あ]けてある, “the window is open (someone opened it, probably to let air in)”. Same snapshot, but now you can see someone's hand and an intention behind it.

filas: 窓[まど]が 開[あ]いている
The window is open (a state, nothing more)
窓[まど]が 開[あ]けてある
The window is open because someone opened it on purpose
窓[まど]を 開[あ]けている
Someone is opening the window (or keeps it open)
✗ 窓[まど]が 開[あ]いてある
Doesn't exist: てある needs someone who did it

items.jp: 部屋[へや]の 電気[でんき]が ついている。
items.es: The light's on in the room.
items.nota: You're just stating a fact: who left it on?

items.jp: テーブルに ケーキが 置[お]いてある。
items.es: There's a cake set out on the table.
items.nota: Someone put it there on purpose. For Nyan? Here's hoping!

items.jp: ポンさんの 店[みせ]は もう 閉[し]まっている。
items.es: Pon's shop is already closed.

bloques.md: ✗ 窓[まど]が 開[あ]いてある doesn't exist, because てある means “someone did it and left it like that”, and with an intransitive there's no someone. ✗ 窓[まど]が 開[あ]けている doesn't work either: it would say the window is opening something. Rule of thumb: **が + intransitive + ている** or **が + transitive + てある**.

secciones.titulo: Blame, luck and nobody in particular

bloques.md:
Japanese uses intransitives far more than English to report what happens: 電車[でんしゃ]が 止[と]まった (the train has stopped), 旅行[りょこう]の 日[ひ]が 決[き]まった (the date for the trip is settled), 鍵[かぎ]が 見[み]つからない (the keys won't turn up). You describe the event without pointing at anyone, and that sounds natural and polite.

But there's one moment when this habit turns against you: **when it's your fault**. If you break something that belongs to someone else and say 壊[こわ]れました, “it broke”, it sounds like you're dodging responsibility, as if the cup had decided to break all by itself. To apologise properly, use the transitive and own it: 壊[こわ]しました, “I broke it”.

items.jp: 財布[さいふ]を 落[お]とした。
items.es: I've lost my wallet. (I dropped it.)
items.nota: Transitive: you're the one who let it fall, even if by accident.

items.jp: あっ、 財布[さいふ]が 落[お]ちている。
items.es: Oh, there's a wallet on the ground.
items.nota: Intransitive with ている: you're describing what you see.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]、 すみません。 花瓶[かびん]を 割[わ]ってしまいました。
items.es: Sensei, I'm sorry. I've broken the vase.
items.nota: てしまう adds the “by accident”; you'll see it in its own lesson.

lineas.jp: タマ……。 コップが 割[わ]れた。
lineas.es: Tama… The glass broke.

lineas.jp: 割[わ]れたの？ それとも、 ニャンが 割[わ]ったの？
lineas.es: It broke? Or did you break it?

lineas.jp: ……わたしが 割[わ]りました。 ごめんなさい。
lineas.es: …I broke it. I'm sorry.

lineas.jp: 正直[しょうじき]で よろしい。 新[あたら]しいのを 買[か]いに 行[い]こう。
lineas.es: Good on you for being honest. Let's go and buy a new one.

ejercicios.pregunta: “The door opened.”
ejercicios.jp: ドア＿ 開[あ]いた。
ejercicios.explica: 開[あ]く is intransitive: no one is acting on the door, which is the subject and takes が. With を you'd need 開[あ]ける.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Nyan opened the window.”
ejercicios.jp: ニャンが 窓[まど]を ＿。
ejercicios.explica: Someone, Nyan, is acting on the window, which has を: that calls for the transitive 開[あ]ける.

ejercicios.pregunta: “The lesson starts at nine.”
ejercicios.jp: 授業[じゅぎょう]が 九時[くじ]に ＿。
ejercicios.explica: The lesson takes が and nobody in the sentence is starting it: intransitive, 始[はじ]まる. Clue: it ends in -aru.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Please switch off the light.”
ejercicios.jp: 電気[でんき]を ＿ ください。
ejercicios.explica: You're asking someone to act on the light, which has を: transitive, 消[け]す. Clue: it ends in -su.
Intransitive + ている describes the state: 開[あ]いている, “it's open”.
てある goes with transitives and says someone left it that way on purpose: つけてある, “it's been switched on”.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I've lost my wallet.”
ejercicios.jp: 財布[さいふ]＿ 落[お]とした。
ejercicios.explica: 落[お]とす is transitive: you let the wallet fall, so it takes を. With が you'd need 落[お]ちた.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I leave the house at eight.”
ejercicios.jp: 八時[はちじ]に 家[いえ]＿ 出[で]る。
ejercicios.explica: 出[で]る is intransitive, but with verbs of movement を marks the place you leave. It isn't an object: nothing is being done to the house.

ejercicios.pregunta: The window is open: someone opened it on purpose to let air in.
ejercicios.jp: 窓[まど]が ＿。
ejercicios.explica: A state plus someone's intention = transitive with てある. 開[あ]けている would say the window is opening something, and 開[あ]いてある doesn't exist because nobody does 開[あ]く.
The partner of 落[お]とす (to drop) is 落[お]ちる (to fall), and its past is 落[お]ちた.

ejercicios.es: My house keys won't turn up.
ejercicios.explica: 見[み]つかる is the intransitive of 見[み]つける: the keys are the subject (が) and “won't be found”. It's the most natural way to say it.

ejercicios.es: The light's on in the room.
ejercicios.explica: Intransitive つく + ている to describe how the light is, with が.

ejercicios.pregunta: You've broken your teacher's vase. Which sentence owns up?
opciones: 花瓶[かびん]を 割[わ]りました。
花瓶[かびん]が 割[わ]れました。
花瓶[かびん]が 割[わ]りました。
ejercicios.explica: The transitive with を says you broke it. 割[わ]れました says it broke, which sounds like dodging the blame. The third mixes が with the transitive and makes no sense.

lecciones.titulo: Can do: the potential form
lecciones.resumen: You'll learn to say what you can and can't do: read kanji, swim, eat natto… with the potential form and with ことができる. And you'll find out why “seeing” Mt Yōtei isn't the same as “being able to watch” a film.

secciones.titulo: A new verb that means “can”

bloques.md:
In English, to say you can do something you add a helper word: “I can read”, “I'm able to swim”. Japanese doesn't work like that. Instead of adding “can”, it **transforms the verb itself**: 読[よ]む (to read) becomes **読[よ]める** (to be able to read). It's a bit like English turning “read” into “readable”, except the result is a verb.

And that new verb is a perfectly ordinary one from the 食[た]べる group, so it conjugates like one: 読[よ]めない (can't read), 読[よ]めた (could read), 読[よ]めます (can read, polite).

Just like English “can”, the potential covers both **ability** (“I can swim”, I know how) and **circumstances** (“I can't swim today, it's too cold”). Both are 泳[およ]げる; context tells you which one is meant.

items.jp: タマは 泳[およ]げる。
items.es: Tama can swim.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 寒[さむ]くて 泳[およ]げない。
items.es: It's too cold to swim today.
items.nota: Same verb, but now it's about circumstances, not skill.

items.jp: この 漢字[かんじ]、 読[よ]める？
items.es: Can you read this kanji?

items.jp: やっと 読[よ]めた！
items.es: I finally managed to read it!
items.nota: In the past, the potential says you succeeded on a specific occasion.

secciones.titulo: How to form it

bloques.md:
**う-verbs**: the final u becomes e, then add る.
読[よ]む → 読[よ]める ・ 書[か]く → 書[か]ける ・ 話[はな]す → 話[はな]せる ・ 待[ま]つ → 待[ま]てる
泳[およ]ぐ → 泳[およ]げる ・ 遊[あそ]ぶ → 遊[あそ]べる ・ 帰[かえ]る → 帰[かえ]れる ・ 買[か]う → 買[か]える
**る-verbs**: drop る and add られる.
食[た]べる → 食[た]べられる ・ 見[み]る → 見[み]られる ・ 起[お]きる → 起[お]きられる
**Irregulars**: する → **できる** ・ 来[く]る → **来[こ]られる**

If you've got the negative form down, you're halfway there: う-verbs swap their last syllable for the “e” version of the same consonant (む → め, く → け, う → え), just as for the negative you swapped it for the “a” version (む → ま). And since the result always ends in -eru, every potential is a る-verb: that's why you conjugate it by dropping る.

Some verbs already have “can” built in and have no potential. **分[わ]かる** already means “to understand”, so “I don't understand” is 分[わ]からない, and ✗ 分[わ]かれない would mean something else, because 分[わ]かれる means “to split up”. **ある** has no potential either, nor do verbs that don't depend on you, like 降[ふ]る (to fall, of rain): rain doesn't “know how” to rain.

secciones.titulo: What you can do takes が (or を)

bloques.md:
With the potential, the thing you can do traditionally takes **が**: 日本語[にほんご]が 話[はな]せる, 漢字[かんじ]が 読[よ]める. Why が and not を? Because the potential turns the action into a **state**, an ability, just like 好[す]き or 分[わ]かる, which also take が. The Japanese idea is something like “Japanese is speakable for me”.

These days you'll also hear **を** all the time: 日本語[にほんご]を 話[はな]せる. Both are correct; が sounds a touch more classic, and を is more noticeable in longer sentences and in conversation. Other particles don't change: 一人[ひとり]で 行[い]ける, 駅[えき]まで 歩[ある]ける.

items.jp: ニャンは ひらがなが 全部[ぜんぶ] 書[か]ける。
items.es: Nyan can write all the hiragana.

items.jp: ポンさんの 店[みせ]で おいしい お 茶[ちゃ]が 買[か]える。
items.es: You can buy lovely tea at Pon's shop.

items.jp: この 道[みち]は 自転車[じてんしゃ]で 行[い]けますか。
items.es: Can you get along this road by bike?

items.jp: わたしには 無理[むり]。 そんなに 食[た]べられない。
items.es: Not me. I can't eat that much.
items.nota: には marks the person for whom something is or isn't possible, with a hint of contrast (“me, personally…”).

secciones.titulo: The forms without ら: 食べれる

bloques.md:
Out and about you'll hear **食[た]べれる**, **見[み]れる**, **来[こ]れる** over and over, without the ら. This “ら-less” form is very widespread in everyday speech, especially among younger people, though people of all ages use it.

Why did it appear? Because られる has several jobs in Japanese (it also forms the passive and a kind of respectful language, which you'll meet later), and dropping the ら makes the potential shorter and unambiguous. It also matches the う-verb pattern: 読[よ]める, 帰[かえ]れる… 食[た]べれる.

Even though you hear it everywhere, exams, formal writing, job interviews and careful speech expect the form with ら, and some people find the other one sloppy. So: **say 食[た]べられる yourself, and recognise 食[た]べれる** when you hear it. And note that this only affects る-verbs and 来[く]る: you don't add anything to う-verbs. ✗ 行[い]けれる or ✗ 書[か]けれる are mistakes.

secciones.titulo: Seeing and hearing: 見える and 聞こえる

bloques.md:
For seeing and hearing, Japanese has four verbs, and English actually helps here, because it also distinguishes “see” from “watch” and “hear” from “listen”. The key is whether the thing reaches you by itself or whether you have the chance to do it.

- **見[み]える**: something is in view, it reaches your eyes without you doing anything (“I can see…”). What's seen takes が.
- **聞[き]こえる**: a sound reaches your ears, whether you like it or not (“I can hear…”).
- **見[み]られる** and **聞[き]ける**: the regular potentials. You can watch or listen because the circumstances allow it: you have a ticket, it's on TV, you're allowed to (“I get to see…”, “I can listen to…”).

filas: ここから 羊蹄山[ようていざん]が 見[み]える。 (You can see Mt Yōtei from here.)
You get the chance to watch it
この 映画[えいが]は ネットで 見[み]られる。 (You can watch this film online.)
隣[となり]の 部屋[へや]から 音楽[おんがく]が 聞[き]こえる。 (I can hear music from next door.)
You get the chance to listen
この アプリで 日本[にほん]の ラジオが 聞[き]ける。 (You can listen to Japanese radio with this app.)

items.jp: もしもし、 聞[き]こえますか。
items.es: Hello? Can you hear me?
items.nota: You're asking whether the sound is reaching them. 聞[き]けますか would be “are you in a position to listen?”, which isn't what you want to know.

items.jp: 冬[ふゆ]の オホーツク 海[かい]では 流氷[りゅうひょう]が 見[み]られる。
items.es: In winter you can see drift ice on the Sea of Okhotsk.
items.nota: It's an opportunity the season offers on Hokkaido's northern coast: hence 見[み]られる.

items.jp: 眼鏡[めがね]が ないと、 よく 見[み]えない。
items.es: I can't see well without my glasses.

bloques.md: By the way, **見[み]える** has a second, very common use: “to look, to seem”. カゲは 怖[こわ]く 見[み]えるけど、 本当[ほんとう]は 優[やさ]しい, “Kage looks scary, but he's actually kind”.

secciones.titulo: 〜ことができる: the formal version

bloques.md:
There's another way to say “can”: the dictionary-form verb + **ことができる**. Literally, “the act of X is possible”. It means the same as the potential but sounds more formal and neutral, so it's what you'll see on signs, rules, leaflets and explanations: ここで 写真[しゃしん]を 撮[と]ることが できます, “you may take photos here”.

It's also a lifesaver: if you're not sure how to make a verb's potential, ことができる always works.

Dictionary-form verb + **ことが できる**
読[よ]む → 読[よ]むことが できる
泳[およ]ぐ → 泳[およ]ぐことが できない
行[い]く → 行[い]くことが できました

items.jp: 図書館[としょかん]では 本[ほん]を 三冊[さんさつ] 借[か]りることが できます。
items.es: You can borrow three books from the library.

items.jp: この 店[みせ]では カードで 払[はら]うことが できます。
items.es: You can pay by card in this shop.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]は 雪[ゆき]で 学校[がっこう]に 行[い]くことが できなかった。
items.es: I couldn't get to school yesterday because of the snow.

bloques.md: With ことができる, the verb inside is an ordinary verb, so it keeps its **を**: 漢字[かんじ]を 読[よ]むことが できる. The が belongs to こと. What you can't do is mix them: ✗ 漢字[かんじ]が 読[よ]むことが できる, because 読[よ]む, without the potential, doesn't take が for what's read.

And **できる** on its own, with an activity noun in front, means “to be able to do”: 料理[りょうり]が できる (I can cook), 日本語[にほんご]が できる (I can speak Japanese), テニスが できる. できる also means “to be done, to be ready”, which is what any Japanese grandmother calls out at mealtime: ご 飯[はん]が できたよ！, “dinner's ready!”.

lineas.jp: 俺[おれ]は 漢字[かんじ]が 五百字[ごひゃくじ] 書[か]ける。 お 前[まえ]は？
lineas.es: I can write five hundred kanji. What about you?

lineas.jp: わたしは…… 読[よ]めるけど、 書[か]けない。
lineas.es: I… can read them, but I can't write them.

lineas.jp: わたしは 納豆[なっとう]が 食[た]べられるよ！
lineas.es: Well, I can eat natto!

lineas.jp: 俺[おれ]は…… 食[た]べられない。
lineas.es: I… can't.

lineas.jp: やった！ カゲにも できない ことが ある！
lineas.es: Yes! There are things even Kage can't do!

ejercicios.explica: う-verb: the final u becomes e and you add る. む → め: 読[よ]める.
る-verb: drop る and add られる. You'll hear 食[た]べれる a lot, but the standard form is 食[た]べられる.
する is irregular: its potential is a different verb altogether, できる.
来[く]る is irregular: 来[こ]られる, read with こ. The ら-less version, 来[こ]れる, is casual.
The potential is 泳[およ]げる, a る-verb: drop る and add ない. 泳[およ]げない.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I can speak Japanese.”
ejercicios.jp: 日本語[にほんご]＿ 話[はな]せます。
ejercicios.explica: With the potential, what you can do takes が (を is also heard). The potential works like a state, just like 好[す]き or 分[わ]かる.

ejercicios.pregunta: “You can watch this film online.”
ejercicios.jp: この 映画[えいが]は ネットで ＿。
ejercicios.explica: It's an opportunity (it's available online), not something that just drifts into view: 見[み]られる. 見[み]える is “to be in view”, and 見[み]せる is “to show”.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I can hear music from the next room.”
ejercicios.jp: 隣[となり]の 部屋[へや]から 音楽[おんがく]が ＿。
ejercicios.explica: The sound reaches you by itself, without you doing anything: 聞[き]こえる. 聞[き]ける would be “to get the chance to listen”, as with an app or a ticket.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I can read kanji.” (formal)
ejercicios.jp: 漢字[かんじ]を 読[よ]む＿ できる。
ejercicios.explica: The formula is fixed: dictionary form + ことが できる. What's possible is “the act”, こと, and it takes が because できる works like a state.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I don't understand.”
ejercicios.explica: 分[わ]かる already has “can” built in and has no potential. 分[わ]かれない would come from 分[わ]かれる, “to split up”, and 分[わ]かられない doesn't exist.

ejercicios.es: You can pay by card in this shop.
ejercicios.explica: The place as topic, この 店[みせ]では; how, カードで; and the formal formula: 払[はら]うことが できます.

ejercicios.es: Kage can't eat natto.
ejercicios.explica: The person who can or can't takes は; what can be done takes が; and the negative potential goes at the end: 食[た]べられない.

ejercicios.pregunta: In a job interview, which sentence is the safest?
opciones: 朝[あさ] 早[はや]く 来[こ]られます。
朝[あさ] 早[はや]く 来[こ]れます。
朝[あさ] 早[はや]く 来[き]られます。
ejercicios.explica: In a formal situation, go with the ら form: 来[こ]られます. 来[こ]れます is the casual ら-less form, and 来[き]られます doesn't exist: the potential of 来[く]る is read with こ.

lecciones.titulo: Try it out or try hard: てみる and ようとする
lecciones.resumen: Trying natto to see what it tastes like isn't the same as trying to eat it and failing. Japanese splits these with two forms, てみる and ようとする, and by the end you'll know which one fits each situation.

secciones.titulo: Trying out isn't trying hard

bloques.md:
English uses one word, “try”, for two quite different ideas, but it quietly tells them apart with grammar:

- **Try doing** something, to see how it goes: try on some shoes, try a new dish, try calling someone. The action **gets done**; what you don't know is the result. That's **〜てみる**.
- **Try to do** something, with effort: try to get up at five, try to open a jar that won't budge. You have a goal; what you don't know is whether you'll manage. That's **〜ようとする**.

items.jp: 納豆[なっとう]を 食[た]べてみた。
items.es: I tried natto.
items.nota: You ate it to find out what it tastes like.

items.jp: 納豆[なっとう]を 食[た]べようとした。
items.es: I tried to eat the natto.
items.nota: You made an effort… and probably didn't manage.

bloques.md: The English “try doing / try to do” split is a great guide: “try calling her” (to see if she picks up) is 電話[でんわ]してみて, an experiment, not a struggle. So the question to ask yourself is: **is the action done to see what happens (てみる), or are you fighting to achieve it (ようとする)?**

secciones.titulo: 〜てみる: do it and see

bloques.md: **てみる** is the て form of a verb + みる, the verb “to see”. Literally, “do it and see”. It's the same idea as “give it a go and see” or “let's see how it turns out”. You do it out of curiosity, as an experiment, to check what something is like.

て form + **みる**
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて → **食[た]べてみる**
行[い]く → 行[い]って → **行[い]ってみる**
する → して → **してみる**
みる conjugates like 見[み]る: てみた, てみない, てみます, てみよう…

Here **みる** is written in hiragana, not as 見[み]る. Why? Because it no longer means “to look with your eyes”: it has become a piece of grammar that only adds “and see what happens”. In Japanese, when a verb loses its original meaning and works as a helper, it's usually written in kana. That's why 見[み]てみる (try looking) is perfectly normal: the first is real looking, the second is the “and see”.

filas: 新[あたら]しい 店[みせ]に 行[い]ってみる。 (I'll try out the new shop.)
着[き]てみたけど、 小[ちい]さかった。 (I tried it on, but it was too small.)
いつか 小樽[おたる]に 行[い]ってみたい。 (I'd love to visit Otaru one day.)
これ、 食[た]べてみて！ (Try this!)
もう 一度[いちど] やってみよう。 (Let's give it another go.)
先生[せんせい]に 聞[き]いてみたら？ (Why don't you ask the teacher?)

items.jp: この 靴[くつ]、 履[は]いてみても いいですか。
items.es: May I try these shoes on?
items.nota: A shop phrase worth its weight in gold. てもいいですか, “may I…?”, is covered properly later on.

items.jp: 分[わ]からない 時[とき]は、 辞書[じしょ]で 調[しら]べてみて。
items.es: When you don't know something, try looking it up in the dictionary.

items.jp: ラベンダーの ソフトクリームを 食[た]べてみたい！
items.es: I want to try the lavender ice cream!
items.nota: In Furano, in Hokkaido, it's a classic during lavender season.

bloques.md: てみる is often followed by けど and an unexpected result. That's its natural habitat: you tried something without knowing how it would turn out, and now you're reporting what happened. 食[た]べてみたけど、 辛[から]すぎた, “I tried it, but it was way too spicy”.

secciones.titulo: 〜ようとする: trying hard

bloques.md: **ようとする** is built on the volitional form, the “let's…” form you already know: 食[た]べよう, 行[い]こう, しよう. Then comes **とする**. The idea is “to set about doing something, to go for it with intent”. That's why the attempt usually **doesn't quite succeed** or gets cut short: if you'd simply managed it, you'd just say you did it.

Volitional + **とする**
起[お]きる → 起[お]きよう → **起[お]きようとする**
開[あ]ける → 開[あ]けよう → **開[あ]けようとする**
話[はな]す → 話[はな]そう → **話[はな]そうとする**
する → しよう → **しようとする** ・ 来[く]る → 来[こ]よう → **来[こ]ようとする**

items.jp: 五時[ごじ]に 起[お]きようとしたけど、 起[お]きられなかった。
items.es: I tried to get up at five, but I couldn't.

items.jp: コタローは 瓶[びん]の ふたを 開[あ]けようとしている。
items.es: Kotarō is trying to get the lid off the jar.
items.nota: With ている: he's trying right now, with all his might (and all his hunger).

items.jp: カゲに 話[はな]そうとしたけど、 恥[は]ずかしくて 言[い]えなかった。
items.es: I tried to talk to Kage, but I got embarrassed and couldn't say it.

bloques.md: In the negative, **〜ようとしない** is very expressive: it means someone **won't even try**, that they refuse. It's the Japanese way of grumbling about someone else's stubbornness.

items.jp: カゲは 全然[ぜんぜん] 謝[あやま]ろうとしない。
items.es: Kage has absolutely no intention of apologising.

items.jp: ニャンは 野菜[やさい]を 食[た]べようとしない。
items.es: Nyan refuses to eat his vegetables.

secciones.titulo: Just as I was about to…

bloques.md: **ようとする** has a second use: the moment when the intention is already in motion, **just before** the action happens. It almost always comes with 時[とき] and something that interrupts: “just as I was about to go out, the phone rang”.

items.jp: 出[で]かけようとした 時[とき]、 電話[でんわ]が 鳴[な]った。
items.es: Just as I was about to go out, the phone rang.

items.jp: 寝[ね]ようとしたら、 タマから メッセージが 来[き]た。
items.es: Just as I was going to sleep, I got a message from Tama.

bloques.md: With things that have no will of their own, like doors or the sun, ようとしている describes something **about to happen**, with a slightly literary feel: 電車[でんしゃ]の ドアが 閉[し]まろうとしている, “the train doors are about to close”; 日[ひ]が 沈[しず]もうとしている, “the sun is about to set”. Nobody thinks the door is “trying” to close: it's the action that's already on its way.

For an everyday “about to”, the most natural choice is still dictionary form + **ところ**: 今[いま] 出[で]るところ. ようとする is mainly for telling what happened at that very instant (ようとした 時[とき]…) or for describing scenes.

secciones.titulo: Try out or try hard? Side by side

filas: Yes: the unknown is the result
Not always: the unknown is whether you'll manage
✗ 食[た]べようとして (sounds odd)
てみない？: an invitation, “why not give it a try?”
しない: refuses to do it

items.jp: 早[はや]く 寝[ね]てみる。
items.es: I'll try going to bed early (and see if it helps).

items.jp: 早[はや]く 寝[ね]ようとする。
items.es: I try to get to sleep early (but it's hard).

bloques.md: You don't ask someone to “make an attempt”: ✗ 食[た]べようとしてください sounds very strange, because ようとする describes an effort, usually a failed one, not something you can hand out as a task. To encourage someone to try something, use てみてください. And don't confuse ようとする with **ようにする** (to make a point of doing something, as a habit), which looks very similar: you'll meet it in the lesson on なる and する.

lineas.jp: いらっしゃい！ 新[あたら]しい お 菓子[かし]だよ。 食[た]べてみる？
lineas.es: Welcome! It's a new sweet. Want to try it?

lineas.jp: 食[た]べてみたい！ ……ん、 おいしい！
lineas.es: Yes please! …Mmm, delicious!

lineas.jp: コタローも 食[た]べてみて。
lineas.es: Kotarō, you try it too.

lineas.jp: もう 箱[はこ]を 開[あ]けようとしてる！
lineas.es: I'm already trying to open the box!

lineas.jp: あっ、 それは 売[う]り 物[もの]！
lineas.es: Hey, that one's for sale!

ejercicios.explica: て form, 食[た]べて, + みる: 食[た]べてみる, “try eating it”.
The て form of 行[い]く is irregular, 行[い]って; then みたい: “I'd like to go and see what it's like”.
して + みる: してみる, “try doing it”.
Volitional of a る-verb: 起[お]きよう; then とする.
Volitional of a う-verb: す → そう, 話[はな]そう; then とした.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan wanted to know what natto tastes like, so he ate some.
ejercicios.jp: 納豆[なっとう]を 食[た]べ＿。
ejercicios.explica: He ate it to see what it was like: that's trying out, てみた. ようとした would say he made an effort and maybe didn't manage.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan tried to get up at five, but couldn't.
ejercicios.jp: 五時[ごじ]に 起[お]き＿けど、 起[お]きられなかった。
ejercicios.explica: There's a goal and a failed attempt: ようとした. てみた would say he got up to see how it went, which clashes with “I couldn't”.

ejercicios.pregunta: Just as I was about to go out, it started to rain.
ejercicios.jp: 出[で]かけ＿ 時[とき]、 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]り 始[はじ]めた。
ejercicios.explica: ようとした 時[とき] marks the instant when the intention was already in motion, just before going out.

ejercicios.pregunta: Kage has no intention whatsoever of apologising.
ejercicios.jp: カゲは 全然[ぜんぜん] 謝[あやま]ろうと＿。
ejercicios.explica: ようとしない means someone refuses, won't even try. みない and ならない don't form this expression.

ejercicios.pregunta: The train doors are about to close.
ejercicios.jp: ドアが 閉[し]まろうと＿。
ejercicios.explica: With things that have no will, ようとしている describes something about to happen. The door isn't “trying” anything: the action is already on its way.

ejercicios.es: I tried asking the teacher.
ejercicios.explica: Who you ask, 先生[せんせい]に; then the て form, 聞[き]いて; and みました for the “and see what she says”.

ejercicios.es: I want to go to Otaru (and see what it's like).
ejercicios.explica: て form + みたい: you'd like to go and see what it's like.

ejercicios.pregunta: Pon offers you a new sweet. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: 新[あたら]しい お 菓子[かし]です。 ＿。
opciones: 食[た]べてみてください
食[た]べようとしてください
食[た]べてみようとしてください
ejercicios.explica: To invite someone to try something, use てみてください. ようとする describes an effortful attempt, usually a failed one, and isn't something you ask of people.

lecciones.titulo: Becoming, deciding and making sure: なる and する
lecciones.resumen: なる is what happens and する is what you decide. With that pair you'll say you're over your cold, that you'll have tea, that you've decided to study every day, that you're being moved to Sapporo, and that you can finally read kanji.

secciones.titulo: What happens and what you do

bloques.md:
If you've seen the lesson on transitive and intransitive verbs, this will sound familiar. **なる** and **する** are the most important pair in Japanese. なる is “to become”: a change that **happens**, with nobody pushing it. する is “to do”: something **you cause or decide**.

This whole lesson is that one idea repeated across three pairs. In each, the なる version reports a result, something that happened or that circumstances decided; the する version reports your will.

filas: 〜にする: to choose, to make something be
〜ようになる: to come to (be able to, do)
〜ようにする: to make sure to

secciones.titulo: Becoming: になる and くなる

bloques.md: English has a whole range of words for change: to “get” nervous, to “grow” old, to “go” mad, to “become” a doctor, to “turn” twenty. Japanese handles nearly all of it with **なる**. The only thing that changes is how it hooks onto what comes before.

**Noun + に なる**: 先生[せんせい]に なる, 春[はる]に なる
**な-adjective + に なる**: 元気[げんき]に なる, 好[す]きに なる
**い-adjective: い → く + なる**: 寒[さむ]い → 寒[さむ]く なる
いい → **よく なる** ・ ない → **なく なる** ・ 〜たい → **〜たく なる**

items.jp: タマは 先生[せんせい]に なりたい。
items.es: Tama wants to be a teacher.

items.jp: もう 春[はる]に なった。
items.es: Spring is here already.
items.nota: In Japanese, seasons and times “become”: 春[はる]に なった, 十時[じゅうじ]に なった.

items.jp: 来月[らいげつ]、 二十歳[はたち]に なります。
items.es: I turn twenty next month.

items.jp: カゲが 好[す]きに なった。
items.es: I've started to like Kage.
items.nota: 好[す]きに なる is “to come to like”: the fondness wasn't there before, and now it is.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]は 十月[じゅうがつ]から 寒[さむ]く なる。
items.es: Hokkaido starts getting cold from October.

items.jp: 風邪[かぜ]が よく なった。
items.es: My cold has got better.

items.jp: 時間[じかん]が なく なった！
items.es: We've run out of time!

items.jp: ケーキを 見[み]たら、 食[た]べたく なった。
items.es: When I saw the cake, I started wanting to eat it.

bloques.md: With い-adjectives, the い turns into **く**, just as when you use them as adverbs: 寒[さむ]く なる, not ✗ 寒[さむ]いに なる. Think of it this way: に is for nouns and な-adjectives, which can't conjugate on their own; い-adjectives already have their own form for hooking onto a verb, the く form. And remember that いい conjugates from よい: **よく なる**, never ✗ いく なる.

In shops and restaurants you'll hear **〜に なります** a lot where nothing is actually changing: こちら、 お 茶[ちゃ]に なります, “here's your tea”, or 千円[せんえん]に なります, “that'll be a thousand yen”. It's a politeness habit that softens things, as if the item “turned out” to be that. Some people find it grating because nothing is transforming, but you'll hear it constantly, so it's worth recognising.

secciones.titulo: Choosing and making: にする and くする

bloques.md: **〜に する** has two uses. The first is **choosing, deciding on**: literally “making the choice be X”. It's what you'll say in any café in Japan: コーヒーに します, “I'll have a coffee”. And the classic question between friends when ordering is 何[なに]に する？, “what are you having?”. It also works for dates, places and plans: 日曜日[にちようび]に しよう, “let's make it Sunday”.

lineas.jp: 何[なに]に する？
lineas.es: What are you having?

lineas.jp: わたしは ケーキと 紅茶[こうちゃ]に する。
lineas.es: I'll have cake and a tea.

lineas.jp: また ケーキ？ じゃあ、 わたしは パフェに しようかな。
lineas.es: Cake again? Then I think I'll go for a parfait.

lineas.jp: パフェも いいね……。 やっぱり 両方[りょうほう]に する！
lineas.es: The parfait looks good too… Actually, I'll have both!

bloques.md: The second use is **making something become a certain way**. It's the transitive of なる: you change something yourself, on purpose. It's formed the same way (noun or な-adjective + に; い-adjective with く), but with する, and with the thing being changed marked by を.

items.jp: 部屋[へや]を きれいに した。
items.es: I tidied up the room.
items.nota: Compare: 部屋[へや]が きれいに なった, “the room got tidy”, without saying who did it.

items.jp: テレビの 音[おと]を 小[ちい]さく して。
items.es: Turn the TV down.

items.jp: 静[しず]かに して ください。
items.es: Quiet, please.

items.jp: ポンさん、 もう 少[すこ]し 安[やす]く して！
items.es: Pon, knock a bit more off the price!

bloques.md: Careful when ordering: ✗ コーヒーに なります means “I'm turning into coffee”. It sounds just as odd as it does in English, and a Japanese waiter will probably laugh. To order, always use **する**: you're choosing. **なる** is for things that change by themselves.

secciones.titulo: Deciding: ことにする

bloques.md: When what you're choosing isn't a thing but **an action**, you turn the action into a noun with こと and add にする: “to make my choice the act of…”, in other words **to decide to do something**. It's the most natural way to announce a decision of your own.

Verb in dictionary or ない form + **ことにする**
毎日[まいにち] 勉強[べんきょう]する → 毎日[まいにち] 勉強[べんきょう]する **ことに した** (I've decided to study every day)
お 菓子[かし]を 食[た]べない → お 菓子[かし]を 食[た]べない **ことに した** (I've decided not to eat sweets)

items.jp: 冬休[ふゆやす]みは 北海道[ほっかいどう]へ 行[い]く ことに した。
items.es: I've decided to go to Hokkaido for the winter holidays.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]から ダイエットする ことに しました。
items.es: I've decided to go on a diet, starting today.
items.nota: Nyan announces this every Monday.

items.jp: もう カゲとは 喧嘩[けんか]しない ことに した。
items.es: I've decided not to fight with Kage any more.

bloques.md: With **ことに している**, the decision has become a **personal rule**, a habit you keep up: 寝[ね]る 前[まえ]に 甘[あま]い 物[もの]を 食[た]べない ことに している, “I make it a rule not to eat sweets before bed”.

secciones.titulo: It's been decided: ことになる

bloques.md: Now the なる version: **ことになる** says something **has been decided**, but not by you, or at least not only by you: circumstances decided it, or the company, the family, the teacher. It's a result that comes to you, like everything with なる.

items.jp: 来月[らいげつ]、 札幌[さっぽろ]に 引[ひ]っ 越[こ]す ことに なった。
items.es: It turns out I'm moving to Sapporo next month.
items.nota: Maybe for work, maybe for family reasons: the point is it wasn't only up to you.

items.jp: 雨[あめ]で、 運動会[うんどうかい]は 来週[らいしゅう]に する ことに なりました。
items.es: Because of the rain, sports day has been moved to next week.

items.jp: わたしが クラスの リーダーを する ことに なった。
items.es: I've ended up as class representative.

bloques.md: An important cultural detail: many Japanese people use **ことに なりました** even for decisions they actually made themselves, especially in formal announcements. For example, 結婚[けっこん]する ことに なりました, “I'm getting married” (lit. “it has come about that I'm marrying”). Why? Because presenting it as the outcome of circumstances sounds more modest and less “me, me, me” than ことに しました. It isn't lying: it's a way of not putting yourself centre stage.

And **ことに なっている** describes a **rule or an arrangement** that already exists: 教室[きょうしつ]では 靴[くつ]を 脱[ぬ]ぐ ことに なっている, “you're supposed to take your shoes off in the classroom”, or 明日[あした]、 タマと 会[あ]う ことに なっている, “I'm meeting Tama tomorrow (it's arranged)”.

filas: Circumstances, other people (or I present it that way)
ことにしている: a rule I've set myself
ことになっている: it's the rule, it's arranged

secciones.titulo: Coming to: ようになる

bloques.md: **ようになる** describes a **gradual** change in what you can do or what you usually do: before, no; now, yes. It's perfect for talking about your progress in Japanese. In English we'd say “I can now…”, “I've started to…”, “I've got to the point where…”.

Verb (often in the potential) + **ように なる**
読[よ]める → 読[よ]める **ように なった** (I can read now)
走[はし]る → 毎朝[まいあさ] 走[はし]る **ように なった** (I've started running every morning)

items.jp: やっと 漢字[かんじ]が 読[よ]める ように なった！
items.es: I can finally read kanji!

items.jp: コタローは 泳[およ]げる ように なった。
items.es: Kotarō can swim now.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 住[す]んでから、 雪[ゆき]の 日[ひ]も 外[そと]で 遊[あそ]ぶ ように なった。
items.es: Since moving to Hokkaido, I've started playing outside even on snowy days.

bloques.md: Why isn't ✗ 読[よ]めるに なった enough? Because に なる needs a noun or an adjective in front, and 読[よ]める is a verb. ように is the bridge: it turns the action into “a state where I can read”, which can then “come about”. To say you've stopped doing something, the most natural form is **なく なる**: 食[た]べなく なった, “doesn't eat it any more”. 食[た]べない ように なった also exists, but it's less common.

secciones.titulo: Making sure: ようにする

bloques.md: And the last pair: **ようにする** is a conscious effort to **make something happen** or keep up a habit: “to make sure to”, “to make a point of”, “to try to always”. It isn't a one-off decision but an ongoing effort. That's why it very often comes in **ている**: you do it as a habit.

items.jp: 毎日[まいにち] 野菜[やさい]を 食[た]べる ように している。
items.es: I make a point of eating vegetables every day.

items.jp: 遅[おく]れない ように します。
items.es: I'll make sure I'm not late.

items.jp: 寝[ね]る 前[まえ]は スマホを 見[み]ない ように している。
items.es: I try not to look at my phone before bed.

items.jp: 明日[あした]は 遅[おく]れない ように して ください。
items.es: Please make sure you're not late tomorrow.
items.nota: Softer than 遅[おく]れないで ください: it doesn't forbid, it asks you to take care.

bloques.md:
Don't mix up three forms that look alike:
- **ことにする**: you make the decision (once).
- **ようにする**: you work at keeping it (every day).
- **ようとする**: you attempt something at one particular moment, often unsuccessfully (you saw it in the lesson on てみる).
毎日[まいにち] 走[はし]る ことに した (I've decided) → 毎日[まいにち] 走[はし]る ように している (I make sure I do) → 今朝[けさ]も 走[はし]ろうと したけど… (this morning I tried to, but…).

lineas.jp: ニャンさん、 漢字[かんじ]が 上手[じょうず]に なりましたね。
lineas.es: Nyan, your kanji have really improved.

lineas.jp: ありがとうございます！ 毎日[まいにち] 十個[じゅっこ] 書[か]く ことに したんです。
lineas.es: Thank you! I decided to write ten every day.

lineas.jp: それで 書[か]ける ように なったんですね。
lineas.es: So that's how you've learned to write them.

lineas.jp: はい。 寝[ね]る 前[まえ]に 必[かなら]ず 練習[れんしゅう]する ように しています。
lineas.es: Yes. I make sure I always practise before bed.

lineas.jp: でも、 練習[れんしゅう]の 途中[とちゅう]で よく 寝[ね]ているよね。
lineas.es: But you often fall asleep halfway through.

ejercicios.pregunta: “It's got cold.”
ejercicios.jp: 寒[さむ]＿ なった。
ejercicios.explica: 寒[さむ]い is an い-adjective: the い becomes く and hooks onto なる. に is for nouns and な-adjectives.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I'm feeling better.”
ejercicios.jp: 元気[げんき]＿ なった。
ejercicios.explica: 元気[げんき] is a な-adjective, so it takes に before なる.

ejercicios.pregunta: At the café: “I'll have tea.”
ejercicios.jp: わたしは 紅茶[こうちゃ]に ＿。
ejercicios.explica: Choosing is にする: you decide. 紅茶[こうちゃ]に なります would be “I'm turning into tea”.
な-adjective + に + する in the て form: 静[しず]かに して, “be quiet”, literally “make it quiet”.
い-adjective: い → く + なった. 大[おお]きく なった, “has grown”.
いい conjugates from よい: よく なった, “has got better”. Never いくなった.
Negative 食[た]べない; ない behaves like an い-adjective, so it becomes なく + なった: “doesn't eat it any more”.

ejercicios.pregunta: You're moving to Sapporo because of your parents' work.
ejercicios.jp: 来年[らいねん]、 札幌[さっぽろ]に 引[ひ]っ 越[こ]す＿ なった。
ejercicios.explica: ことになる reports a decision that comes from outside. ようになる would be a gradual change in habit or ability.

ejercicios.pregunta: It was your own decision: you'll study Japanese every day.
ejercicios.jp: 毎日[まいにち] 日本語[にほんご]を 勉強[べんきょう]する ことに ＿。
ejercicios.explica: If the decision is yours, ことにする. ことになった would sound as if it had been imposed on you (or as if you were being modest).

ejercicios.pregunta: “I can finally read kanji!”
ejercicios.jp: やっと 漢字[かんじ]が 読[よ]める＿ なった。
ejercicios.explica: A gradual change in ability is ようになる. に on its own won't do: なる needs ように as a bridge when there's a verb in front.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Make sure you don't forget your homework.”
ejercicios.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]を 忘[わす]れない ように ＿ ください。
ejercicios.explica: ようにする is putting effort into making something happen (or not happen). ようになる would be a change that comes by itself.

ejercicios.es: I've decided not to eat sweets at night.
ejercicios.explica: The negative action, 食[た]べない, becomes a noun with こと, and にした reports your decision.

ejercicios.es: Kotarō can swim now.
ejercicios.explica: Potential, 泳[およ]げる, + ように なった: he couldn't before, and now he can.

ejercicios.pregunta: You're modestly announcing at work that you're getting married.
ejercicios.jp: 結婚[けっこん]する＿。
opciones: ことに なりました
ように なりました
ことに なってください
ejercicios.explica: ことになりました presents the news as an outcome, without putting yourself centre stage: it's the usual formula. ようになりました would mean you've gradually got into the habit of marrying, and the third makes no sense.

lecciones.titulo: Saying and thinking: quoting with と
lecciones.resumen: With a single particle, と, you'll be able to report what someone said, what you think, and what you've heard on the grapevine. It's the Japanese version of quotation marks, and its casual cousin, って, turns up in every conversation.

secciones.titulo: と, Japanese quotation marks

bloques.md:
In English, to report what someone said or thought, the verb comes first and the content after: “Tama **said that** it was tasty”, “**I think** it'll rain”. In Japanese, as ever, the verb goes last. So the order is flipped: first what was said or thought, then **と**, and the verb at the very end.

Think of **と** as closing quotation marks: it shows where the quoted part ends. Everything before it is “the content”, and the verb after it says what was done with that content: saying it, thinking it, hearing it, writing it.

**What's said or thought + と + verb**
おいしい **と** 言[い]った (said it was tasty)
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]る **と** 思[おも]う (I think it'll rain)
北海道[ほっかいどう]は 寒[さむ]い **と** 聞[き]いた (I heard Hokkaido is cold)

There are two ways to quote, just as in English: word for word (**direct quote**, Tama said: “Yum!”) or reporting the content in your own words (**indirect quote**, Tama said it was tasty). Both use と.

secciones.titulo: Direct quotes: word for word

bloques.md: To quote the exact words, put them inside **「」**, the Japanese quotation marks, and add と after them. Inside the brackets everything stays exactly as it was said: if someone spoke politely, it stays polite; if they shouted, it stays a shout. No comma is needed before と.

items.jp: タマは 「おいしい！」と 言[い]った。
items.es: Tama said, “Yum!”

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]は 「 静[しず]かに してください」と 言[い]いました。
items.es: The teacher said, “Quiet, please.”

items.jp: カゲは 「 俺[おれ]の 勝[か]ちだ！」と 叫[さけ]んだ。
items.es: Kage shouted, “I win!”

items.jp: 日本[にほん]の 猫[ねこ]は 「ニャー」と 鳴[な]く。
items.es: Japanese cats go “nyaa”.
items.nota: Animal noises and sound effects are “quoted” with と too.

bloques.md: A very handy use: **と 書[か]いてある**, “it says…”, for reading signs and notes. 入口[いりぐち]に 「 禁煙[きんえん]」と 書[か]いてある, “the sign at the entrance says ‘no smoking’”. That's the てある from the lesson on transitive verbs in action: someone wrote it, and there it stays.

secciones.titulo: Indirect quotes: in plain form

bloques.md: In an indirect quote you report the **content**, not the exact words. So it goes without 「」 and with the sentence in **plain form**, even if the person spoke politely. Why? Because politeness is something you owe to the person listening to you now, not to the sentence you're quoting. So it goes on once, at the end, in your own verb: タマは 来[く]ると 言[い]いました, “Tama said she'd come”.

filas: タマは 「 明日[あした] 行[い]きます」と 言[い]った。
タマは 明日[あした] 行[い]くと 言[い]った。

bloques.md: Now for the detail that trips people up at first: if the quote ends in a **noun or a な-adjective**, you need **だ** before と. カゲは 学生[がくせい]**だ**と 思[おも]う, 静[しず]か**だ**と 思[おも]う. Why? Because と also means “and” and “with”. Without だ, 学生[がくせい]と 思[おも]う could be read as “think with the student”. The だ closes the sentence and makes it clear that と is the quotation mark. い-adjectives and verbs don't need it, because they already end in a complete form: おいしいと 思[おも]う, 来[く]ると 思[おも]う.

filas: 学生[がくせい]だったと
学生[がくせい]じゃないと

bloques.md: Don't put だ after an い-adjective: ✗ おいしいだと 思[おも]う. だ is only there to close what can't close itself, and い-adjectives are already complete. And don't forget it with nouns: without だ, the sentence wobbles.

secciones.titulo: と思う: what you think

bloques.md: **と 思[おも]う** is probably the most useful quote of all: “I think”, “it seems to me”. Japanese uses it constantly to soften opinions, because stating something flatly can sound blunt. Adding と 思[おも]います is like saying “in my view”.

items.jp: 明日[あした]は 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]ると 思[おも]います。
items.es: I think it'll snow tomorrow.

items.jp: この 答[こた]えは 違[ちが]うと 思[おも]う。
items.es: I think this answer is wrong.

items.jp: ポンさんの お 茶[ちゃ]が 一番[いちばん] おいしいと 思[おも]う。
items.es: I think Pon's tea is the best.

bloques.md: Plain **と 思[おも]う** is for **your own** thoughts. To report what someone else thinks, the norm is **と 思[おも]っている**: タマは ニャンが 犯人[はんにん]だと 思[おも]っている, “Tama thinks Nyan's the culprit”. Why? Because you can't get inside someone else's head: you can only describe the state they're in (“she's going around thinking that…”). You also use と 思[おも]っている about yourself for an idea you've held for a while, rather than something that's just occurred to you.

Two more details. To ask for an opinion, Japanese says **どう 思[おも]う？**, literally “how do you think?”, with どう, not 何[なに]. That's a false friend for English speakers: if you ask 何[なん]だと 思[おも]う？ you're asking something else, for someone to guess what a thing is. And when your thought is negative, English likes “I don't think it'll rain”, but Japanese prefers to put the negative inside: 雨[あめ]は 降[ふ]らないと 思[おも]う, “I think it won't rain”. 降[ふ]ると 思[おも]わない sounds more like you're contradicting someone.

secciones.titulo: と言う and と聞く

bloques.md:
**と 言[い]う** reports what someone said. When you're passing on a message, **と 言[い]っていた** (“was saying that…”, “told me that…”) is very common: it presents the message as something the person was going around saying, and sounds more natural than a bare past tense.

**と 聞[き]く** is “to hear that”: what you've been told. And since 聞[き]く also means “to ask”, with **か** before と it reports questions: 何時[なんじ]に 来[く]るかと 聞[き]いた, “I asked what time they were coming”.

items.jp: カゲが 明日[あした] 来[く]ると 言[い]っていたよ。
items.es: Kage said he's coming tomorrow.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 冬[ふゆ]は 長[なが]いと 聞[き]いた。
items.es: I heard winters in Hokkaido are long.

items.jp: タマに 明日[あした] 暇[ひま]かと 聞[き]いた。
items.es: I asked Tama if she was free tomorrow.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]は 宿題[しゅくだい]は ないと 言[い]いました。
items.es: The teacher said there's no homework.
items.nota: The best quote there is!

secciones.titulo: って: と in its slippers

bloques.md: Among friends, **と** very often becomes **って**, shorter and looser: タマが 来[く]るって 言[い]ってた, “Tama said she's coming”. And often the verb drops out altogether: **って** at the end of a sentence already means “she says”, “they say”: 明日[あした]は 休[やす]みだって, “apparently there's no school tomorrow”.

items.jp: カゲ、 今日[きょう]は 来[こ]ないって。
items.es: Kage says he's not coming today.

items.jp: 明日[あした] 雪[ゆき]だって！
items.es: They say it's going to snow tomorrow!
items.nota: With nouns, だ stays in front of って, just as with と.

items.jp: えっ、 何[なん]だって？
items.es: Huh? What did you say?
items.nota: Or, depending on the tone, “You what?!”

bloques.md: **って** is casual: perfect with friends, but with your teacher or in a shop, use と and the full verb. And remember the だ for nouns goes here too: 雪[ゆき]だって, not ✗ 雪[ゆき]って (that would mean something else, “this snow thing…”, a use of って you'll see in the lesson on という).

lineas.jp: ねえ、 カゲが 明日[あした]の 勝負[しょうぶ]は 中止[ちゅうし]だって。
lineas.es: Hey, Kage says tomorrow's duel is off.

lineas.jp: えっ、 本当[ほんとう]？ なんで？
lineas.es: Really? Why?

lineas.jp: お 腹[なか]が 痛[いた]いと 言[い]っていたよ。
lineas.es: He said he had a tummy ache.

lineas.jp: ふうん……。 わたしが 勝[か]つと 思[おも]ったから だと 思[おも]う。
lineas.es: Hmm… I think it's because he thought I'd win.

lineas.jp: カゲに そう 言[い]ったら、 怒[おこ]ると 思[おも]うよ。
lineas.es: If you say that to Kage, I think he'll get angry.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Tama said, ‘Thank you.’”
ejercicios.jp: タマは 「ありがとう」＿ 言[い]った。
ejercicios.explica: と is the closing quotation mark: it marks what's being quoted. を would treat the sentence as an ordinary object, which isn't how 言[い]う works with quotes.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I think Kage is a student.”
ejercicios.jp: カゲは 学生[がくせい]＿と 思[おも]う。
ejercicios.explica: With a noun at the end of the quote you need だ; otherwise と could be read as “with” or “and”.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I think this ramen is tasty.”
ejercicios.jp: この ラーメンは ＿と 思[おも]う。
ejercicios.explica: An い-adjective is already complete: it doesn't take だ. おいしいだ is a classic mistake.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Tama thinks Nyan is the culprit.”
ejercicios.jp: タマは ニャンが 犯人[はんにん]だと ＿。
ejercicios.explica: For someone else's thoughts, use と 思[おも]っている: you describe their state, since you can't be inside their head. And たい doesn't work for other people's wishes either.
静[しず]か is a な-adjective: it needs だ before と. 静[しず]かだと 思[おも]う.
With nouns, だ stays in front of って: 雨[あめ]だって, “they say it'll rain”.
With verbs, って goes straight after the plain form: 行[い]くって, “she says she's going”.

ejercicios.pregunta: “What do you think of these clothes?”
ejercicios.jp: この 服[ふく]、 ＿ 思[おも]う？
ejercicios.explica: To ask for an opinion, Japanese asks “how” you think: どう 思[おも]う. 何[なん]だと 思[おも]う would be “what do you think it is?”, for guessing.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I heard winters in Hokkaido are long.”
ejercicios.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 冬[ふゆ]は 長[なが]い＿ 聞[き]いた。
ejercicios.explica: What you heard is a quote: it takes と before 聞[き]く.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Cats go ‘nyaa’.”
ejercicios.jp: 猫[ねこ]は 「ニャー」＿ 鳴[な]く。
ejercicios.explica: Sounds are quoted with と too, just like words.

ejercicios.es: Kage said he'd come tomorrow.
ejercicios.explica: First who, then the content, 明日[あした] 来[く]る, the quotation mark と, and the verb of saying at the end.

ejercicios.es: I don't think it'll rain tomorrow.
ejercicios.explica: The negative goes inside the quote, 降[ふ]らないと, which is the most natural choice in Japanese; 思[おも]う closes the sentence.

ejercicios.pregunta: You pass on to a friend what Tama said: “Tama says she's coming tomorrow.”
ejercicios.jp: タマ、 明日[あした] 来[く]る＿。
ejercicios.explica: Among friends, って at the end already means “she says”. だって doesn't go after a verb (only after nouns), and a bare と leaves the sentence hanging.

lecciones.titulo: Called, the fact that, and what it means: という
lecciones.resumen: という is a Swiss Army knife: it tells you what something is called, sums up what a piece of news says, defines words and asks “what does… mean?”. And its short form, って, turns up in every conversation.

secciones.titulo: Where という comes from

bloques.md:
You already know that と marks a quote and that 言[い]う means “to say”. Well, **という** is exactly that: “that is said”, “called”. The underlying idea is to take a label, a name or a piece of content, and hang it on a noun.

When **いう** is used like this, as a piece of grammar, it's usually written in hiragana, because it no longer literally means “to say”. In conversation it almost always sounds like **ゆう**: とゆう. Don't be surprised to hear it that way.

filas: 「ポン 屋[や]」という 店[みせ]
雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]るという ニュース
the news that it's going to snow
「 猫舌[ねこじた]」というのは…

secciones.titulo: Naming: “a place called…”

bloques.md: The most basic use: **X という Y**, “a Y called X”. It introduces something your listener might not know: the name of a shop, a town, a person, a dish.

items.jp: 駅[えき]の 近[ちか]くに 「ポン 屋[や]」という 店[みせ]が あります。
items.es: There's a shop called “Pon-ya” near the station.

items.jp: ニャンという 猫[ねこ]を 知[し]っていますか。
items.es: Do you know a cat called Nyan?

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 美瑛[びえい]という 町[まち]が ある。
items.es: There's a town in Hokkaido called Biei.

bloques.md: The same piece, with no noun after it, is how you introduce yourself: **ニャンと いいます**, “my name is Nyan”. Best of all, you can use it to ask what something is called or how to say it, which is probably what you'll need most in Japan.

items.jp: これは 何[なん]という 花[はな]ですか。
items.es: What's this flower called?

items.jp: 「cat」は 日本語[にほんご]で 何[なん]と いいますか。
items.es: How do you say “cat” in Japanese?
items.nota: A sentence worth tattooing somewhere. Note that the question word is 何[なん], “what”, not どう, “how”, even though English says “how do you say”.

bloques.md: Don't use という for things everyone knows. If you say 東京[とうきょう]という 町[まち] to a Japanese person, it sounds as if you're introducing Tokyo to someone who's never heard of it, just as “a city called London” would sound odd said to a Londoner. という signals “this may not ring a bell”.

secciones.titulo: Giving the content: “the news that…”

bloques.md: Second use: attaching a whole sentence to a noun of **information** (news, a rumour, a story, a message, an idea) to say **what it's about**. In English we use “that”: “the news **that** it's going to snow”. In Japanese, that “that” is という: 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]るという ニュース.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]が 結婚[けっこん]するという 噂[うわさ]を 聞[き]いた。
items.es: I heard a rumour that our teacher is getting married.

items.jp: カゲから 「 明日[あした] 勝負[しょうぶ]だ」という メッセージが 来[き]た。
items.es: I got a message from Kage saying: “Duel tomorrow.”

items.jp: いつか 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 住[す]みたいという 夢[ゆめ]が ある。
items.es: I have a dream of living in Hokkaido one day.

bloques.md: Why isn't an ordinary relative clause enough, the kind you already know? Because they mean different things. 先生[せんせい]が 話[はな]した 話[はなし] is “the story the teacher **told**”: the sentence describes the noun from the outside. 先生[せんせい]が 結婚[けっこん]するという 話[はなし] is “the story **that** the teacher is getting married”: the sentence **is** the content. When the sentence is what the news, rumour or message actually says, you use という. English makes the same distinction: “the story (that) she told” versus “the story that she's getting married”.

With some nouns, like 話[はなし], という is sometimes dropped in conversation. With others, like ニュース or 噂[うわさ], leaving it out sounds odd. The practical rule: **with という you're never wrong**; without it, sometimes you are.

secciones.titulo: Defining and clarifying: というのは and ということ

bloques.md: Third use: defining words. **X というのは Y のことだ** means “X means Y”, literally “the thing called X is a matter of Y”. It's the formula teachers and dictionaries use.

items.jp: 「 猫舌[ねこじた]」というのは、 熱[あつ]い 物[もの]が 苦手[にがて]な 人[ひと]の ことです。
items.es: “Nekojita” (cat's tongue) means someone who can't handle very hot food.
items.nota: A word made for Nyan: cats wait for their food to cool down.

items.jp: 「 花見[はなみ]」というのは、 桜[さくら]を 見[み]ながら 食[た]べたり 飲[の]んだり する ことです。
items.es: “Hanami” means eating and drinking while admiring the cherry blossoms.

bloques.md: And **ということ** is for **summing up or rephrasing** what's been said: “so…”, “in other words…”. It's the Japanese way of checking you've understood, and it's very handy when the conversation is moving fast.

items.jp: じゃあ、 明日[あした]は 休[やす]みという ことですね。
items.es: So there's no school tomorrow, then?
items.nota: Literally, “so that means tomorrow is a day off, right?”.

items.jp: チケットが ないという ことは、 入[はい]れないという こと？
items.es: If we don't have tickets, does that mean we can't get in?

bloques.md: In writing, in dictionaries and headings, you'll also see **とは** with the same meaning as というのは: 「 猫舌[ねこじた]」とは…, “nekojita: a person who…”. It's drier and more formal; you won't need it in conversation.

secciones.titulo: って: the short version of everything

bloques.md: Among friends, almost all of the above gets shortened to **って**: it stands in for という, for というのは and for the と of quotes. It's used for naming, for asking what something is and, very often, for bringing up a topic to say what you think of it: “this… thing”, “you know X?”, “X, well, is…”.

items.jp: 「 猫舌[ねこじた]」って 何[なに]？
items.es: What's this “nekojita” thing?

items.jp: ポン 屋[や]って 店[みせ]、 知[し]ってる？
items.es: Do you know a shop called Pon-ya?

items.jp: カゲって、 本当[ほんとう]は 優[やさ]しいよね。
items.es: Kage's actually really kind, isn't he?
items.nota: って brings Kage up as the topic in order to comment on him: “as for Kage, you know…”.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 冬[ふゆ]って、 本当[ほんとう]に 寒[さむ]いの？
items.es: Are winters in Hokkaido really that cold?

bloques.md: って is for relaxed settings. With your teacher, use というのは or simply は: 「 猫舌[ねこじた]」は どういう 意味[いみ]ですか。 With friends, on the other hand, って sounds natural and warm; saying というのは all the time would make you sound like a walking dictionary.

secciones.titulo: What does it mean? And というか

bloques.md: To ask what something means, the go-to question is **〜って どういう 意味[いみ]？** (with friends) or **〜は どういう 意味[いみ]ですか** (polite). **どういう** means “what kind of”, literally “called how”: you're asking what sort of meaning it has. From the same family come **こういう**, **そういう** and **ああいう**: “this kind of”, “that kind of”, “that kind of (over there)”.

items.jp: 「よろしく」って どういう 意味[いみ]？
items.es: What does “yoroshiku” mean?

items.jp: えっ、 どういう こと？
items.es: Huh? What do you mean?
items.nota: For when something catches you off guard and you don't understand what's going on.

items.jp: わたしも こういう 店[みせ]が 好[す]き。
items.es: I like this kind of shop too.

bloques.md: False friend: **何[なん]の 意味[いみ]が ある？** doesn't ask what anything means. It means “what's the point?”, “what good is it?”, and it usually sounds like a complaint: 勉強[べんきょう]して 何[なん]の 意味[いみ]が あるの？, “what's the point of studying?”. To ask what a word means, always use どういう 意味[いみ].

And finally, **というか** (on the street, **っていうか**): “or rather”, “I mean”, “well, actually”. It's for correcting yourself on the fly or qualifying what you've just said. Young people also use it at the start of a sentence to change the subject abruptly, a bit like “anyway, the thing is…”.

items.jp: おいしい……というか、 最高[さいこう]！
items.es: It's tasty… actually, no, it's amazing!

items.jp: カゲは 怖[こわ]い……というか、 ちょっと 変[へん]。
items.es: Kage's scary… or rather, a bit weird.

lineas.jp: タマ、 「 猫舌[ねこじた]」って どういう 意味[いみ]？
lineas.es: Tama, what does “nekojita” mean?

lineas.jp: 熱[あつ]い 物[もの]が 食[た]べられない 人[ひと]の ことだよ。
lineas.es: It's someone who can't eat very hot things.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 わたしの ことだ！ ラーメンは いつも 冷[さ]ましてから 食[た]べる。
lineas.es: Then that's me! I always let my ramen cool down before I eat it.

lineas.jp: というか、 猫[ねこ]は みんな 猫舌[ねこじた]でしょ。
lineas.es: Well, actually, all cats are nekojita, aren't we?

ejercicios.pregunta: “Do you know a shop called Pon-ya?”
ejercicios.jp: 「ポン 屋[や]」＿ 店[みせ]を 知[し]っていますか。
ejercicios.explica: To name something they might not know: X という Y, “a Y called X”. With と alone, the piece linking the name to the noun is missing.

ejercicios.pregunta: Among friends: “What's this ‘nekojita’ thing?”
ejercicios.jp: 「 猫舌[ねこじた]」＿ 何[なに]？
ejercicios.explica: って is the short form of というのは: it raises the topic so you can ask about it. という on its own can't close off the topic before 何[なに].

ejercicios.pregunta: “How do you say this in Japanese?”
ejercicios.jp: これは 日本語[にほんご]で ＿と いいますか。
ejercicios.explica: You're asking for the word, which is what sits inside the quote: 何[なん]と いいますか. どう would ask “in what way” and doesn't fit with と.

ejercicios.pregunta: “What does ‘Nyango’ mean?”
