ejercicios.jp: 「ニャンゴ」って どういう ＿？
ejercicios.explica: どういう 意味[いみ] is “what kind of meaning”: the standard question about what a word means.

ejercicios.es: Do you know a cat called Kage?
ejercicios.explica: The name + と いう + the noun: カゲという 猫[ねこ], then を 知[し]っている.

ejercicios.es: I heard a rumour that our teacher is getting married.
ejercicios.explica: The sentence is what the rumour says, so it links to 噂[うわさ] with という, like the English “that”.

ejercicios.pregunta: “So there's no school tomorrow, then?”
ejercicios.jp: じゃあ、 明日[あした]は 休[やす]み＿ ことですね。
ejercicios.explica: ということ sums up or rephrases what's been said: “so that means…”. な can't follow the noun 休[やす]み.

ejercicios.pregunta: You want to ask what “nekojita” means.
opciones: 「 猫舌[ねこじた]」って どういう 意味[いみ]？
「 猫舌[ねこじた]」って 何[なん]の 意味[いみ]が ある？
「 猫舌[ねこじた]」って どう 意味[いみ]？
ejercicios.explica: どういう 意味[いみ] asks for the meaning. 何[なん]の 意味[いみ]が ある means “what's the point?”, and どう can't go directly before a noun.

ejercicios.base: 猫舌[ねこじた]というのは
ejercicios.explica: Among friends, というのは shrinks to って: 猫舌[ねこじた]って.
With a noun you can say 休[やす]みという こと or 休[やす]みだという こと: both are used.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Kage's scary… or rather, a bit weird.”
ejercicios.jp: カゲは 怖[こわ]い……＿、 ちょっと 変[へん]。
ejercicios.explica: というか corrects or qualifies what you've just said: “or rather…”.

ejercicios.pregunta: “the rumour that Pon is closing his shop”
ejercicios.jp: ポンさんが 店[みせ]を 閉[し]める＿ 噂[うわさ]
ejercicios.explica: The sentence is the content of the rumour, so it needs という. Without it, the sentence would be describing the rumour from the outside, which makes no sense here.

ejercicios.es: “Nekojita” means someone who can't handle hot things.
ejercicios.explica: X というのは, “the thing called X”, + the definition + の ことです: the dictionary formula.

lecciones.titulo: Only, nothing but and how far: だけ, しか, ばかり and ほど
lecciones.resumen: Japanese has three ways of saying “only”, each with its own attitude: the neutral one, the one that grumbles it's too little, and the one that grumbles it's too much. And with ほど you'll measure how far something goes, all the way to “the more I eat, the hungrier I get”.

secciones.titulo: Three ways to say “only”

bloques.md:
Imagine Nyan opens his wallet at Pon's shop and finds a hundred yen. He can say it three ways, and each one says something different about how he feels:

- 百円[ひゃくえん]**だけ** ある: “I've got just a hundred yen”. A fact, no drama.
- 百円[ひゃくえん]**しか** ない: “I've only got a hundred yen”. And it's nowhere near enough.
- And if Nyan always spends his money on the same thing, Tama will say: お 菓子[かし]**ばかり** 買[か]っている, “you buy nothing but sweets”. Too much of one thing.

All three can be translated as “only”, but Japanese never mixes them up, because each carries an attitude.

secciones.titulo: だけ: just that, full stop

bloques.md: **だけ** sets a limit: this and nothing more. It's neutral, so it works for good and bad things alike. It goes right after whatever you're limiting: a noun, a number or a verb.

After a noun; が and を usually disappear (or come after it): 水[みず]**だけ** 飲[の]む, タマ**だけ**が 知[し]っている
With other particles, before or after them: ニャン**にだけ** 話[はな]した (I told only Nyan)
After a number: 一[ひと]つ**だけ**
After a verb: 見[み]る**だけ** (just look)

items.jp: 朝[あさ]は コーヒーだけ 飲[の]む。
items.es: In the morning I just have coffee.

items.jp: この 秘密[ひみつ]は タマにだけ 話[はな]した。
items.es: I've only told Tama this secret.

items.jp: ケーキを 一[ひと]つだけ ください。
items.es: Just one cake, please.

items.jp: 見[み]ているだけです。
items.es: I'm just looking.
items.nota: Your survival phrase in any Japanese shop when an assistant comes over.

bloques.md: Two expressions with だけ you'll use a lot: **できるだけ**, “as much as possible” (できるだけ 早[はや]く 来[き]て, “come as soon as you can”), and **〜だけで**, “just by…”: 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 写真[しゃしん]を 見[み]るだけで 幸[しあわ]せに なる, “just looking at photos of Hokkaido makes me happy”.

secciones.titulo: しか〜ない: nothing but

bloques.md: **しか** also means “only”, but with one condition: the verb **is always negative**. Why? Because what it really says is “apart from this, there's **nothing**”. English has a close match in “I've got **nothing but** a hundred yen” or “I **don't** have **more than** a hundred yen”. And just like those, it sounds like it's too little, it won't do, you expected more.

items.jp: お 金[かね]が 百円[ひゃくえん]しか ない。
items.es: I've only got a hundred yen.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]は 三時間[さんじかん]しか 寝[ね]なかった。
items.es: I only slept three hours last night.

items.jp: カゲは 日曜日[にちようび]にしか 会[あ]えない。
items.es: I can only see Kage on Sundays.
items.nota: With particles other than が or を, しか goes after them: にしか, でしか, からしか.

items.jp: この お 菓子[かし]は 北海道[ほっかいどう]でしか 買[か]えない。
items.es: You can only buy these sweets in Hokkaido.
items.nota: Here しか isn't grumbling: it highlights that it's exclusive, that you won't find it anywhere else.

bloques.md: ✗ 百円[ひゃくえん]しか ある is a classic mistake. しか without a negative is like dropping the “no” from “I have no more than a hundred yen”: “I have more than a hundred yen” says the opposite. If the verb is positive, use だけ. And watch out for the opposite misunderstanding: しか ない doesn't mean you have nothing; it means you have that, and nothing more.

secciones.titulo: ばかり: nothing but (and enough already)

bloques.md: **ばかり** says something happens **so much** that it fills all the space: always the same thing, all the time, usually with a tone of criticism or fed-up-ness. It's every Japanese mum's favourite word. In conversation it very often sounds like **ばっかり**.

Noun + **ばかり** + verb: お 菓子[かし]**ばかり** 食[た]べる
て form + **ばかり いる**: 寝[ね]て**ばかり** いる (does nothing but sleep)

items.jp: コタローは 肉[にく]ばかり 食[た]べている。
items.es: Kotarō eats nothing but meat.

items.jp: ニャンは 休[やす]みの 日[ひ]は 寝[ね]てばかり いる。
items.es: On his days off, Nyan does nothing but sleep.

items.jp: ゲームばっかり してないで、 宿題[しゅくだい]を しなさい！
items.es: Stop playing games all the time and do your homework!

items.jp: 最近[さいきん]、 雨[あめ]ばかりだね。
items.es: It's been nothing but rain lately, hasn't it?

bloques.md: You've already met another ばかり in the lesson on ながら and ところ: **食[た]べたばかり**, “I've just eaten”. Don't get them tangled: after a verb in **た** it means “have just”; after a **noun**, or a **て form** with いる, it means “nothing but”. What comes before it always tells you which.

secciones.titulo: The three, face to face

bloques.md: See how the tone shifts in the same scene: Kotarō and his vegetables.

filas: 野菜[やさい]だけ 食[た]べる。
He only eats vegetables. A fact: maybe he's on a diet.
野菜[やさい]しか 食[た]べない。
He eats nothing but vegetables. And that seems too little, or odd.
野菜[やさい]ばかり 食[た]べる。
He eats vegetables all the time and nothing else. It's getting old.

bloques.md: A very handy pair for feeling the difference: **少[すこ]しだけ 食[た]べた**, “I only had a little bit” (don't worry, I didn't overdo it), and **少[すこ]ししか 食[た]べなかった**, “I only had a tiny bit” (and I'm still hungry). Same amount; different face. And if you want to stress even more that it's too little, you can stack them: 百円[ひゃくえん]**だけしか** ない.

secciones.titulo: ほど: how far something goes

bloques.md: **ほど** means “degree, the point something reaches”. It has three main uses, and all three are about measuring.

bloques.titulo: 1. A は B ほど〜ない: not as… as
bloques.md:
B sets the bar, and you say A **doesn't** reach it. That's why the verb or adjective is always **negative**.
東京[とうきょう]は 札幌[さっぽろ]ほど 寒[さむ]くない. (Tokyo isn't as cold as Sapporo.)
カゲは ニャンほど 食[た]べない. (Kage doesn't eat as much as Nyan.)

✗ 東京[とうきょう]は 札幌[さっぽろ]ほど 寒[さむ]い isn't said. ほど sets B as the ceiling, and the natural thing is to say A falls short of it. To say “as cold as” in the positive, you use 同[おな]じくらい, which you'll see in the lesson on comparisons.

Something + **ほど** + adjective or verb: you exaggerate the degree with an image.
泣[な]きたいほど うれしい. (So happy I could cry.)
死[し]ぬほど 疲[つか]れた. (I'm dead tired.)

Number + **ほど**: a rough amount, with a polite touch. It's similar to ぐらい, but sounds a little more careful.
十分[じゅっぷん]ほど 待[ま]ってください. (Please wait about ten minutes.)
And two everyday expressions: **それほど** and **そんなに**, with a negative, mean “not that much”, “not so”: この 問題[もんだい]は それほど 難[むずか]しくない, “this problem isn't that hard”.

secciones.titulo: 〜ば〜ほど: the more…, the more…

bloques.md: Finally, a lovely formula: **〜ば〜ほど**, “the more…, the more…”. You repeat the same verb or adjective twice: first in the ば conditional form, then in its normal form + ほど. Literally, “if you do it, to the extent that you do it…”.

You'll see the ば form (the conditional “if…”) properly later on; for this formula, this is all you need:
う-verbs: u → e + ば: 読[よ]む → **読[よ]めば**, 行[い]く → **行[い]けば**
る-verbs: る → れば: 食[た]べる → **食[た]べれば**
する → **すれば** ・ 来[く]る → **来[く]れば**
い-adjectives: い → ければ: 高[たか]い → **高[たか]ければ**, いい → **よければ**

items.jp: 食[た]べれば 食[た]べるほど お 腹[なか]が すく。
items.es: The more I eat, the hungrier I get.
items.nota: Nyan's philosophy of life.

items.jp: 日本語[にほんご]は 勉強[べんきょう]すれば するほど 面白[おもしろ]い。
items.es: The more you study Japanese, the more interesting it gets.

items.jp: 早[はや]ければ 早[はや]いほど いい。
items.es: The sooner the better.

items.jp: 考[かんが]えれば 考[かんが]えるほど 分[わ]からなく なる。
items.es: The more I think about it, the less I understand.

bloques.md: In conversation you'll also hear a shorter version, without the ば part: 練習[れんしゅう]するほど 上手[じょうず]に なる, “the more you practise, the better you get”. And with な-adjectives, なら is used instead of ば: 静[しず]かなら 静[しず]かなほど いい, “the quieter, the better”.

lineas.jp: ポンさん、 この ケーキ、 いくら？
lineas.es: Pon, how much is this cake?

lineas.jp: 三百円[さんびゃくえん]だよ。
lineas.es: Three hundred yen.

lineas.jp: えっ…… 百円[ひゃくえん]しか ない。
lineas.es: What…? I've only got a hundred yen.

lineas.jp: お 菓子[かし]ばかり 買[か]うからだよ。
lineas.es: That's what you get for buying nothing but sweets.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 今日[きょう]だけ 百円[ひゃくえん]で いいよ。
lineas.es: Go on then, just for today, you can have it for a hundred.

lineas.jp: ポンさん、 泣[な]きたいほど うれしい！
lineas.es: Pon, I'm so happy I could cry!

ejercicios.pregunta: “I've only got a hundred yen (and it's not enough).”
ejercicios.jp: お 金[かね]が 百円[ひゃくえん]＿ ない。
ejercicios.explica: With a negative verb and a complaint that it's not enough: しか. だけ with ない would mean “it's only a hundred yen that I don't have”, which makes no sense.

ejercicios.pregunta: In a shop: “I'm just looking.”
ejercicios.jp: 見[み]ている＿です。
ejercicios.explica: だけ sets a limit without complaint: you're just looking. しか would need a negative verb.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Nyan does nothing but sleep.”
ejercicios.jp: ニャンは 寝[ね]て＿ いる。
ejercicios.explica: て form + ばかり いる: doing that all the time, with a critical tone.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Tokyo isn't as cold as Sapporo.”
ejercicios.jp: 東京[とうきょう]は 札幌[さっぽろ]＿ 寒[さむ]くない。
ejercicios.explica: B ほど〜ない: B sets the bar and A doesn't reach it.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Kotarō eats nothing but meat (and it's a bit much).”
ejercicios.jp: コタローは 肉[にく]＿ 食[た]べる。
ejercicios.explica: Positive verb and criticism of excess: ばかり. しか would need 食[た]べない.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I only had a little bit (don't worry, I didn't overdo it).”
ejercicios.jp: 少[すこ]し＿ 食[た]べた。
ejercicios.explica: The verb is positive and the tone neutral: だけ. With しか you'd need 食[た]べなかった, and it would sound like you're still hungry.

ejercicios.es: There's only one cake left.
ejercicios.explica: Number + しか + negative: 一[ひと]つしか ない, “there's nothing but one”.

ejercicios.es: You can only buy it here.
ejercicios.explica: With で, しか goes after the particle: ここでしか. And the verb in the negative potential.
る-verb: 食[た]べれば, then the verb again + ほど: 食[た]べれば 食[た]べるほど.

respuestas: たかければたかいほど
ejercicios.explica: い-adjective: い → ければ, then the adjective + ほど: 高[たか]ければ 高[たか]いほど.

ejercicios.pregunta: “The sooner the better.”
ejercicios.jp: 早[はや]ければ 早[はや]い＿ いい。
ejercicios.explica: The formula is 〜ば〜ほど: the second half always takes ほど.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I'm so happy I could cry.”
ejercicios.jp: 泣[な]きたい＿ うれしい。
ejercicios.explica: ほど measures the degree: so happy it reaches the point of wanting to cry.

ejercicios.es: The more I practise, the more I like it.
piezas: 練習[れんしゅう]すれば
ejercicios.explica: すれば + する + ほど, and the change at the end: 好[す]きに なる.

lecciones.titulo: More than, the most and the way to: より, 方 and 一番
lecciones.resumen: You'll learn to compare: say Hokkaido is colder than Tokyo, ask whether someone prefers ramen or sushi, pick your favourite fruit, say Tama eats as much as Nyan… and, as a bonus, ask someone to explain “the way to” do something.

secciones.titulo: Japanese adjectives have no “-er”

bloques.md:
First surprise: Japanese has no “colder” or “bigger”, and no “more” in front of adjectives either. The adjective doesn't change: **寒[さむ]い** is “cold” and also “colder”; **大[おお]きい** is “big” and also “bigger”. What turns a sentence into a comparison are the pieces around it: **より** (compared with), **の 方[ほう]が** (the side that wins) and **一番[いちばん]** (the most).

It sounds odd, but it's actually very logical: if you say “Hokkaido is cold, compared with Tokyo”, it's already clear that it's colder. Japanese doesn't repeat what the context makes obvious.

secciones.titulo: より: compared with

bloques.md: **より** goes after the point of reference, the thing you're comparing against. It's the “than” in “colder **than** Tokyo”, but in Japanese it sticks to Tokyo, and comes before the adjective.

**A は B より 〜**: A is more ~ than B
北海道[ほっかいどう]は 東京[とうきょう]より 寒[さむ]い. (Hokkaido is colder than Tokyo.)
To say how much more: **ずっと** (much more), **少[すこ]し** or **ちょっと** (a bit more).

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]は 東京[とうきょう]より ずっと 寒[さむ]い。
items.es: Hokkaido is much colder than Tokyo.

items.jp: カゲは ニャンより 少[すこ]し 背[せ]が 高[たか]い。
items.es: Kage is a bit taller than Nyan.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 昨日[きのう]より 暖[あたた]かいね。
items.es: It's warmer today than yesterday, isn't it?

bloques.md: **より** also works with verbs and whole sentences. An expression you'll use all the time: **思[おも]ったより**, “than I thought”. And when you don't say what you're comparing with, because it's obvious, “more” is **もっと**: もっと 食[た]べたい, “I want to eat more”.

items.jp: 試験[しけん]は 思[おも]ったより 簡単[かんたん]だった。
items.es: The exam was easier than I thought.

items.jp: 見[み]るより、 やってみる ほうが 楽[たの]しい。
items.es: Having a go is more fun than watching.

items.jp: もっと ゆっくり 話[はな]して ください。
items.es: Please speak more slowly.

secciones.titulo: の方が: the side that wins

bloques.md:
**方[ほう]** means “side, direction”. **A の 方[ほう]が 〜** is “A's side is more ~”: you point at the winner of the comparison. It takes **が** because you're identifying which of the two it is, just as when you answer “who?” with が.

Most often you combine the two pieces: **B より A の 方[ほう]が 〜**, “A is more ~ than B”. The order can shift, because より and の 方[ほう]が already say who's who.

items.jp: 犬[いぬ]より 猫[ねこ]の 方[ほう]が 好[す]き。
items.es: I like cats more than dogs.
items.nota: Nyan's opinion. Kotarō, being a dog, begs to differ.

items.jp: ラーメンより 寿司[すし]の 方[ほう]が 高[たか]い。
items.es: Sushi is more expensive than ramen.

items.jp: バスより 歩[ある]く 方[ほう]が 速[はや]いよ。
items.es: It's quicker to walk than take the bus.
items.nota: With verbs, the verb goes in the dictionary form before 方[ほう].

bloques.md: Don't confuse this with **〜た 方[ほう]が いい**, “you'd better…”, from the lesson on wishes and suggestions: 早[はや]く 寝[ね]た 方[ほう]が いい, “you should go to bed early”. It's the same 方[ほう], but as a set phrase for advice, and it takes the verb in the past. To compare actions without giving advice, the verb goes in the dictionary form: 歩[ある]く 方[ほう]が 速[はや]い.
You'll often see 方[ほう] written in hiragana, **ほう**, especially in these constructions. Both spellings are correct.

secciones.titulo: Which of the two? どちら and どっち

bloques.md: To ask which of two things wins, use **どちら** (polite) or **どっち** (among friends), which literally mean “which side?”. It fits perfectly with the 方[ほう], “side”, in the answer.

**A と B と どちらが 〜ですか**: which is more ~, A or B?
Among friends: **A と B、 どっちが 〜？**
Answer: **A の 方[ほう]が 〜** / Both: **どちらも** / **どっちも**

lineas.jp: 夏[なつ]と 冬[ふゆ]と どちらが 好[す]きですか。
lineas.es: Which do you like better, summer or winter?

lineas.jp: 冬[ふゆ]の 方[ほう]が 好[す]きです。 雪[ゆき]が 大好[だいす]きですから。
lineas.es: I like winter better. I love snow.

lineas.jp: ラーメンと 寿司[すし]、 どっちが いい？
lineas.es: Ramen or sushi, which do you fancy?

lineas.jp: うーん…… どっちも！
lineas.es: Hmm… Both!

bloques.md: **どちら** is only for **two** options, because it asks about a “side”, and there are only two sides. With three or more, you use **何[なに]**, **どれ**, **誰[だれ]** or **どこ** with 一番[いちばん], as you'll see next. That's why ✗ 犬[いぬ]と 猫[ねこ]と 鳥[とり]と どちらが 好[す]き？ sounds odd, a bit like asking “which do you prefer of the two: dogs, cats and birds?”.

secciones.titulo: 一番: the most

bloques.md: **一番[いちばん]** literally means “number one”, and before an adjective it's “the most” or “-est”: **一番[いちばん] 大[おお]きい**, “the biggest”. To say what group it's the most in, use **〜の 中[なか]で** (among…, out of…) or just **で** with a place or a group.

**Group + の 中[なか]で + question word + が 一番[いちばん] 〜ですか**
The question word depends on what you're comparing: **何[なに]** (things), **誰[だれ]** (people), **どこ** (places), **いつ** (times), **どれ** (among specific items in front of you).

items.jp: 果物[くだもの]の 中[なか]で 何[なに]が 一番[いちばん] 好[す]き？
items.es: What's your favourite fruit?

items.jp: メロンが 一番[いちばん] 好[す]き。 夕張[ゆうばり]メロンは 最高[さいこう]！
items.es: Melon, definitely. Yubari melons are the best!
items.nota: Yubari, in Hokkaido, is famous for its melons.

items.jp: クラスで 誰[だれ]が 一番[いちばん] 速[はや]い？
items.es: Who's the fastest in the class?

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]で どこが 一番[いちばん] きれいですか。
items.es: Where's the most beautiful place in Hokkaido?

bloques.md: In writing and formal texts you'll see **最[もっと]も** instead of 一番[いちばん]: 日本[にほん]で 最[もっと]も 高[たか]い 山[やま]は 富士山[ふじさん]です. It means the same, but sounds bookish or like the news.

secciones.titulo: The same as: 同じ and 同じくらい

bloques.md: To say two things are the same, there's **同[おな]じ**, “same”. And to say two things reach the same degree, **と 同[おな]じくらい**, “as… as”, “just as much as”.

items.jp: ニャンと タマは 同[おな]じ クラスです。
items.es: Nyan and Tama are in the same class.

items.jp: わたしも タマと 同[おな]じ ケーキに する。
items.es: I'll have the same cake as Tama.

items.jp: タマは ニャンと 同[おな]じくらい 食[た]べる。
items.es: Tama eats as much as Nyan.
items.nota: And that's saying something!

items.jp: 小樽[おたる]と 札幌[さっぽろ]は 全然[ぜんぜん] 違[ちが]う。
items.es: Otaru and Sapporo are nothing alike.
items.nota: 違[ちが]う means “to be different”.

bloques.md: **同[おな]じ** is an odd word: before a noun it goes on **directly**, with no な or の: 同[おな]じ クラス, not ✗ 同[おな]じな クラス. It looks like a な-adjective, but in that position it does its own thing, so learn it as it is. And remember its partner from the previous lesson: in the negative, “not as… as” uses **ほど**: 東京[とうきょう]は 札幌[さっぽろ]ほど 寒[さむ]くない.

secciones.titulo: 〜方: the way to do something

bloques.md: And a parting gift with the same kanji, but a different reading. Stick **方[かた]** onto a verb stem and you get “the way of doing it”: 食[た]べ 方[かた] (the way to eat), 読[よ]み 方[かた] (the way to read, the reading), 作[つく]り 方[かた] (the recipe, how it's made). It's one of the handiest constructions in Japanese, because it lets you ask how to do anything at all.

Verb stem (the ます form without ます) + **方[かた]**
読[よ]みます → **読[よ]み 方[かた]** ・ 書[か]きます → **書[か]き 方[かた]** ・ 使[つか]います → **使[つか]い 方[かた]**
行[い]きます → **行[い]き 方[かた]** (how to get there)
する verbs use **仕方[しかた]**: 勉強[べんきょう]の 仕方[しかた] (the way to study)

items.jp: この 漢字[かんじ]の 読[よ]み 方[かた]を 教[おし]えてください。
items.es: Please tell me how to read this kanji.

items.jp: 駅[えき]への 行[い]き 方[かた]が 分[わ]かりません。
items.es: I don't know how to get to the station.

items.jp: タマの ケーキの 作[つく]り 方[かた]を 知[し]りたい！
items.es: I want to know how Tama makes her cakes!

items.jp: 雪[ゆき]だから、 仕方[しかた]が ない。
items.es: It's snowing, so there's nothing we can do.
items.nota: 仕方[しかた]が ない, lit. “there's no way of doing it”, is the Japanese way of accepting the inevitable.

bloques.md: Because **〜 方[かた]** turns the verb into a **noun**, what used to take を now takes **の**: 漢字[かんじ]を 読[よ]む → 漢字[かんじ]**の** 読[よ]み 方[かた]. ✗ 漢字[かんじ]を 読[よ]み 方[かた] doesn't work, because を needs a verb after it, and 読[よ]み 方[かた] isn't one any more. English does the same: you “read kanji”, but you learn “the reading **of** kanji”.

To round off, a summary of the readings of the kanji 方: **ほう** is “side” (the winner in comparisons, and the one in 〜た 方[ほう]が いい); **かた** after a verb is “way”; and **かた** on its own, as in あの 方[かた], is a very respectful word for “person”.

lineas.jp: クラスで 一番[いちばん] 速[はや]いのは 俺[おれ]だ。
lineas.es: The fastest in the class is me.

lineas.jp: でも、 コタローの 方[ほう]が カゲより 速[はや]いよ。
lineas.es: But Kotarō's faster than you.

lineas.jp: 犬[いぬ]は…… 別[べつ]だ。
lineas.es: Dogs… don't count.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 ご 飯[はん]を 食[た]べるのは ニャンが 一番[いちばん] 速[はや]いね。
lineas.es: Well, when it comes to eating, Nyan's the fastest.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Hokkaido is colder than Tokyo.”
ejercicios.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]は 東京[とうきょう]＿ 寒[さむ]い。
ejercicios.explica: より marks the point of reference, what you're comparing with. ほど would need a negative adjective, and の 方[ほう] without が doesn't work there.

ejercicios.pregunta: “I like cats more than dogs.”
ejercicios.jp: 犬[いぬ]より 猫[ねこ]の 方[ほう]＿ 好[す]きです。
ejercicios.explica: の 方[ほう]が points at the winner and takes が, because it identifies which of the two it is. Besides, 好[す]き always takes が.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Which do you like better, summer or winter?”
ejercicios.jp: 夏[なつ]と 冬[ふゆ]と ＿が 好[す]きですか。
ejercicios.explica: With two options, どちら: it asks about a “side”, and there are two sides. どれ and 何[なに] are used with three or more.

ejercicios.pregunta: “What's your favourite fruit?”
ejercicios.jp: 果物[くだもの]の 中[なか]で 何[なに]が ＿ 好[す]き？
ejercicios.explica: For “the most” within a group, 一番[いちばん]. より and 方[ほう] only compare two things.
Verb stem, 読[よ]み, + 方[かた]: 読[よ]み 方[かた], “the way to read, the reading”.
作[つく]ります → 作[つく]り + 方[かた]: “how it's made, the recipe”.
する verbs use 仕方[しかた], and the noun links up with の: 勉強[べんきょう]の 仕方[しかた].

ejercicios.es: Ramen is cheaper than sushi.
ejercicios.explica: A は B より + adjective. The adjective doesn't change: 安[やす]い already means “cheaper” thanks to より.

ejercicios.es: Tama eats as much as Nyan.
ejercicios.explica: A は B と 同[おな]じくらい + verb: “A does it just as much as B”.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Tell me how to read this kanji.”
ejercicios.jp: この 漢字[かんじ]＿ 読[よ]み 方[かた]を 教[おし]えて。
ejercicios.explica: 読[よ]み 方[かた] is a noun, so it links to 漢字[かんじ] with の. を would need a verb after it.

ejercicios.pregunta: “The exam was easier than I thought.”
ejercicios.jp: 試験[しけん]は 思[おも]った＿ 簡単[かんたん]だった。
ejercicios.explica: 思[おも]ったより, “than I thought”: より also compares with whole sentences.

ejercicios.pregunta: “Nyan and Tama are in the same class.”
ejercicios.jp: ニャンと タマは ＿ クラスです。
ejercicios.explica: 同[おな]じ goes directly before the noun, with no な or の. It's an exception: learn it as it is.

ejercicios.es: Which do you fancy, ramen or sushi? (among friends)
ejercicios.explica: Among friends: A と B、 どっちが…？ The answer might be 寿司[すし]の 方[ほう]が いい.

lecciones.titulo: And then…: connectors for chatting and telling stories
lecciones.capitulo: If…, maybe… and I have to…
lecciones.resumen: Link your sentences the way Japanese speakers do: add reasons, draw conclusions, change the subject smoothly and tell a story from start to finish without losing anyone along the way.

secciones.titulo: Sentences that hold hands

bloques.md:
So far you've joined ideas by attaching something to the end of the first clause: 雨[あめ]だから、 行[い]かない, «it's raining, so I'm not going»; 高[たか]いけど、 買[か]う, «it's expensive, but I'll buy it». That works beautifully inside a single sentence. But in real conversation, ideas arrive one at a time, each with its own full stop, and you need a different tool: a word at the **start** of the new sentence that says how it fits with the last one.
Those are **connectors**, which Japanese calls 接続詞[せつぞくし], literally «joining words». They're the road signs of conversation: before your listener even hears the sentence, they know whether a consequence, an objection, an extra point or a change of subject is coming. Japanese speakers use them constantly, and your Japanese will sound far more alive once you have them at hand.

End of sentence + full stop + **connector** + new sentence.
雨[あめ]だ。 **だから**、 行[い]かない。
Many connectors are actually pieces you already know with a «that» in front: だから is だ + から («it's so, and therefore»); それで is それ + で («with that»). That's why they make sense on their own: they sum up the previous sentence in one little word and hook it onto the next.

items.jp: 雨[あめ]だから、 行[い]かない。
items.es: It's raining, so I'm not going.
items.nota: One sentence: から sticks to the end of the reason.

items.jp: 雨[あめ]だ。 だから、 行[い]かない。
items.es: It's raining. So I'm not going.
items.nota: Two sentences: the connector opens the second. It sounds more measured, as if you'd thought about it before giving your conclusion.

bloques.md: A connector doesn't replace the grammar inside a sentence. If you say 雨[あめ]だ、 だから 行[い]かない with no full stop, it sounds to a Japanese ear like two sentences taped together. Either join with から inside one sentence, or close the sentence and open the next with だから: each tool has its own place.

secciones.titulo: Connectors for conversation

bloques.md: Let's start with the ones you'll hear in any conversation. Notice that each one doesn't translate a particular English word so much as an **intention**: carry on, conclude, object, add, sum up, change the subject or decide.

filas: What happened next or as a result; also «and then what?»
A conclusion or decision based on what came before
Something that clashes with what came before
One more point pushing the same way
The same thing put another way, in short
A reaction or decision based on what was just said

bloques.md:
**それで** is the calmest connector: it reports what came next or what followed from it, without passing judgement. On its own, with a questioning tone, it's the most natural way to ask someone to keep going: 「それで？」, «and? what happened?».
**だから** also links cause and effect, but with more weight: the speaker draws a conclusion and stands behind it. That's why you can follow だから with an order, a plan or an opinion, but not それで: それで only narrates what happened.

items.jp: 寝坊[ねぼう]した。 それで、 学校[がっこう]に 遅[おく]れた。
items.es: I overslept. So I was late for school.
items.nota: A fact and its result: それで simply reports it.

items.jp: 明日[あした]は テストだ。 だから、 今夜[こんや]は 勉強[べんきょう]する。
items.es: There's a test tomorrow. That's why I'm studying tonight.
items.nota: A decision: this is where だから feels natural.

items.jp: だから 言[い]ったのに！
items.es: I told you so!
items.nota: だから at the start of a complaint means «see?»: it's used like this all the time, with a certain edge.

bloques.md: Be careful with だから when you're speaking politely to someone. Its polite version, ですから, at the start of a reply can sound like «as I already told you…», as if you were correcting the other person for not keeping up. With a teacher or in a shop, それで or a sentence with ので sounds gentler when you're explaining a result.

**でも** is the «but» that opens a sentence; けど, which you already know, is the one that attaches to the end. でも is also how excuses begin: when someone tells you off, a long でも… is the good old «yeah, but…». In serious writing you'll see しかし, which means the same thing in a suit and tie.
**それに** adds: you've given one reason and you add another pushing in the same direction. If the second point went the other way, それに wouldn't work; you'd need でも.

items.jp: ケーキは 大好[だいす]き。 でも、 今日[きょう]は 食[た]べない。
items.es: I love cake. But I'm not having any today.
items.nota: Nyan's words, which nobody believes.

items.jp: 「 宿題[しゅくだい]は？」「でも… 眠[ねむ]かったから…」
items.es: “What about your homework?” “But… I was sleepy…”
items.nota: でも as the start of an excuse.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 寒[さむ]い。 それに、 雨[あめ]も 降[ふ]って いる。
items.es: It's cold today. And on top of that, it's raining.
items.nota: Two reasons to stay home: they add up.

bloques.md:
**つまり** sums up what came before or turns it into its logical consequence: «so basically». It's perfect for checking you've understood, and the question つまり、 どういう こと？ («so what do you mean?») will get you out of trouble more than once.
**ところで** opens a new topic. It's polite and clear, but it's a sharp turn: drop it while someone is telling you something important and it'll seem you weren't listening. When the new topic grows out of something just said, people use そういえば, «speaking of which», which sounds much more natural.
**じゃあ** reacts to what you've just heard and moves to action: «well then…». It's also the word that wraps up a chat (じゃあ、 またね, «OK, see you»). Its polite form is では, which Fukuro-sensei uses to start class.

items.jp: 「 駅[えき]から 歩[ある]いて 一時間[いちじかん]です。」「つまり、 遠[とお]いって ことですね。」
items.es: “It's an hour's walk from the station.” “So basically, it's far.”
items.nota: つまり + your conclusion: a way to check you've got it.

items.jp: ところで、 明日[あした]の お 祭[まつ]り、 行[い]く？
items.es: By the way, are you going to the festival tomorrow?

items.jp: 「 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]って きたね。」「じゃあ、 家[いえ]で 映画[えいが]を 見[み]よう。」
items.es: “It's started raining.” “Well then, let's watch a film at home.”
items.nota: じゃあ takes what was said and decides.

items.jp: では、 授業[じゅぎょう]を 始[はじ]めましょう。
items.es: Right, let's begin the lesson.
items.nota: では: the polite version of じゃあ, very teacher-like.

secciones.titulo: Telling things in order

bloques.md: To tell a story, give a recipe or explain the way to Tama's house, you need words that mark the steps. The basics are **まず** (first), **次[つぎ]に** (next), **それから** (after that, and then) and **最後[さいご]に** (lastly). With them, any sequence becomes crystal clear.

items.jp: まず、 お 湯[ゆ]を 沸[わ]かします。 次[つぎ]に、 麺[めん]を 入[い]れます。 最後[さいご]に、 ねぎを のせます。
items.es: First, boil the water. Next, add the noodles. Lastly, top with spring onion.
items.nota: That's how every ramen packet at Pon's shop starts.

items.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]を して、 それから 遊[あそ]びに 行[い]った。
items.es: I did my homework, and then I went out to play.

items.jp: 牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]と 卵[たまご]、 それから パンも 買[か]って きて。
items.es: Get some milk and eggs, and some bread too.
items.nota: それから can also add an item to a list: «and also».

bloques.md:
**そして** is an «and» that links sentences. In everyday conversation it sounds a little solemn, like a book or a documentary narrator; in writing and in stories told with a bit of drama, on the other hand, it's everywhere. Chatting with friends, それから or それで will sound more natural.
And within a single sentence, to say «after doing something», you have **〜てから**: the て-form + から. It's the attached cousin of それから: 宿題[しゅくだい]を して から、 遊[あそ]ぶ, «I'll play after I do my homework». Careful, this isn't the から of «because»: here から follows the て-form and marks a starting point in time.

Verb in て-form + から
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて から　　買[か]う → 買[か]って から　　する → して から
The 〜てから action has to be finished before the next one starts: it's strict order, «first this, and once it's done, the other».

items.jp: 手[て]を 洗[あら]って から、 食[た]べて ね。
items.es: Wash your hands before you eat, OK?
items.nota: Literally «eat after washing your hands»: Japanese says it in the order it happens.

items.jp: 日本[にほん]に 来[き]て から、 納豆[なっとう]が 好[す]きに なった。
items.es: Since coming to Japan, I've got to like natto.
items.nota: With verbs of arriving or starting, 〜てから can mean «since».

secciones.titulo: Finally, in the end, at last: four different endings

bloques.md: Here's the sneakiest trap for English speakers. We say «finally», «in the end» and «at last» almost without thinking, and often use them interchangeably. Japanese has four words, and each tells a different kind of ending: the last step in a list, the outcome after a lot of back and forth, the relief after a wait, and the culmination of something that had been coming for a while.

filas: The last step in a series
How it all turned out after doubts or twists
Something you wanted finally comes, after effort or waiting
The outcome of a long process, good or bad

items.jp: 最後[さいご]に、 みんなで 写真[しゃしん]を 撮[と]った。
items.es: To finish, we all took a photo together.
items.nota: The last item on the trip. No particular emotion.

items.jp: 一日中[いちにちじゅう] 迷[まよ]って、 結局[けっきょく] 何[なに]も 買[か]わなかった。
items.es: I dithered all day and in the end I didn't buy anything.
items.nota: 結局[けっきょく]: after going round in circles, the outcome.

items.jp: 二時間[にじかん] 並[なら]んで、 やっと 買[か]えた！
items.es: Two hours in the queue, and I finally got one!
items.nota: やっと: you wanted it and it took effort.

items.jp: 古[ふる]い 自転車[じてんしゃ]が ついに 壊[こわ]れた。
items.es: The old bike finally gave up.
items.nota: ついに: it had been coming for a long time.

bloques.md: Don't use やっと for something you didn't want. やっと carries the speaker's wish inside it: «at last, what I was waiting for has happened». If you say the bike やっと broke, you're confessing you'd been hoping for months that it would. For bad or neutral outcomes, use ついに (or its more colloquial sibling とうとう), which just says the process has reached its end.

«Finally» is a double false friend. If it means «lastly», it's 最後[さいご]に. If it means «so in the end…», it's 結局[けっきょく]. And if it means «at last!», it's やっと. Before translating, ask yourself which of the three endings you're telling.

secciones.titulo: The rhythm of an anecdote

bloques.md:
A good anecdote in Japanese has its own rhythm, and knowing it will help you both tell them and listen to them.
**1. The opening.** You set the time, with 昨日[きのう], この 間[あいだ] («the other day») or 先週[せんしゅう], and you often open with **〜んだけど**: 昨日[きのう]、 変[へん]な ことが あったんだけど…, «so, something weird happened yesterday…». That dangling けど isn't a «but»: it's an invitation for the other person to say «yeah?» and hand you the floor.
**2. The middle.** The events, in the past tense and in order, linked with それで, それから or, among friends, their short versions: **で** (それで squeezed into one syllable) and **そしたら** («and then, out of nowhere…», for what you didn't see coming). In books, すると does the same job.
**3. The ending.** 結局[けっきょく] for the outcome, やっと if there was relief, and a verdict: 大変[たいへん]だった, 面白[おもしろ]かった.

Two more details. First: at the most exciting point, Japanese speakers sometimes switch from past to present so the listener lives it live, just as we do in English with «so I open the door and bam!». For example: そしたら、 目[め]の 前[まえ]に カゲが いるの！
Second: the listener doesn't stay quiet. They keep dropping うん, へえ, それで？, うそ！ at every step. These responses, called 相槌[あいづち], tell the speaker you're following. In Japanese, a long silence can be taken to mean you're not listening or that something has upset you, so when someone tells you a story, react.

lineas.jp: ねえ、 昨日[きのう]の 秋祭[あきまつ]り、 大変[たいへん]だったんだけど…
lineas.es: Hey, so yesterday at the autumn festival, it was crazy…

lineas.jp: へえ、 どう したの？
lineas.es: Oh yeah? What happened?

lineas.jp: まず、 ポンさんの 屋台[やたい]で たこ 焼[や]きを 買[か]ったの。
lineas.es: First, I bought some takoyaki at Pon's stall.

lineas.jp: うん。 それで？
lineas.es: Uh-huh. And?

lineas.jp: それから、 金魚[きんぎょ]すくいを やった。 でも、 一匹[いっぴき]も 取[と]れなかった。
lineas.es: Then I had a go at goldfish scooping. But I didn't catch a single one.

lineas.jp: そしたら、 カゲが 来[き]て、 「 下手[へた]だな」って 言[い]ったの！
lineas.es: And then Kage turns up and goes, «you're rubbish at this»!

lineas.jp: うそ！ ひどい！
lineas.es: No way! That's so mean!

lineas.jp: だから、 勝負[しょうぶ]した。 一時間[いちじかん]も！
lineas.es: So I challenged him. For a whole hour!

lineas.jp: で、 結局[けっきょく] どっちが 勝[か]ったの？
lineas.es: So who won in the end?

lineas.jp: 結局[けっきょく]、 二人[ふたり]とも ゼロ。 でも 最後[さいご]に、 ポンさんが 一匹[いっぴき]ずつ くれたんだ。 やっと 金魚[きんぎょ]が もらえた！
lineas.es: In the end, zero each. But to finish, Pon gave us one each. I finally got my goldfish!

lineas.jp: よかったね。 ところで、 たこ 焼[や]きは？
lineas.es: Aww, nice. By the way, what about the takoyaki?

lineas.jp: あ…… カゲが 食[た]べた。
lineas.es: Oh… Kage ate them.

bloques.md: See how each connector does its job: まず and それから set the order, でも marks the setback, そしたら brings the surprise, だから the reaction, で and 結局[けっきょく] lead to the outcome, やっと adds the relief and ところで opens the takoyaki question, with the ending we all feared. And Tama keeps signalling that she's listening: へえ, それで？, うそ！

secciones.titulo: Depending on who you're talking to

bloques.md: Almost all of these connectors work the same with or without です/ます, but some have versions for each occasion. With friends, the short, chatty ones; with a teacher, the full forms; in writing, the most formal.

filas: そのため、 したがって

bloques.md: Don't let で become a verbal tic, which is easy to do: で、 で、 で… Among friends it's normal, but used nonstop it sounds nervous. And with Fukuro-sensei, stick to the full それで: to someone older, the short version sounds too loose.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan gives a second reason not to go out. Which connector fits?
ejercicios.jp: 今日[きょう]は 寒[さむ]いね。 ＿、 雪[ゆき]も 降[ふ]って いる。
ejercicios.explica: それに adds a point pushing the same way: cold, and snow as well, two reasons to stay in. でも would announce something against it, and ところで would change the subject.

ejercicios.pregunta: A fact and its result, simply reported. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 寝坊[ねぼう]した。 ＿、 バスに 乗[の]れなかった。
ejercicios.explica: それで reports what followed: he overslept and, as a result, missed the bus. でも doesn't fit because nothing clashes, and ところで would change the subject.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama reacts to what she just heard and suggests a plan. What does she say?
ejercicios.jp: 「 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]って きた。」「＿、 家[いえ]で ゲームを しよう。」
ejercicios.explica: じゃあ takes what was just said and decides from there: «well then…». それに would add another reason, and 最後[さいご]に would mark the last step in a list.

ejercicios.pregunta: After a long wait, what you wanted arrives. Which word fits?
ejercicios.jp: 二時間[にじかん] 待[ま]って、 ＿ バスが 来[き]た！
ejercicios.explica: やっと expresses relief that something you were waiting for has finally happened. 最後[さいご]に would only say it's the last step in a series, without the emotion of waiting.

ejercicios.pregunta: Lots of dithering and a disappointing result. Which word fits?
ejercicios.jp: 三日[みっか] 悩[なや]んだけど、 ＿ 何[なに]も 買[か]わなかった。
ejercicios.explica: 結局[けっきょく] tells how it all turned out after the back and forth: three days of dithering and, in the end, nothing. やっと doesn't fit, because buying nothing is no relief.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which of these sentences sounds natural?
opciones: 明日[あした]は テストだ。 だから、 早[はや]く 寝[ね]なさい。
明日[あした]は テストだ。 それで、 早[はや]く 寝[ね]なさい。
明日[あした]は テストだ。 ところで、 早[はや]く 寝[ね]なさい。
ejercicios.explica: だから can be followed by an order, because it draws a conclusion and acts on it. それで only narrates what happened, so it can't take orders or plans; and ところで would change the subject just when the order depends on what came before.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan wants to change the subject after talking about class. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: 今日[きょう]の 授業[じゅぎょう]、 楽[たの]しかったね。 ＿、 明日[あした] ひま？
ejercicios.explica: ところで opens a new topic: from class to tomorrow's plans. だから would present the plan as a result of the class and つまり as a summary of it, and neither makes sense here.

ejercicios.pregunta: The old bike had been giving trouble for ages. Which word fits?
ejercicios.jp: 古[ふる]い 自転車[じてんしゃ]が ＿ 壊[こわ]れた。
ejercicios.explica: ついに tells the outcome of a long process, even a bad one. With やっと you'd be saying you'd been hoping it would break, because やっと always carries the speaker's wish.

ejercicios.es: First I'll do my homework, and then I'll play.
ejercicios.explica: まず opens the series, the first action goes in the て-form and それから introduces the second. The main verb, 遊[あそ]ぶ, closes the sentence, as always in Japanese.

ejercicios.es: So basically, there's no class tomorrow, right?
ejercicios.explica: つまり opens the sentence because it sums up what came before. Then the usual order: first the topic, 明日[あした]は; then the subject, 授業[じゅぎょう]が; then the verb and, at the end, って こと？ to check you've understood.

ejercicios.es: In the end, Kage ate the takoyaki.
ejercicios.explica: 結局[けっきょく] goes first because it announces the outcome of the whole story. Then who, カゲが; what, たこ 焼[や]きを; and the verb in the past.
It's the て-form + から: 食[た]べて + から. It says the first action ends before the next one starts.
買[か]う makes its て-form with って, 買[か]って, like every う-group verb ending in う, つ or る. Then add から.
だから is だ + から, so its polite version swaps だ for です: ですから. Use it with care, because at the start of a reply it can sound like «as I already told you».

lecciones.titulo: Without doing: 〜ないで and 〜ずに
lecciones.capitulo: If…, maybe… and I have to…
lecciones.resumen: Going out without an umbrella, studying instead of sleeping, begging «don't go!»: by the end you'll be able to say what WASN'T done, tell it apart from «because… didn't», and recognise the old negative that still pops up in proverbs and in grandpa's speech.

secciones.titulo: In Japanese, «without» is a negative verb

bloques.md:
In English we say «I went out without having breakfast» with a preposition, **without**, plus a verb in -ing. Japanese has no preposition like that for actions. What it does is more logical than it looks: it puts the verb in the negative and hooks it on with で. «I went out without having breakfast» is thought of as «not eating breakfast, I went out»: 朝[あさ]ごはんを 食[た]べないで 出[で]かけた.
The ないで part describes **how** you did the main action, under what conditions. The main action comes at the end, as always, and it's the only one that carries the tense: if it happened yesterday, the past goes on the last verb, not on ないで.

ない-form + で
食[た]べない → **食[た]べないで**　　行[い]かない → **行[い]かないで**
しない → **しないで**　　来[こ]ない → **来[こ]ないで**
If you can make the plain negative, you can already make this form: there isn't a single new exception.

items.jp: 傘[かさ]を 持[も]たないで 出[で]かけた。
items.es: I went out without an umbrella.
items.nota: Literally «I went out without holding an umbrella»: Japanese needs a verb where English makes do with just the object.

items.jp: 朝[あさ]ごはんを 食[た]べないで 学校[がっこう]に 来[き]た。
items.es: I came to school without having breakfast.

items.jp: 辞書[じしょ]を 使[つか]わないで 読[よ]めた！
items.es: I managed to read it without using a dictionary!

items.jp: ニャンは 歯[は]を 磨[みが]かないで 寝[ね]た。
items.es: Nyan went to bed without brushing his teeth.
items.nota: Classic Nyan, who's a bit lazy.

bloques.md: ないで has a second, very close meaning: **instead of**. When the normal thing would have been to do A and you do B, 〜ないで names the option you dropped. Japanese doesn't separate «without sleeping» from «instead of sleeping»: to it they're the same idea, «not doing this, I did that».

items.jp: 寝[ね]ないで 勉強[べんきょう]した。
items.es: I studied instead of sleeping. / I studied without sleeping.

items.jp: バスに 乗[の]らないで、 歩[ある]いて 帰[かえ]った。
items.es: Instead of taking the bus, I walked home.

bloques.md: ないで goes after verbs. For «without + thing», like «coffee without sugar», Japanese has two routes: bring in a verb, as in 砂糖[さとう]を 入[い]れないで («without putting in sugar»), or use **なしで**, which attaches to nouns: コーヒー、 砂糖[さとう]なしで お 願[ねが]いします. Try to stick ないで onto a noun and a Japanese listener will feel something's missing: without doing what with the sugar?

secciones.titulo: 〜ないで at the end: «please don't…»

bloques.md:
You already know 〜ないで ください for asking someone not to do something. Now you can see where it comes from: it's the same «without» form followed by ください, «please give me / do me the favour». In other words: «do me the favour of carrying on without doing that».
Among friends, people usually cut off ください and leave the sentence at 〜ないで. It sounds like a close, almost pleading request, and the listener fills in the rest. With ね it gets sweeter; with よ, more insistent.

items.jp: 行[い]かないで！
items.es: Don't go!
items.nota: A proper plea: you'll hear it in every drama.

items.jp: カゲ、 わたしの プリン、 食[た]べないで ね。
items.es: Kage, don't eat my pudding, OK?

items.jp: 笑[わら]わないで よ！
items.es: Stop laughing!

items.jp: ここで 写真[しゃしん]を 撮[と]らないで ください。
items.es: Please don't take photos here.
items.nota: The polite version, the one on signs and in museums.

bloques.md: Don't mix up 行[い]かないで and 行[い]くな. 行[い]くな, with the prohibitive な, is a curt order, from someone with authority or someone very angry. 行[い]かないで is a request, and can even sound tender. If you want someone not to leave and also want them to still be talking to you tomorrow, use ないで.

secciones.titulo: 〜ずに: the same, but bookish

bloques.md: There's another form that means exactly «without doing»: **〜ずに**. It's older, sounds more formal and shows up mostly in writing, in the news, on signs and in speeches. But don't think it's only for books: a handful of set phrases with ずに are heard every day on the street, and it's worth having them in your ear.

ない-form, minus ない, + ずに
食[た]べない → **食[た]べずに**　　行[い]かない → **行[い]かずに**　　飲[の]まない → **飲[の]まずに**
The irregulars: する → **せずに** (not しずに)　　来[く]る → **来[こ]ずに**
Why せずに and not しずに? Because ずに comes from classical Japanese, where the negative of する was built on せ. That せ has survived stuck to ず like a fossil: you'll always see it in せずに and せず.

items.jp: 遠慮[えんりょ]せずに 食[た]べて ください。
items.es: Please help yourself, don't be shy.
items.nota: 遠慮[えんりょ] is holding back out of politeness. Every good Japanese host says this.

items.jp: 忘[わす]れずに 傘[かさ]を 持[も]って いって ね。
items.es: Remember to take your umbrella, OK?
items.nota: Literally «without forgetting, take your umbrella». 忘[わす]れずに is one of the most common ずに forms in speech.

items.jp: カゲは 一度[いちど]も 休[やす]まずに 走[はし]った。
items.es: Kage ran without stopping for a rest even once.

items.jp: 何[なに]も 言[い]わずに 帰[かえ]った。
items.es: He left without saying a word.
items.nota: 言[い]わないで would work here too; 言[い]わずに sounds more like storytelling.

bloques.md: ずに can't make a request. 食[た]べずに ください doesn't exist, because ずに always needs another verb after it saying what's done «without eating», and only ないで has the habit of being cut off and left hanging. To ask someone not to do something: 食[た]べないで ください. On signs you will see ずに followed by another polite verb, as in 忘[わす]れずに お 持[も]ちください, «please don't forget to take it with you».

secciones.titulo: Without…, or because… didn't? ないで versus なくて

bloques.md:
There's another form that looks very similar: **なくて**. It's the て-form of ない treated as an adjective (just as 高[たか]い gives 高[たか]くて, ない gives なくて). They sound almost the same, but they tell different stories:
**ないで** describes how the main action was done, or what was done in its place: «without…», «instead of…».
**なくて** presents a cause: «because… didn't», «since… wasn't». What follows is the result: a feeling, a problem, something that couldn't be done.
The trick is to translate in your head. If «without» or «instead of» comes out, it's ないで. If «because… not» comes out, it's なくて.

filas: 宿題[しゅくだい]を しないで 遊[あそ]んだ。
宿題[しゅくだい]が 終[お]わらなくて、 遊[あそ]べなかった。
I played without doing my homework.
I couldn't play because I didn't finish my homework.
Yes: 高[たか]くなくて, 学生[がくせい]じゃなくて

items.jp: 友達[ともだち]が 来[こ]なくて、 寂[さび]しかった。
items.es: My friend didn't come, so I felt lonely.
items.nota: Cause (didn't come) and feeling (loneliness): なくて.

items.jp: バスが 来[こ]なくて、 困[こま]った。
items.es: The bus didn't come and I was stuck.

items.jp: 漢字[かんじ]が 読[よ]めなくて、 恥[は]ずかしかった。
items.es: I was embarrassed that I couldn't read the kanji.

items.jp: コタローは 狐[きつね]じゃなくて、 犬[いぬ]だよ。
items.es: Kotarō isn't a fox, he's a dog.
items.nota: じゃなくて also corrects: «not A, but B». Kotarō is a shiba, and with that foxy face he has to say this a lot.

bloques.md: 友達[ともだち]が 来[こ]ないで 寂[さび]しかった sounds odd. ないで says how someone does the main action, but feeling lonely isn't something your friend did «without coming»: it's what happened to you because they didn't come. When a feeling or a problem follows, the link is cause and effect, and causes go with なくて.

secciones.titulo: ず, ぬ and ん: grandpa's negative

bloques.md: Centuries ago, Japanese said «not» with **ず** and **ぬ**, not ない. That old negative never went away: it lives on in corners of the language, and you'll run into it even if you never use it. You don't need to produce it, but you do need to recognise it.

filas: Texts and news: a written «without» or «because… not»
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]らず、 水[みず]が 足[た]りない。 (There's no rain and not enough water.)
相変[あいか]わらず (as ever), 思[おも]わず (without meaning to), 残[のこ]らず (every last one)
見知[みし]らぬ 人[ひと] (a stranger)
Western Japan, older people, anime characters
分[わ]からん (I don't get it), 知[し]らん (no idea)

bloques.md:
Some of these words are so ordinary that nobody feels the negative inside any more: **相変[あいか]わらず** is «without having changed», that is, «as ever»; **思[おも]わず** is «without thinking», «before you know it». And the proverb **知[し]らぬが 仏[ほとけ]**, literally «not knowing is being a Buddha», is the Japanese «ignorance is bliss»: whoever doesn't find out lives in peace.
ん deserves a special mention. In Kansai and other parts of the west it's used in everyday speech, in forms like 分[わ]からん or 行[い]かん, and in the rest of Japan it's the classic voice of grandpas, movie samurai and serious anime characters. And here's the surprise: you already use it. The ません you say every day is ませ + ん, the old negative, hidden inside the polite form.

items.jp: カゲは 相変[あいか]わらず 元気[げんき]だね。
items.es: Kage's as full of beans as ever, huh?

items.jp: ケーキを 見[み]て、 思[おも]わず 笑[わら]った。
items.es: When I saw the cake, I couldn't help smiling.
items.nota: 思[おも]わず: without thinking, without being able to stop yourself.

items.jp: そんな こと、 知[し]らん。
items.es: How should I know?
items.nota: That's how a grumpy grandpa would say it, or anyone in Osaka.

bloques.md: Don't start saying 分[わ]からん because you heard it in an anime. Unless you're from western Japan, it'll sound like a costume in your mouth, like a learner of English who starts talking like a pirate. Recognise it, enjoy it and stick to 分[わ]からない or 分[わ]かりません.

secciones.titulo: All together

bloques.md: Nyan turns up late for class, and all three forms appear in this scene: what he did without doing something else, what he couldn't do because of something, and a couple of bookish ずに.

lineas.jp: ニャンさん、 どう したんですか。 びしょびしょですよ。
lineas.es: Nyan, what happened? You're soaking wet.

lineas.jp: 傘[かさ]を 持[も]たないで 家[いえ]を 出[で]たんです。
lineas.es: I left home without an umbrella.

lineas.jp: 天気[てんき]予報[よほう]を 見[み]なかったんですか。
lineas.es: Didn't you check the weather forecast?

lineas.jp: はい… 朝[あさ]、 起[お]きられなくて、 見[み]る 時間[じかん]が なかったんです。
lineas.es: No… I couldn't get up this morning, so I didn't have time to look.

lineas.jp: 朝[あさ]ごはんも 食[た]べないで 来[き]たの？
lineas.es: And you came without breakfast too?

lineas.jp: うん… お 腹[なか]、 すいた…
lineas.es: Yeah… I'm starving…

lineas.jp: ふん。 俺[おれ]は 一日[いちにち]も 休[やす]まずに、 毎朝[まいあさ] 天気[てんき]予報[よほう]を 見[み]て いる。
lineas.es: Hmph. I check the forecast every morning, without missing a single day.

lineas.jp: カゲさん、 えらいですね。 ニャンさん、 明日[あした]からは 忘[わす]れずに 見[み]て くださいね。
lineas.es: Well done, Kage. Nyan, from tomorrow on, please remember to check it.

lineas.jp: はい… あ、 カゲ、 笑[わら]わないで よ！
lineas.es: Yes, miss… Hey, Kage, stop laughing!

bloques.md: Go back over the scene: 持[も]たないで and 食[た]べないで tell how Nyan came; 起[お]きられなくて gives the reason he couldn't check the forecast; 休[やす]まずに and 忘[わす]れずに are the more serious versions, fittingly from Kage and the teacher; and 笑[わら]わないで よ is the good old cut-off request.

ejercicios.explica: The negative of 食[た]べる is 食[た]べない (る verb: drop the る). Add で and you have «without eating».
う-group verb: the final u becomes a, 行[い]かない, then add で. It works both for «without going» and for begging «don't go!».
Start from 飲[の]まない, remove ない and add ずに: 飲[の]まずに. It means the same as 飲[の]まないで, but sounds more formal.
This is the lesson's irregular: せずに, not しずに. The せ is a leftover from classical Japanese, where the negative of する was built on せ.
As in 来[こ]ない, the vowel changes to o: 来[こ]ずに. Same kanji, but read こ.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan went out without an umbrella. Which form fits?
ejercicios.jp: 傘[かさ]を ＿ 出[で]かけた。
ejercicios.explica: It's a «without»: it describes how he went out. なくて would present a cause, «because he didn't have it…», and we'd expect a problem after it; and 持[も]たなかった would end the sentence too early.

ejercicios.pregunta: The friend didn't come and Nyan felt lonely. Which form fits?
ejercicios.jp: 友達[ともだち]が ＿、 寂[さび]しかった。
ejercicios.explica: A feeling follows, so the first part is its cause: «because he didn't come». Causes take なくて. ないで and ずに would describe how someone did something «without coming», which makes no sense here.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama asks Kage not to eat her cake. What does she say?
ejercicios.jp: カゲ、 わたしの ケーキを ＿！
ejercicios.explica: To ask something by leaving the sentence cut off, only ないで works: it's 〜ないで ください without the ください. ずに always needs another verb after it, and なくて would announce a cause.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does 思[おも]わず mean here?
ejercicios.jp: ケーキを 見[み]て、 思[おも]わず 笑[わら]った。
opciones: Without meaning to, before I could stop myself
ejercicios.explica: 思[おも]わず is 思[おも]う with the old negative ず: «without thinking». It's used for things that just come out of you, without deciding.

ejercicios.pregunta: Someone mistakes Kotarō for a fox. How do you correct them?
ejercicios.jp: コタローは 狐[きつね]＿、 犬[いぬ]だよ。
ejercicios.explica: With nouns only じゃなくて exists, because ないで is for verbs only. じゃなくて corrects: «not A, but B».

ejercicios.es: Instead of taking the bus, I walked home.
ejercicios.explica: The option you dropped comes first with ないで, then how you went home, 歩[ある]いて, and finally the main verb with the tense: 帰[かえ]った.

ejercicios.es: Kage left without saying a word.
ejercicios.explica: 何[なに]も with a negative verb means «nothing»; here the negative is ずに. The topic goes first and the main verb, 帰[かえ]った, closes the sentence.

ejercicios.es: Please don't take photos here.
ejercicios.explica: First the place with で, then the object with を, the verb in ないで, and ください at the end to turn it into a polite request.

lecciones.titulo: Have to, may and mustn't
lecciones.capitulo: If…, maybe… and I have to…
lecciones.resumen: Obligations, permissions and prohibitions: by the end you'll be able to say what you have to do and what you needn't, ask permission politely and understand any rule, from a museum sign to Fukuro-sensei's warnings.

secciones.titulo: The Japanese detour: «if you don't, it won't do»

bloques.md:
In English, obligation is direct: «I have to study». Japanese has no verb like «have to». Instead, it builds obligation out of a **double negative**: 勉強[べんきょう]しなければ ならない, which inside means «if I don't study, it won't do».
Let's take it piece by piece. しない is «not study». Swap ない for **なければ** and you get «if I don't study» (that ば is one of the Japanese «ifs», and you'll see it properly in the next lesson). And **ならない** means «it doesn't become», «it can't be». All together: «not studying isn't an option».
You can think of it like this: instead of saying «you must», Japanese describes the situation and makes it clear there's no alternative. It sounds less like somebody's order and more like the way things are.

ない-form → swap ない for **なければ** + **ならない** (or **いけない**)
食[た]べない → **食[た]べなければ ならない**
行[い]かない → **行[い]かなければ ならない**
しない → **しなければ ならない**　　来[こ]ない → **来[こ]なければ ならない**
Polite: なければ なりません / なければ いけません. Past: なければ ならなかった, «I had to».

items.jp: 明日[あした]までに 宿題[しゅくだい]を 出[だ]さなければ なりません。
items.es: I have to hand in my homework by tomorrow.

items.jp: 毎朝[まいあさ] 七時[しちじ]に 起[お]きなければ ならない。
items.es: I have to get up at seven every morning.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]は 病院[びょういん]に 行[い]かなければ ならなかった。
items.es: Yesterday I had to go to the doctor's.
items.nota: The past goes at the end, on ならなかった: what was compulsory.

bloques.md:
**ならない** or **いけない**? In practice, in speech they're used almost the same way. But they each have a character: ならない sounds more objective, like a general rule or a law, and is common in texts and official notices; いけない («it's no good») sounds more personal, about what you or the situation require, and is more frequent in conversation. When in doubt, いけない never sounds odd in daily life.
There's also a variant with て: **なくては ならない / なくては いけない**. It means the same and is built from なくて + は: «not doing it, it won't do». It's worth knowing because one of the most common short forms comes from it.

filas: 書類[しょるい]を 出[だ]さなければ なりません。
薬[くすり]を 飲[の]まなければ いけません。
早[はや]く 帰[かえ]らなくては いけない。
Neutral and very common in speech
もう 行[い]かないと いけない。

secciones.titulo: The short forms: なきゃ, なくちゃ and ないと

bloques.md:
Saying 行[い]かなければ ならない in full is tiring, and in speech Japanese people squeeze it as much as they can:
**なければ → なきゃ** (けれ and ば melt together)
**なくては → なくちゃ** (ては turns into ちゃ)
**ないと**, with と, another «if» you'll meet in the next lesson: «if not…».
And the most curious thing: very often the second half vanishes altogether. 行[い]かなきゃ。 That's it: «I've got to go». Why is it understood? Because «if I don't go…» can only end one way: «…it won't do». It's what we do in English when we say «if I don't hurry…» and leave it there: everyone knows how it ends.

items.jp: あっ、 もう 八時[はちじ]だ。 行[い]かなきゃ！
items.es: Oh, it's already eight! I've got to go!

items.jp: 明日[あした] テストだから、 勉強[べんきょう]しなくちゃ。
items.es: There's a test tomorrow, so I've got to study.

items.jp: そろそろ 帰[かえ]らないと。
items.es: I'd better be getting home.
items.nota: Literally «if I don't go home soon…». One of the most commonly heard forms.

items.jp: 薬[くすり]を 飲[の]まないと いけませんよ。
items.es: You do need to take your medicine.
items.nota: ないと いけません is short but polite: even doctors use it.

bloques.md: なきゃ and なくちゃ are for people you're close to. If you say もう 帰[かえ]らなきゃ to Fukuro-sensei, you'll sound as if you were talking to Tama: it's not an insult, but it is a small lapse in respect, because older people expect the full form. With her: もう 帰[かえ]らなければ なりません, or the in-between 帰[かえ]らないと いけません.

secciones.titulo: No need: 〜なくても いい

bloques.md: To say something isn't compulsory, Japanese builds with loose pieces again: **なくて** («not doing it») + **も** («even») + **いい** («it's fine»). In other words: «even if you don't, it's fine».

ない-form → swap ない for **なくても** + いい
来[こ]ない → **来[こ]なくても いい**　　急[いそ]がない → **急[いそ]がなくても いい**
Polite: なくても いいです, なくても 大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]です or, more formally, なくても かまいません.

items.jp: 明日[あした]は 来[こ]なくても いいよ。
items.es: You don't need to come tomorrow.

items.jp: 全部[ぜんぶ] 食[た]べなくても いいですよ。
items.es: You don't have to eat it all.
items.nota: Words Nyan has never needed to hear.

items.jp: 急[いそ]がなくても 大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]です。
items.es: There's no need to hurry.

items.jp: 靴[くつ]を 脱[ぬ]がなくても いいですか。
items.es: Is it OK if I keep my shoes on?
items.nota: A very useful question in Japan, where many homes, temples and even some restaurants ask you to take your shoes off.

bloques.md: Here's a big false friend. In English, «you don't have to come» means there's no need (なくても いい), but «you mustn't come» means it's forbidden. Both have a «not» and a verb of obligation, and yet they say very different things. Japanese keeps them completely apart: 来[こ]なくても いい is «no need», and 来[き]ては いけない, which you'll see in a moment, is «don't come». Before translating, ask yourself: is it forbidden, or just not required?

secciones.titulo: Asking and giving permission: 〜ても いい

bloques.md: Take away the negative and you have permission: て-form + **も** + **いい**, «even if you do it, it's fine». As a question, you're asking permission; as a statement, you're giving it. It's the form you'll use most as a guest, a customer and a student.

items.jp: 入[はい]っても いい？
items.es: Can I come in?
items.nota: Among friends, poking your head into Tama's room.

items.jp: ここに 座[すわ]っても いいですか。
items.es: May I sit here?

items.jp: 窓[まど]を 開[あ]けても よろしいですか。
items.es: Would you mind if I opened the window?
items.nota: よろしい is the refined version of いい: perfect with customers or important people.

items.jp: もう 帰[かえ]っても いいですよ。
items.es: You can go home now.
items.nota: Not a question: the teacher is giving permission.

bloques.md:
To say yes: いいよ, どうぞ or いいですよ. To say no, on the other hand, Japanese people almost never come out with a flat «no, you can't». The usual thing is to leave the sentence hanging with an awkward look: すみません、 ここは ちょっと…, «sorry, here it's a bit…». That ちょっと… is a full-blown «no», and everyone gets it straight away. If you hear it, don't push.
The same idea works with adjectives and nouns: 〜くても いい with い-adjectives, and 〜でも いい with nouns and な-adjectives. That's how you say something will do even if it's not ideal.

items.jp: 少[すこ]し 高[たか]くても いいです。
items.es: I don't mind if it's a bit expensive.

items.jp: 「 今日[きょう]、 手伝[てつだ]える？」「 明日[あした]でも いい？」
items.es: “Can you help me today?” “Would tomorrow be OK?”

secciones.titulo: Forbidden: 〜ては いけない and 〜ちゃ だめ

bloques.md: To forbid something, Japanese uses the twin structure: て-form + **は** + **いけない** (or **だめ**, or **ならない**). That is: «if you do it, it's no good». If the て-form ends in で, it becomes では: 泳[およ]いでは いけない.

〜ては **ならない**: a rule, a law, an official sign.
〜ては **いけない**: a clear ban, the kind teachers and parents give.
〜ては **だめ**: the one at home, more direct and familiar.
In speech, ては contracts to **ちゃ** and では to **じゃ**: 触[さわ]っちゃ だめ, 飲[の]んじゃ だめ.

items.jp: この 川[かわ]で 泳[およ]いでは いけません。
items.es: Swimming in this river is not allowed.

items.jp: 美術館[びじゅつかん]の 中[なか]で 写真[しゃしん]を 撮[と]っては いけません。
items.es: You can't take photos inside the museum.

items.jp: それ、 触[さわ]っちゃ だめ！
items.es: Don't touch that!
items.nota: How a mother talks to a small child.

items.jp: この ケーキ、 食[た]べちゃ だめ？
items.es: Can't I eat this cake?
items.nota: 〜ちゃ だめ？ as a question: Nyan's favourite plea.

bloques.md: 〜ては いけません states a rule, and that implies authority. So don't say it to someone above you: if you tell Fukuro-sensei ここで 食[た]べては いけません, it'll sound like you're reading the rules to your own teacher. To ask someone not to do something, use 〜ないで ください, which is a request rather than a law, and even then, gently.

secciones.titulo: All four together: a mirror

bloques.md: Now that you have all four forms, look at the lovely symmetry they hide. They're all built from the same pieces: the verb, positive or negative; て + **も** («even if») or て + **は** («if»); and **いい** («fine») or **いけない** («no good»).

filas: 食[た]べても いい: you may eat it
食[た]べなくても いい: you needn't eat it
食[た]べては いけない: you mustn't eat it
食[た]べなくては いけない: you have to eat it

bloques.md: Read it aloud and the logic jumps out: «even if you eat it, it's fine» is permission; «even if you don't eat it, it's fine» is no need; «if you eat it, it's no good» is a ban; and «if you don't eat it, it's no good» is an obligation. Four combinations, four meanings, and not a single new word.

lineas.jp: 明日[あした]は 小樽[おたる]へ 遠足[えんそく]です。 八時[はちじ]に 駅[えき]に 集[あつ]まらなければ なりません。
lineas.es: Tomorrow we're going on a school trip to Otaru. We have to meet at the station at eight.

lineas.jp: 先生[せんせい]、 お 弁当[べんとう]を 持[も]って こなければ いけませんか。
lineas.es: Miss, do we have to bring a packed lunch?

lineas.jp: いいえ、 持[も]って こなくても いいですよ。 お 昼[ひる]は みんなで お 寿司[すし]を 食[た]べます。
lineas.es: No, you don't need to bring one. We'll all have sushi together for lunch.

lineas.jp: やった！ お 寿司[すし]、 たくさん 食[た]べても いいですか。
lineas.es: Yay! Can we eat lots of sushi?

lineas.jp: いいですよ。 でも、 ガラスの お 店[みせ]では 走[はし]っては いけません。
lineas.es: Of course. But no running in the glass shops.

lineas.jp: ニャン、 ガラスを 割[わ]っちゃ だめだよ。
lineas.es: Nyan, try not to break any glass.

lineas.jp: 割[わ]らないよ！
lineas.es: I'm not going to break anything!

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 今夜[こんや]は 早[はや]く 寝[ね]なきゃ ね。
lineas.es: Well then, we'd better get to bed early tonight.

bloques.md: Otaru, in Hokkaido, is famous for its sushi and its glassware shops, so the teacher's rules make perfect sense. Notice the registers: the teacher uses the full, polite forms, Nyan asks her with いけませんか and いいですか, and among classmates out come ちゃ だめ and なきゃ.

respuestas: 行かなければならない
いかなければならない
ejercicios.explica: Negative: 行[い]かない. Swap ない for なければ and add ならない: «if I don't go, it won't do», in other words, «I have to go».
Negative: しない. なければ contracts to なきゃ, and the rest drops off because it's understood: しなきゃ, «I've got to do it».
Negative: 食[た]べない. ない becomes なくても and you add いい: «even if you don't eat it, it's fine».
座[すわ]る is a う-group verb, so its て-form is 座[すわ]って. Then も and いい: «even if you sit, it's fine».
The て-form of 飲[の]む is 飲[の]んで, which ends in で. では contracts to じゃ, not ちゃ: 飲[の]んじゃ だめ.

ejercicios.pregunta: There's a test tomorrow. What does Nyan say?
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした]は テストだから、 勉強[べんきょう]＿。
ejercicios.explica: With a test tomorrow, studying is an obligation: しなきゃ, the short form of しなければ ならない. しても いい would be mere permission, and しなくても いい would say there's no need.

ejercicios.pregunta: The museum attendant answers Nyan. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 「ここで 写真[しゃしん]を 撮[と]っても いいですか。」「すみません、 ここでは 撮[と]っては ＿。」
ejercicios.explica: 撮[と]っては いけません is the ban: «if you do it, it's no good». いいです would be permission, and the apology すみません wouldn't make sense; ください can't follow ては.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama tells Nyan he needn't come tomorrow. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした]は 来[こ]＿ いいよ。
ejercicios.explica: なくても いい is «even if you don't come, it's fine»: no need. なくては would go with いけない to oblige, and 来[き]ては, without the negative, would be used to allow or forbid coming.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan wants the last dorayaki and asks permission. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: この どら 焼[や]き、 ＿？
opciones: 食[た]べなければ ならない
食[た]べては いけない
ejercicios.explica: To ask permission: て-form + も いい as a question. The other two would ask whether eating it is compulsory or forbidden, and what Nyan wants is to be allowed.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan tells Fukuro-sensei he has to leave now. Which sentence is appropriate?
opciones: もう 帰[かえ]らなければ なりません。
もう 帰[かえ]らなきゃ。
もう 帰[かえ]らなくちゃ。
ejercicios.explica: With the teacher you use the full, polite form. なきゃ and なくちゃ are for people you're close to: to her they'd sound like he was talking to a classmate.

ejercicios.pregunta: Pon tells Nyan the tea is free: «you don't have to pay». What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: お 茶[ちゃ]は ＿ よ。
opciones: 払[はら]わなくても いい
払[はら]っては いけない
払[はら]わなければ ならない
ejercicios.explica: «You don't have to pay» means there's no need, not that it's forbidden: なくても いい. 払[はら]っては いけない would be «you're not allowed to pay», the classic false friend of «you mustn't».

ejercicios.es: I have to hand in my homework by tomorrow.
ejercicios.explica: First the deadline (までに, «by»), then the object with を, and finally the obligation: 出[だ]さなければ なりません, «if I don't hand it in, it won't do».

ejercicios.es: Excuse me, may I sit here?
ejercicios.explica: あの opens politely, ここに marks where, and the request for permission closes the sentence: 座[すわ]っても いいですか.

ejercicios.es: Swimming in this river is not allowed.
ejercicios.explica: The place where the action happens takes で, and the ban is て-form + は + いけません. Since 泳[およ]いで ends in で, it becomes 泳[およ]いでは.

lecciones.titulo: If…: と, ば, たら and なら
lecciones.capitulo: If…, maybe… and I have to…
lecciones.resumen: English has one «if»; Japanese has four. By the end you'll know which one to pick in each situation, how to kick yourself over what you didn't do («I should have…!») and how to play with hypotheses like «supposing…» or «even if that were so…».

secciones.titulo: One «if» in English, four in Japanese

bloques.md:
Think about these four sentences: «if you press this button, the door opens»; «if you hurry, you'll make it»; «when you get home, call me»; «if you're going to Hokkaido, take a coat». In English, they all get by with «if» or «when». But the relationship between the two halves isn't the same. In the first, B happens on its own, like a law of physics. In the second, what matters is the condition: all it takes is hurrying. In the third, first A happens and then B. And in the fourth, you start from something you've been told in order to give advice.
Japanese has a form for each of those relationships: **と**, **ば**, **たら** and **なら**. Don't panic: they overlap quite a lot, and in many sentences two or three will do. What you'll learn here is what each one brings and when only one of them sounds right.

filas: If A is met (and that's what counts), B
Conditions, advice, どう すれば
急[いそ]げば、 間[ま]に 合[あ]う。
着[つ]いたら、 電話[でんわ]して。
If it's the case that A (going by what was said), B
行[い]くなら、 コートを。

bloques.md: One rule all four share: **the condition always comes first**. In English you can say «call me if you're late»; in Japanese, never: the «if» part goes first and the rest after it. It's the usual logic: whatever comes last is the main point.

secciones.titulo: と: whenever A happens, B happens

bloques.md:
Dictionary form or ない-form + **と**
押[お]す → **押[お]すと**　　押[お]さない → **押[お]さないと**
い-adjectives: 寒[さむ]い → **寒[さむ]いと**. Nouns and な-adjectives, with だ: 雨[あめ]だ → **雨[あめ]だと**.

と says B follows A in a **natural, automatic, inevitable** way: every time A occurs, B occurs. That's why it's the «if» of instruction manuals, laws of nature, fixed habits and directions to get somewhere. Think of it as a formula: put in A and out comes B.

items.jp: この ボタンを 押[お]すと、 ドアが 開[あ]きます。
items.es: If you press this button, the door opens.

items.jp: 春[はる]に なると、 雪[ゆき]が 溶[と]ける。
items.es: When spring comes, the snow melts.
items.nota: It happens every year, without anyone deciding it.

items.jp: この 道[みち]を まっすぐ 行[い]くと、 ポンさんの 店[みせ]が あります。
items.es: Go straight down this street and you'll come to Pon's shop.
items.nota: Directions are と territory: do this and you'll find that.

items.jp: ニャンは お 腹[なか]が すくと、 機嫌[きげん]が 悪[わる]く なる。
items.es: Whenever Nyan gets hungry, he gets grumpy.
items.nota: A habit: it always happens.

items.jp: 急[いそ]がないと、 遅[おく]れるよ。
items.es: If you don't hurry, you'll be late.
items.nota: ないと makes warnings. It's the same ないと as in «have to» from the previous lesson.

bloques.md: After と you can't put requests, invitations, wishes or plans. 駅[えき]に 着[つ]くと、 電話[でんわ]して ください sounds odd, because と describes how the world works, and someone calling you isn't something that happens by itself, like melting snow: it's a request. That's what たら is for: 駅[えき]に 着[つ]いたら、 電話[でんわ]して ください.

One more use: in the past, と tells of a **discovery**, «I did A and found B». It has a storytelling, bookish feel: 窓[まど]を 開[あ]けると、 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]って いた, «I opened the window, and it was snowing». You'll see it a lot in books; in speech, people prefer たら for the same thing, which you'll see shortly.

secciones.titulo: ば: the condition that decides everything

bloques.md:
**う-group verbs**: the final u becomes e + ば. 行[い]く → **行[い]けば**, 飲[の]む → **飲[の]めば**, 待[ま]つ → **待[ま]てば**, 買[か]う → **買[か]えば**.
**る-group verbs**: る → **れば**. 食[た]べる → **食[た]べれば**, 見[み]る → **見[み]れば**.
**Irregulars**: する → **すれば**, 来[く]る → **来[く]れば**.
**い-adjectives**: い → **ければ**. 安[やす]い → **安[やす]ければ**, いい → **よければ**.
**Negative**: ない → **なければ**. The «have to» piece from the previous lesson!
**Nouns and な-adjectives**: **なら** (in formal writing, であれば). 雨[あめ]なら, 静[しず]かなら.

ば puts the spotlight on **the condition**: what it takes for B to happen. It has a flavour of «if, and only if» or «all it takes is…». That's why it's the favourite «if» of advice, proverbs and questions about what to do.
And here's an expression you'll use every day: **どう すれば いい？**, literally «if I do how, is it good?», that is, «what should I do?». And its natural answer, **〜ば いい**: «all you need to do is…», «just…».

items.jp: 急[いそ]げば、 間[ま]に 合[あ]う。
items.es: If you hurry, you'll make it.
items.nota: Hurrying is the key: that's the condition.

items.jp: 安[やす]ければ、 買[か]います。
items.es: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.

items.jp: 天気[てんき]が よければ、 羊蹄山[ようていざん]が 見[み]えますよ。
items.es: If the weather's good, you can see Mount Yōtei.
items.nota: よければ: the ば of いい is built on its old form, よい.

items.jp: 「 宿題[しゅくだい]が 分[わ]からない。 どう すれば いい？」「 先生[せんせい]に 聞[き]けば いいよ。」
items.es: “I don't get the homework. What should I do?” “Just ask the teacher.”

items.jp: 雨[あめ]なら、 家[いえ]で 遊[あそ]ぼう。
items.es: If it rains, let's play at home.
items.nota: With nouns, ば turns into なら. It's the same なら you'll see further down.

bloques.md: If the first part is an **action**, ば doesn't usually take requests or plans after it: 駅[えき]に 着[つ]けば、 電話[でんわ]して ください sounds forced. The reason is that ば sets up a general condition, «in the event that this is met», and a one-off request for a specific moment fits better with たら. But if the first part is a **state** (ある, いる, できる, an adjective, a negative), a request is fine: 時間[じかん]が あれば、 遊[あそ]びに 来[き]て ください, «if you have time, come and see me».

secciones.titulo: たら: if… and when…, the all-rounder

bloques.md:
Past form + **ら**
行[い]った → **行[い]ったら**　　食[た]べた → **食[た]べたら**　　した → **したら**　　来[き]た → **来[き]たら**
安[やす]かった → **安[やす]かったら**　　雨[あめ]だった → **雨[あめ]だったら**　　行[い]かなかった → **行[い]かなかったら**

Why the past form? Because たら pictures A as **already done**: «once A has happened, then B». That past isn't about yesterday, it's about order: first A, then B.
That makes たら the most versatile «if». It works for what might happen (**if**) and also for what will definitely happen (**when**): 家[いえ]に 着[つ]いたら doesn't doubt you'll get home, it just says what you'll do after. And it happily takes everything と refused: requests, invitations, wishes and plans.

items.jp: 雨[あめ]だったら、 行[い]かない。
items.es: If it rains, I'm not going.

items.jp: 家[いえ]に 着[つ]いたら、 電話[でんわ]するね。
items.es: I'll call you when I get home.
items.nota: Getting home is certain: here たら means «when».

items.jp: 大人[おとな]に なったら、 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 住[す]みたい。
items.es: When I grow up, I want to live in Hokkaido.

items.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]が 終[お]わったら、 遊[あそ]ぼう。
items.es: Let's play once we've finished our homework.

items.jp: 家[いえ]に 帰[かえ]ったら、 テーブルに ケーキが あった。
items.es: When I got home, there was a cake on the table.
items.nota: In the past, たら tells of a discovery or a surprise, like と but with a conversational tone.

bloques.md: たら isn't the «when» for everything. It only works if B happens **after** A is complete. For a «when» that marks a period or a moment during which things happen, Japanese uses 時[とき]: 子[こ]どもの 時[とき], «when I was a child». If you say 子[こ]どもだったら, you'll be saying «if I were a child», which is something else entirely.

And you already know one use of たら from the lesson on suggestions: **〜たら どう？**, «why don't you…?». Now you can see where it comes from: «if you did it, how would that be?». 休[やす]んだら どう？, «why don't you take a break?».

secciones.titulo: なら: if that's so, then…

bloques.md:
Plain form + **なら**
Verbs: 行[い]く → **行[い]くなら**, 行[い]った → **行[い]ったなら**.
Nouns and な-adjectives, directly, without だ: **雨[あめ]なら**, **暇[ひま]なら**.

なら starts from something **already on the table**: what you've just been told, what you can see, or what's known. It's like saying «if that's the case…», «if that's what we're talking about…», «since…». That's why it shines in replies and advice: the other person mentions a plan, and you answer with なら to comment on that plan.

items.jp: 「 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]きたい。」「 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]くなら、 冬[ふゆ]が いいよ。 雪[ゆき]まつりが あるから。」
items.es: “I want to go to Hokkaido.” “If you're going to Hokkaido, winter's best. There's the snow festival.”
items.nota: The Sapporo Snow Festival is held in February.

items.jp: 「ラーメンが 食[た]べたい。」「ラーメンなら、 ポンさんの 店[みせ]が 一番[いちばん]だよ。」
items.es: “I feel like ramen.” “If it's ramen you want, Pon's shop is the best.”
items.nota: With nouns, なら is almost a topic: «speaking of ramen…».

items.jp: 「 明日[あした]、 暇[ひま]？」「 午後[ごご]なら 暇[ひま]だよ。」
items.es: “Are you free tomorrow?” “In the afternoon, yes.”
items.nota: なら narrows it down: «if we're talking about the afternoon, yes».

items.jp: 疲[つか]れて いるなら、 休[やす]んだ ほうが いい。
items.es: If you're tired, you'd better rest.
items.nota: Based on what you can see: the other person looks tired.

bloques.md: Now for the detail that makes なら unique: with it, **B can happen before A**. With たら, on the other hand, B always comes after. Compare:

filas: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]くなら、 コートを 買[か]った ほうが いい。
If you're going to Hokkaido, you'd better buy a coat.
北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]ったら、 コートを 買[か]おう。
When I get to Hokkaido, I'll buy a coat.

bloques.md: Don't use なら for things that simply happen one after another. 春[はる]に なるなら、 雪[ゆき]が 溶[と]ける sounds very strange, as if someone had said spring might be coming and you replied «if it's true that it's coming…». なら always has that «going by what you say» flavour, so it needs something on the table.

secciones.titulo: Which one do I pick?

bloques.md: Here's the same topic, the Furano lavender that blooms in July, told with all four forms. Each one says something different:

items.jp: 七月[しちがつ]に なると、 富良野[ふらの]は ラベンダーで 紫[むらさき]に なる。
items.es: When July comes, Furano turns purple with lavender.
items.nota: と: it happens every year, it's how nature works.

items.jp: 七月[しちがつ]まで 待[ま]てば、 ラベンダーが 見[み]られるよ。
items.es: Just wait till July and you'll get to see the lavender.
items.nota: ば: the condition is what matters; all it takes is waiting.

items.jp: 七月[しちがつ]に なったら、 富良野[ふらの]へ 行[い]こう！
items.es: When July comes, let's go to Furano!
items.nota: たら: a plan for when A is fulfilled.

items.jp: 「 七月[しちがつ]に 北海道[ほっかいどう]へ 行[い]くんだ。」「 七月[しちがつ]なら、 ラベンダーが 見[み]られるね。」
items.es: “I'm going to Hokkaido in July.” “If it's July, you'll get to see the lavender.”
items.nota: なら: it starts from what the other person just said.

filas: Describe something that always happens, a machine, a route
Say what it takes, give advice, ask what to do
Make plans, ask for something, say «when…»
Reply to what you're told, advise on a plan
It starts from what's been said

bloques.md: When in doubt, **たら**. In conversation it's the «if» least likely to go wrong, because it takes requests and plans and works for both «if» and «when». It won't always be the most elegant choice, but it'll rarely sound wrong.

secciones.titulo: もし, and what you didn't do: 〜ば よかった

bloques.md: **もし** is an adverb placed at the start to signal that a hypothesis is coming: «in case…», «if by any chance…». It doesn't make the condition; the condition is made by たら, ば or なら at the end of the first part. もし is just the sign announcing what's coming, and it helps the listener get ready.

items.jp: もし 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]ったら、 遠足[えんそく]は 中止[ちゅうし]です。
items.es: If it rains, the school trip is cancelled.

items.jp: もし よかったら、 一緒[いっしょ]に 行[い]きませんか。
items.es: If you'd like, why not come with us?
items.nota: もし よかったら, «if it suits you»: the kindest way to invite someone.

bloques.md: A typical learner mistake: putting もし and forgetting the ending. もし 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]る、 中止[ちゅうし]です doesn't work, because もし doesn't mean «if»: without たら or ば, the sentence has no condition. Think of もし as an «in case» that still needs its verb in a conditional form.

And now, regret. **〜ば よかった** literally means «if I had done A, it would have been good», that is, **«I should have…»**. With たら, **〜たら よかった** means the same, with a slightly more conversational tone. In the negative, **〜なければ よかった**: «I shouldn't have…». Add のに and out comes a sigh: «and it would have been so easy!». Aimed at someone else, it's a gentle reproach: «you could have told me!».

items.jp: もっと 早[はや]く 起[お]きれば よかった。
items.es: I should have got up earlier.

items.jp: 傘[かさ]を 持[も]って くれば よかった。
items.es: I should have brought an umbrella.

items.jp: あんなに 食[た]べなければ よかった…
items.es: I shouldn't have eaten so much…
items.nota: Nyan's standard line after every festival.

items.jp: 言[い]って くれれば よかったのに。
items.es: You could have told me!
items.nota: のに adds «and it would've been so easy». It's a reproach, but an affectionate one.

bloques.md: Looking forward, the same structure expresses wishes: **〜たら いいね** or **〜と いいね**, «I hope…»: 明日[あした]、 晴[は]れたら いいね, «I hope it's sunny tomorrow».

secciones.titulo: Supposing…: としたら, としても and にしても

bloques.md: To finish, three expressions for playing with hypotheses. All three are built from pieces you already know: と (the quoting «that…»), する («to consider», «to take as») and an «if» or an «even if».

Plain form + **と したら**: supposing…, then…
Plain form + **と しても**: even if that were so, (nothing changes)
**にしても**, after nouns or the plain form: even granting that…
