With nouns, the first two take だ: 本当[ほんとう]だと したら, 冗談[じょうだん]だと しても.

**としたら** sets up a hypothesis and draws its consequences: «let's say A; then B». It's the one for «what would you do if…?» games and for «if that's true, wow». You'll also see とすれば and とすると, which work almost the same.
**としても** sets up a hypothesis in order to say **nothing changes**: «even if that were so, B». It's often reinforced with たとえ at the start, an «even if» announced in advance.
**にしても** looks like としても, but it doesn't imagine: it **accepts** something as true and still objects. «Fine, it's a joke; even so, it's cruel». It also forms pairs, «whether… or…», and in conversation you'll often hear **それに しても**, «even so», «boy, is it…!».

items.jp: 宝[たから]くじが 当[あ]たったと したら、 何[なに]を する？
items.es: Supposing you won the lottery, what would you do?

items.jp: もし それが 本当[ほんとう]だと したら、 大変[たいへん]だ。
items.es: If that's true, we're in trouble.

items.jp: 今[いま]から 走[はし]ったと しても、 間[ま]に 合[あ]わない。
items.es: Even if I ran now, I wouldn't make it.

items.jp: たとえ 雨[あめ]だと しても、 お 祭[まつ]りに 行[い]く。
items.es: Even if it rains, I'm going to the festival.

items.jp: 冗談[じょうだん]に しても、 ひどいよ。
items.es: Even as a joke, that's harsh.
items.nota: にしても takes it for granted that it's a joke. With 冗談[じょうだん]だと しても, on the other hand, you'd be doubting that it was.

items.jp: 行[い]くに しても 行[い]かないに しても、 連絡[れんらく]して ね。
items.es: Whether you go or not, let me know, OK?

items.jp: それに しても、 寒[さむ]いね。
items.es: Boy, is it cold, though!
items.nota: それに しても: «that aside», «even so». It brings you back to what's really striking you.

secciones.titulo: All together: winter plans

lineas.jp: 冬休[ふゆやす]みに なったら、 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]かない？
lineas.es: How about we go to Hokkaido when the winter holidays come?

lineas.jp: 行[い]く！ でも、 わたし、 寒[さむ]いと 動[うご]けなく なるよ。
lineas.es: Yes! But whenever it's cold, I freeze up.

lineas.jp: 暖[あたた]かい コートを 着[き]れば 大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だよ。
lineas.es: Just wear a warm coat and you'll be fine.

lineas.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]くなら、 札幌[さっぽろ]で 味噌[みそ]ラーメンを 食[た]べたい！
lineas.es: If we're going to Hokkaido, I want miso ramen in Sapporo!

lineas.jp: いいね。 もし 時間[じかん]が あったら、 小樽[おたる]にも 行[い]こう。
lineas.es: Nice. And if we have time, let's go to Otaru too.

lineas.jp: 宝[たから]くじが 当[あ]たったと したら、 毎日[まいにち] カニを 食[た]べるのに…
lineas.es: If I won the lottery, I'd eat crab every single day…

lineas.jp: 当[あ]たったと しても、 ニャンは 一日中[いちにちじゅう] 寝[ね]てるよ。
lineas.es: Even if you won, you'd spend all day asleep.

lineas.jp: ひどい！ …ああ、 夏[なつ]に お 小遣[こづか]いを 貯[た]めて おけば よかった…
lineas.es: That's so mean! …Oh, I should have saved my pocket money over the summer…

bloques.md: Go back over the scene: たら for the holiday plan and for what they'll do if they have time to spare; と for what always happens to Nyan when it's cold; ば for the condition that fixes everything, wearing a coat; なら to react to Tama's plan; としたら and としても to daydream about the lottery; and ば よかった for the final lament. Crab and miso ramen are two of Hokkaido's most famous foods, so Nyan knows exactly what he wants.

ejercicios.explica: う-group verb: the final u becomes e and you add ば. く → け: 行[い]けば.
る-group verb: る becomes れば. 食[た]べれば.
い-adjectives swap い for ければ: 安[やす]ければ, «if it's cheap».
いい always conjugates from its old form, よい: よければ. That's where もし よければ, «if you like», comes from.
たら is the past form + ら. The past of 来[く]る is 来[き]た, so you get 来[き]たら.
見[み]る is a る-group verb: 見[み]れば. With よかった after it, «it would have been good if I'd seen it»: I should have seen it.

ejercicios.pregunta: Instructions for the electric kettle. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: この ボタンを 押[お]す＿、 お 湯[ゆ]が 出[で]ます。
ejercicios.explica: It's an automatic result, like any machine's: every time you press, hot water comes out. That's と territory. なら would start from something someone else said, and のに is «even though», which makes no sense here.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan asks Tama to call him. Which form fits?
ejercicios.jp: 駅[えき]に ＿、 電話[でんわ]して ください。
ejercicios.explica: A request follows, and with requests the natural «if» is たら: «once you arrive, call me». と can't take requests because it describes things that happen on their own, and ば after an action doesn't suit a one-off request either.

ejercicios.pregunta: Kage says he's off to Sapporo and Tama gives him advice. What does she say?
ejercicios.jp: 「 今度[こんど]、 札幌[さっぽろ]に 行[い]くんだ。」「 札幌[さっぽろ]に ＿、 味噌[みそ]ラーメンを 食[た]べてね。」
ejercicios.explica: Tama takes what Kage just said as her starting point to advise him: that's なら, «if you're going to Sapporo…». With と you can't advise or request, and ば would make going sound like the required condition, when the trip is already decided.

ejercicios.pregunta: The coat needs buying before the trip. Which form fits?
ejercicios.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に ＿、 コートを 買[か]って おいた ほうが いいよ。
ejercicios.explica: With なら, the second part can happen before the first: you buy the coat here, before going. 行[い]ったら would mean buying it after you arrive, and と can't give advice.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan got soaked and is kicking himself. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 雨[あめ]に 濡[ぬ]れた… 傘[かさ]を 持[も]って くれば ＿。
ejercicios.explica: 〜ば よかった looks back: «it would have been good if I'd brought it», that is, «I should have brought it». 〜ば いい would be advice for the future, and よければ would leave the sentence unfinished.

ejercicios.pregunta: It's already too late and nothing can be done. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 今[いま]から 走[はし]った＿、 もう 間[ま]に 合[あ]わない。
ejercicios.explica: としても sets up a hypothesis to say nothing changes: «even if I ran, I wouldn't make it». としたら would draw a consequence from the hypothesis, and here the whole point is that it's no use.

ejercicios.es: If it rains, the school trip is cancelled.
ejercicios.explica: もし announces the hypothesis, the condition ends in たら and always comes first. Then the topic, 遠足[えんそく]は, and the conclusion.

ejercicios.es: Supposing you won the lottery, what would you do?
piezas: 当[あ]たったと したら、
ejercicios.explica: The hypothesis, with としたら, goes first; then the question, with 何[なに]を and the verb at the end. Japanese doesn't need a special «would» form here: the plain form does the job.

lecciones.titulo: Maybe, probably, definitely: how sure are you?
lecciones.capitulo: If…, maybe… and I have to…
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to dial your certainty up and down like a Japanese speaker: from «might be» to «no doubt about it», by way of the weather forecast's «probably» and the «right?» that fishes for agreement.

secciones.titulo: A flat statement is a commitment

bloques.md:
If you say 明日[あした]は 雨[あめ]だ, you're stating that it'll rain tomorrow, as if you'd seen it. About the future, about what other people think, or about anything you haven't checked, Japanese speakers rarely talk like that. The normal thing is to mark **how sure you are**: «it might rain», «it'll probably rain», «it's bound to rain».
English does this too, but mostly with separate words («maybe», «probably»). Japanese does it above all **at the end of the sentence**, with endings that work like a certainty thermometer. Get used to them and you'll sound more careful, more natural and far less blunt.

filas: Medium: could be, could not be
〜に 決[き]まって いる

bloques.md:
They all go after the **plain form**: 来[く]る, 来[こ]ない, 来[き]た, 寒[さむ]い…
With **nouns** and **な-adjectives**, they attach directly, **without だ**: 雨[あめ]かもしれない, 雨[あめ]でしょう, 暇[ひま]に 違[ちが]いない.
Why no だ? Because だ is a flat assertion, «it is so», and these endings take its place precisely to say «it is so, with this degree of certainty». Using both would mean asserting and doubting at the same time.

secciones.titulo: かもしれない: maybe

bloques.md:
かもしれない looks long, but it makes sense as soon as you take it apart: **か** (the question particle, «whether…») + **も** («even») + **知[し]れない** («can't be known»). That is: «whether it's so or not can't be known». That's why it's a 50/50: you lean neither towards yes nor towards no.
The polite form is **かもしれません**. And in casual speech, young people especially chop it down to plain **かも**, which you'll hear (and see in text messages) all the time.

items.jp: 明日[あした]は 雪[ゆき]かもしれない。
items.es: It might snow tomorrow.
items.nota: Noun + かもしれない, with no だ.

items.jp: カゲも 来[く]るかもしれない。
items.es: Kage might come too.

items.jp: もう 売[う]り 切[き]れたかもしれません。
items.es: It may have sold out already.
items.nota: With the past before it: maybe it's already happened.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 来[こ]ないかも。
items.es: Maybe he's not coming today.
items.nota: かも: the short, chatty version.

bloques.md: かもしれません also has a very Japanese use: **softening an opinion** even when you're fairly sure. If something in a shop seems expensive, saying 高[たか]いです sounds like a straight complaint; ちょっと 高[たか]いかもしれませんね, «it might be a little pricey, perhaps?», says the same thing without anyone feeling attacked. In Japan, not imposing your opinion is a form of respect, and かもしれない is one of its favourite tools.
Don't put だ in front: 雨[あめ]だかもしれない is a classic mistake. かもしれない already does だ's job, so with nouns and な-adjectives it attaches directly: 雨[あめ]かもしれない, 静[しず]かかもしれない.

secciones.titulo: でしょう and だろう: probably

bloques.md:
**でしょう** is the speaker's guess, made with a fair amount of confidence: «probably», «most likely». It's the form you'll hear every morning in the weather forecast: 明日[あした]は 晴[は]れるでしょう, «tomorrow will be sunny». The forecaster isn't a hundred per cent sure, but nearly.
**だろう** is exactly the same thing in plain form. In writing it's neutral, and in thoughts too: when people wonder something to themselves, they use だろう or だろうか. But said out loud, だろう sounds rather blunt and, traditionally, masculine. Many people prefer と 思[おも]う instead: たぶん 来[く]ると 思[おも]う, «I think he'll come».

items.jp: 明日[あした]は 晴[は]れるでしょう。
items.es: Tomorrow will probably be sunny.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]は もう 寒[さむ]いでしょう。
items.es: It must be cold in Hokkaido by now.

items.jp: カゲは たぶん 知[し]って いるだろう。
items.es: Kage probably knows.

items.jp: どこに 置[お]いたんだろう…
items.es: Now where did I put it…?
items.nota: だろう in a thought spoken aloud: here it sounds natural from anyone.

bloques.md: And a golden use for shops and the phone: **でしょうか**. Instead of asking with ですか, which demands an answer, でしょうか asks what the other person «supposes», and that sounds much more delicate. これは いくらでしょうか, «how much might this be?», is the polite way to ask a price.

Don't use でしょう for your own plans. 明日[あした]、 わたしは 行[い]くでしょう sounds as if you're forecasting yourself, like the weather: «tomorrow, Nyan will probably go». For things you decide, say 行[い]こうと 思[おも]います or, if you're sure, 行[い]きます.

secciones.titulo: でしょ？ and だろ？: right?

bloques.md:
With a questioning intonation, でしょう changes jobs: it no longer guesses, it **asks the other person to agree with you**. It's nearly always shortened to **でしょ？**, and it's stronger than ね: not «isn't it?», but «come on, admit it!». When the other person didn't listen to you, it becomes a small reproach: ほら、 言[い]ったでしょ！, «see? I told you!».
The plain version, **だろ？**, is rougher and more masculine. Very Kage.

items.jp: この ケーキ、 おいしいでしょ？
items.es: This cake is amazing, right?
items.nota: Tama isn't asking: she's expecting Nyan to say yes.

items.jp: ほら、 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]ったでしょ！
items.es: See? It rained!

items.jp: 俺[おれ]の 方[ほう]が 速[はや]いだろ？
items.es: I'm faster than you, right?
items.nota: Kage showing off, naturally.

bloques.md: With someone older or your boss, avoid でしょう？ to fish for agreement: it sounds like «you know this, don't you?», as if you were testing them. That's what ですよね is for, which seeks agreement without pushing: この 本[ほん]、 面白[おもしろ]いですよね.

secciones.titulo: に違いない and に決まっている: no doubt about it

bloques.md:
At the top of the thermometer there are two expressions, and although both mean «definitely», they don't reach that certainty by the same road.
**に 違[ちが]いない** literally means «there's no mistake», «it can't be otherwise». It's the certainty of the **detective**: you've seen clues and drawn a conclusion. It sounds a little serious, like a novel or a line of reasoning, so in everyday chat it's used with a touch of theatre.
**に 決[き]まって いる**, nearly always **に 決[き]まってる**, means «it's settled that…», that is, «obviously», «no question». No clues needed: it's the certainty of someone who **won't hear any argument**, sometimes rightly and sometimes out of sheer prejudice. It's very conversational, and very emotional.

items.jp: 雪[ゆき]の 上[うえ]に 足跡[あしあと]が ある。 誰[だれ]か 来[き]たに 違[ちが]いない。
items.es: There are footprints in the snow. Someone must have come.
items.nota: A deduction from a clue.

items.jp: あれは カゲの 声[こえ]に 違[ちが]いない。
items.es: That's Kage's voice, no doubt about it.

items.jp: ポンさんの コロッケは おいしいに 決[き]まってる！
items.es: Pon's croquettes are delicious, obviously!

items.jp: そんなの 無理[むり]に 決[き]まってるよ。
items.es: That's obviously impossible.

items.jp: 「どっちが 勝[か]つと 思[おも]う？」「 俺[おれ]に 決[き]まってるだろ。」
items.es: “Who do you think will win?” “Me, obviously. Who else?”

bloques.md: に 決[き]まってる shuts the conversation down: «that's how it is, full stop». Among friends, with a bit of humour, it's perfect. But to a superior or in a serious discussion, you'll sound arrogant, as if their opinion didn't count. If you're sure and want to say so politely, きっと 〜と 思[おも]います works much better.

secciones.titulo: The full scale, with its adverbs

bloques.md: These endings usually come with an adverb at the start of the sentence that announces the level of certainty, just as in English. Each adverb has its favourite endings, and pairing them well is what makes your sentence sound complete.

filas: もしかしたら, ひょっとしたら
たぶん (おそらく, more formal)
〜でしょう, 〜だろう, 〜と 思[おも]う
〜でしょう, 〜と 思[おも]う, 〜に 違[ちが]いない
〜に 決[き]まってる, plain form

bloques.md: False friend: たぶん isn't «maybe», even though that's how it often gets translated. «Maybe» is a 50/50, and that's もしかしたら 〜かもしれない. たぶん sits well above that, at «probably». And きっと isn't based on evidence but on what you feel: that's why it works for encouraging someone, きっと 大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だよ, «I'm sure it'll be fine».
And now, a mystery at Tama's house. Notice how each character commits more or less depending on what they know:

lineas.jp: あれ？ どら 焼[や]きが ない！
lineas.es: Huh? The dorayaki's gone!

lineas.jp: もしかしたら、 カゲが 食[た]べたかもしれない。
lineas.es: Maybe Kage ate it.

lineas.jp: 俺[おれ]じゃない！ ニャンが 食[た]べたに 決[き]まってる！
lineas.es: It wasn't me! It was Nyan, obviously!

lineas.jp: わたしでも ないよ！ …たぶん。
lineas.es: It wasn't me either! …Probably.

lineas.jp: 見[み]て。 床[ゆか]に あんこが 落[お]ちてる。 それに、 小[ちい]さい 足跡[あしあと]…
lineas.es: Look. There's anko on the floor. And some tiny footprints…

lineas.jp: 小[ちい]さい 足跡[あしあと]？ じゃあ、 コタローだろう。
lineas.es: Tiny footprints? Then it was probably Kotarō.

lineas.jp: コタロー、 口[くち]に あんこが ついてるよ。
lineas.es: Kotarō, you've got anko on your mouth.

lineas.jp: …おいしかった。
lineas.es: …It was yummy.

lineas.jp: やっぱり。 コタローに 違[ちが]いないと 思[おも]った！
lineas.es: I knew it! I was sure it had to be Kotarō!

lineas.jp: ほら、 わたしじゃ なかったでしょ？
lineas.es: See? Told you it wasn't me!

bloques.md: Nyan starts with a timid かもしれない; Kage jumps in with に 決[き]まってる and no evidence at all (and gets it wrong); Kage's later だろう at least leans on a clue; and Tama, with the footprints and the anko, arrives at the detective's に 違[ちが]いない. Anko, by the way, is the sweet red bean paste inside a dorayaki: the perfect piece of evidence.

ejercicios.explica: With nouns, かもしれない attaches directly, without だ: 雨[あめ]かもしれない, «it might rain».
でしょう goes after the plain form of the verb, which stays as it is: 来[く]るでしょう, «he'll probably come».
かも is the chopped-down version of かもしれない. The い-adjective stays as it is: 寒[さむ]いかも, «it might be cold».

ejercicios.forma: past + に 違[ちが]いない
ejercicios.explica: The past of 行[い]く is irregular, 行[い]った, followed by に 違[ちが]いない: «he must have gone», a deduction.

ejercicios.pregunta: The TV weather forecast. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした]は 晴[は]れる＿。
ejercicios.explica: The forecaster gives a very likely prediction in a formal tone: でしょう. に 決[き]まってる would be too casual and too categorical, and かも too much like a chat between friends.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which form is right?
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした]は 雨[あめ]＿。
ejercicios.explica: With nouns, かもしれない attaches directly, with no だ or な. かもしれない already takes だ's place, and using both would mean asserting and doubting at once.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama wants Nyan to agree with her. What does she say?
ejercicios.jp: この ケーキ、 おいしい＿？
ejercicios.explica: でしょ？ with a questioning tone asks the other person to agree: «right?». かもしれない would express doubt about her own cake, and に 違[ちが]いない would be a detective's deduction.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama has seen the footprints and draws a conclusion. What does she say?
ejercicios.jp: 雪[ゆき]の 上[うえ]に 足跡[あしあと]が ある。 誰[だれ]か 来[き]た＿。
ejercicios.explica: There's a clear clue and the conclusion is firm: に 違[ちが]いない, the certainty that comes from deduction. かもしれない would be too timid, and でしょうか is a question.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan very politely asks a price in a shop. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: すみません、 これは いくら＿。
ejercicios.explica: でしょうか asks what the other person «supposes», so it sounds gentler than ですか. だろう is plain and would sound like talking to yourself, and に 決[き]まってる doesn't ask anything.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan has no idea whether Kage will come: he might, he might not. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: カゲは 来[く]る＿。
ejercicios.explica: A 50/50 is かもしれない: «whether he comes or not can't be known». The other two express near-total certainty, the exact opposite.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which adverb goes best with this ending?
ejercicios.jp: ＿、 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]るかもしれない。
ejercicios.explica: かもしれない is a 50/50 doubt, and its natural partner is もしかしたら, «maybe». 絶対[ぜったい]に and きっと announce a lot of certainty and would clash with the doubt at the end.

ejercicios.es: Kage might already know.
ejercicios.explica: The topic first, then the adverb もう («already»), the verb in plain form, and finally the degree of certainty: かもしれない.

ejercicios.es: That's obviously impossible.
ejercicios.explica: 無理[むり] is a な-adjective, so it goes straight in front of に 決[き]まってる. よ at the end adds the «take it from me» tone.

lecciones.titulo: な, かな, さ, わ, ぞ, ぜ: the colour at the end
lecciones.capitulo: If…, maybe… and I have to…
lecciones.resumen: The last syllables of a sentence tell you who's talking and what mood they're in. By the end you'll recognise at a glance the sentence-ending particles that fill anime and the streets, and you'll know which ones to use yourself and which to simply enjoy.

secciones.titulo: The last syllable carries the feeling

bloques.md:
You already know よ (I'm telling you, I insist) and ね (let's agree). But Japanese has many more sentence-ending particles, and they all do the same kind of job: **they don't change what you say, they change how you say it**. They add attitude: doubt, enthusiasm, nonchalance, warning, complicity.
In English we do this with intonation and with fillers like «eh?», «man», «mate» or «you know». And just like those fillers, sentence-ending particles say a lot about **who's speaking**: their age, their personality, sometimes their region and, traditionally, whether they're a man or a woman.

Here's an important warning. Anime and manga exaggerate these particles on purpose, so you recognise each character the moment they open their mouth: the swaggering hero, the refined young lady, the wise old man. Japanese linguists even have a name for this character speech: 役割語[やくわりご], «role language». In real life, especially among young people, the differences are much milder.
So the goal of this lesson is twofold: **recognise them all** (you'll hear them every day) and **use only a few**. A particle that sounds natural from a sixty-year-old man from Osaka can sound like a costume in your mouth.

secciones.titulo: な: thinking out loud

bloques.md:
The most common use of な (often stretched to **なあ**) is talking **to yourself**: exclaiming, sighing, wishing. Here everyone uses it, men and women, kids and grandparents, because it isn't aimed at anyone: it's what slips out when you see something.
With **〜たい** before it, it voices a wish, almost a sigh: «oh, I'd love to…». And **いいなあ** is the classic way of saying «I'm so jealous!» or «lucky you!».

items.jp: いい 天気[てんき]だなあ。
items.es: What a lovely day!
items.nota: Nyan, sprawled in the sun, talking to himself.

items.jp: 眠[ねむ]いな…
items.es: So sleepy…

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]きたいな。
items.es: I'd love to go to Hokkaido.

items.jp: 「 来週[らいしゅう]、 札幌[さっぽろ]に 行[い]くんだ。」「いいなあ！」
items.es: “I'm going to Sapporo next week.” “Lucky you!”

bloques.md: When な **is aimed at someone else**, it works like a more direct, matey ね. You mostly hear it among guys and from older men speaking to younger people: 明日[あした]な, «tomorrow, yeah?», or じゃあな, «right, see ya». Women use it less towards others and more in those comments to themselves.

Don't confuse it with the prohibitive な you already know. 食[た]べるな！, stuck curtly onto the dictionary form with a sharp tone, is «don't eat!». よく 食[た]べるなあ, with a long, admiring なあ, is «wow, he really can eat!». The difference is in the tone (curt or drawn out) and the context: one forbids and the other comments. And there's a third you'll hear from mums and grandmas: verb stem + な, a short form of なさい. 早[はや]く 寝[ね]な, «go on, off to bed».

secciones.titulo: かな: I wonder…

bloques.md: **かな** combines the question particle か with that thinking-aloud な: the result is «I wonder if…», «could it be…?». It's a question that doesn't demand an answer: you toss it into the air, and if the other person feels like it, they reply. That's why it's so comfortable and so common, and everyone uses it.

items.jp: 明日[あした]、 雪[ゆき]かな。
items.es: I wonder if it'll snow tomorrow.

items.jp: 晩[ばん]ごはん、 何[なに]かな。
items.es: I wonder what's for dinner.
items.nota: The big question of the day, according to Nyan.

items.jp: そろそろ 帰[かえ]ろうかな。
items.es: I think I might head off now.
items.nota: Volitional + かな: you announce an intention without imposing it, as if you're still thinking it over.

items.jp: ちょっと 手伝[てつだ]って くれないかな。
items.es: Any chance you could give me a hand?
items.nota: A request wrapped in doubt, very soft.

bloques.md: Its polite relative is でしょうか, which you saw in the last lesson. And its traditional feminine relative is **かしら**, which means the same. Today かしら sounds like an elegant lady, a novel or a refined anime character; very few young people use it day to day. Recognise it, but for you, かな covers everything.

secciones.titulo: さ: offhand, or keeping the rhythm

bloques.md:
**さ** leads two lives. At the end of a sentence, it states something in a laid-back way, like «meh» or «well, obviously»: いいさ, «meh, whatever»; 何[なん]とか なるさ, «it'll work itself out». It's somewhat masculine and can sound calm and self-assured or, depending on the tone, a bit condescending.
But where you'll hear it most is **mid-sentence**, as a filler after each chunk: 昨日[きのう]さ、 カゲがさ、 急[きゅう]にさ… It's very typical of casual speech around Tokyo and works like our «you know» or «like». Above all, **あのさ** is the most typical way to get a friend's attention: «hey, listen…».

items.jp: あのさ、 明日[あした] 暇[ひま]？
items.es: Hey, are you free tomorrow?

items.jp: 負[ま]けても いいさ。 楽[たの]しかったから。
items.es: Meh, who cares if I lost. It was fun.

bloques.md: The odd さ sounds natural among friends; one after every chunk of the sentence sounds childish or grating, like someone who puts «like» every three words. And with a teacher or strangers, not a single one: it's speech for people you're close to.

secciones.titulo: わ: soft… or from Osaka

bloques.md:
You need to be careful with わ, because there are really two of them, told apart by intonation.
**The rising わ**, soft, from Tokyo-style Japanese: traditionally feminine, it adds a delicate emphasis. きれいだわ, «how pretty». Today, among young women in Tokyo, you hear it rarely in daily life; it lives mainly in fiction (refined ladies, well-bred young women) and in combinations like わよ and わね.
**The falling わ**, flat: anyone uses it, men included, and it's especially common in western Japan, in Kansai. It announces what you've decided or how you feel: もう 帰[かえ]るわ, «right, I'm off». これ、 おいしいわ, «this is good, y'know».
As you can see, region and generation matter a lot here. When you hear a わ, notice who's speaking and how it sounds before drawing conclusions.

items.jp: まあ、 すてきだわ。
items.es: Oh, how lovely!
items.nota: Rising わ: the tone of an elegant lady, very much fiction.

items.jp: ほな、 帰[かえ]るわ。
items.es: Right then, I'm off.
items.nota: Falling わ, from someone in Osaka. ほな is «well then» in Kansai speech.

secciones.titulo: ぞ and ぜ: the rough voice

bloques.md:
**ぞ** asserts forcefully: it warns, threatens, spurs on. Aimed at others, it sounds masculine and rough: 行[い]くぞ！, «let's go!», from whoever's leading the group; 危[あぶ]ないぞ, «watch out, that's dangerous!». But said **to yourself**, to psych yourself up, far more people use it: よし、 がんばるぞ, «right, let's do this!», is something people say to themselves even if they'd never talk to anyone else that way.
**ぜ** is the «c'mon, buddy!» of the likeable tough guy: 行[い]こうぜ, «let's go, man!». It's masculine, cocky and a little old-fashioned. In real life only some young men use it among friends; in anime, it's the badge of the hot-headed hero. Guess who uses it in Nyango.

items.jp: おい、 ニャン。 競争[きょうそう]しようぜ。
items.es: Oi, Nyan. Let's race.
items.nota: Kage, of course.

items.jp: 負[ま]けないぞ！
items.es: I'm not going to lose!

items.jp: よし、 今日[きょう]は 漢字[かんじ]を 十個[じゅっこ] 覚[おぼ]えるぞ。
items.es: Right, today I'm learning ten kanji!
items.nota: ぞ to psych yourself up.

bloques.md: ぞ and ぜ are the most dangerous ones for a learner. Aimed at a teacher, a customer or someone you've just met, they sound cocky, almost aggressive, and very cartoonish too. If you want to sound energetic but polite, よ is more than enough: 行[い]きましょう よ, «come on, let's go!».

secciones.titulo: All together, and which ones to use

filas: あのさ, yes; the rest, sparingly

bloques.md: Now look at the Nyango characters in the park. Each one sounds like who they are:

lineas.jp: おい、 ニャン。 競争[きょうそう]しようぜ。
lineas.es: Oi, Nyan. Let's race.

lineas.jp: えー、 今日[きょう]は 暑[あつ]いなあ… 明日[あした]に しようかな。
lineas.es: Ugh, it's so hot today… Maybe tomorrow?

lineas.jp: 逃[に]げるな！ 行[い]くぞ！
lineas.es: Don't you dare chicken out! Here I go!

lineas.jp: カゲ、 速[はや]いね。 ニャン、 勝[か]てるかな。
lineas.es: Kage's fast, isn't he? I wonder if Nyan can win.

lineas.jp: あのさ、 タマ… わたし、 もう 疲[つか]れたんだけど。
lineas.es: Hey, Tama… I'm already tired, you know.

lineas.jp: ふん、 俺[おれ]の 勝[か]ちだぜ。
lineas.es: Hah, I win.

lineas.jp: いいさ。 アイスが 食[た]べられれば、 それで いいんだ。
lineas.es: Meh, whatever. As long as I get an ice cream, I'm happy.

lineas.jp: ニャンは 相変[あいか]わらずだね。
lineas.es: Nyan, you never change.

bloques.md: Kage throws out ぜ and ぞ, cocky and competitive; lazy Nyan sighs with なあ, hesitates with かな, grabs attention with あのさ and consoles himself with a very laid-back いいさ; and kind Tama sticks to ね and かな. Notice 逃[に]げるな too: the curt prohibitive な, right next to Nyan's long, drawn-out 暑[あつ]いなあ.

ejercicios.forma: volitional + かな (I think I might…)
ejercicios.explica: The volitional of 行[い]く is 行[い]こう. With かな after it, you announce an intention as if you're still thinking it over: «I think I might go».
Stem 食[た]べ + たい, and な to sigh it out loud: 食[た]べたいな, «oh, I'd love to eat…».

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan looks at the sky and talks to himself. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: いい 天気[てんき]だ＿。
ejercicios.explica: To exclaim to yourself, the particle is な, often stretched to なあ. ぞ and ぜ are aimed forcefully at other people, and there's no one here to warn or challenge.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan wonders whether it'll snow tomorrow. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした]、 雪[ゆき]＿。
ejercicios.explica: かな is a question tossed into the air: «will it snow?». だぞ would forcefully assert that it will, and さ would say it offhandedly, as if it were obvious.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does this sentence mean, said in a curt, sharp tone?
ejercicios.jp: 食[た]べるな！
ejercicios.explica: な stuck curtly onto the dictionary form is the prohibition: «don't eat!». The admiring exclamation would be よく 食[た]べるなあ, with a long なあ.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does this sentence mean, said admiringly?
ejercicios.jp: よく 食[た]べるなあ。
ejercicios.explica: Here the drawn-out なあ comments on something that surprises you: «what an appetite!». It's not a prohibition: that would be 食[た]べるな, curt and without よく.

ejercicios.pregunta: Kage challenges Nyan, cocky and matey. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: 走[はし]ろう＿！
ejercicios.explica: ぜ is the cocky, masculine invitation that suits Kage. かしら is a feminine, refined «I wonder», and わね sounds like an elegant lady: nothing like him.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan wants to tell Fukuro-sensei the test was hard. Which sentence is appropriate?
opciones: 難[むずか]しかったです。
ejercicios.explica: With the teacher you speak with です/ます and no rough particles. ぜ and ぞ would sound cocky, almost defiant, as if he were talking to a rival.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama wants to get Nyan's attention. How does she start?
ejercicios.jp: ＿、 ニャン。 これ 見[み]て。
ejercicios.explica: あのさ is the «hey, look» used between friends. いいさ is «meh, whatever» and 行[い]くぞ is «let's go!», and neither of them asks for attention.

ejercicios.pregunta: What is Nyan doing when he says this to himself?
ejercicios.jp: よし、 がんばるぞ！
ejercicios.explica: ぞ asserts forcefully, and said to yourself it's a pep talk: «right, let's do this!». To hesitate he'd use かな, and to ask permission, 〜ても いい？.

ejercicios.es: Hey, shall we go to the park tomorrow?
ejercicios.explica: あのさ opens to get attention, then when and where, and finally the invitation in the negative with a question tone, 行[い]かない？, «why don't we go?».

ejercicios.es: I wonder if Tama's at home.
ejercicios.explica: The ordinary plain-form sentence, タマは 家[いえ]に いる, and かな at the end to turn it into a doubt tossed into the air.

ejercicios.es: Lucky you! I want to go too.
ejercicios.explica: いいなあ is the good old «lucky you!». Then わたしも, the wish with たい, and another な to sigh it out loud.

lecciones.titulo: It seems…: そう, みたい, よう and らしい
lecciones.capitulo: If…, maybe… and I have to…
lecciones.resumen: «That looks tasty», «seems nobody's home», «they say it'll snow», «that's so Nyan!»: by the end you'll handle every Japanese «seems» without mixing them up, and even tell people about the thing that almost happened to you.

secciones.titulo: Four ways of «seeming»

bloques.md:
In English, «seems» and «looks» cover almost everything: «it looks tasty» (you're looking at it), «it seems nobody's home» (you work it out because the lights are off), «it seems it'll snow tomorrow» (you heard so). Japanese, on the other hand, pays close attention to **where your information comes from**: whether you see it with your own eyes, deduce it from clues or were told it. And it has a form for each source.
This isn't a whim: it's tied to a very Japanese habit of not stating as fact what you don't know first-hand. When you use the right form, you give the information and how you got it, all at once.

filas: What you see at a glance, before checking
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]りそう。 (The sky looks like rain.)
Plain form + みたい / ようだ
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]って いるみたい。 (People are carrying umbrellas.)
Something heard around, kept at a distance
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]るらしい。 (Apparently it's going to rain.)
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]るそうだ。 (They say it's going to rain.)

secciones.titulo: 〜そう: looks like…

bloques.md:
**Verbs**: stem + そう. 降[ふ]る → **降[ふ]りそう**, 落[お]ちる → **落[お]ちそう**.
**い-adjectives**: drop the い. おいしい → **おいしそう**, 高[たか]い → **高[たか]そう**.
**な-adjectives**: directly. 元気[げんき] → **元気[げんき]そう**, 暇[ひま] → **暇[ひま]そう**.
**Exceptions**: いい → **よさそう**; ない → **なさそう** (and the same with negative adjectives: おいしくない → おいしくなさそう). The extra さ stops the word shrinking to a single syllable, よそう or なそう, which would sound odd.
**Nouns**: it doesn't work. 学生[がくせい]そう doesn't exist; that's what みたい is for.

With adjectives, そう gives **an impression at a glance, before checking**. If you see a cake in a shop window, it's おいしそう, «it looks delicious». Once you've tasted it, it's simply おいしい. So stem + そう only makes sense when you're judging by appearance.
And it's the perfect form for talking about **what other people feel**. In Japanese, flatly saying タマは 悲[かな]しい sounds strange, as if you could climb into Tama's head and know what she feels. The natural thing is to report what you see: タマは 悲[かな]しそう, «Tama looks sad». It's the same idea that stops other people's wishes being expressed with たい.

items.jp: わあ、 この ケーキ、 おいしそう！
items.es: Wow, this cake looks delicious!

items.jp: カゲは 今日[きょう]、 暇[ひま]そうだね。
items.es: Kage looks bored today, doesn't he?

items.jp: タマ、 眠[ねむ]そうだね。
items.es: Tama, you look sleepy.
items.nota: You don't know whether she's sleepy: you see it in her face.

items.jp: この 本[ほん]、 よさそうですね。
items.es: This book looks good, doesn't it?

bloques.md: With verbs, そう says **something is about to happen**, judging by what you can see: a grey sky, a button hanging by a thread, Nyan's watery eyes. And since the whole form behaves like a な-adjective, you can put it before a noun (おいしそうな ケーキ) or turn it into an adverb with に (おいしそうに 食[た]べる, «eats with obvious relish»).

items.jp: 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]りそうだ。
items.es: It looks like it's going to rain.

items.jp: ボタンが 取[と]れそう。
items.es: Your button's about to come off.

items.jp: ニャンは 今[いま]にも 泣[な]きそうな 顔[かお]を して いる。
items.es: Nyan looks like he's about to burst into tears any second.

items.jp: コタローは いつも おいしそうに 食[た]べる。
items.es: Kotarō always eats with such gusto.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]りそうに ない。
items.es: It doesn't look like it'll rain today.
items.nota: The negative of the verb form: そうに ない or そうも ない.

bloques.md: Don't use そう for what you can see perfectly clearly. If you've got a red apple in front of you, saying 赤[あか]そう is absurd: it doesn't «look red», it is red. そう is for guessing what you can't see directly: taste, feelings, personality, what's going to happen.

secciones.titulo: 〜そうだ: they say…

bloques.md: And now, this lesson's trap: there's another そうだ that looks very similar and means something completely different. When it follows the **full plain form** (not the stem), it means **«they say»**: it passes on information you've received from someone else, the TV or a sign. The source is often given with によると, «according to».

Plain form + **そうだ** (polite: そうです)
降[ふ]る → **降[ふ]るそうだ**　　来[こ]ない → **来[こ]ないそうだ**　　おいしい → **おいしいそうだ**
Nouns and な-adjectives, with だ: 雪[ゆき]だ → **雪[ゆき]だそうだ**, 静[しず]かだ → **静[しず]かだそうだ**.
This そうだ never changes: it has no past or negative of its own. What changes is the sentence before it.

items.jp: 天気[てんき]予報[よほう]に よると、 明日[あした]は 雪[ゆき]だそうです。
items.es: According to the forecast, it'll snow tomorrow.

items.jp: ポンさんの 新[あたら]しい パンは すごく おいしいそうだよ。
items.es: They say Pon's new bread is really good.

items.jp: カゲは 明日[あした] 来[こ]ないそうだ。
items.es: Apparently Kage isn't coming tomorrow.

columnas: Stem + そう (I can see it)
Plain form + そうだ (I was told)
filas: 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]りそうだ。 It looks like rain.
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]るそうだ。 They say it'll rain.
おいしそうだ。 It looks tasty.
おいしいそうだ。 They say it's tasty.
元気[げんき]そうだ。 He looks well.
元気[げんき]だそうだ。 I hear he's well.

bloques.md: Sometimes there's only a single syllable between the two columns, but the meaning changes completely. A trick to get it right: if you **saw** it, stem + そう; if you **heard** it, full form + そうだ. In casual speech, for things you've been told, people also use って a lot, which you saw with quoting: 明日[あした]、 雪[ゆき]だって, «they say it'll snow tomorrow».

secciones.titulo: みたい and ようだ: it seems… and «like»

bloques.md:
**みたい** and **ようだ** mean the same; the difference is register. みたい belongs to conversation, and ようだ is more formal and bookish (ようです is the neutral polite version). Both have two uses.
The first is **deducing from clues** you've picked up yourself: you see the lights off and conclude nobody's home. Unlike そう, which judges an appearance, みたい draws a conclusion about the whole situation.
The second is **comparing**: «like», «just like». 夢[ゆめ]みたい, «it's like a dream»; 雪[ゆき]のように 白[しろ]い, «white as snow».

**みたい**: plain form. Nouns and な-adjectives, directly: **学生[がくせい]みたい**, **暇[ひま]みたい**. Verbs and い-adjectives: **来[き]たみたい**, **寒[さむ]いみたい**.
**ようだ**: nouns + **の**: **学生[がくせい]のようだ**; な-adjectives + **な**: **暇[ひま]なようだ**; verbs and い-adjectives, directly: **来[き]たようだ**.
Both behave like な-adjectives: みたいな / ような before a noun, みたいに / ように before a verb or adjective.

items.jp: 電気[でんき]が 消[き]えて いる。 誰[だれ]も いないみたい。
items.es: The lights are off. Seems like nobody's home.
items.nota: A deduction: みたい.

items.jp: カゲは 怒[おこ]って いるみたいだ。
items.es: Kage seems to be angry.

items.jp: どうも 風邪[かぜ]を ひいたようです。
items.es: I think I've caught a cold.
items.nota: ようです: the more formal version, perfect with the teacher.

items.jp: 富良野[ふらの]の ラベンダー 畑[ばたけ]、 夢[ゆめ]みたい！
items.es: The lavender fields in Furano are like a dream!
items.nota: A comparison: it isn't a dream, but it feels like one.

items.jp: 雪[ゆき]のように 白[しろ]い 猫[ねこ]。
items.es: A cat as white as snow.

items.jp: ニャンみたいな 猫[ねこ]は どこにも いない。
items.es: There's no other cat like Nyan.

bloques.md:
Notice the difference from そう with the same adjective. おいしそう is «it looks tasty»: you say it looking at the cake. おいしいみたい is «it seems to be tasty»: you say it because there's a queue out the door or because everyone who tries it smiles. The first judges by appearance; the second draws a conclusion.
And in passing: in casual speech you'll also see **っぽい**, meaning something like «-ish»: 子[こ]どもっぽい, «childish»; 嘘[うそ]っぽい, «sounds like a lie». It's explained properly in the lesson «〜っぽい and 〜がち: -ish, and prone to…».

secciones.titulo: らしい: apparently… and «so typical of»

bloques.md:
**らしい** also has two faces.
The first is **«apparently», «it seems»**: information that has reached you indirectly, that you haven't checked and that you keep at arm's length. It's like the «they say» そうだ, but vaguer: そうだ usually has a specific source; らしい is more «word is…». It attaches to the plain form, and to nouns and な-adjectives directly, without だ: 雨[あめ]らしい. It conjugates like an い-adjective.
The second face is as a **suffix after a noun**: «typical of», «just as it should be». ニャンらしい, «so Nyan»; 春[はる]らしい 天気[てんき], «real spring weather», the kind you expect from spring. In the negative, らしくない, «not like…».

items.jp: 明日[あした]は 授業[じゅぎょう]が ないらしいよ。
items.es: Apparently there's no class tomorrow.

items.jp: あの 店[みせ]、 来月[らいげつ] 閉[し]まるらしい。
items.es: Word is that shop's closing next month.

items.jp: ケーキを 三[みっ]つ 食[た]べて、 すぐ 寝[ね]た？ ニャンらしいね。
items.es: He ate three cakes and fell straight asleep? That's so Nyan.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 春[はる]らしい 天気[てんき]ですね。
items.es: Real spring weather today, isn't it?

items.jp: 諦[あきら]めるの？ カゲらしくないね。
items.es: You're giving up? That's not like you, Kage.

bloques.md: Compare **子[こ]どもみたい** and **子[こ]どもらしい**. みたい compares you to something you're not: «like a child», said of an adult acting like one, and almost always as criticism: «how childish». らしい, on the other hand, describes someone who really is a child and behaves the way a child should: «so childlike», and it sounds like praise. Say 子[こ]どもみたい to Kage and he'll be furious; say it about a little kid playing happily in the snow and 子[こ]どもらしい is what you want.

secciones.titulo: 〜そうに なる: almost…, without meaning to

bloques.md: Combine the «looks like» そう with なる, «to become», and you get a very handy expression: **stem + そうに なる**, «to get to the point of almost». It's nearly always used in the past to tell of something that **almost happened to you, involuntarily**, and in the end didn't: «I almost fell», «I nearly cried», «I nearly nodded off».

Verb stem + **そうに なる**
転[ころ]ぶ → **転[ころ]びそうに なった**　　泣[な]く → **泣[な]きそうに なった**　　寝[ね]る → **寝[ね]そうに なった**

items.jp: 雪[ゆき]の 道[みち]で 転[ころ]びそうに なった。
items.es: I nearly slipped over on the snowy street.
items.nota: A Sapporo winter classic.

items.jp: 映画[えいが]が 悲[かな]しくて、 泣[な]きそうに なった。
items.es: The film was so sad I almost cried.

items.jp: 授業中[じゅぎょうちゅう]に 寝[ね]そうに なった。
items.es: I nearly fell asleep in class.
items.nota: Guess who.

bloques.md: It only works for **involuntary** things, because そう is about what «looks set to happen», not what you decide. For something you were going to do on purpose, 行[い]きそうに なった sounds odd. And to tell of a close call where something nearly went wrong, there's also 〜ところだった: もう 少[すこ]しで 遅[おく]れる ところだった, «I very nearly ended up late».

secciones.titulo: All together, at Pon's shop

lineas.jp: わあ、 この ケーキ、 おいしそう！
lineas.es: Wow, this cake looks delicious!

lineas.jp: 今日[きょう]の 新作[しんさく]です。 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]を 使[つか]って います。
lineas.es: It's new today. It's made with Hokkaido milk.

lineas.jp: テレビで 言[い]って いたけど、 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]は 濃[こ]くて おいしいそうだよ。
lineas.es: They said on TV that Hokkaido milk is rich and really tasty.

lineas.jp: 本当[ほんとう]？ …あれ、 カゲも 来[き]て いるみたい。
lineas.es: Really? …Oh, looks like Kage's here too.

lineas.jp: その ケーキ、 最後[さいご]の 一[ひと]つらしいぜ。
lineas.es: Apparently that cake's the last one.

lineas.jp: えっ… 泣[な]きそう…
lineas.es: What…? I think I'm going to cry…

lineas.jp: 大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]ですよ。 奥[おく]に もう 一[ひと]つ ありますから。
lineas.es: Don't worry, there's another one in the back.

lineas.jp: よかった！ さっき、 本当[ほんとう]に 泣[な]きそうに なったよ。
lineas.es: Phew! I really nearly cried just now.

lineas.jp: ふん、 ニャンらしいな。
lineas.es: Hmph. So Nyan.

bloques.md: Go back over the scene: おいしそう judges the cake by how it looks; おいしいそう passes on what was said on TV; 来[き]て いるみたい is a deduction (maybe Nyan spotted Kage's bike outside); 最後[さいご]の 一[ひと]つらしい is an «apparently» that Kage heard or worked out; 泣[な]きそう and 泣[な]きそうに なった tell of the tears that almost fell; and ニャンらしい is the good old «so Nyan». Six different «seems», and not one of them interchangeable.

ejercicios.explica: い-adjectives drop the い and take そう: おいしそう, «looks tasty».
With verbs, そう follows the stem: 降[ふ]り + そう. It says something is about to happen, judging by what you see.
One of the two exceptions: いい starts from its old form よい and adds さ, よさそう, so it doesn't shrink to a one-syllable word.
The «they say» そうだ follows the full plain form, not the stem: 降[ふ]るそうだ, «they say it'll rain».
Stem 転[ころ]び + そうに なった: «I nearly fell», something that almost happened to you without meaning to.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan sees a cake in the shop window and hasn't tasted it yet. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: この ケーキ、 ＿！
ejercicios.explica: He's judging by appearance, without having tasted it: stem + そう, おいしそう. おいしいそう would be «they say it's tasty» and おいしいらしい «apparently it's tasty»: both are about what he's heard, not what he sees.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama repeats what the weather forecast said. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 天気[てんき]予報[よほう]に よると、 明日[あした]は 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]る＿。
ejercicios.explica: によると gives the source, and after it comes the «they say» そうだ, attached to the full plain form 降[ふ]る. そうに なる is «almost» and らしくない is «not like».

ejercicios.pregunta: The lights at Tama's house are off. What does Nyan conclude?
ejercicios.jp: 電気[でんき]が 消[き]えて いる。 誰[だれ]も いない＿。
ejercicios.explica: Nyan draws a conclusion from a clue: みたい. そうに なる would tell of something that almost happened to you, and らしくない would say something isn't like someone.

ejercicios.pregunta: Kage flies off the handle over nothing. How does Tama criticise him?
ejercicios.jp: カゲは 小[ちい]さい ことで すぐ 怒[おこ]る。 子[こ]ども＿。
ejercicios.explica: Kage isn't a child but acts like one: みたい compares you with something you're not. 子[こ]どもらしい would be said of an actual child, as praise; and そう can't follow a noun.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan ate three cakes and fell asleep. What does Tama say?
ejercicios.jp: ニャンは ケーキを 三[みっ]つ 食[た]べて、 すぐ 寝[ね]た。 ニャン＿ね。
ejercicios.explica: It's Nyan behaving exactly like Nyan: らしい as a suffix, «so typical of». ニャンみたい would be said of someone else who's like Nyan, and そう doesn't follow nouns.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which of these sentences is well formed?
opciones: あの 人[ひと]は 学生[がくせい]みたいだ。
あの 人[ひと]は 学生[がくせい]そうだ。
あの 人[ひと]は 学生[がくせい]なそうだ。
ejercicios.explica: The «looks like» そう doesn't attach to nouns, so with 学生[がくせい] you need みたい. And なそうだ doesn't exist: «I hear he's a student» would be 学生[がくせい]だそうだ.

ejercicios.es: I nearly slipped over on the snowy street.
ejercicios.explica: First the place, 雪[ゆき]の 道[みち]で, and at the end what almost happened: 転[ころ]びそうに なった.

ejercicios.es: Apparently there's no class tomorrow.
ejercicios.explica: The plain-form sentence, 明日[あした]は 授業[じゅぎょう]が ない, and らしい at the end to mark it as something heard around. よ adds that you're telling the other person.

ejercicios.es: These croquettes look so good!
ejercicios.explica: The topic, この コロッケ, then おいしそう, because you're judging by appearance. だね invites the other person to agree.

lecciones.titulo: こと, ところ and もの: the wildcard words
lecciones.capitulo: If…, maybe… and I have to…
lecciones.resumen: Three nouns that barely mean anything, which is exactly why they're good for everything. With them you'll talk about what you've experienced («have you ever been to Hokkaido?»), say how things are, make pouty excuses and hand out wise advice.

secciones.titulo: Three almost empty words (and why they're so useful)

bloques.md:
English has wildcard words like «thing», «place» or «matter». Japanese has three that get used far more, because on top of their ordinary meaning they build a whole range of grammatical expressions:
**こと** is an **abstract** thing: a fact, a matter, something done, said or thought. You can't touch it.
**もの** is a **concrete** thing: an object, something you can pick up. And, by extension, «the way things are».
**ところ** is a **place**, both on the map and off it: an aspect of someone, a moment, a point.
All three have kanji, 事[こと], 物[もの] and 所[ところ], but when they work as grammar they're usually written in hiragana, as you'll see in this lesson.

filas: 大切[たいせつ]な こと (something important: an idea, a piece of advice)
大切[たいせつ]な もの (something important: an object, a treasure)
A place, an aspect, a moment
静[しず]かな ところ (a quiet place)

items.jp: 変[へん]な ことを 言[い]わないで。
items.es: Don't say weird things.
items.nota: こと: something said.

items.jp: カゲの 部屋[へや]に 変[へん]な ものが ある。
items.es: There's something weird in Kage's room.
items.nota: もの: an object.

items.jp: ニャンの ことが 好[す]き。
items.es: I like Nyan.
items.nota: Literally «I like the things of Nyan»: everything that he is.

items.jp: わたしの こと、 覚[おぼ]えてる？
items.es: Do you remember me?

bloques.md: Look at the last two examples. With people, Japanese uses **〜の こと** a lot: it doesn't just talk about the person, but about «everything to do with them». ニャンが 好[す]き is correct, but ニャンの ことが 好[す]き sounds more natural when you're talking about feelings for someone: it takes in the whole person, their personality, what they do.

secciones.titulo: こと: what you've lived and what happens sometimes

bloques.md: The most useful expression with こと is **〜たことが ある**: «I have the experience of having done something», «I've… before». Inside, it's very logical: the た-form + こと turns the past action into a **fact**, and ある says that fact **exists** in your life. In the negative, **〜たことが ない**, «I've never…». And as a question, **〜たことが ありますか**, «have you ever…?».

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]った ことが ある。
items.es: I've been to Hokkaido.
items.nota: An experience: at some point in your life.

items.jp: スキーを した ことが ありますか。
items.es: Have you ever been skiing?

items.jp: オーロラは 一度[いちど]も 見[み]た ことが ない。
items.es: I've never once seen the northern lights.
items.nota: 一度[いちど]も + negative strengthens the «never».

bloques.md: Here's a false friend with English. «I've eaten sushi» can mean «I've had sushi today» or «I've eaten sushi at some point». Japanese keeps the two apart: what happened at a specific time is 食[た]べた, and life experience is 食[た]べた ことが ある. That's why 昨日[きのう] 寿司[すし]を 食[た]べた ことが ある makes no sense: with 昨日[きのう] you're no longer talking about an experience but a specific event. Nor is it used for things everyone does every day: saying you «have the experience» of eating rice would sound like a joke.
With the dictionary form in front, **〜ことが ある** means something else: **«sometimes»**, «there are times when». It isn't about your past, but about something that happens every now and then.

items.jp: 朝[あさ]ごはんを 食[た]べない ことが ある。
items.es: Sometimes I skip breakfast.

items.jp: カゲも 負[ま]ける ことが ある。
items.es: Even Kage loses sometimes.
items.nota: Though he'd never admit it.

filas: 雪[ゆき]を 見[み]た ことが ある。 (I've seen snow.)
雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]る ことが ある。 (It sometimes snows.)

secciones.titulo: ところ: places that aren't on the map

bloques.md:
**ところ** is first and foremost a place: 静[しず]かな ところ, «a quiet spot»; 寒[さむ]い ところ, «a cold place». But its real usefulness lies in the places that aren't on any map.
**A person's «place».** In Japanese you can't «go to a person» with に or へ: 先生[せんせい]に 行[い]く doesn't work, because a person isn't a destination. You have to say 先生[せんせい]の ところに 行[い]く, «go to where the teacher is». Likewise わたしの ところ, «my place», «where I am».
**An aspect of someone.** タマの 優[やさ]しい ところ is «how kind Tama is», that side of her. It's the natural way to talk about good and bad points: いい ところ, 悪[わる]い ところ.
**A moment.** 今[いま]の ところ, «for now»; いい ところに 来[き]た, «you've come at a good moment». This is where the verb forms you saw in «While, right now and every time» come from, like 食[た]べる ところ or 食[た]べた ところ, and even the connector ところで, «by the way», literally «at this point».

items.jp: 静[しず]かな ところで 本[ほん]を 読[よ]みたい。
items.es: I want to read somewhere quiet.

items.jp: 後[あと]で 先生[せんせい]の ところに 行[い]きます。
items.es: I'll go and see the teacher later.

items.jp: タマの 優[やさ]しい ところが 好[す]き。
items.es: I love how kind Tama is.

items.jp: 今[いま]の ところ、 雪[ゆき]は 降[ふ]って いません。
items.es: It isn't snowing for now.

items.jp: いい ところに 来[き]たね！ ちょうど ケーキを 切[き]る ところだよ。
items.es: Good timing! I was just about to cut the cake.

bloques.md: Remember the rule for people: to go, come or take something **to someone**, add の ところ. ポンさんに 行[い]く sounds as if Pon were a town. ポンさんの ところに 行[い]く, on the other hand, is exactly «go and see Pon», at his shop or wherever he is.

secciones.titulo: もの: real things, and the way things are

bloques.md: **もの** is anything you can touch. It turns up in loads of compounds: 食[た]べ 物[もの] (food, «thing to eat»), 飲[の]み 物[もの] (a drink), 買[か]い 物[もの] (shopping), 着物[きもの] («thing to wear», the kimono). And after an adjective or a verb it makes very handy phrases: 甘[あま]い もの, «something sweet»; 何[なに]か 飲[の]む もの, «something to drink».

With **〜ものだ** at the end of a sentence, もの stops being an object and becomes **«the way things are»**. It's how you state general truths, with an air of folk wisdom: «that's life», «that's how it goes». Sometimes it also carries a touch of «that's how it should be», and in the negative, **〜ものではない**, it's an older person's «that's not done».
With the past, **〜たものだ**, it turns into a nostalgic memory of what you **used to do**: «those were the days when…». It's very typical of grandparents.

items.jp: 子[こ]どもは 遊[あそ]ぶ ものだ。
items.es: Kids are meant to play.
items.nota: A general truth: that's how things are.

items.jp: 楽[たの]しい 時間[じかん]は すぐ 過[す]ぎる ものだ。
items.es: Time flies when you're having fun.

items.jp: 人[ひと]の 悪口[わるぐち]を 言[い]う ものでは ない。
items.es: You shouldn't speak ill of people.
items.nota: A «that's not done»: it sounds like advice from an older person.

items.jp: 子[こ]どもの 頃[ころ]、 よく この 川[かわ]で 泳[およ]いだ ものだ。
items.es: As a kid, I used to swim in this river all the time. Those were the days!
items.nota: たものだ: nostalgia for what you used to do.

bloques.md: And now, the cutest もの: the one for **excuses**. At the end of a sentence, nearly always in its colloquial form **もん**, it justifies what you did with a very pouty «but…!». It often comes with **だって** at the start, «but…». Children use it, and young people when they want to sound sweet or whiny. From a serious adult it sounds childish, unless they're joking.

items.jp: だって、 眠[ねむ]いんだもん。
items.es: But I'm sleepy!
items.nota: Nyan's motto in life.

items.jp: 「どうして 全部[ぜんぶ] 食[た]べたの？」「おいしかったんだもん。」
items.es: “Why did you eat it all?” “But it was so good!”

bloques.md: Careful with もん outside close relationships. If you explain to Fukuro-sensei why you didn't do your homework with 眠[ねむ]かったんだもん, you're not giving her a reason: you're pouting at her. With her, 眠[ねむ]かったので… and an apology.

secciones.titulo: ことは ない: no need to

bloques.md: **Dictionary form + ことは ない** literally means «there's no matter of…», that is, **«there's no need to»**, **«there's no reason to»**. It's like なくても いい, which you already know, but firmer, and it's usually used to **reassure** someone or to tell them they're overreacting: «don't stress, there's no need».

items.jp: 心配[しんぱい]する ことは ないよ。
items.es: There's nothing to worry about.

items.jp: わざわざ 来[く]る ことは ないよ。 電話[でんわ]で いいから。
items.es: No need to come all the way here. A phone call's fine.

items.jp: そんなに 謝[あやま]る ことは ありません。
items.es: There's no need to apologise so much.

bloques.md: Don't confuse it with たことが ない. 行[い]く ことは ない is «no need to go»; 行[い]った ことが ない is «I've never been». Two small things change, the verb tense and the particle (は or が), and the meaning flips completely.

A bonus you'll hear a lot: the double negative **〜ない ことは ない**, «it's not that I can't…». It's for half-admitting something, without much enthusiasm: 食[た]べられない ことは ない, «I mean, I can eat it…», with the face of someone who'd rather not.

secciones.titulo: ことだ: the best thing you can do

bloques.md: Finally, **dictionary form (or ない-form) + ことだ**: «what you need to do is…», «the best thing is to…». It's firm advice, from someone with experience to someone with less. That's why it's so typical of teachers, parents and coaches, and for the same reason you don't say it to a superior: it would sound like you were lecturing them.

items.jp: 上手[じょうず]に なりたいなら、 毎日[まいにち] 練習[れんしゅう]する ことです。
items.es: If you want to get better, what you need to do is practise every day.

items.jp: 風邪[かぜ]の 時[とき]は、 無理[むり]を しない ことだ。
items.es: When you've got a cold, the best thing is not to push yourself.

lineas.jp: 皆[みな]さん、 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]った ことが ありますか。
lineas.es: Has anyone here been to Hokkaido?

lineas.jp: はい、 一度[いちど] あります。 富良野[ふらの]は とても きれいな ところでした。
lineas.es: Yes, once. Furano is a beautiful place.

lineas.jp: わたしは 行[い]った ことが ありません。 でも、 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 食[た]べ 物[もの]は 大好[だいす]きです！
lineas.es: I've never been. But I love food from Hokkaido!

lineas.jp: 俺[おれ]は 小[ちい]さい 頃[ころ]、 毎年[まいとし] スキーに 行[い]った もんだ。
lineas.es: When I was little, I used to go skiing every year. Those were the days.

lineas.jp: カゲ、 おじいさんみたい。
lineas.es: Kage, you sound like a grandpa.

lineas.jp: でも 先生[せんせい]、 わたし、 寒[さむ]い ところは 苦手[にがて]です…
lineas.es: But, miss, I'm not good with cold places…

lineas.jp: 心配[しんぱい]する ことは ありませんよ。 暖[あたた]かい 服[ふく]を 着[き]て、 楽[たの]しむ ことです。
lineas.es: There's nothing to worry about. What you need to do is wrap up warm and enjoy yourself.

lineas.jp: だって、 寒[さむ]いと 眠[ねむ]く なるんだもん。
lineas.es: But the cold makes me sleepy…

lineas.jp: ニャンは いつも 眠[ねむ]いでしょ。 でも、 ニャンの そういう ところ、 好[す]きだよ。
lineas.es: You're always sleepy, aren't you? But I like that about you.

bloques.md: See how well the three wildcards work: こと for experiences, 行[い]った ことが ある; for reassurance, 心配[しんぱい]する ことは ない; and for advice, 楽[たの]しむ ことです; ところ for the lovely place and for «that about you»; and もの for the food, for Kage's put-on nostalgia (a grandpa's もんだ from a youngster, hence Tama's teasing) and for Nyan's pouty excuse.

ejercicios.explica: The past of 行[い]く, which is irregular: 行[い]った. Then ことが ある: «the fact of having gone exists», in other words «I've been».

ejercicios.forma: 〜た ことが ない (I've never…)
ejercicios.explica: Past 見[み]た + ことが ない: «the fact of having seen it doesn't exist», that is, «I've never seen it».

respuestas: しんぱいすることはない
ejercicios.explica: Dictionary form + ことは ない: 心配[しんぱい]する ことは ない, «there's no need to worry». It's used to reassure.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan asks about an experience. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 小樽[おたる]に 行[い]った ＿ ありますか。
ejercicios.explica: Experience is expressed with 〜た ことが ある, because having gone is a fact, something abstract: こと. もの would be an object and ところ a place.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan wants to say he sometimes skips breakfast. Which sentence is it?
opciones: 朝[あさ]ごはんを 食[た]べない ことが ある。
朝[あさ]ごはんを 食[た]べなかった ことが ある。
朝[あさ]ごはんを 食[た]べない ことは ない。
ejercicios.explica: With the dictionary form (here, negative), ことが ある means «sometimes». With the past it would be a one-off experience («there's been a time I didn't have breakfast»), and ない ことは ない is «it's not that I don't…», something else.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama is thirsty and wants something to drink. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 何[なに]か 飲[の]む ＿が 欲[ほ]しい。
ejercicios.explica: A drink is something you can touch: an object, so it's もの. 飲[の]む こと would be «the act of drinking», and 飲[の]む ところ a place to drink.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan is off to see the teacher. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 先生[せんせい]の ＿に 行[い]って くる。
ejercicios.explica: A person isn't a destination, so to go and see them you say «to where they are»: 先生[せんせい]の ところに. こと and もの aren't places.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan makes a pouty excuse. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 「どうして 宿題[しゅくだい]を しなかったの？」「だって、 眠[ねむ]かったんだ＿。」
ejercicios.explica: もん at the end justifies what you did with a pouty «but…!», and it often goes with だって. こと and ところ don't work as excuses.

ejercicios.pregunta: Fukuro-sensei gives firm advice. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 上手[じょうず]に なりたいなら、 毎日[まいにち] 練習[れんしゅう]する ＿です。
ejercicios.explica: Dictionary form + ことだ: «what you need to do is…». ものだ would state a general truth, and ところだ would say you're just about to practise.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does this sentence mean?
ejercicios.jp: 行[い]く ことは ない。
ejercicios.explica: Dictionary form + ことは ない is «no need to». «I've never been» would be 行[い]った ことが ない, with the past and with が.

ejercicios.pregunta: A grandpa fondly remembers his childhood. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 子[こ]どもの 頃[ころ]、 よく この 川[かわ]で 泳[およ]いだ ＿だ。
ejercicios.explica: Past + ものだ is the nostalgic memory of what you used to do. 泳[およ]いだ ところだ would be «I've just been swimming», and 泳[およ]いだ ことだ means nothing.

ejercicios.es: I've never been to Sapporo.
ejercicios.explica: The destination with に, the verb in the past, and ことが ない: «the fact of having gone doesn't exist».

ejercicios.es: I love how kind Tama is.
ejercicios.explica: ところ here is an aspect of Tama: «Tama's kind side». Like anything you like, it takes が and 好[す]き.

ejercicios.es: There's no need to worry so much.
ejercicios.explica: そんなに, «so much», comes before the verb. Then ことは ありません, the polite version of ことは ない, and よ to reassure.

lecciones.titulo: What for, why, and whose fault
lecciones.capitulo: If…, maybe… and I have to…
lecciones.resumen: Purposes, conclusions, credit and blame: by the end you'll be able to say what you're doing something for, come out with a «no wonder!», half-deny with «it's not that…», thank or blame whoever deserves it, and finish off with a good «and on top of that…!».

secciones.titulo: In order to: ために and ように

bloques.md:
In English, «to» or «so that» cover any purpose: «I'm saving to go to Hokkaido», «I sit at the front to see properly», «I take notes so I don't forget». Japanese distinguishes two kinds of goal and uses a different form for each.
**ために**: the goal is **an action you do and decide on**. Going to Hokkaido is something you'll do, on purpose. You save so you can do it.
**ように**: the goal is **a state or result you can't do directly**, only make possible. Seeing properly isn't something you decide: you sit at the front so it happens. Not forgetting isn't either: you take notes so it doesn't happen.

bloques.titulo: ために: in order to (do something)
bloques.md:
Dictionary form + **ために**
Noun + **の ために**: «for», «for the sake of».
The goal is a voluntary action, usually by the same subject as the main sentence.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]く ために、 お 金[かね]を 貯[た]めて いる。
items.es: I'm saving up to go to Hokkaido.

items.jp: 日本語[にほんご]の 本[ほん]を 読[よ]む ために、 毎日[まいにち] 漢字[かんじ]を 勉強[べんきょう]して いる。
items.es: I study kanji every day so I can read books in Japanese.

items.jp: 健康[けんこう]の ために、 毎朝[まいあさ] 歩[ある]く。
items.es: I walk every morning for my health.

items.jp: 家族[かぞく]の ために 働[はたら]いて います。
items.es: I work for my family.

bloques.titulo: ように: so that (something happens or doesn't)
bloques.md:
Dictionary form or ない-form + **ように**
It's used with verbs you can't simply decide: the potential form, like 泳[およ]げる or 読[よ]める; 見[み]える, 聞[き]こえる and 分[わ]かる; intransitive verbs; negatives… and also when the goal belongs to someone else.

items.jp: 忘[わす]れない ように、 メモを 取[と]る。
items.es: I take notes so I don't forget.

items.jp: よく 見[み]える ように、 前[まえ]に 座[すわ]った。
items.es: I sat at the front so I could see properly.

items.jp: 子[こ]どもにも 分[わ]かる ように、 ゆっくり 話[はな]します。
items.es: I speak slowly so that even children can understand.
items.nota: The goal belongs to others: that the children understand.

items.jp: 風邪[かぜ]を ひかない ように、 暖[あたた]かく して 寝[ね]てね。
items.es: Keep warm in bed so you don't catch a cold.

bloques.md:
A trick for choosing: try turning the goal into an order to yourself. «Go to Hokkaido!» works: it's an action you can decide on, so ために. «See properly!» or «understand it!» don't work as orders, because they don't depend on your will alone: ように.
Look how clear it is with the same verb: 泳[およ]ぐ ために プールに 行[い]く, «I go to the pool to swim» (swimming is your choice), versus 泳[およ]げる ように 毎日[まいにち] 練習[れんしゅう]する, «I practise every day so that I'll be able to swim» (being able to swim isn't decided, it's achieved). It's the same ように you saw with ようになる and ようにする.

見[み]える ために or 分[わ]かる ために sound wrong, because ために presents the goal as something you'll do on purpose, and neither seeing nor understanding is done on purpose: they happen. And one more use of ために you'll see in the news: after a noun or a past-tense verb, it means «due to». 雪[ゆき]の ために、 電車[でんしゃ]が 止[と]まりました, «due to snow, the train stopped». It's very formal; in speech people say 雪[ゆき]で or 雪[ゆき]だから.

secciones.titulo: わけ: the logic of things

bloques.md: **わけ** means «reason», «logic», «sense». Three expressions come from it that are used constantly in speech, and they let you reason out loud like a Japanese speaker. (By the way: an excuse is a 言[い]い 訳[わけ], literally «saying the reason».)

filas: 寒[さむ]い わけだ。 (No wonder it's cold!)
嫌[きら]いな わけでは ない。 (It's not that I dislike it.)
勝[か]てる わけが ない。 (There's no way we can win.)

bloques.md:
Plain form + わけ. With な-adjectives, **な**: 好[す]きな わけ. With nouns, **な** or **である**: 学生[がくせい]な わけ.
In speech, わけでは ない nearly always becomes **わけじゃ ない**.
**わけだ** draws a logical conclusion from something you've just found out: «so that means…», «that explains…», «no wonder!». It's the moment when the pieces click into place.

items.jp: 「タマは 札幌[さっぽろ]育[そだ]ちなんだ。」「だから 寒[さむ]さに 強[つよ]い わけだ。」
items.es: “Tama grew up in Sapporo.” “No wonder she handles the cold so well!”

items.jp: 窓[まど]が 開[あ]いて いる。 寒[さむ]い わけだ。
items.es: The window's open. No wonder it's cold!

items.jp: 毎日[まいにち] 三時間[さんじかん]なら、 一年[いちねん]で 千時間[せんじかん]以上[いじょう]に なる わけだ。
items.es: Three hours a day means over a thousand hours in a year.

bloques.md: **わけでは ない** denies a conclusion the other person might draw. It doesn't say «no», but «that's not exactly it». It's perfect for adding nuance without sounding blunt, or for denying just part of something: 全部[ぜんぶ] 分[わ]かる わけでは ない, «it's not that I understand everything».

items.jp: 納豆[なっとう]が 嫌[きら]いな わけじゃ ない。 ただ、 今[いま]は お 腹[なか]が いっぱいなんだ。
items.es: It's not that I don't like natto. I'm just full right now.

items.jp: 日本人[にほんじん]が みんな 寿司[すし]を 好[す]きな わけでは ない。
items.es: It's not as if every Japanese person likes sushi.

bloques.md: **わけが ない** is the most emphatic: «there's no logic that allows it», that is, **«there's no way»**, «not a chance». It's a subjective, forceful denial, very conversational. It's like はずが ない, which you'll see in the lesson on はず and べき, but はずが ない leans more on facts and わけが ない on your conviction.

items.jp: カゲが 泣[な]く わけが ない。
items.es: There's no way Kage would cry.

items.jp: こんな 難[むずか]しい 問題[もんだい]、 一日[いちにち]で できる わけが ないよ。
items.es: A problem this hard? No way it can be done in a day.

secciones.titulo: おかげで and せいで: credit and blame

bloques.md: When something has a cause, Japanese also lets you say whether that cause **deserves thanks or blame**. **おかげで** is «thanks to»: the result is good and you're grateful. **せいで** is «because of», in the sense of «it's X's fault»: the result is bad and you're pointing at the culprit. Both are formed the same way: noun + の, or the plain form of a verb.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]の おかげで、 試験[しけん]に 合格[ごうかく]しました。
items.es: Thanks to you, miss, I passed the exam.

items.jp: タマが 手伝[てつだ]って くれた おかげで、 早[はや]く 終[お]わった。
items.es: Thanks to Tama helping me, I finished early.

items.jp: 雨[あめ]の せいで、 試合[しあい]が 中止[ちゅうし]に なった。
items.es: The match was called off because of the rain.

items.jp: カゲの せいで 遅[おく]れたんだよ！
items.es: It's Kage's fault I was late!

bloques.md:
Two set phrases you'll hear every day. **おかげさまで** is the polite answer to «how are you?»: 「お 元気[げんき]ですか。」「おかげさまで。」 Literally «thanks to you»: even if the other person hasn't done anything for you, you thank them for asking and, more broadly, everyone around you. And **気[き]の せい** is «it's just your imagination», «your mind's fault»: 「 今[いま]、 何[なに]か 聞[き]こえた？」「 気[き]の せいだよ。」
Just like in English, おかげで can be ironic: 君[きみ]の おかげで、 大変[たいへん]だったよ, «thanks to you, I had a terrible time». The tone says it all.

Don't use せいで for something good or おかげで for something bad, unless you're joking. And if you just want to give the cause, without thanking or blaming, you don't need either: から, ので or, in writing, ために will do. せいで always comes with a pointing finger, and if you use it by accident you can sound like a moaner.

secciones.titulo: くせに: and on top of that…!

bloques.md: **くせに** joins two things that clash, like のに, but with an extra ingredient: **reproaching a person**. «He knows, and yet he won't tell me»; «for a kid, he sure is cocky». The speaker is annoyed, sometimes with a hint of contempt.

Plain form + **くせに**
Noun + **の くせに**; な-adjective + **な くせに**.

items.jp: 知[し]って いる くせに、 教[おし]えて くれない。
items.es: He knows perfectly well, and still won't tell me.

items.jp: 自分[じぶん]は 何[なに]も しない くせに、 文句[もんく]ばかり 言[い]う。
items.es: He does nothing himself, and yet all he does is complain.

items.jp: 子[こ]どもの くせに、 生意気[なまいき]だ。
items.es: He's just a kid, and he's so cheeky.

items.jp: 知[し]ってる くせに！
items.es: You know perfectly well!
items.nota: Left hanging at the end, between people who are close, it sounds like playful teasing, with a pout.

bloques.md: So how is it different from のに, which also means «even though»? のに expresses disappointment at **a situation**, and works with any subject, yourself included: たくさん 勉強[べんきょう]した のに、 だめだった, «I studied so much, and it was no good». くせに, on the other hand, **criticises someone** for how they behave, and both halves have the same subject: the person being criticised. That's why nobody uses くせに about themselves: it would be scolding yourself with contempt.

くせに is strong. Said to a superior, a customer or someone you don't know well, it's an outright insult, because on top of complaining you're being disrespectful. If you want to express your surprise politely, のに or けど is enough: 知[し]って いるのに、 どうして 教[おし]えて くれないんですか.

secciones.titulo: All together: the kanji test results

lineas.jp: やった！ 漢字[かんじ]の テスト、 合格[ごうかく]した！
lineas.es: Yes! I passed the kanji test!

lineas.jp: おめでとう！ 毎日[まいにち] 練習[れんしゅう]した おかげだね。
lineas.es: Congratulations! That's thanks to practising every day.

lineas.jp: タマが 教[おし]えて くれた おかげだよ。 忘[わす]れない ように、 ノートに 何回[なんかい]も 書[か]いたんだ。
lineas.es: It's thanks to you teaching me. So I wouldn't forget, I wrote them in my notebook loads of times.

lineas.jp: カゲは？
lineas.es: What about you, Kage?

lineas.jp: … 昨日[きのう]は 雨[あめ]の せいで 勉強[べんきょう]できなかった。
lineas.es: …I couldn't study yesterday because of the rain.

lineas.jp: 雨[あめ]と 勉強[べんきょう]、 関係[かんけい] ある？
lineas.es: What's rain got to do with studying?

lineas.jp: うるさい！ 勉強[べんきょう]が 嫌[きら]いな わけじゃ ない。 時間[じかん]が なかった だけだ。
lineas.es: Shut up! It's not that I don't like studying. I just didn't have time, that's all.

lineas.jp: 昨日[きのう]、 公園[こうえん]で 三時間[さんじかん]も 走[はし]って いた くせに。
lineas.es: And yet you spent three whole hours running in the park yesterday.

lineas.jp: あ、 だから 公園[こうえん]で 見[み]かけた わけだ！
lineas.es: Oh, so that's why I saw you in the park!

lineas.jp: … 次[つぎ]は 絶対[ぜったい] 勝[か]つ ために、 今日[きょう]から 勉強[べんきょう]する！
lineas.es: …To make sure I win next time, I'm starting to study today!

bloques.md: Go back over the scene: おかげ for Nyan's credit (and Tama's); ように for the goal that can't just be decided, not forgetting; せいで for Kage's excuse, blaming the rain; わけじゃ ない for his half-denial; くせに for Tama's reproach, now that she's caught him out; わけだ for Nyan's conclusion, as he finally works out what Kage was doing in the park; and ために for the goal Kage really can decide on: winning.

ejercicios.forma: 〜ない ように (so as not to…)
ejercicios.explica: Not forgetting isn't something you do on purpose, but a result you're after: negative 忘[わす]れない + ように.
With nouns, おかげで comes after の: 先生[せんせい]の おかげで, «thanks to the teacher».

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan is saving for a trip he's planning. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]く ＿、 お 金[かね]を 貯[た]めて いる。
ejercicios.explica: Going to Hokkaido is an action Nyan decides on and will do himself: ために. ように is for goals you can't just decide, and せいで would blame something.

ejercicios.pregunta: Kotarō practises so he'll be able to swim. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 泳[およ]げる ＿、 毎日[まいにち] 練習[れんしゅう]して いる。
ejercicios.explica: 泳[およ]げる, «being able to swim», is an ability you achieve, not an action you decide on. With the potential form, purpose takes ように.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama helped and the job was done early. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: タマが 手伝[てつだ]って くれた ＿、 早[はや]く 終[お]わった。
ejercicios.explica: The result is good and Tama gets the thanks: おかげで. せいで would blame her for something bad, and くせに would reproach her.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama is cross: they missed the bus because Kage overslept. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: カゲが 寝坊[ねぼう]した ＿、 バスに 乗[の]れなかった。
ejercicios.explica: The result is bad and Tama points at the culprit: せいで. おかげで would only work ironically, and ように expresses a purpose, not a cause.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan learns something that explains what he already knew. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: 「タマは 札幌[さっぽろ]育[そだ]ちなんだ。」「だから 寒[さむ]さに 強[つよ]い ＿。」
ejercicios.explica: The pieces click and a logical conclusion follows: わけだ, «no wonder!». わけが ない would say it's impossible, and わけでは ない that it's not exactly so.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama can't believe Kage would cry. What does she say?
ejercicios.jp: カゲが 泣[な]く ＿よ。
ejercicios.explica: わけが ない is an emphatic denial: «there's no way…». わけだ would draw the opposite conclusion, and おかげだ would be thanking someone.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan turns down the natto but doesn't want to seem rude. What does he say?
ejercicios.jp: 納豆[なっとう]が 嫌[きら]いな ＿。 ただ、 今[いま]は お 腹[なか]が いっぱいなんだ。
ejercicios.explica: わけじゃ ない half-denies the conclusion the other person might draw: «it's not that I don't like it». That way he declines without offending.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama reproaches Kage for knowing and not telling. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 知[し]って いる ＿、 教[おし]えて くれない。
ejercicios.explica: It's a reproach aimed at a person for how they behave: くせに, «he knows, and still won't tell me». ために would be a purpose and おかげで a thank-you.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan laments: he studied hard and still failed. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: たくさん 勉強[べんきょう]した ＿、 テストが だめだった。
ejercicios.explica: Nyan is talking about himself and expressing disappointment at the situation: のに. くせに is a contemptuous reproach aimed at someone else, and nobody says it about themselves.

ejercicios.es: I write it in my notebook so I don't forget.
piezas: 忘[わす]れない ように、
ejercicios.explica: The purpose goes first with ように, because not forgetting is a result you're after. Then where you write it and the verb.

ejercicios.es: Thanks to Tama, I understood it really well.
ejercicios.explica: Noun + の おかげで gives the credit. Then the good result: よく 分[わ]かった.

ejercicios.es: It's not that I understand everything.
ejercicios.explica: The sentence you're half-denying, 全部[ぜんぶ] 分[わ]かる, and わけでは ない at the end: «it's not exactly that…».

lecciones.titulo: Everyday Japanese, the way it's really spoken
lecciones.resumen: It's not in the textbooks, but it's how people talk: contractions, vanishing particles, back-to-front sentences, じゃん, っけ and なんか. By the end you'll understand your Japanese friends when they really talk, and you'll know when you can talk like that yourself and when you can't.

secciones.titulo: What the textbook leaves out (but you hear everywhere)

bloques.md:
So far you've learned complete Japanese, with every piece in place. It's correct, and it's what you'll use with your teacher, in shops and in writing. But listen to two friends chatting on a train in Sapporo and it'll sound like another language: words melt together, particles vanish and the word order turns upside down.
They're not speaking badly. It happens in every language: among friends, English speakers say «gonna», «wanna» or «whatcha doin'?», and nobody would dream of writing that in an exam. Spoken language is after **speed** and **closeness**, and Japanese has its own way of getting there.
In this lesson you'll learn that way. The goal is twofold: **understand all of it**, because you'll hear it as soon as you talk with Japanese people (and in any anime or TV series), and **use it little by little**, only with the right people.

secciones.titulo: Everyday contractions

bloques.md: Contractions aren't random: they follow the logic of sound. When two vowels meet, one swallows the other; when a syllable is hard to say quickly, it gets squeezed. You've already met many of them separately; here they are all together.

filas: 何[なに] 見[み]てるの？ 読[よ]んでる。
傘[かさ]、 持[も]ってく？
パン、 買[か]っとく。 読[よ]んどいて。
〜て しまう / 〜で しまう
食[た]べちゃった。 飲[の]んじゃった。
分[わ]かんない。 何[なに] してんの？
ニャンって 猫[ねこ]。
今[いま]、 出[で]る とこ。

bloques.md:
Notice how they work: in 〜て いる, the い gets lost after the e; in 〜て おく, て and お merge into と; in ては, the rub between て and は ends up as ちゃ. And in 分[わ]からない, the ら softens into ん before な, just as 何[なに] してるの becomes 何[なに] してんの. Read them aloud really fast and you'll find they come out on their own.
The 〜て しまう one (ちゃう, じゃう) is so common that it has a lesson of its own, «〜てしまう: ending up doing it (and sometimes regretting it)»: that's where you'll see the nuance it adds.

There's another family of contractions you'll hear a lot in anime: the vowels **ai** and **oi** turning into **ee**. すごい → すげえ, うまい → うめえ, 痛[いた]い → いてえ. They sound rough and very masculine, like a tough guy or a grumpy bloke: perfect for Kage, but from you they may come across as a pose. Recognise them and leave them to the characters.

secciones.titulo: Vanishing particles

bloques.md: Among friends, lots of particles disappear: **は**, **が**, **を** and the destination **に** or **へ** drop out all the time. Why? Because in a face-to-face chat the context already makes it clear who's doing what, and pronouncing them all sounds careful, almost formal. In their place there's usually a tiny pause, which in writing is marked with a comma.

items.jp: わたし、 ニャン。
items.es: Me, Nyan.
items.nota: わたしは ニャンです, the relaxed version.

items.jp: ごはん、 食[た]べた？
items.es: Eaten yet?

items.jp: 明日[あした]、 学校[がっこう] 行[い]く？
items.es: You going to school tomorrow?

items.jp: これ、 おいしい。
items.es: This is good.

bloques.md: But not all of them go. The ones that **carry information you can't guess** stay put: **で** (where or with what), **と** (with whom), **から** and **まで** (from and until), **より** (comparison) and the time **に**. If you say 公園[こうえん] 遊[あそ]ぶ instead of 公園[こうえん]で 遊[あそ]ぶ, people will understand, but it'll sound like robot Japanese. And the question particle か usually drops too: raising your intonation at the end is enough.

Contrastive は is never dropped, because it carries meaning. ケーキは 好[す]きだけど、 クッキーは ちょっと…, «cake I like, but biscuits…»: take out the は and you'd lose exactly what you want to say, the contrast between the two things.

secciones.titulo: Back-to-front order

bloques.md: You know the verb goes at the end in Japanese. Well, in speech that rule bends: what matters most comes out first (the question, the feeling, the reaction), and the rest follows, almost like a clarification. Japanese grammarians call it 倒置[とうち], «inversion», and English does something very similar: «Have you seen it, the film?», «It's gorgeous, this cake».

items.jp: 食[た]べた？ ケーキ。
items.es: Did you eat it? The cake.

items.jp: おいしいね、 これ。
items.es: It's good, this.

items.jp: 行[い]こうよ、 早[はや]く。
items.es: Come on, let's go, hurry up.

items.jp: 誰[だれ]？ あの 人[ひと]。
items.es: Who's that?

bloques.md: In writing, in a careful text or an exam, the normal order stays as it is. Back-to-front order belongs to the voice: it comes from thinking as you speak. You will see it in messages between friends, though, because those are written the way people talk.

secciones.titulo: じゃん, っけ, なんか and って

bloques.md:
**じゃん** comes from じゃない, but it doesn't negate anything: it's the «isn't it?» of someone presenting something as obvious, often with enthusiasm or a touch of reproach. いいじゃん is «that's great!» or «come on, it's fine!»; 言[い]ったじゃん is «I told you so!». It's very casual and very youthful; in Kansai the equivalent is やん.
**っけ** is the particle of a failing memory: it asks about something **you knew but have forgotten**, or double-checks it. 何[なん]だっけ, «what was it again?». It almost always goes with だ or the past (だっけ, たっけ), because you're recalling something already said. It even has a polite version, でしたっけ, handy when you've forgotten someone's name.

items.jp: この 絵[え]、 かわいいじゃん！
items.es: Hey, this drawing's really cute!

items.jp: だから 言[い]ったじゃん。
items.es: I told you so.

items.jp: あの 人[ひと]、 名前[なまえ] 何[なん]だっけ？
items.es: What was his name again?

items.jp: 明日[あした]って テストだっけ？
items.es: Wait, is there a test tomorrow?

items.jp: すみません、 お 名前[なまえ]、 何[なん]でしたっけ。
items.es: Sorry, what was your name again?
items.nota: The polite version: a lifesaver in very awkward moments.

bloques.md:
**なんか** has three uses, all very chatty.
As a **filler**, it's our «kind of», «like»: なんか 眠[ねむ]い, «I'm kind of sleepy»; なんか 変[へん]だね, «that's kind of weird».
To **soften a suggestion**, it's «or something»: ケーキなんか どう？, «how about some cake or something?».
And to **look down on something**, after a noun: カゲなんか 知[し]らない！, «I don't care about Kage!». In this use it's related to なんて, which you'll see later, in the lesson on speaking forcefully.
**って** you already know as the short form of と and という. In speech it also works as a **topic**, with a touch of emphasis or surprise: ニャンって、 優[やさ]しいね, «Nyan's so sweet, isn't he?». And it reports what you've heard: 明日[あした] 休[やす]みだって, «they say there's no school tomorrow»; or asks someone to repeat: 何[なん]だって？, «what did you say?».

items.jp: なんか、 今日[きょう]の カゲ、 優[やさ]しくない？
items.es: Is it just me, or is Kage kind of nice today?

items.jp: お 茶[ちゃ]なんか 飲[の]む？
items.es: Fancy a tea or something?

items.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]なんか 大嫌[だいきら]い！
items.es: I hate homework!
items.nota: Scornful なんか: «stuff like homework».

items.jp: タマって、 本当[ほんとう]に 絵[え]が 上手[じょうず]だね。
items.es: Tama, you're so good at drawing.

secciones.titulo: Words you'll hear on the street

bloques.md:
Besides grammar, casual speech has its own vocabulary. You'll hear these three words every day among young people, and it's worth knowing what they really mean:
**マジ** means «seriously». マジで？, «seriously?», is the most common reaction of surprise.
**めっちゃ** means «really», «super». It's associated with western Japan, but today you hear it all over the country.
