**やばい** literally means «dangerous», «dodgy». But among young people it also works for good things: この ケーキ、 やばい！ can mean «this cake is insane!». Only the tone and the face will tell you whether it's good or bad.

Slang ages fast and changes from one generation to the next. These three words have been on the street for years and are unlikely to sound odd, but don't try to memorise lists of trendy slang: what's cool today will sound dated in a few years. Better to pick up the slang you hear from real people.

secciones.titulo: When yes and when no

bloques.md:
Everything in this lesson is **speech for people you're close to**. Use it with friends, family, people younger than you, animals and yourself; in messages between friends, too. But with your teacher, your boss, in a shop, with strangers or with older people you're not close to, it sounds disrespectful: like saying «what's up, dude?» to the head teacher.
There's a middle ground worth knowing: polite Japanese contracts a little too. 食[た]べてます, instead of 食[た]べて います, is heard all the time in polite conversation, just like the 〜んです form. What never fits in a polite conversation are the rough forms, じゃん, plain だっけ and scornful なんか.

lineas.jp: ねえ、 ニャン、 何[なに] してんの？
lineas.es: Hey, Nyan, whatcha doing?

lineas.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]。 でも、 全然[ぜんぜん] 分[わ]かんない。
lineas.es: Homework. But I don't get it at all.

lineas.jp: どれ？ 見[み]せて。 …あ、 これ、 簡単[かんたん]じゃん。
lineas.es: Which one? Let's see. …Oh, this is easy!

lineas.jp: え、 マジで？
lineas.es: Seriously?

lineas.jp: うん。 あ、 明日[あした]って テストだっけ？
lineas.es: Yeah. Oh, wait, is there a test tomorrow?

lineas.jp: そうだよ。 やばい、 勉強[べんきょう]しなきゃ。 ケーキ 食[た]べてる 場合[ばあい]じゃ ない！
lineas.es: Yep. Uh-oh, I've gotta study. This is no time to be eating cake!

lineas.jp: じゃ、 一緒[いっしょ]に やっとこう。
lineas.es: OK, let's get it done together, then.

lineas.jp: こんにちは。 二人[ふたり]とも、 勉強[べんきょう]して いますか。
lineas.es: Hello. Are you both studying?

lineas.jp: あ、 先生[せんせい]！ はい、 今[いま] 勉強[べんきょう]して います！
lineas.es: Oh, miss! Yes, we're studying right now!

lineas.jp: ニャン、 急[きゅう]に まじめじゃん。
lineas.es: Nyan, you've gone all proper all of a sudden.

bloques.md: Between themselves, Tama and Nyan use the lot: してんの, 分[わ]かんない, じゃん, マジで, っけ, なきゃ, やっとこう (from やって おこう) and vanishing particles. The moment Fukuro-sensei walks in, Nyan snaps straight back to 勉強[べんきょう]して います, in full and with ます. That gear change, which Japanese people make without thinking, is exactly what you need to learn: the same language, two speeds.

ejercicios.explica: In 〜て いる, the い gets lost after the e when you speak fast: 食[た]べてる.
て and お merge into と: 買[か]って おく → 買[か]っとく, «I'll get it in».
Before な, ら softens into ん: 分[わ]からない → 分[わ]かんない. The same happens with つまらない → つまんない.

ejercicios.base: 飲[の]んで しまった
ejercicios.explica: でしまう contracts to じゃう (でしま → じゃ), and in the past it becomes じゃった: 飲[の]んじゃった.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan can't remember someone's name. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: あの 人[ひと]、 名前[なまえ] 何[なん]だ＿？
ejercicios.explica: っけ asks about something you knew and have forgotten: «what was it again?». じゃん would present something as obvious, and とく is the contraction of ておく, which has no business here.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama sees Nyan's drawing and loves it. What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: この 絵[え]、 かわいい＿！
ejercicios.explica: じゃん presents something as obvious, often with enthusiasm: «hey, this is cute!». っけ would ask whether it was cute, as if she'd forgotten, and とこ is the short form of ところ.

ejercicios.pregunta: Among friends, which of these particles usually does NOT get dropped?
ejercicios.explica: で carries information you can't guess, the place or the means, so it stays. を and non-contrastive は are understood from context, and in casual speech they drop out constantly.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan asks Fukuro-sensei what she's reading. Which sentence is appropriate?
opciones: 何[なに]を 読[よ]んで いるんですか。
何[なに] 読[よ]んでんの？
何[なに] 読[よ]んでるっけ？
ejercicios.explica: With the teacher you use the full, polite form. 読[よ]んでんの, contracted and with no particle, is how friends talk; and っけ would ask about something Nyan already knew and has forgotten, which isn't the case.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does Tama mean by this, shouted with her arms folded?
ejercicios.jp: カゲなんか 知[し]らない！
ejercicios.explica: なんか after a noun looks down on it, and 知[し]らない here isn't «I don't know him» but «I'm done with him». It's the kind of huff that's over in five minutes.

ejercicios.es: Nyan, whatcha doing?
ejercicios.explica: First who you're talking to, then 何[なに] with no particle (among friends を drops) and してんの, the contraction of しているの.

ejercicios.es: Wait, is there a test tomorrow?
ejercicios.explica: って marks the topic casually, and だっけ at the end asks about something you knew but can't quite remember.

ejercicios.es: It's so good, this croquette.
ejercicios.explica: Back-to-front order: first the reaction, おいしいね, and then, as a clarification, what you're talking about: この コロッケ.

lecciones.titulo: 〜てしまう: ending up doing it (and sometimes regretting it)
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to confess that you accidentally ate the whole cake, apologise to the teacher properly and boast that your homework is completely done. And you'll understand why you hear ちゃった everywhere in Japan.

secciones.titulo: A verb for putting away… and for regretting

bloques.md:
Picture it: Tama leaves a cake on the table, steps out for a moment and, when she comes back, there's nothing left but crumbs and a guilty-looking Nyan. Nyan won't just say «I ate it», which would be 食[た]べた. He'll say **食[た]べてしまった** or, more likely, **食[た]べちゃった**. That little addition changes everything: it's no longer a statement of fact, it's a confession.

The star of this lesson is しまう. On its own, it's a verb meaning «to put away, to tidy away»: you put the plates away in the cupboard, you pack your winter clothes into a box. Whatever you put away is closed up, out of sight, finished. When しまう attaches to the て-form of another verb, it keeps that sense of closure: the action has gone all the way to the end and **there's no taking it back**.

Both uses of 〜てしまう grow out of that «no taking it back» feeling:

**1. Doing something completely**, all the way to the end: reading the whole book, getting your homework done.
**2. Ending up doing something you didn't mean to, or something you regret**: you drop your wallet, you forget your umbrella, you eat what wasn't yours.

Often the two go together: if you've eaten **all** of Tama's cake, you've done it completely **and** you're sorry. Context and tone of voice will tell you which one weighs more.

items.jp: お 皿[さら]を 棚[たな]に しまう。
items.es: I put the plates away on the shelf.
items.nota: しまう on its own, as an ordinary verb: to put away.

items.jp: ケーキを 全部[ぜんぶ] 食[た]べてしまった。
items.es: I've eaten the whole cake (oh dear).
items.nota: Completely and regrettably at once: both meanings together.

secciones.titulo: How to form it

bloques.md:
Put the verb in the て-form and add しまう. The first verb doesn't change any further: all the conjugating is done by しまう, which is a perfectly ordinary う-verb (しまう, しまった, しまわない, しまいます, しまいました…).

If the て-form ends in で, as in 飲[の]んで, 読[よ]んで or 泳[およ]いで, you get でしまう: 飲[の]んでしまう.

You'll hear it in the **past** most of the time: 〜てしまった. That makes sense: what you usually regret is something that has already happened, and what you celebrate finishing is already finished. But it's also used in the present, as you'll see further down, to talk about something that **is going to end up happening** unless someone does something.

In polite speech, the politeness goes on しまう, the last verb: 〜てしまいます, 〜てしまいました. The verb in front stays comfortably in its て-form. It's the same logic as 〜ています: Japanese marks politeness **only once, at the end of the sentence**, so the verbs in the middle stay in their simple form.

items.jp: コーヒーを こぼしてしまいました。
items.es: I've spilt the coffee.
items.nota: Polite: ます only on しまう, at the end.

secciones.titulo: By accident: the «oops» built into the verb

bloques.md: English has plenty of ways to soften a mishap: «I **went and** forgot my keys», «I **accidentally** broke the glass», «I **ended up** eating the lot». Japanese packs that whole feeling into one ending. The person is still the one doing the action, the thing still takes を, and てしまう adds the «I didn't mean to» or the «there's no fixing this now».

items.jp: 財布[さいふ]を 落[お]としてしまった。
items.es: I've lost my wallet (I dropped it somewhere).
items.nota: 落[お]とす is «to drop»: the speaker is still the subject. てしまう adds the pained face.

items.jp: 傘[かさ]を 電車[でんしゃ]に 忘[わす]れてしまった。
items.es: I left my umbrella on the train.
items.nota: 忘[わす]れる also means «to leave something behind somewhere»; the place takes に.

items.jp: 今朝[けさ]、 寝坊[ねぼう]してしまった！
items.es: I overslept this morning!
items.nota: 寝坊[ねぼう]する is to sleep in and get up late.

items.jp: カゲの 前[まえ]で 泣[な]いてしまった。
items.es: I burst into tears in front of Kage.
items.nota: Nobody cries on purpose in front of their rival: double disaster.

bloques.md: English often shifts the blame onto the object: «my wallet **fell out** of my pocket». てしまう doesn't do that: it doesn't change the subject or the particles, it simply attaches to whatever verb you pick and adds the regret. If you'd rather tell it as something that happened by itself, Japanese uses a different verb, the intransitive one: 財布[さいふ]が 落[お]ちてしまった, «my wallet fell», as you saw in the lesson on transitive and intransitive verbs. Both versions are fine; what doesn't work is mixing the parts, because 落[お]とす takes を and 落[お]ちる takes が.

Two little words go wonderfully with 〜てしまう:

**つい**: without being able to help it, almost without noticing. It's the word for temptations: you knew you shouldn't, but…
**うっかり**: absent-mindedly. It's the word for slip-ups: you didn't even realise what you were doing.

items.jp: ダイエット 中[ちゅう]なのに、 つい ケーキを 買[か]ってしまった。
items.es: I'm on a diet, and yet I couldn't resist buying a cake.
items.nota: つい: temptation won.

items.jp: うっかり 先生[せんせい]を 「お 母[かあ]さん」と 呼[よ]んでしまった。
items.es: Without thinking, I called the teacher «Mum».
items.nota: うっかり: one of those slips that make you want the floor to swallow you up.

secciones.titulo: Completely: getting it out of the way

bloques.md: The other meaning has no drama at all. 〜てしまう can also say that an action has been done **completely**, right to the end, and that you don't need to worry about it any more. It's «I've read the whole thing», «that's done and dusted», «come on, let's get this over with».

items.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]は もう やってしまった。
items.es: I've already got my homework done.
items.nota: No regret: just the relief of having finished.

items.jp: タマは その 本[ほん]を 一日[いちにち]で 読[よ]んでしまった。
items.es: Tama read the whole book in a single day.
items.nota: She read it cover to cover.

items.jp: 先[さき]に 掃除[そうじ]を してしまおう。
items.es: Let's get the cleaning out of the way first.
items.nota: With the volitional しまおう: finishing something off so it's done.

items.jp: 早[はや]く 食[た]べてしまいなさい。
items.es: Come on, eat up.
items.nota: Classic mum talk: なさい on top of しまう (しまいなさい).

bloques.md: English has its own trick for this nuance, and you use it without thinking: little words like **up**, **through** and **off**. «Eat your dinner» is not quite «eat **up** your dinner»; «I read the book» is not quite «I read **through** the book»; «finish» becomes «finish **off**». Those particles say «all of it, to the very end», and that's exactly the job 〜てしまう is doing here.

How do you know which meaning you're dealing with? From the context and the speaker's face. 宿題[しゅくだい]を やってしまった, said with a smile, is «I've finished my homework». 秘密[ひみつ]を 言[い]ってしまった, said with a look of horror, is «I let the secret slip». When there's anything to regret, listeners will tend to hear the «oops», because it's the more frequent use; if you just mean you've finished, people often add もう or 全部[ぜんぶ] to make it clear.

secciones.titulo: What's going to happen if nobody stops it

bloques.md: In the present tense, 〜てしまう looks at the future with a worried frown: it says something **is going to end up happening**, and it won't be good. It often comes with このままだと («if things go on like this») or an «if we don't…».

items.jp: 急[いそ]がないと、 電車[でんしゃ]が 行[い]ってしまう。
items.es: If we don't hurry, we're going to miss the train.
items.nota: The train isn't leaving «by accident»: the regret is yours, because you'll miss it.

items.jp: このままだと、 アイスが 溶[と]けてしまう！
items.es: At this rate the ice cream's going to melt!

items.jp: 冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に 入[い]れておかないと、 コタローが 食[た]べてしまうよ。
items.es: If you don't put it in the fridge, Kotarō's going to eat it.
items.nota: Kotarō does the eating; you'd be the one who's sorry.

bloques.md: Look closely at that last example: it's Kotarō who eats the food, but it's the speaker who'd be sorry. This matters: てしまう doesn't say that **the subject** regrets anything, it says that **the speaker** sees it as a shame, something that won't be fixable. That's why it works equally well for your own slip-ups, for trains that leave without you and for greedy dogs.

secciones.titulo: ちゃう and じゃう: how it sounds on the street

bloques.md: In the lesson on casual speech you already saw that 〜てしまう is hardly ever said in full between friends. It melts into a single, shorter, faster word:

filas: 忘[わす]れちゃいました

bloques.md:
The trick is simple: て and しま merge into ち, and で and しま merge into じ. That's how 行[い]ってしまった becomes 行[い]っちゃった, and 転[ころ]んでしまった becomes 転[ころ]んじゃった («I fell over»).

ちゃった has a light, almost mischievous tone. Said with a grin, 買[か]っちゃった！ isn't a lament at all: it's «I went and bought it!», with the thrill of someone who's just done something a bit naughty. Among friends you'll hear it all the time.

There's also a rougher version, ちまう and じまう, as in 食[た]べちまった, which you'll hear from gruff anime characters, in period dramas or from the odd older man. It's worth recognising, but you don't need to use it: coming from you, it would sound like a costume.

With the teacher, in Pon's shop or anywhere polite, use the full form: 忘[わす]れてしまいました. ちゃいました does exist, and you'll hear it between colleagues who get on well, but it sounds breezy. With someone you owe respect to, the contraction can give the impression that you're not taking your mistake seriously.

A heads-up for your travels: in Kansai speech (Osaka, Kyoto…), ちゃう on its own at the start of a reply is something else entirely: it's the local form of 違[ちが]う, «no, that's not it». ちゃうちゃう！ means «no, no, no!». If you hear it on its own, with no verb in front, it has nothing to do with てしまう.

secciones.titulo: しまった! and how to apologise

bloques.md: しまった on its own is an exclamation: what slips out the very moment you realise you've messed up. «Oh no!», «Dang!», «Now I've done it!». You say it to yourself more than to anyone else, and it's usually followed by what you got wrong.

lineas.jp: しまった！ 弁当[べんとう]を 家[いえ]に 忘[わす]れた！
lineas.es: Oh no! I've left my lunch at home!

lineas.jp: わたしの おにぎり、 半分[はんぶん] あげようか。
lineas.es: Want half my onigiri?

lineas.jp: …べつに いらない。 でも、 もらって おく。
lineas.es: …Not that I need it. But fine, I'll take it.

bloques.md: And when it's time to apologise, てしまう is your best friend. If you tell the teacher 宿題[しゅくだい]を 忘[わす]れました, it sounds almost like an official report: «I forgot the homework». With 忘[わす]れてしまいました, on the other hand, you own up to the mistake and make it clear it wasn't deliberate and that you're sorry. That's why it turns up so often in apologies: 〜てしまって、 すみません («I'm sorry for…»).

items.jp: 遅[おく]れてしまって、 すみません。
items.es: I'm sorry I'm late.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]、 宿題[しゅくだい]を 家[いえ]に 忘[わす]れてしまいました。
items.es: Sensei, I've left my homework at home.

items.jp: お 皿[さら]を 割[わ]ってしまいました。 本当[ほんとう]に ごめんなさい。
items.es: I've broken a plate. I'm really, really sorry.

bloques.md: Don't stick てしまう on everything. If you announce that you 結婚[けっこん]してしまった, people will hear «I've gone and got married… oh dear», as if you regretted it (people sometimes say it that way as a joke, precisely for that reason). For good or neutral news, the ordinary past, 結婚[けっこん]した, is what you want: てしまう **always** adds a nuance, and if you don't want that nuance, leave it out.

secciones.titulo: At Tama's house

lineas.jp: タマ、 ごめん…。
lineas.es: Tama, I'm sorry…

lineas.jp: どうしたの？
lineas.es: What's wrong?

lineas.jp: 冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]の プリン、 食[た]べちゃった。
lineas.es: The pudding in the fridge… I ate it.

lineas.jp: えっ、 二[ふた]つ あったよね。 両方[りょうほう]？
lineas.es: What? There were two, weren't there? Both of them?

lineas.jp: うん…。 一[ひと]つだけ 食[た]べようと 思[おも]ったけど、 つい 全部[ぜんぶ] 食[た]べちゃった。
lineas.es: Yeah… I was only going to have one, but I couldn't stop and ate the lot.

lineas.jp: もう、 ニャン！
lineas.es: Honestly, Nyan!

lineas.jp: ふん。 俺[おれ]は そんな 失敗[しっぱい]は しない。
lineas.es: Hmph. I never make mistakes like that.

lineas.jp: …あっ、 しまった！ 財布[さいふ]を 家[いえ]に 忘[わす]れちゃった。
lineas.es: …Oh no! I've left my wallet at home.

lineas.jp: カゲも やっちゃったね。
lineas.es: Looks like you messed up too, huh?

bloques.md: Notice that last line: やっちゃった (from やってしまった) is used all by itself to mean «I've messed up» or «now I've done it», without saying what was done. The context says it all.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan confesses he's eaten the whole cake. What completes the sentence?
ejercicios.jp: ケーキを 全部[ぜんぶ] 食[た]べて＿。
ejercicios.explica: しまった says he finished it completely and it can't be undone. おいた would mean «I ate it in advance, on purpose» and みた «I tried eating it»: neither has that confessional tone.
て-form, 忘[わす]れて, + しまった. The first verb doesn't change any further; しまう carries the past tense.
The て-form of 飲[の]む is 飲[の]んで, so you get でしまった: the で of the て-form stays.
食[た]べてしまった: て and しま merge into ち, giving 食[た]べちゃった.
The て-form is 読[よ]んで; で and しま merge into じ, giving 読[よ]んじゃった.

ejercicios.pregunta: What is the contracted form of 行[い]ってしまった?
ejercicios.explica: The contraction starts from the て-form: 行[い]って + しまった = 行[い]っちゃった. Since the て-form ends in て (not で), you get ち, not じ.

ejercicios.es: I forgot my umbrella.
ejercicios.explica: Object with を, then the verb in the て-form, and finally しまった, which does the conjugating.

ejercicios.pregunta: You arrive late to class. What do you say to Fukuro-sensei?
opciones: 遅[おく]れてしまって、 すみません。
遅[おく]れて おいて、 すみません。
ejercicios.explica: With the teacher, use the full form and an apology: てしまって admits it wasn't deliberate. 遅[おく]れちゃった！ sounds like a remark between friends, and 遅[おく]れて おいて would mean you were late on purpose, in advance.

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama says happily: 宿題[しゅくだい]は もう やってしまった。 What does she mean?
opciones: She did her homework by accident.
She's about to do her homework.
ejercicios.explica: Said cheerfully and with もう, it's the «completely» meaning: it's finished and out of the way. There's nothing to regret.

ejercicios.es: If we don't hurry, we're going to miss the train.
ejercicios.explica: The condition comes first, 急[いそ]がないと, and てしまう in the present warns of something bad that's going to end up happening.
The て-form of する, して, + しまいました. In polite speech, ます goes only at the end, on しまう.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which sentence talks about something that might happen and would be a shame?
opciones: このままだと、 アイスが 溶[と]けてしまう。
アイスが 溶[と]けてしまった。
アイスを 冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に しまった。
ejercicios.explica: In the present, てしまう warns of what's going to end up happening: «at this rate, it'll melt». The second has already happened. In the third, しまった is just the verb «put away»: «I put the ice cream in the fridge».

ejercicios.es: I couldn't help laughing.
ejercicios.explica: つい (without being able to help it) goes before the verb, and てしまった closes the sentence with the «I didn't mean to».

ejercicios.pregunta: Kage says his big brother has got married, and he's happy about it. Which fits?
ejercicios.jp: 兄[あに]が 結婚[けっこん]＿。
ejercicios.explica: For good news told straight, the ordinary past. してしまった or しちゃった would add an «oh dear» or a «who'd have thought!» that he doesn't mean here.

lecciones.titulo: 〜やすい and 〜にくい: easy or hard to do
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to say that a book is a breeze to read, that some boots are hard to walk in, or that some things are awkward to ask, all with a single word stuck onto the verb.

secciones.titulo: A verb that turns into an adjective

bloques.md:
In English, to say something is easy to do you need a little construction: «easy to read», «hard to understand», «comfortable to use». Japanese does it in one stroke: take the verb's stem and stick **やすい** (easy to) or **にくい** (hard to) onto it. The result is a brand-new word, and it's a fully fledged **い-adjective** too.

読[よ]む (to read) → 読[よ]みやすい (easy to read) → 読[よ]みにくい (hard to read)

Think how handy that is: a single adjective you can put in front of a noun, put in the past or make negative, just as you would with 高[たか]い or おいしい.

items.jp: この 本[ほん]は 読[よ]みやすい。
items.es: This book is easy to read.

items.jp: フクロウ 先生[せんせい]の 説明[せつめい]は 分[わ]かりやすいです。
items.es: Fukuro-sensei's explanations are really easy to follow.
items.nota: 分[わ]かりやすい is one of the most-used words in Japanese: «clear, easy to understand».

items.jp: この 漢字[かんじ]は 覚[おぼ]えにくい。
items.es: This kanji is hard to remember.

secciones.titulo: How to form it

bloques.titulo: Verb stem + やすい / にくい
bloques.md:
The stem is what's left when you take ます off the polite form: 読[よ]みます → 読[よ]み, 食[た]べます → 食[た]べ, します → し. Stick やすい or にくい straight onto that stem, with nothing in between.

う-verbs change the final u to i: 読[よ]む → 読[よ]み, 使[つか]う → 使[つか]い. る-verbs just lose る: 食[た]べる → 食[た]べ. And the two irregulars: する gives し, and 来[く]る gives 来[き].
And since the result is an い-adjective, it conjugates exactly like any other: change the final い and you're done.

filas: 読[よ]みやすくなかった
読[よ]みやすい 本[ほん]
読[よ]みにくい 字[じ]
分[わ]かりやすく 話[はな]す

items.jp: この ペンは 書[か]きやすいね。
items.es: This pen writes really nicely, doesn't it?
items.nota: Literally «it's easy to write with»: that's how Japanese praises a comfortable pen.

items.jp: 昨日[きのう]の テストは 思[おも]ったより 解[と]きやすかった。
items.es: Yesterday's test was easier to do than I expected.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]は いつも 分[わ]かりやすく 説明[せつめい]して くれる。
items.es: Sensei always explains things clearly for us.
items.nota: やすい → やすく: the adverb is formed as with any い-adjective.

secciones.titulo: What's easy becomes the topic

bloques.md:
Here's a detail that trips a lot of people up at first. The verb 読[よ]む takes its object with を: 本[ほん]を 読[よ]む. But 読[よ]みやすい isn't a verb any more; it's an adjective that **describes** something. And what it describes is the book. So the book stops being the object and becomes the topic or subject: **本[ほん]は 読[よ]みやすい**, **本[ほん]が 読[よ]みやすい**.

English actually does the same thing without you noticing: you say «I read the book», but «the book **is** easy to read». The book has moved from object to subject.

Don't say この 本[ほん]を 読[よ]みやすい. If the book is what you're describing, the book has to be the topic: を needs a verb acting on something, and やすい has turned the sentence into a description. Whatever is easy or hard takes は or が.

Mind you, を can survive when what you're describing is **something else**: この アプリは 写真[しゃしん]を 送[おく]りやすい, «this app makes it easy to send photos». Here it's the app being described, and the photos are still the object of 送[おく]る. The key question is: what am I saying is easy or hard?

items.jp: この 箸[はし]は 使[つか]いやすい。
items.es: These chopsticks are easy to use.

items.jp: 札幌[さっぽろ]は 住[す]みやすい 町[まち]だね。
items.es: Sapporo's a nice, easy place to live, isn't it?
items.nota: 住[す]みやすい, «easy to live in»: comfortable to live in.

items.jp: カゲは ちょっと 話[はな]しにくい。
items.es: Kage's a bit hard to talk to.
items.nota: 話[はな]しやすい 人[ひと] is someone who's easy to talk to; 話[はな]しにくい, the opposite.

secciones.titulo: Easily happens: things that tend to occur

bloques.md: やすい and にくい don't only talk about things someone does on purpose. With verbs for things that **happen**, they say whether something happens easily or not: it's English «breaks easily». And here にくい is often good news: something that is 割[わ]れにくい is hard to break, in other words, sturdy.

items.jp: この コップは 割[わ]れやすいから、 気[き]を つけて。
items.es: This glass breaks easily, so be careful.

items.jp: この コップは 割[わ]れにくいです。
items.es: This glass is sturdy; it doesn't break easily.

items.jp: 冬[ふゆ]は 風邪[かぜ]を 引[ひ]きやすい。
items.es: It's easy to catch a cold in winter.

items.jp: ニャンは 太[ふと]りやすい 体質[たいしつ]だ。
items.es: Nyan's the type who puts on weight easily.
items.nota: 体質[たいしつ]: your constitution, the way your body is.

bloques.md: This use will be your bridge to the lesson on 〜っぽい and 〜がち, which also talk about tendencies, but with different nuances.

secciones.titulo: 〜づらい: hard because it's a struggle for you

bloques.md:
There's a third piece that attaches the same way: **づらい**. It comes from 辛[つら]い, meaning «hard to bear, painful». That's why づらい isn't about technical difficulty but about what it **costs the person**: physical discomfort, awkwardness, embarrassment, strain.

Compare:
**にくい**: the difficulty lies in the thing or the situation. It's objectively hard to do.
**づらい**: the difficulty lies in the person doing it. They have a rough time doing it.

items.jp: この 靴[くつ]は 歩[ある]きづらい。
items.es: These shoes are a pain to walk in (they hurt, they're uncomfortable).

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]には ちょっと 聞[き]きづらい。
items.es: I feel a bit awkward asking the teacher.

items.jp: 字[じ]が 小[ちい]さくて 読[よ]みづらい。
items.es: The writing's so small it's a strain to read.

items.jp: 言[い]いにくいんだけど…、 それ、 わたしの プリンだよ。
items.es: I don't quite know how to say this, but… that's my pudding.
items.nota: 言[い]いにくいんだけど or 言[い]いづらいんだけど: the classic way to warn that something awkward is coming.

bloques.md: In practice the two overlap a lot, and many Japanese speakers use にくい and づらい almost interchangeably when there's a person struggling: 読[よ]みにくい and 読[よ]みづらい, 言[い]いにくい and 言[い]いづらい. But there's one place づらい doesn't go: when there's **nobody** having a hard time. A material that doesn't burn easily is 燃[も]えにくい; 燃[も]えづらい sounds odd to most people, because it's no struggle for the material: it just doesn't burn much.

It doesn't fully work the other way round either: if you want to say you feel awkward asking something, 聞[き]きにくい is understandable, but 聞[き]きづらい gets the awkwardness across better, because it puts the focus on how you feel. Rule of thumb: is the difficulty someone's feeling or discomfort? づらい fits like a glove. Is it a property of the thing? にくい.

In written texts you'll also come across **〜がたい**, which is more formal and stronger, almost «impossible to»: 信[しん]じがたい (hard to believe), 忘[わす]れがたい (unforgettable). It's rare in everyday conversation, but it's worth recognising.

secciones.titulo: Traps of sound and meaning

bloques.md: **やすい is not 安[やす]い.** They sound the same, but 安[やす]い on its own means «cheap». この 店[みせ]は 安[やす]い is «this shop is cheap»; この 店[みせ]は 入[はい]りやすい is «this shop is easy to walk into», which says nothing about prices. The «easy to» やすい always hangs off a verb stem, which is why it's almost always written in hiragana.

**やすい isn't やさしい either.** 易[やさ]しい (easy) and 優[やさ]しい (kind) are standalone adjectives. To say something is easy in general, with no verb, you say 易[やさ]しい or 簡単[かんたん]: この 問題[もんだい]は 簡単[かんたん]だ. To say it's easy **to do something specific**, you stick やすい onto the verb: この 問題[もんだい]は 解[と]きやすい. Same with にくい and 難[むずか]しい: 難[むずか]しい stands alone; にくい always needs its verb in front.

secciones.titulo: At Pon's shop

lineas.jp: ポンさん、 北海道[ほっかいどう]に 行[い]くので、 雪道[ゆきみち]でも 歩[ある]きやすい 靴[くつ]が 欲[ほ]しいんですが…。
lineas.es: Pon, I'm going to Hokkaido, so I'd like some shoes that are easy to walk in, even on snowy roads…

lineas.jp: それなら、 この ブーツは どうですか。 滑[すべ]りにくいですよ。
lineas.es: In that case, how about these boots? They don't slip.

lineas.jp: うーん、 ちょっと 重[おも]くて 歩[ある]きづらいです。
lineas.es: Hmm, they're a bit heavy and hard work to walk in.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 こちらは？ 軽[かる]くて、 はきやすいですよ。
lineas.es: Then what about these? They're light and easy to slip on.

lineas.jp: あ、 本当[ほんとう]だ！ これに します。
lineas.es: Oh, you're right! I'll take these.

bloques.md: Notice how Nyan tells them apart without even thinking: the first boots are 滑[すべ]りにくい (a property of the boots: they don't slip), but he finds them 歩[ある]きづらい (he's the one suffering, with all that weight). And はきやすい comes from はく, the verb for putting on shoes and trousers.

ejercicios.explica: The stem of 読[よ]む is 読[よ]み, because the u becomes i. Then add やすい.
る-verbs just drop る: 食[た]べ + にくい.
使[つか]う → 使[つか]い (u → i) + やすい.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which particle goes after the thing that's easy to read?
ejercicios.jp: この 本[ほん]＿ 読[よ]みやすい。
ejercicios.explica: 読[よ]みやすい is an adjective describing the book, so the book is the topic (は) or subject (が). を only makes sense with a verb acting on something.
分[わ]かり + やすい, then past like any い-adjective: い becomes かった.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does この 店[みせ]は 安[やす]い mean?
opciones: This shop is easy to walk into.
ejercicios.explica: 安[やす]い on its own is «cheap». The «easy to» やすい always hangs off a verb stem, as in 入[はい]りやすい.

ejercicios.es: This pen writes really nicely.
ejercicios.explica: この + ペン with は (what we're describing), and the adjective 書[か]きやすい at the end.

ejercicios.pregunta: A fabric that hardly burns. Which is the natural word?
ejercicios.jp: この 布[ぬの]は 燃[も]え＿。
ejercicios.explica: It's no struggle for the fabric: it simply doesn't burn much. づらい needs someone having a hard time, so にくい is the one here.

ejercicios.pregunta: You feel awkward asking the teacher something. What do you say?
ejercicios.jp: 先生[せんせい]には ちょっと 聞[き]き＿。
ejercicios.explica: The awkwardness is your own feeling, and that's exactly what づらい is for: what's hard on the inside. やすい would say the opposite, and にくくない means «it isn't hard».

ejercicios.es: The teacher explains things in a way that's easy to understand.
ejercicios.explica: 分[わ]かりやすい turns into an adverb (やすく) and goes right before the verb it goes with.
歩[ある]き + にくい, then past: にくかった.

ejercicios.es: It's easy to catch a cold in winter.
ejercicios.explica: Here やすい is about something that happens easily. 風邪[かぜ]を 引[ひ]く, to catch a cold, keeps its を because what we're talking about is winter, not the cold.

lecciones.titulo: まま: just as it is, unchanged
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to say that Kage walked into the house with his shoes on, that you fell asleep with the light on or that something's fine just as it is, and you'll know when っぱなし adds a telling-off.

secciones.titulo: A freeze-frame

bloques.md:
There are situations English describes with a participle or a «with… on»: «he came in with his shoes on», «she fell asleep with the TV on», «leave it open». Japanese has a single word for all of them: **まま**.

まま is like a freeze-frame: it says something **stays in the same state**, unchanged, while something else happens. Quite often that state should have changed and didn't (shoes come off at the door, lights go off at bedtime), which is why まま often carries a little hidden «wait, what?». But it can also be neutral, for asking that something be left just as it is.

items.jp: カゲは 靴[くつ]の まま 部屋[へや]に 入[はい]った。
items.es: Kage walked into the room with his shoes on.
items.nota: In a Japanese home, shoes come off at the entrance; that's why this sentence sounds scandalous.

items.jp: 電気[でんき]を つけた まま 寝[ね]て しまった。
items.es: I fell asleep with the light on.
items.nota: まま and てしまう together: the state that didn't change, plus the «I didn't mean to».

items.jp: そのままで いいですよ。
items.es: It's fine as it is, leave it like that.

secciones.titulo: How to form it

bloques.titulo: まま behaves like a noun
bloques.md:
Grammatically, まま is a noun meaning «the state as it is». So it hooks onto other words just the way any noun would:

Noun + **の** まま: 靴[くつ]の まま, パジャマの まま
Past-tense verb + まま: 開[あ]けた まま, 座[すわ]った まま
Negative verb + まま: 食[た]べない まま, 分[わ]からない まま
い-adjective + まま: 若[わか]い まま, 温[あたた]かい まま
な-adjective + **な** まま: きれいな まま, 元気[げんき]な まま
この・その・あの + まま: この まま, その まま

After まま you can put whatever you'd put after a noun. The most common:

**〜まま(で) + verb**: doing something in that state. 靴[くつ]の ままで 入[はい]る.
**〜ままだ**: staying that way, still being like that. ドアが 開[あ]いた ままだ, «the door's been left open».
**〜ままに する / 〜ままに して おく**: leaving something that way on purpose. 窓[まど]を 開[あ]けた ままに して おく.

items.jp: パジャマの まま 学校[がっこう]に 来[き]ちゃった！
items.es: I've come to school in my pyjamas!

items.jp: ずっと 若[わか]い ままで いたいなあ。
items.es: I wish I could stay young forever.
items.nota: 若[わか]い まま: unchanged, just as I am now.

items.jp: おばあちゃんの 家[いえ]は 昔[むかし]の ままだ。
items.es: Grandma's house is just the way it always was.
items.nota: 昔[むかし]の まま: as it used to be, unchanged. It has a lovely nostalgic ring to it.

items.jp: エアコンは つけた ままに して おいて。
items.es: Leave the air conditioning on, OK?
items.nota: ままに して おく: leave it like that on purpose.

secciones.titulo: Why does the verb go in the past?

bloques.md: With verbs, まま nearly always comes after the **past** form: 開[あ]けた まま, つけた まま, 着[き]た まま. The reason is logical: まま talks about a state that's being kept up, and that state begins once the action is **done**. First you open the window; from then on the window is open, and that state is what まま freezes. It's exactly what the participle does in English: you don't say «he left the window open-ing», you say «he left it **open**», «with his coat **on**».

開[あ]ける まま doesn't work, because 開[あ]ける in the dictionary form is about the act of opening, not the result, and there's nothing to freeze yet. Same with 着[き]る (to put on clothes): 服[ふく]を 着[き]た まま, «with your clothes on», because first you put them on and then they stayed on.

With the negative, on the other hand, the present is used: 食[た]べない まま, «without eating». Not having done something is already a state in itself, so there's no need for the past.

items.jp: 窓[まど]を 開[あ]けた まま 出[で]かけた。
items.es: I went out and left the window open.

items.jp: コタローは 朝[あさ]ごはんを 食[た]べない まま 散歩[さんぽ]に 行[い]った。
items.es: Kotarō went for his walk without having breakfast.
items.nota: Unusual for him: he's always hungry.

items.jp: 意味[いみ]が 分[わ]からない まま、 本[ほん]を 最後[さいご]まで 読[よ]んだ。
items.es: I read the book to the end without ever really understanding it.

items.jp: ニャンは 座[すわ]った まま 寝[ね]て いる。
items.es: Nyan has fallen asleep sitting up.

secciones.titulo: そのまま: the wild card

bloques.md: Of all the combinations, the one you'll hear most is **そのまま**: «just like that, as it is, without further ado». It's a wild card that fits a whole range of situations:

items.jp: この トマトは そのまま 食[た]べられるよ。
items.es: You can eat this tomato just as it is.
items.nota: No cooking, no peeling, nothing.

items.jp: 授業[じゅぎょう]の 後[あと]、 そのまま 家[いえ]に 帰[かえ]った。
items.es: After class I went straight home.
items.nota: No stops along the way: the plan didn't change.

items.jp: そのまま 待[ま]って いて ください。
items.es: Please wait right there, don't move.

items.jp: このままだと、 遅刻[ちこく]するよ。
items.es: If things carry on like this, you'll be late.
items.nota: このまま: «if nothing changes». You saw it with てしまう.

bloques.md: Here's one that'll come in handy in Japan: when a shop asks whether you want a bag and you don't need one, you can answer **そのままで いいです**, «it's fine as it is, I'll take it like that». It's a friendly way of saying no, because you're not turning anything down: you're just saying it suits you the way it is.

lineas.jp: 袋[ふくろ]に 入[い]れましょうか。
lineas.es: Shall I put it in a bag for you?

lineas.jp: あ、 そのままで いいです。
lineas.es: Oh, no need, it's fine as it is.

secciones.titulo: まま is not ながら

bloques.md:
It's easy to mix up まま and ながら, because both sometimes come out as «while» in English. But they think differently:

**ながら** joins **two actions** you do at the same time: eating and watching TV, walking and singing.
**まま** joins **a state that doesn't change** with an action: the TV stays on while you sleep.

テレビを 見[み]ながら 食[た]べる is «eating while watching TV»: your eyes are on the screen. テレビを つけた まま 寝[ね]る is «sleeping with the TV on»: you're not watching it, it's simply still on. If you use ながら for the second one, you're saying you watch TV while you sleep, which is impossible.

items.jp: 音楽[おんがく]を 聞[き]きながら 勉強[べんきょう]する。
items.es: I study while listening to music.
items.nota: Two actions at once: ながら.

items.jp: 音楽[おんがく]を かけた まま 寝[ね]た。
items.es: I fell asleep with the music on.
items.nota: A state that stays as it is: まま.

secciones.titulo: っぱなし: leaving it like that out of carelessness

bloques.md: まま has a crankier cousin: **〜っぱなし**. It attaches to the verb stem (the ます form without ます) and comes from 放[はな]す, «to let go». Picture someone doing something and just letting go of it, never tidying up after themselves. That's why っぱなし almost always carries a **telling-off**: something has been left that way through carelessness, and it shouldn't have been.

items.jp: また 電気[でんき]を つけっぱなしに して！
items.es: You've left the light on again!

items.jp: 水[みず]を 出[だ]しっぱなしに しないで。
items.es: Don't leave the tap running.

items.jp: ドアが 開[あ]けっぱなしだよ。
items.es: The door's been left wide open (someone didn't close it).

bloques.md:
Compare: 窓[まど]を 開[あ]けた まま 寝[ね]た just states the fact, «I slept with the window open». 窓[まど]を 開[あ]けっぱなしで 寝[ね]た adds that it was careless and not a good idea.

っぱなし has a second use too: something that **keeps going** for a long stretch, usually tiring or annoying. 一日中[いちにちじゅう] 立[た]ちっぱなしだった, «I was on my feet all day long». カゲに 負[ま]けっぱなしだ, «Kage beats me every single time».

secciones.titulo: A winter night at Tama's house

lineas.jp: さむっ！ ニャン、 窓[まど]が 開[あ]けっぱなしだよ！
lineas.es: Brr, it's freezing! Nyan, you've left the window wide open!

lineas.jp: あ、 ごめん。 雪[ゆき]を 見[み]て いて、 開[あ]けた まま 寝[ね]ちゃった。
lineas.es: Oh, sorry. I was watching the snow and fell asleep with it open.

lineas.jp: おい、 入[はい]るぞ。
lineas.es: Oi, I'm coming in.

lineas.jp: カゲ！ 靴[くつ]！ 靴[くつ]の まま 入[はい]らないで！
lineas.es: Kage! Your shoes! Don't come in with your shoes on!

lineas.jp: … 分[わ]かってる。 わざとじゃない。
lineas.es: …I know. I didn't do it on purpose.

lineas.jp: カゲ、 顔[かお]に 雪[ゆき]が ついた ままだよ。
lineas.es: Kage, you've still got snow on your face.

lineas.jp: …そのままで いい。 かっこいいだろ。
lineas.es: …Leave it. Looks cool, right?

ejercicios.pregunta: What goes between the noun and まま?
ejercicios.jp: 靴[くつ]＿ まま 入[はい]った。
ejercicios.explica: まま works like a noun, and between two nouns you put の: 靴[くつ]の まま, «with your shoes on».

ejercicios.pregunta: Which verb form goes before まま?
ejercicios.jp: 窓[まど]を ＿ まま 出[で]かけた。
ejercicios.explica: まま freezes the state left by an action that's already done, so the verb goes in the past: first you open it, then the window stays open.

ejercicios.pregunta: な-adjective + まま:
ejercicios.jp: ずっと 元気[げんき]＿ ままで いてね。
ejercicios.explica: な-adjectives take な before a noun, and まま is one: 元気[げんき]な まま, «healthy, just as you are».
The past of 着[き]る is 着[き]た, then + まま: «with your clothes on». Past, because first you put them on and then they stay on.
With the negative, the present is used: not having eaten is already a state. 食[た]べない + まま = «without eating».

ejercicios.es: I fell asleep with the light on.
ejercicios.explica: The state that didn't change, 電気[でんき]を つけた まま, comes before the action, and てしまった adds the «I didn't mean to».

ejercicios.pregunta: A shop offers you a bag and you don't need one. What do you say?
opciones: そのままで いいです。
そのままが いいです。
このままだと いいです。
ejercicios.explica: そのままで いいです is the set phrase: «it's fine as it is». このままだと means «if things go on like this» and warns of something bad, so it doesn't fit.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan fell asleep with the TV on (he wasn't watching it). Which sentence says that?
opciones: テレビを つけた まま 寝[ね]た。
テレビを 見[み]ながら 寝[ね]た。
テレビを つけて から 寝[ね]た。
ejercicios.explica: まま joins an unchanging state with another action. ながら would say he was watching it while asleep, and てから would only say he switched it on first and then went to sleep.
っぱなし goes on the stem: 出[だ]します → 出[だ]し + っぱなし. 水[みず]を 出[だ]しっぱなし is leaving the tap running through carelessness.

ejercicios.es: Grandma's house is just the way it always was.
ejercicios.explica: 昔[むかし]の まま, «as it used to be»: noun + の + まま, with だ at the end because まま works as a noun.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which sentence carries a telling-off for carelessness?
opciones: また ドアを 開[あ]けっぱなしに して！
ドアを 開[あ]けた ままに して おいて。
ドアは 開[あ]けた ままで いいよ。
ejercicios.explica: っぱなし says something was left that way through carelessness and shouldn't have been. The other two ask for the door to be left open on purpose, with no reproach.

lecciones.titulo: はず and べき: what should happen and what you should do
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to say that Tama should be here by now, that there's no way Nyan would leave cake on his plate and that promises should be kept, without ever mixing up logic and morals.

secciones.titulo: One «should», two ideas

bloques.md:
English makes a single word do an awful lot of work: **should**. Look at these two sentences:

«Tama **should** be home by now.»
«You **should** apologise to Tama.»

They look alike, but they have nothing to do with each other. The first is a **calculation**: you know when she left, you know how long it takes, and you work out that she must have arrived. Nobody is telling Tama what to do. The second is a **judgement**: you think apologising is the right thing to do.

Japanese keeps these two apart. For the calculation it uses **はず**; for the judgement, **べき**. And if what you want is to give practical advice, you already know 〜ほうがいい, from the lesson on wishes and suggestions.

items.jp: タマは もう 家[いえ]に 着[つ]いた はずだ。
items.es: Tama should have got home by now.
items.nota: はず: by my reckoning.

items.jp: タマに 謝[あやま]る べきだよ。
items.es: You should apologise to Tama.
items.nota: べき: it's the right thing to do.

secciones.titulo: はず: it's supposed to be…

bloques.md:
はず is a noun meaning something like «what's expected to be the case, logically». You use it when you have **grounds** for believing something: a timetable, something you were told, something you know about someone. It's not a hunch: it's a conclusion.

In English it comes out as «should», «is supposed to», «must»… (that last one in its deducing sense: «she must be home, the light's on»).

Since it's a noun, it hooks on just like any noun would, followed by だ or です:

Plain-form verb + はず: 来[く]る はず, 来[こ]ない はず, 来[き]た はず
い-adjective + はず: 寒[さむ]い はず
な-adjective + **な** はず: 静[しず]かな はず
Noun + **の** はず: 休[やす]みの はず

items.jp: フクロウ 先生[せんせい]は 今日[きょう] 学校[がっこう]に いる はずです。
items.es: Fukuro-sensei should be at school today.
items.nota: You know because it's Tuesday, and she's always in on Tuesdays.

items.jp: ポンさんの 店[みせ]は 十時[じゅうじ]に 開[あ]く はずだ。
items.es: Pon's shop is supposed to open at ten.
items.nota: It says so on the door, so you take it as given.

items.jp: 二月[にがつ]の 札幌[さっぽろ]は 寒[さむ]い はずだよ。
items.es: Sapporo in February must be bitterly cold.

items.jp: 明日[あした]は 休[やす]みの はずです。
items.es: Tomorrow's supposed to be a day off.

bloques.md: In the past, **はずだった** is «it was supposed to…», and it nearly always describes a plan or expectation that **didn't** work out. And **はずなのに** is the perfect complaint: «it was supposed to… and yet it didn't».

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 晴[は]れる はずだったのに…。
items.es: It was supposed to be sunny today…

items.jp: 鍵[かぎ]を かけた はずなのに、 ドアが 開[あ]いて いる！
items.es: I'm sure I locked it, and the door's open!
items.nota: はずなのに: logic says one thing, reality another.

secciones.titulo: はずがない: that can't be

bloques.md: Add がない to はず and you're saying there's **no possible expectation** of something happening: «it's impossible», «that can't be», «no way!». It's very strong, because it denies the very possibility. You'll also hear はずは ない, with は, which sounds a touch more emphatic.

items.jp: ニャンが ケーキを 残[のこ]す はずが ない。
items.es: There's no way Nyan would leave any cake.
items.nota: Knowing Nyan, logic simply won't allow it.

items.jp: カゲが 泣[な]いた？ そんな はずは ない。
items.es: Kage cried? That can't be right.

items.jp: そんな はずは ない！
items.es: That's impossible!
items.nota: A set phrase: you'll hear it in every drama when someone discovers something they never expected.

bloques.md:
Don't confuse **〜ない はずだ** with **〜はずが ない**. They look alike, but the strength is very different:

カゲは 来[こ]ない はずだ: «Kage isn't supposed to be coming» (that's what I was told; that's the expectation).
カゲが 来[く]る はずが ない: «there's no way Kage's coming» (it's not even on the cards).

The first is a negative expectation; the second denies that the possibility even exists. When in doubt, the first is the cautious one: the second sounds categorical. In the lesson on ために, わけ and おかげ you met わけがない, which is used in a very similar way.

secciones.titulo: What はず is not

bloques.md: **はず is not obligation.** If you want to tell Nyan «you should study», 勉強[べんきょう]する はずだ **won't** do: it would mean «he's supposed to be studying», as if you were deducing it from something. It's the sneakiest false friend in this lesson, precisely because English uses the same «should» for both ideas. To nudge someone into doing something, use べき or ほうがいい.

**はず looks from the outside.** Because it's a calculation, using it about your own plans makes them sound as if someone else decided them for you. 明日[あした] 大阪[おおさか]に 行[い]く はずです means «I'm supposed to be going to Osaka tomorrow» (it's on the schedule, the company arranged it…), not «I intend to go». For your own will, use what you learned with the volitional: 行[い]こうと 思[おも]って います.

secciones.titulo: べき: what you ought to do

bloques.md: **べき** is the «should» of judgement: what it's **right** to do according to your principles, the rules, common sense. It's a weighty word inherited from classical Japanese, which is why it sounds serious: you'll hear it in opinions, debates, important advice and reproaches. Think of English «ought to».

Dictionary-form verb + べき + だ / です.

守[まも]る → 守[まも]る べきだ
言[い]う → 言[い]う べきだ
する → すべきだ or するべきだ (both are correct; すべき is the more classical one and very common)

Negative: **べきではない** (べきじゃない in plain speech). Past: **べきだった**, «should have…». Before a noun: べき + noun, as in やる べき こと, «the things you ought to do».

filas: you should say it, it's right
言[い]う べきではない
言[い]う べきだった
読[よ]む べき 本[ほん]
a book you ought to read

items.jp: 約束[やくそく]は 守[まも]る べきだ。
items.es: Promises ought to be kept.
items.nota: A principle: it applies to everyone.

items.jp: 人[ひと]の 悪口[わるぐち]は 言[い]う べきではない。
items.es: You shouldn't speak ill of others.

items.jp: もっと 早[はや]く 相談[そうだん]すべきだった。
items.es: I should have talked it over sooner.
items.nota: べきだった looks back with regret, like 〜ばよかった, but with more of an «it was my duty» weight.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]で 絶対[ぜったい]に 食[た]べる べき ものは 何[なん]ですか。
items.es: What's the one thing you absolutely have to eat in Hokkaido?
items.nota: べき + noun: what you really must eat. Here べき sounds enthusiastic, not preachy.

bloques.md: **The negative goes after べき, not before.** 食[た]べない べきだ isn't said: べき only rests on the dictionary form, and the negation goes after it, on the copula: 食[た]べる べきではない. Think of べき as the opinion («the right thing is…»), and what you negate is the whole opinion: «it's not right to eat that».

secciones.titulo: Watch out for preaching

bloques.md: べき sounds like a principle, a moral rule. Used in general («promises ought to be kept»), it's fine. But when you aim it at a specific person, **you're judging them**: you're saying what they're doing isn't right. Between close friends it can happen, especially when the matter is serious. But day to day it's far more common, and kinder, to give advice with **〜ほうがいい**, which sounds like «if I were you…».

items.jp: 早[はや]く 寝[ね]た ほうが いいよ。
items.es: You'd better get to bed early.
items.nota: Kind, practical advice.

items.jp: 早[はや]く 寝[ね]る べきだ。
items.es: One ought to go to bed early.
items.nota: Sounds like a rule, or a sermon.

bloques.md: With the teacher, a customer or anyone older, avoid saying 先生[せんせい]は 〜べきです. Even if you're right, it sounds as though you're lecturing the very person who should be lecturing you. If you really want to suggest something, it's done much more indirectly, for example by asking: 〜たら どうでしょうか.

secciones.titulo: All the «shoulds» together

bloques.md: So you can see them at a glance, here are the various «should / have to» forms you already know, all in the same situation: it's going to rain.

filas: Logical expectation: from what I know
天気[てんき] 予報[よほう]では 午後[ごご]から 降[ふ]る はずだ。
人[ひと]の 傘[かさ]を 勝手[かって]に 使[つか]う べきではない。
傘[かさ]を 持[も]って 行[い]った ほうが いいよ。
傘[かさ]を 返[かえ]さなければ ならない。

bloques.md: Translations: «according to the forecast, it should rain from the afternoon»; «you shouldn't use someone else's umbrella without asking»; «you'd better take an umbrella»; «I have to give the umbrella back». Four «should / have to» in English, four different tools in Japanese.

secciones.titulo: Where's Tama?

lineas.jp: タマ、 遅[おそ]いね。 もう 来[き]て いる はずなのに。
lineas.es: Tama's late, isn't she? She should be here by now.

lineas.jp: 寝坊[ねぼう]した？ あいつが？ そんな はずは ない。
lineas.es: Overslept? Her? No way.

lineas.jp: 電車[でんしゃ]が 遅[おく]れて いる はずだよ。 雪[ゆき]が すごいから。
lineas.es: The train must be running late. With all this snow…

lineas.jp: タマさんから 連絡[れんらく]が ありました。 やはり 電車[でんしゃ]が 止[と]まって いるそうです。
lineas.es: Tama has been in touch. As we thought, it seems the train has stopped.

lineas.jp: ほらな。 でも、 もっと 早[はや]く 連絡[れんらく]すべきだろ。
lineas.es: See? Still, she ought to have let us know sooner, right?

lineas.jp: カゲ、 心配[しんぱい]して いたの？
lineas.es: Kage, were you worried?

lineas.jp: …して いる はずが ないだろ。
lineas.es: …As if I'd be worried.

bloques.md: Look at Kage's last line: はずが ないだろ, «how could I possibly…?». He denies it with all the force of はずがない… and that's exactly why nobody believes him.

ejercicios.pregunta: You know Tama left an hour ago and the walk takes twenty minutes. What do you say?
ejercicios.jp: タマは もう 着[つ]いた ＿だ。
ejercicios.explica: It's a calculation from what you know, not a moral judgement: はず. べき would say arriving is her duty.

ejercicios.pregunta: You believe promises must be kept. What completes the sentence?
ejercicios.jp: 約束[やくそく]は 守[まも]る ＿だ。
ejercicios.explica: It's a principle, the right thing to do: べき. はず would say «in theory, they get kept», as if you were deducing it.

ejercicios.pregunta: な-adjective + はず:
ejercicios.jp: 図書館[としょかん]は 静[しず]か＿ はずだ。
ejercicios.explica: はず is a noun, and な-adjectives take な before a noun: 静[しず]かな はず.

ejercicios.pregunta: Noun + はず:
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした]は 休[やす]み＿ はずです。
ejercicios.explica: Between two nouns you put の: 休[やす]みの はず, «it's supposed to be a day off».

ejercicios.es: There's no way Nyan would leave any cake.
ejercicios.explica: The whole idea (ニャンが ケーキを 残[のこ]す) comes before はずが ない, which denies it's even possible.
With する, both work: すべきだ, the classical form, and するべきだ. Both are correct and very common.
べき goes with the dictionary form and the negation comes after: 言[い]う べきではない. You don't say 言[い]わない べき.
べきだった looks back: «I should have apologised». The past goes on the copula (だった), not on the verb.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which one means «I'm sure I locked it, and it's open!»?
opciones: 鍵[かぎ]を かけた はずなのに、 開[あ]いて いる！
鍵[かぎ]を かける べきなのに、 開[あ]いて いる！
鍵[かぎ]を かけた はずが ない、 開[あ]いて いる！
ejercicios.explica: はずなのに is the complaint of «logic says one thing, reality another». べき would be about duty, and はずが ない would say there's no way you locked it.

ejercicios.pregunta: Kage isn't supposed to be coming today (that's what you were told). Which is the cautious sentence?
opciones: カゲは 来[こ]ない はずだ。
カゲが 来[く]る はずが ない。
カゲは 来[こ]ない べきだ。
ejercicios.explica: 〜ない はずだ is a negative expectation: «he's not supposed to come». はずが ない is categorical, «there's no way he's coming», and べき would say he ought not to come.

ejercicios.pregunta: You want to kindly suggest that Tama wrap up warm. What sounds most natural?
opciones: コートを 着[き]た ほうが いいよ。
コートを 着[き]る べきだ。
コートを 着[き]る はずだ。
ejercicios.explica: For kind advice, ほうがいい. べき would sound like a rule or a sermon, and はず would mean «she's supposed to be putting her coat on», which isn't advice at all.

ejercicios.es: I should have talked it over sooner.
ejercicios.explica: もっと 早[はや]く (sooner) goes before the verb, and べきだった closes with the regret: it was the right thing and I didn't do it.

ejercicios.pregunta: Nyan wants to say «I'm planning to go to Otaru tomorrow». Which sentence expresses his intention?
opciones: 明日[あした]、 小樽[おたる]に 行[い]こうと 思[おも]って いる。
明日[あした]、 小樽[おたる]に 行[い]く はずだ。
明日[あした]、 小樽[おたる]に 行[い]く べきだ。
ejercicios.explica: For your own intention, the volitional with と 思[おも]う. はず would describe your plan from outside, like a schedule someone else set, and べき would say it's your duty to go.

lecciones.titulo: 〜っぽい and 〜がち: -ish, and prone to…
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to say that Kage is a bit childish, that Nyan is forgetful beyond belief and that in winter you tend to stay indoors, with two suffixes you hear every day in Japan.

secciones.titulo: Two suffixes for describing what something's like

bloques.md:
English has plenty of ways to hedge a description: a **reddish** shirt, a **greyish** sky, a **forgetful** child, a **sickly** person. You're not saying the shirt is red, just that it leans that way; you're not saying the child forgot one particular thing, but that they tend to forget.

Japanese has two suffixes that cover a lot of that ground:

**〜っぽい**: has an air of, -ish, seems like; and also «tends to» as a character trait.
**〜がち**: often happens, is prone to… and it's nearly always something you'd rather didn't happen.

Both are very conversational, and both will make you sound much more natural.

secciones.titulo: 〜っぽい: -ish, with an air of…

bloques.md:
っぽい sticks onto almost anything, and the result is always an **い-adjective**:

Noun + っぽい: 子[こ]どもっぽい, 秋[あき]っぽい
い-adjective minus い + っぽい: 白[しろ]い → 白[しろ]っぽい, 安[やす]い → 安[やす]っぽい (cheap-looking, tacky)
な-adjective minus な + っぽい: 変[へん]な → 変[へん]っぽい (a bit colloquial)
Verb stem + っぽい: 忘[わす]れる → 忘[わす]れっぽい, 怒[おこ]る → 怒[おこ]りっぽい

Like any い-adjective: っぽくない, っぽかった, っぽく.
**1. Has an air of, -ish.** With colours and things, っぽい is exactly English «-ish»: 赤[あか]っぽい is reddish; 白[しろ]っぽい, whitish. With people and atmospheres, it's «has an air of», «feels like».

items.jp: タマは 白[しろ]っぽい マフラーを して いる。
items.es: Tama's wearing a whitish scarf.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]の 風[かぜ]は 秋[あき]っぽいね。
items.es: Today's wind feels autumnal, doesn't it?

items.jp: カゲは 大人[おとな]っぽい 服[ふく]が 好[す]きだ。
items.es: Kage likes clothes that make him look grown-up.

items.jp: その 話[はなし]、 ちょっと 嘘[うそ]っぽいな。
items.es: That story sounds a bit like a lie.

bloques.md: **2. Tends to, as a character trait.** With verb stems, っぽい describes someone who does something **easily and often**, so much so that it's part of who they are. Think of English adjectives like forgetful or short-tempered.

items.jp: ニャンは 忘[わす]れっぽい。
items.es: Nyan is really forgetful.

items.jp: カゲは 怒[おこ]りっぽいけど、 本当[ほんとう]は 優[やさ]しい。
items.es: Kage's quick to lose his temper, but deep down he's a good sort.

items.jp: わたし、 飽[あ]きっぽいから、 趣味[しゅみ]が すぐ 変[か]わるの。
items.es: I get bored of things so quickly that my hobbies keep changing.

bloques.md: **3. Seems like (very colloquial).** Among young people, っぽい does the job of みたい, which you met in the lesson on appearances: 風邪[かぜ]っぽい, «I think I'm coming down with a cold»; あの 二人[ふたり]、 付[つ]き 合[あ]って いるっぽいよ, «looks like those two are going out». It's relaxed, street-level speech: with the teacher, stick with みたいです or ようです.

secciones.titulo: っぽい versus らしい

bloques.md:
In the lesson on appearances you saw らしい in its «typical of» sense. It might seem to say the same as っぽい, but the intention is the opposite, and English has the perfect pair to show it: **childlike** versus **childish**.

**らしい**: has what's typical of what it **is**. 子[こ]どもらしい is said of a child who behaves the way a child should: cheerful, spontaneous. Childlike. It's praise.
**っぽい**: has the air of something it **isn't** (or shouldn't be). 子[こ]どもっぽい is said mostly of an adult who acts like a kid. Childish. It's usually a criticism.

That's why カゲは 子[こ]どもっぽい stings, while タマは 女[おんな]の 子[こ]らしい or 日本[にほん]らしい 景色[けしき] («a very Japanese landscape») describe something being true to itself.

items.jp: コタローは 子[こ]どもらしくて かわいい。
items.es: Kotarō is so full of puppyish fun, he's adorable.
items.nota: らしい: he's a youngster and acts like one. Praise.

items.jp: カゲって、 たまに 子[こ]どもっぽいよね。
items.es: Kage can be a bit childish sometimes, can't he?
items.nota: っぽい: he isn't a child, but he acts like one. A gentle dig.

bloques.md: Words like 男[おとこ]っぽい (masculine-looking, manly) or 女[おんな]っぽい (feminine-looking) exist and are used a lot, but they rest on stereotypes about what's «for boys» or «for girls». Depending on who you say it to and how, it can land badly, just as in English. Be careful using them to describe someone standing right in front of you.

secciones.titulo: 〜がち: it tends to happen (and you wish it didn't)

bloques.md: **がち** describes something that happens **often**, more than would be ideal. It almost always has a negative ring: nobody uses がち to say they «tend to» do something good. It's like «tends to…» said with a sigh, or «prone to».

Verb stem + がち: 遅[おく]れる → 遅[おく]れがち, 忘[わす]れる → 忘[わす]れがち, する → しがち
Noun + がち: 病気[びょうき]がち, 曇[くも]りがち

It behaves like a **な-adjective**: 〜がちだ, 〜がちな + noun, 〜がちに なる. Before a noun you'll also hear がちの, especially when がち is attached to another noun: 曇[くも]りがちの 天気[てんき].

items.jp: この バスは 雪[ゆき]の 日[ひ]は 遅[おく]れがちだ。
items.es: On snowy days this bus tends to run late.

items.jp: おじいちゃんは 最近[さいきん] 病気[びょうき]がちだ。
items.es: Grandpa's been rather poorly lately.
items.nota: 病気[びょうき]がち: falls ill often, sickly.

items.jp: 冬[ふゆ]は 家[いえ]に こもりがちに なる。
items.es: In winter you tend to shut yourself away indoors.

items.jp: 小[ちい]さい 間違[まちが]いは 見落[みお]としがちです。
items.es: Little mistakes tend to get overlooked.

items.jp: 今週[こんしゅう]は 曇[くも]りがちの 天気[てんき]が 続[つづ]くでしょう。
items.es: The week will stay mostly cloudy.
items.nota: A typical weather-forecast line.

bloques.md: Don't use がち for good things. 勉強[べんきょう]しがちだ would sound as if studying were a bad habit you can't kick, because がち comes with a built-in «this happens too much and I don't like it». For a good habit, just say よく 勉強[べんきょう]する or 〜ことが 多[おお]い.

A very handy combination: **ありがち**, from ある + がち. It means «typical, the sort of thing that always happens», and it's used for hackneyed or predictable things: ありがちな 話[はなし] is a story you've heard a hundred times; ありがちな 間違[まちが]い, a textbook mistake.

And don't confuse this がち with **ガチ** in katakana, a youth-slang word meaning «seriously, for real»: ガチで おいしい, «it's seriously delicious». They sound the same, but they're different words.

secciones.titulo: っぽい, がち or やすい: which one?

bloques.md: With 忘[わす]れる you can use all three pieces you've met in these last few lessons, and each one tells a different story:

filas: It's part of their character: forgetful
ニャンは 忘[わす]れっぽい。
傘[かさ]は 忘[わす]れがちだ。
この 名前[なまえ]は 忘[わす]れやすい。

bloques.md: Translations: «Nyan is forgetful» (about Nyan); «umbrellas tend to get left behind» (something that often happens, annoyingly); «this name is easy to forget» (about the name). っぽい describes the **person**; がち, an unwelcome **habit**; やすい, how **easy** it is, often a property of the thing itself.

secciones.titulo: Gossip in the park

lineas.jp: ねえ、 カゲって 怒[おこ]りっぽいけど、 ちょっと 子[こ]どもっぽいところも あるよね。
lineas.es: Hey, Kage's quick-tempered, but he's got a bit of a childish side too, hasn't he?

lineas.jp: うん。 でも わたしも 人[ひと]の ことは 言[い]えないよ。 忘[わす]れっぽいし、 朝[あさ]は 遅[おく]れがちだし…。
lineas.es: Yeah. But I can't talk. I'm forgetful, I tend to be late in the mornings…

lineas.jp: たしかに。 それに、 最近[さいきん] ちょっと 太[ふと]りがちじゃない？
lineas.es: True. And haven't you been putting on a bit of weight lately?

lineas.jp: それは 秋[あき]の せいだよ！ 食[た]べものが おいしい 季節[きせつ]だから。
lineas.es: That's autumn's fault! It's the season when everything tastes good.

lineas.jp: ありがちな 言[い]い 訳[わけ]だね。
lineas.es: That's the oldest excuse in the book.

bloques.md: A cultural note: in Japan people talk a lot about the «autumn of appetite», 食欲[しょくよく]の 秋[あき], because it's the season for chestnuts, sweet potatoes, mushrooms and fish at their best. Nyan's excuse is so predictable that Tama dismisses it with an ありがち.

ejercicios.pregunta: A scarf that's more or less white:
ejercicios.jp: ＿ マフラー
ejercicios.explica: For colours, っぽい is «-ish»: 白[しろ]っぽい, whitish. がち is about things that tend to happen, and らしい about what's typical of something.
The stem of 忘[わす]れる is 忘[わす]れ, and with っぽい you get «forgetful», a character trait.
怒[おこ]る is an う-verb, so its stem is 怒[おこ]り. With っぽい: someone who loses their temper easily.
Stem 遅[おく]れ + がち: «tends to run late», with the sense that it's not a good thing.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which one praises a child for acting like a child?
ejercicios.explica: らしい says something has what's typical of what it is, and in a child that's good: childlike. っぽい is used mostly when someone seems like a child without being one: childish, usually a criticism. 子[こ]どもがち doesn't exist.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which sentence sounds odd?
opciones: タマは 毎日[まいにち] 勉強[べんきょう]しがちだ。
冬[ふゆ]は 家[いえ]に こもりがちだ。
おじいちゃんは 病気[びょうき]がちだ。
ejercicios.explica: がち carries a negative «this happens too much». Studying every day is a good thing, so 勉強[べんきょう]しがち sounds like a vice. Better: よく 勉強[べんきょう]する.

ejercicios.es: Kage's quick to lose his temper, but deep down he's a good sort.
ejercicios.explica: First the trait, 怒[おこ]りっぽい, which works like any い-adjective, with けど; then what he's really like: 本当[ほんとう]は 優[やさ]しい.

ejercicios.pregunta: How does the sentence end?
ejercicios.jp: この バスは 雪[ゆき]の 日[ひ]は 遅[おく]れ＿。
ejercicios.explica: がち behaves like a な-adjective, so it closes the sentence with だ: 遅[おく]れがちだ. がちい doesn't exist, and っぽい is an い-adjective, which never takes だ after it.

ejercicios.es: In winter you tend to shut yourself away indoors.
ejercicios.explica: こもる (to shut yourself away) + がち, then がちに なる: «it ends up happening often».

ejercicios.pregunta: A friend tells you a thoroughly predictable story. What do you say?
opciones: ありがちな 話[はなし]だね。
あるっぽい 話[はなし]だね。
ありやすい 話[はなし]だね。
ejercicios.explica: ありがち is the ready-made word for «typical, the sort of thing that always happens». The other two aren't used that way.
大人[おとな] + っぽい, then the negative like any い-adjective: い becomes くない.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which one describes the person rather than something that tends to happen?
opciones: ニャンは 忘[わす]れっぽい。
傘[かさ]は 忘[わす]れがちだ。
この 名前[なまえ]は 忘[わす]れやすい。
ejercicios.explica: 忘[わす]れっぽい describes a character trait: Nyan is forgetful. がち is about an unfortunate habit, and やすい about how easy that name is to forget.

lecciones.titulo: Causative and passive: making, letting and having it done to you
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to say that the teacher made you read aloud, that Nyan was allowed to eat cake, that Kage had his umbrella stolen and that you were made to sing at the festival. And you'll know how to ask, as politely as can be, to be allowed to do something.

secciones.titulo: Three forms that change who does what

bloques.md:
In an ordinary sentence, the subject does the action: Nyan eats, Tama reads. But life is often less simple. Sometimes someone **makes another person** do something (the teacher makes us read), or **lets them** do it (Tama lets Nyan eat her cake). Other times the subject doesn't do anything at all: it's **done to them** (Kage gets his umbrella stolen). And sometimes, worst of all, they're **made to** do something (Nyan is made to sing at the festival).

Japanese handles all of this by conjugating the verb. No helper verb like English «make» or «let» is needed: you just change the ending.

**Causative** (させる): making someone do something, or letting them.
**Passive** (られる): receiving someone else's action.
**Causative-passive** (させられる): being made to do something.

Some good news before we start: all three forms produce a brand-new **る-verb**, which conjugates exactly like 食[た]べる. 読[よ]ませる, 読[よ]まれる and 読[よ]まされる have their negative in ない, their past in た and their て-form in て, like any る-verb you already know. Learn to build them once and the rest comes for free.

secciones.titulo: The causative: making or letting

bloques.md:
**う-verbs**: the final u becomes a, and you add せる. As in the negative, う turns into わ.
読[よ]む → 読[よ]ませる, 行[い]く → 行[い]かせる, 待[ま]つ → 待[ま]たせる, 買[か]う → 買[か]わせる

**る-verbs**: drop る and add させる.
食[た]べる → 食[た]べさせる, 見[み]る → 見[み]させる

**Irregulars**: する → させる, 来[く]る → 来[こ]させる

A tip: the causative looks a lot like the negative. 読[よ]まない → 読[よ]ませる; 食[た]べない → 食[た]べさせる. If you can make the negative, you're halfway there.

Now for the interesting bit: **the same form covers both «make» and «let»**. In English those are two very different verbs (forcing versus allowing), but Japanese sees them as a single idea: someone with the power to decide has another person do something. Whether they force it or permit it is left to context.

items.jp: フクロウ 先生[せんせい]は 学生[がくせい]に 教科書[きょうかしょ]を 読[よ]ませた。
items.es: Fukuro-sensei made the students read the textbook.
items.nota: The teacher's in charge: make.

items.jp: お 母[かあ]さんは 子[こ]どもに 野菜[やさい]を 食[た]べさせた。
items.es: The mother made her child eat vegetables.
items.nota: Probably by force. But it could also mean «she fed her child vegetables».

items.jp: タマは ニャンに ケーキを 食[た]べさせて あげた。
items.es: Tama let Nyan eat her cake.
items.nota: With てあげる, it's clearly a favour: let.

items.jp: ポンさんは 子[こ]どもたちに 店[みせ]の 中[なか]で 遊[あそ]ばせて いる。
items.es: Pon lets the children play inside the shop.

bloques.md:
**Where does everyone go?** The person making or letting is the subject (は or が). The person doing the action takes **に**, especially when the verb already has an object with を: 先生[せんせい]は ニャンに 本[ほん]を 読[よ]ませた. If you gave Nyan を as well, the sentence would have two を and nobody could tell which was which.

With verbs **that have no object**, like 行[い]く, 走[はし]る or 来[く]る, the person can take either を or に, and there's a useful tendency: **を** sounds more like «make» (they're moved like a chess piece, without being asked), and **に** more like «let» (their own wish is respected).

items.jp: コーチは 選手[せんしゅ]を 走[はし]らせた。
items.es: The coach made the players run.
items.nota: を: an order, full stop.

items.jp: お 父[とう]さんは 娘[むすめ]に 一人[ひとり]で 旅行[りょこう]に 行[い]かせた。
items.es: The father let his daughter go travelling on her own.
items.nota: に: she wanted to go, and he allowed it.

secciones.titulo: Making people feel: laugh, cry, wait

bloques.md: The causative is used all the time with verbs of emotion and reaction, to say someone **causes** something in another person. There are no orders or permission here: it's English «make someone laugh» or «make someone cry».

items.jp: ニャンは いつも みんなを 笑[わら]わせる。
items.es: Nyan always makes everyone laugh.

items.jp: 妹[いもうと]を 泣[な]かせちゃった。
items.es: I made my little sister cry.
items.nota: Causative + ちゃった: not on purpose, and with regret.

items.jp: 心配[しんぱい]させて ごめんね。
items.es: Sorry for making you worry.

items.jp: お 待[ま]たせしました。
items.es: Sorry to have kept you waiting.
items.nota: From 待[ま]たせる, «to make someone wait». You'll hear it in every restaurant, every shop and every time someone turns up late.

bloques.md: お 待[ま]たせしました is such a set phrase that Japanese people say it even if you've only waited ten seconds: the waiter says it when bringing your dish, the shop assistant when coming back with your size. They're not apologising for some huge delay; it's a way of acknowledging they've kept you hanging on. Between friends, just お 待[ま]たせ！ will do.

secciones.titulo: Let me do it: させてください and させてもらう

bloques.md: Combine the causative with what you already know about requests and favours, and you get some of the most useful phrases in Japanese. The logic goes like this: if 行[い]かせる is «let go», then 行[い]かせて ください is «please let me go», literally «do me the favour of letting me go».

bloques.titulo: Asking to be allowed to do something
bloques.md:
**〜させて ください**: «let me…», «allow me to…». Polite and direct.
**〜させて もらえますか / もらえませんか**: «could you let me…?». Softer, because you're asking instead of requesting.
**〜させて くれる / もらう**: saying someone let you do something, with gratitude.

In keigo there's also 〜させて いただく, which you'll see in the keigo lesson.

items.jp: ここは わたしに 払[はら]わせて ください。
items.es: Please, let me pay this time.
items.nota: The battle over who pays the bill is a Japanese classic.

items.jp: ちょっと 考[かんが]えさせて ください。
items.es: Let me think about it a little.
items.nota: The polite way of not saying yes just yet.

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は 早[はや]く 帰[かえ]らせて もらえませんか。
items.es: Would you mind if I left early today?

items.jp: タマの お 母[かあ]さんが 泊[と]まらせて くれた。
items.es: Tama's mum let me stay the night.
items.nota: くれた: she let me, and I'm grateful.

bloques.md: Don't confuse 〜させて ください with 〜て ください. 食[た]べて ください is «please eat» (you, the listener, do it). 食[た]べさせて ください is «please let me eat» (I do it, and I'm asking permission). The causative changes who's eating: that's why that させ slips in the middle.

secciones.titulo: The passive: when it's done to you

bloques.md:
**う-verbs**: u → a + れる.
読[よ]む → 読[よ]まれる, 言[い]う → 言[い]われる, 叱[しか]る → 叱[しか]られる, 盗[ぬす]む → 盗[ぬす]まれる

**る-verbs**: る → られる.
食[た]べる → 食[た]べられる, 見[み]る → 見[み]られる

**Irregulars**: する → される, 来[く]る → 来[こ]られる

The person doing the action takes **に**: 先生[せんせい]に 呼[よ]ばれた, «I was called by the teacher».

For る-verbs, the passive is identical to the potential form you met in its own lesson: 食[た]べられる can be «be eaten» or «be able to eat». Context decides, and there's hardly ever any doubt: カゲに ケーキを 食[た]べられた can only be passive, because someone (に) is doing the eating. With う-verbs there's no confusion: 読[よ]める is «can read» and 読[よ]まれる is «be read».

English uses the passive quite a bit, but Japanese uses it even more, and the reason is very Japanese: a Japanese sentence likes to **keep the same point of view**, usually yours. If something happens to you, you stay the star of the sentence, and whoever acted slips into the background with に. Where English might happily switch to «the teacher called me», Japanese tends to stay with you: 先生[せんせい]に 呼[よ]ばれた.

items.jp: ニャンは 先生[せんせい]に ほめられた。
items.es: Nyan was praised by the teacher.
items.nota: Nyan's the star; the teacher is the one acting.

items.jp: カゲは コタローに 追[お]いかけられた。
items.es: Kage got chased by Kotarō.
items.nota: Poor Kage: Kotarō's only a little dog, but a very persistent one.

items.jp: 駅[えき]で 知[し]らない 人[ひと]に 道[みち]を 聞[き]かれた。
items.es: At the station, a stranger asked me for directions.

items.jp: タマに 映画[えいが]に 誘[さそ]われた。
items.es: Tama's asked me to the cinema.
items.nota: 言[い]われる, 誘[さそ]われる, 頼[たの]まれる, 呼[よ]ばれる: the passives you'll hear most in Japanese.

bloques.md: The passive is also used, as in English, when **it doesn't matter who** did something, or to talk about things in general. It's what you'll see in the news, on signs and in books: この 本[ほん]は 世界中[せかいじゅう]で 読[よ]まれて いる, «this book is read all over the world». With things and in formal writing, the doer often takes によって instead of に; you'll see that in the lesson on written Japanese.

secciones.titulo: The passive of annoyance

bloques.md: And now, the gem of Japanese: a passive that **doesn't exist** in most European languages. In Japanese you can put into the passive **things that aren't done directly to you**, but that affect you, nearly always badly. That's why it's called the passive of annoyance, or the suffering passive.

items.jp: 帰[かえ]りに 雨[あめ]に 降[ふ]られた。
items.es: I got rained on on the way home.
items.nota: Rain doesn't do anything «to you»… but you still get soaked.

items.jp: 夜中[よなか]に 赤[あか]ちゃんに 泣[な]かれて、 眠[ねむ]れなかった。
items.es: The baby started crying in the middle of the night and I couldn't sleep.
items.nota: Crying isn't something you do to anyone, but you're the one who suffers.

items.jp: テストの 前[まえ]に 友達[ともだち]に 来[こ]られて、 勉強[べんきょう]できなかった。
items.es: A friend turned up on me before the test and I couldn't study.

bloques.md: The most common case is when someone does something **to something of yours**. In Japanese, you (the one affected) are the star, and the thing keeps its を:

items.jp: 電車[でんしゃ]で 財布[さいふ]を 盗[ぬす]まれた。
items.es: I had my wallet stolen on the train.

items.jp: 満員[まんいん] 電車[でんしゃ]で 足[あし]を 踏[ふ]まれた。
items.es: Someone trod on my foot on the packed train.

items.jp: カゲに ケーキを 食[た]べられた！
items.es: Kage went and ate my cake!
items.nota: It doesn't just say Kage ate it: it says you're the victim.

bloques.md: Come to think of it, English has something quite similar, with other pieces: **«get»** and **«have… done»**. «I **got** rained on», «I **had** my wallet stolen», «the baby cried **on me** all night». Those constructions put the person affected at the centre, just like the subject of the Japanese passive. When translating, reach for them: they're usually the best way to carry the annoyance across.

わたしの 財布[さいふ]が 盗[ぬす]まれた is grammatical, but it sounds like a police report: it tells what happened to the wallet. When the victim is you, the natural version is 財布[さいふ]を 盗[ぬす]まれた, with you as the star (even if unspoken) and the wallet with を. That way the sentence says what really matters: it happened to you.

**No passive for favours.** Since the passive tends to sound like annoyance, when someone does you a good turn the natural choice is てもらう or てくれる, from the lesson on favours. タマに 教[おし]えて もらった is «Tama taught me (and I'm grateful)»; タマに 教[おし]えられた sounds cold, or even as if it was dumped on you unasked. There are some very common exceptions, like ほめられる (be praised) or 誘[さそ]われる (be invited), which are good things in themselves.

secciones.titulo: The causative-passive: being made to…

bloques.md: Put the two forms together, causative first and passive second, and you get the complaining form: **you were made to do something you didn't want to**. You're the star, the one forcing you takes に, and the tone is «I had no choice».

Causative + passive: させる → させ**られる**.

**る-verbs**: 食[た]べる → 食[た]べさせる → 食[た]べさせられる
**Irregulars**: する → させられる, 来[く]る → 来[こ]させられる
**う-verbs**: 読[よ]む → 読[よ]ませる → 読[よ]ませられる. But in conversation the **short form** is far more common: u → a + **される**. 読[よ]まされる, 行[い]かされる, 待[ま]たされる, 歌[うた]わされる.

The short form isn't used with verbs ending in す, because you'd get a clumsy さされる: 話[はな]す → 話[はな]させられる.

items.jp: ニャンは 先生[せんせい]に 漢字[かんじ]を 百回[ひゃっかい] 書[か]かされた。
items.es: Nyan was made to write the kanji a hundred times by the teacher.

items.jp: 病院[びょういん]で 二時間[にじかん]も 待[ま]たされた。
items.es: They kept me waiting at the hospital for a whole two hours.

items.jp: 子[こ]どもの ころ、 母[はは]に ピーマンを 食[た]べさせられた。
items.es: When I was little, my mum used to make me eat green peppers.

items.jp: この 映画[えいが]には 考[かんが]えさせられた。
items.es: This film really made me think.
items.nota: No complaint here: the film «made» you think, and that's praise. Very common with 考[かんが]えさせられる.

bloques.md:
Compare carefully:
先生[せんせい]は ニャンに 書[か]かせた: «the teacher made Nyan write» (told from the teacher's side).
ニャンは 先生[せんせい]に 書[か]かされた: «Nyan was made to write by the teacher» (told from Nyan's side, and you can tell he didn't enjoy it).
Same event, seen from two sides. Japanese picks the second when the speaker is on the side of the person on the receiving end of the order.

secciones.titulo: All three at a glance

filas: 読[よ]まされる / 読[よ]ませられる

bloques.md:
And who plays which part:

**Causative**: the one making or letting is the subject; the one acting takes に (or を).
**Passive**: the one affected or receiving is the subject; the one acting takes に.
**Causative-passive**: the one forced is the subject; the one forcing takes に.

In all three, notice who the star is: Japanese picks the form so that the sentence is told from the point of view of whoever matters most to the speaker.

secciones.titulo: After the autumn festival

lineas.jp: 昨日[きのう]の 秋祭[あきまつ]り、 どうだった？
lineas.es: So how was the autumn festival yesterday?

lineas.jp: 大変[たいへん]だったよ。 カゲに 舞台[ぶたい]で 歌[うた]わされたんだ。
lineas.es: It was a nightmare. Kage made me sing on stage.

lineas.jp: えっ、 ニャンが 歌[うた]ったの？
lineas.es: What? You sang?

lineas.jp: うん。 しかも 途中[とちゅう]で 雨[あめ]に 降[ふ]られて、 びしょびしょ。
lineas.es: Yep. And halfway through I got rained on and ended up soaked.

lineas.jp: でも、 みんな 笑[わら]ってたぞ。 お 前[まえ]は 人[ひと]を 笑[わら]わせる 天才[てんさい]だな。
lineas.es: But everyone was laughing. You're a genius at making people laugh.

lineas.jp: それ、 ほめてるの？
lineas.es: Is that a compliment?

lineas.jp: … 次[つぎ]は 俺[おれ]にも 歌[うた]わせろ。
lineas.es: …Next time, let me sing too.

lineas.jp: ふふ。 本当[ほんとう]は 歌[うた]いたかったんだね。
lineas.es: Hehe. You really wanted to sing, didn't you?

bloques.md: One short dialogue, all three forms: 歌[うた]わされた (causative-passive: I was made to sing), 雨[あめ]に 降[ふ]られて (passive of annoyance), 笑[わら]わせる (causative: make laugh) and 歌[うた]わせろ, the imperative of the causative, «let me sing», said Kage-style, with no beating about the bush.

ejercicios.explica: う-verb: the u becomes a, 読[よ]ま, and you add せる.
る-verb: drop る and add させる.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which particle does the person doing the action take?
ejercicios.jp: 先生[せんせい]は ニャン＿ 本[ほん]を 読[よ]ませた。
ejercicios.explica: The verb already has an object with を, 本[ほん]を, so the reader takes に. Two を in the same sentence wouldn't make clear which is which.
う-verb ending in う: う becomes わ, as in the negative, and you add れる.
盗[ぬす]む → 盗[ぬす]まれる, then the past like any る-verb: 盗[ぬす]まれた.

ejercicios.pregunta: Your wallet has been stolen. Which sentence is the natural one?
opciones: 財布[さいふ]を 盗[ぬす]まれた。
財布[さいふ]を 盗[ぬす]ませた。
財布[さいふ]が 盗[ぬす]んだ。
ejercicios.explica: Passive of annoyance: you're the victim and the wallet keeps its を. 盗[ぬす]ませた would mean you let someone steal it, and 財布[さいふ]が 盗[ぬす]んだ, that the wallet stole something.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does お 待[ま]たせしました mean?
opciones: Sorry to have kept you waiting.
ejercicios.explica: It comes from 待[ま]たせる, «to make someone wait»: the speaker acknowledges keeping you waiting. «Please wait a moment» would be お 待[ま]ちください.

ejercicios.es: Let me think about it a little.
ejercicios.explica: 考[かんが]える in the causative is 考[かんが]えさせる; in the て-form with ください it becomes «do me the favour of letting me think».

ejercicios.pregunta: Tama kindly explained something to you and you want to show you're grateful. What do you say?
opciones: タマに 教[おし]えて もらった。
タマに 教[おし]えられた。
タマに 教[おし]えさせた。
ejercicios.explica: For a favour, てもらう: you receive something good and appreciate it. The passive would sound cold or annoyed, and the causative would mean you made her teach you.

ejercicios.es: I got rained on on the way home.
ejercicios.explica: Passive of annoyance: the rain (に) falls, and you're the one who suffers. 帰[かえ]りに is «on the way back».
With う-verbs, the short form is u → a + される: 待[ま]たされる, «be kept waiting».
Causative 食[た]べさせる + passive: 食[た]べさせられる. る-verbs have no short form.

ejercicios.es: The teacher made me write the kanji a hundred times.
ejercicios.explica: You're the star (no need to say it), the teacher who forces you takes に, and 書[か]かされた is the short form of 書[か]かせられた.

ejercicios.pregunta: «I was made to speak in front of everyone.» Which form is correct?
ejercicios.jp: みんなの 前[まえ]で ＿。
ejercicios.explica: Verbs ending in す don't use the short form, because you'd get a clumsy さされる: 話[はな]させられた. 話[はな]させた would be «I made someone speak».

lecciones.titulo: Keigo: raising others and lowering yourself
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll understand what people say to you in shops, stations and hotels, you'll be able to talk to the teacher or a customer without putting your foot in it, and you'll spot at a glance whether someone is raising you up or lowering themselves.

secciones.titulo: Three steps of politeness

bloques.md:
In English, respect is mostly carried by extra words: «would you mind», «may I», «sir», «madam». Japanese works differently. Instead of wrapping the sentence in polite padding, it **moves people up or down** depending on who is doing each action. This system is called **敬語[けいご]**, keigo, «language of respect», and it has three steps:
