**丁寧語[ていねいご]**, the polite style: です and ます. You've known it from the start. It's courteous to everyone and doesn't raise or lower anybody.
**尊敬語[そんけいご]**, the honorific: **raises the other person**. It's used for the actions of someone you respect: the teacher comes, the customer eats, the boss says.
**謙譲語[けんじょうご]**, the humble: **lowers you**. It's used for your own actions when you do them for, or in front of, someone you respect: I go, I say, I show you.

The key question before every verb is always the same: **who is doing this action?** If it's someone you respect, honorific. If it's you (or your people), humble.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]が 来[き]ます。
items.es: The teacher is coming.
items.nota: Polite: correct, but neutral.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]が いらっしゃいます。
items.es: The teacher is coming.
items.nota: Honorific: the action is hers, so you raise her.

items.jp: 明日[あした]、 わたしが 参[まい]ります。
items.es: I'll come tomorrow.
items.nota: Humble: the action is yours, so you lower yourself.

bloques.md: Behind all this lies a very Japanese idea: **inside and outside**, 内[うち] and 外[そと]. Your group (your family, your company, your school) is «inside», and when you talk to someone from «outside», you lower your own people along with yourself, even if you speak to them respectfully at home. That's why an employee on the phone to a customer refers to their own boss without さん and with humble verbs. It seems odd at first, but there's logic to it: facing a customer, you and your boss are one team bowing to them.

secciones.titulo: The special verbs

bloques.md: The most common verbs have their own honorific word and their own humble word. No rule builds them: you learn them as vocabulary. The good news is that there aren't many, and you'll hear them so often that you'll end up knowing them without trying.

filas: 参[まい]る, 伺[うかが]う (visit)
申[もう]す, 申[もう]し 上[あ]げる
食[た]べる・ 飲[の]む
ご 覧[らん]に なる
聞[き]く・ 訪[たず]ねる
お 目[め]に かかる

bloques.md: Five of these verbs have a slightly rebellious ます form: instead of り, they take い. **いらっしゃる → いらっしゃいます**, **おっしゃる → おっしゃいます**, **なさる → なさいます**, **くださる → くださいます**, and ござる → **ございます**. If you say いらっしゃります, people will understand, but it'll sound like a mistake, because centuries of use have worn that り away.

items.jp: フクロウ 先生[せんせい]は 職員室[しょくいんしつ]に いらっしゃいます。
items.es: Fukuro-sensei is in the staff room.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]が そう おっしゃいました。
items.es: That's what the teacher said.

items.jp: どうぞ、 召[め]し 上[あ]がって ください。
items.es: Please, help yourself.
items.nota: What you say to a guest when offering them food.

items.jp: はじめまして。 ニャンと 申[もう]します。
items.es: How do you do? My name is Nyan.
items.nota: 申[もう]す: you introduce yourself by lowering yourself. The standard way to do a formal introduction.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]の 絵[え]を 拝見[はいけん]しました。
items.es: I've seen your painting, Sensei.
items.nota: The looking is yours, and what's looked at is hers: humble.

items.jp: この 本[ほん]を ご 存[ぞん]じですか。
items.es: Are you familiar with this book?

secciones.titulo: The formula for every other verb

bloques.md: And the verbs without a special word? For those there's a formula that almost always works. It starts from the verb stem (the ます form without ます), puts a respectful お in front and finishes with a verb that sets the direction: up or down.

bloques.titulo: Honorific: お + stem + に なる
bloques.md:
待[ま]つ → お 待[ま]ちに なる
帰[かえ]る → お 帰[かえ]りに なる
読[よ]む → お 読[よ]みに なる

With Chinese-origin words that go with する, like 利用[りよう]する or 説明[せつめい]する, you use ご instead of お: ご 利用[りよう]に なる.

The image is a lovely one: the respected person doesn't simply «go home», they «become someone who goes home». In Japanese, saying things indirectly is a way of not touching the other person with your words.

bloques.titulo: Humble: お + stem + する (or いたす)
bloques.md:
持[も]つ → お 持[も]ちする, «let me carry this for you»
送[おく]る → お 送[おく]りする, «I'll see you off, I'll send it to you»
知[し]らせる → お 知[し]らせする, «I'll let you know»

With Chinese-origin words: ご 案内[あんない]する, ご 連絡[れんらく]する.

With いたす instead of する, it goes up a notch: お 持[も]ちいたします, ご 案内[あんない]いたします. That's what you'll hear in hotels and department stores.

bloques.titulo: Requests: お + stem + ください
bloques.md:
待[ま]つ → お 待[ま]ちください, «please wait»
入[はい]る → お 入[はい]りください, «please come in»
注意[ちゅうい]する → ご 注意[ちゅうい]ください, «please be careful»

It's more refined than 〜て ください, and you'll read it on every sign and hear it on every platform.

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]は もう お 帰[かえ]りに なりました。
items.es: The teacher has already gone home.

items.jp: お 荷物[にもつ]、 お 持[も]ちしましょうか。
items.es: Shall I carry your luggage for you?
items.nota: You're offering to do something for the other person: humble.

items.jp: 黄色[きいろ]い 線[せん]の 内側[うちがわ]まで お 下[さ]がりください。
items.es: Please stand behind the yellow line.
items.nota: The Japanese platform announcement. You'll hear it a thousand times.

bloques.md: **Don't use the humble form for the other person's actions.** 先生[せんせい]、 お 待[ま]ちしますか is a serious slip: お〜する lowers whoever does the action, so you'd be lowering the teacher. The right version is お 待[ま]ちに なりますか. It's the most typical keigo mistake learners make, because お appears in both formulas; the difference is in the ending: になる raises, する lowers.

The formula has its limits. It doesn't work with verbs whose stem is a single syllable (お 見[み]に なる isn't said: that's why ご 覧[らん]に なる exists), or with verbs that already have their own special word (you say いらっしゃる, not お 行[い]きに なる). And be careful about **stacking** keigo: おっしゃられる piles another honorific layer on top of おっしゃる, and although you'll hear it often, many Japanese people find it overdone, much as over-the-top politeness grates in English.

secciones.titulo: The light honorific: 〜れる / 〜られる

bloques.md:
There's a third way to raise someone, lighter and easier: using the **passive form** as an honorific. 先生[せんせい]が 来[こ]られる, 先生[せんせい]が 書[か]かれた. It sounds respectful but less ceremonious than いらっしゃる or お〜に なる, and it's very common at the office, on the news and in older people's speech.

Since it's identical to the passive you saw in the previous lesson, context decides: 先生[せんせい]が 本[ほん]を 書[か]かれた, with the teacher as the one acting, is «the teacher wrote a book», said respectfully.

items.jp: 社長[しゃちょう]は 何時[なんじ]に 戻[もど]られますか。
items.es: What time will the company president be back?

items.jp: 先生[せんせい]は 毎朝[まいあさ] 公園[こうえん]を 歩[ある]かれるそうです。
items.es: I hear the teacher walks in the park every morning.

secciones.titulo: お and ご: dressing words up

bloques.md:
Besides verbs, keigo also touches nouns, with two prefixes: **お** and **ご**. They do two different jobs:

**1. Respecting what belongs to the other person**: お 名前[なまえ] (your name), ご 家族[かぞく] (your family), お 仕事[しごと] (your work).
**2. Speaking elegantly**, without it belonging to anyone in particular: お 茶[ちゃ], お 水[みず], ご 飯[はん], お 金[かね]. Some words carry お almost all the time, and dropping it sounds blunt or rough.

As a tendency, **お** goes with native Japanese words and **ご** with Chinese-origin ones: お 手紙[てがみ], ご 住所[じゅうしょ]. But there are plenty of very common exceptions (お 電話[でんわ], お 時間[じかん], お 元気[げんき]), so it's best to learn them as they come.

**Don't put お on your own things** when it's there to honour them. わたしの お 名前[なまえ]は… sounds as if you're bowing to yourself: what you say is わたしの 名前[なまえ]は… or, better still, ニャンと 申[もう]します. On the other hand, お 茶[ちゃ] or ご 飯[はん] can perfectly well be yours, because there お isn't honouring anyone: it just makes the word prettier.

And you almost never put お on katakana loanwords: nobody says おコーヒー or おパン, because it sounds like a parody of an over-refined lady (sometimes people do it as a joke, precisely for that reason).

secciones.titulo: ございます: the です of hotels

bloques.md:
ございます comes from the old verb ござる, and it's the most polite version of ある. You already know it without realising: it's in **ありがとう ございます** and in **おはよう ございます**. On top of that:

**ございます** = あります, dressed up: お 手洗[てあら]いは 二階[にかい]に ございます.
**で ございます** = です, dressed up: こちらが お 部屋[へや]で ございます.

You'll hear it mostly in hotels, department stores and smart restaurants. You don't need to use it yourself, but you do need to recognise it: when someone speaks to you with でございます, they're treating you as a VIP customer.

items.jp: 申[もう]し 訳[わけ]ございません。
items.es: I do apologise.
items.nota: The formal apology par excellence: the dressed-up version of すみません.

items.jp: こちらは 北海道[ほっかいどう]の ラベンダーで ございます。
items.es: This is lavender from Hokkaido, madam.

secciones.titulo: Shop and phone keigo

bloques.md: There's a kind of keigo you'll hear every single day in Japan, even if you never speak it: the keigo of shops, restaurants and the phone. It's made of set phrases, and it pays to recognise them on the fly.

filas: Walking into any shop. No need to reply.
When the waiter takes your order: it's keigo for 分[わ]かりました.
少々[しょうしょう] お 待[ま]ちください
Before they go and fetch something.
お 待[ま]たせいたしました
When they come back or bring your order.
〜で よろしいでしょうか
When introducing themselves, in person or on the phone.
To announce what they're about to do.

lineas.jp: いらっしゃいませ。
lineas.es: Welcome!

lineas.jp: この お 弁当[べんとう]、 ください。
lineas.es: This bento, please.

lineas.jp: かしこまりました。 温[あたた]めますか。
lineas.es: Certainly. Shall I heat it up for you?

lineas.jp: はい、 お 願[ねが]いします。
lineas.es: Yes, please.

lineas.jp: 少々[しょうしょう] お 待[ま]ちください。 …お 待[ま]たせいたしました。 五百円[ごひゃくえん]で ございます。
lineas.es: One moment, please… Sorry to keep you waiting. That'll be five hundred yen.

lineas.jp: ちょうど いただきます。 ありがとう ございました。
lineas.es: That's exactly right. Thank you very much!

bloques.md: Notice that Nyan doesn't use keigo: です/ます and お 願[ねが]いします are all he needs. In a shop, the keigo comes from the person serving you; the customer just speaks politely. So don't stress: in most situations, your job is to **understand** keigo, not to produce it.

**〜させて いただきます** deserves a word. It comes from the causative plus いただく, as you saw in the previous lesson: literally «I humbly receive your permission to…». It's the height of courtesy for announcing something you're about to do: 説明[せつめい]させて いただきます, «allow me to explain». But it's become so fashionable that it turns up even where nobody has given permission for anything. On the doors of closed shops you'll see 本日[ほんじつ]は 休業[きゅうぎょう]させて いただきます, «we humbly take the liberty of closing today», and more than one Japanese person finds that excessive. Use it to announce something you're doing for the other person, and don't put it in every sentence.

On the phone, the inside/outside principle really shows. If you call a company and ask for Mr Tanaka, the receptionist will tell you 田中[たなか]は ただいま 席[せき]を 外[はず]して おります, «Tanaka is away from his desk right now», **without さん** and with humble おる. She's not being disrespectful to her boss: facing you, an outsider, Tanaka is on her team, and she lowers him to her side.

secciones.titulo: When to use it (and when not to)

bloques.md:
Relax: nobody expects a learner to master keigo, and plenty of young Japanese people only really learn it when they start work. With です and ます, a handful of set phrases and the most common special verbs (いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, 召[め]し 上[あ]がる, 申[もう]す, 参[まい]る, いただく), you'll get a very long way.

**Use it** with the teacher, with customers, with older people you don't know, in interviews and on formal phone calls. **Don't use it** with friends or family: with Tama, an いらっしゃいますか would sound so cold she'd think you were cross with her or pulling her leg.

**Never use the honorific for yourself.** わたしが いらっしゃいます or わたしが 召[め]し 上[あ]がります are mistakes that make any Japanese person smile, because you're raising yourself up: it's like saying «I, Your Excellency, shall deign to come». For your own actions, always humble or, if in doubt, just です/ます. Plain です/ます is never a mistake; a misdirected honorific is.

One last point: keigo isn't the same everywhere or across generations. Some regions have their own forms of respect, and young people use it less, and less rigidly, than their grandparents. What you've seen here is standard keigo, the kind that works all over Japan and in any office.

secciones.titulo: A visit to the staff room

lineas.jp: 失礼[しつれい]します。 フクロウ 先生[せんせい]は いらっしゃいますか。
lineas.es: Excuse me. Is Fukuro-sensei here?

lineas.jp: はい、 ここに いますよ。 どうしましたか。
lineas.es: Yes, I'm here. What is it?

lineas.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]の お 土産[みやげ]を お 持[も]ちしました。
lineas.es: We've brought you a souvenir from Hokkaido.

lineas.jp: 小樽[おたる]の お 菓子[かし]です。 先生[せんせい]は 甘[あま]い ものを 召[め]し 上[あ]がりますか。
lineas.es: They're sweets from Otaru. Do you eat sweet things, Sensei?

lineas.jp: ええ、 大好[だいす]きですよ。 ありがとう。 いただきます。
lineas.es: Oh yes, I love them. Thank you. I'll have some.

lineas.jp: よかった！ 帰[かえ]りの 電車[でんしゃ]で 半分[はんぶん] 食[た]べちゃおうかと 思[おも]ったけど、 我慢[がまん]して よかった。
lineas.es: Phew! On the train back I nearly ate half of them, but I'm glad I held out.

lineas.jp: ニャン、 先生[せんせい]に 聞[き]こえてるよ…。
lineas.es: Nyan, the teacher can hear you…

bloques.md: Look how the keigo is shared out: the students raise the teacher (いらっしゃいますか, 召[め]し 上[あ]がりますか) and lower themselves (お 持[も]ちしました). The teacher answers in ordinary です/ます, because she has no need to raise her students. And when Nyan gets excited and turns to Tama, he drops straight back into plain speech: keigo depends on **who** you're talking to, sentence by sentence.

ejercicios.pregunta: The teacher is coming tomorrow. Which verb raises her?
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした]、 先生[せんせい]が ＿。
ejercicios.explica: The action is the teacher's, so it's honorific: いらっしゃる. 参[まい]る and おる are humble, for your own actions: using them would lower the teacher.

ejercicios.pregunta: You tell a customer that you'll go to their office. Which verb do you use?
ejercicios.jp: 明日[あした]、 わたしが ＿。
ejercicios.explica: The action is yours: humble, 参[まい]る. いらっしゃる and 行[い]かれる are honorific, and using them for yourself would mean raising yourself up.
It's one of the five rebel verbs: in the ます form, り becomes い. いらっしゃいます, not いらっしゃります.
お + the stem 待[ま]ち + ください: the refined «please wait».
Honorific: お + the stem 帰[かえ]り + に なる. The respected person «becomes someone who goes home».
Humble: お + the stem 持[も]ち + します. You're offering to carry something for the other person.

ejercicios.pregunta: What's the honorific of 見[み]る?
opciones: ご 覧[らん]に なる
お 見[み]に なる
ejercicios.explica: 見[み]る has a one-syllable stem, so the formula doesn't work: お 見[み]に なる isn't said. That's why ご 覧[らん]に なる exists. 拝見[はいけん]する is the humble one, for when you're the one looking.

ejercicios.pregunta: You offer the teacher some food. What do you say?
opciones: どうぞ、 召[め]し 上[あ]がって ください。
どうぞ、 いただいて ください。
どうぞ、 食[た]べて ください。
ejercicios.explica: She's the one eating: honorific, 召[め]し 上[あ]がる. いただく is humble, for when you eat, so you'd be asking her to lower herself. 食[た]べて ください isn't wrong, but with the teacher it falls short.

ejercicios.es: My name is Nyan (formal introduction).
ejercicios.explica: 申[もう]す is the humble form of 言[い]う: when introducing yourself, you lower yourself. The name takes と, like a quote.

ejercicios.es: I'll show you the way to the station.
ejercicios.explica: 案内[あんない] is a Chinese-origin word, so it takes ご; with いたします it's humble and very refined. The action is yours, done for the other person.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does かしこまりました mean?
ejercicios.explica: It's keigo for 分[わ]かりました: what the waiter or shop assistant says when taking your order. «Welcome» is いらっしゃいませ, and «I do apologise» is 申[もう]し 訳[わけ]ございません.

ejercicios.pregunta: You work at a company. A customer calls asking for your boss, Tanaka, who's out. What do you say?
opciones: 田中[たなか]は ただいま 席[せき]を 外[はず]して おります。
田中[たなか]さんは ただいま いらっしゃいません。
田中[たなか]様[さま]は ただいま おりません。
ejercicios.explica: In front of an outsider, your boss is on your team: no さん, and humble おる. Raising him with いらっしゃる in front of a customer would put him above the customer.

ejercicios.pregunta: What's the natural way to talk about your own name?
opciones: わたしの 名前[なまえ]は ニャンです。
わたしの お 名前[なまえ]は ニャンです。
わたしの ご 名前[なまえ]は ニャンです。
ejercicios.explica: The お in お 名前[なまえ] honours someone else's name. Putting it on your own would be bowing to yourself. And ご 名前[なまえ] doesn't exist.

ejercicios.pregunta: What do you ask the teacher to find out whether she'll wait?
opciones: 先生[せんせい]、 お 待[ま]ちに なりますか。
先生[せんせい]、 お 待[ま]ちしますか。
先生[せんせい]、 お 待[ま]ちいたしますか。
ejercicios.explica: The action is hers: honorific, お〜に なる. お〜する and お〜いたす are humble, and would lower the teacher. It's the most typical keigo mistake.

lecciones.titulo: 〜ても, さえ and こそ: even if, not even, and this one
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to say that Nyan would keep eating even if he were full, that Kage can't even cook rice, that as long as it's sunny you're happy, and that this year you really are going to see the Sapporo snow.

secciones.titulo: 〜ても: even if

bloques.md:
Picture Nyan in front of a plate of dango. He's already had three helpings. Tama tells him he's going to burst. And Nyan replies: お 腹[なか]が いっぱいでも、 食[た]べる. «Even if I'm full, I'm eating it». That «even if» is **〜ても**: it says something will happen **all the same**, whatever happens with the condition.

It couldn't be simpler to form: て-form + **も**. The も you already know, the «also» one, gives the sentence that flavour of «even so».

**Verbs**: て-form + も. 食[た]べて → 食[た]べても, 読[よ]んで → 読[よ]んでも, 行[い]って → 行[い]っても, して → しても, 来[き]て → 来[き]ても
**Negative**: 〜なくても. 食[た]べなくても, «even if you don't eat».
**い-adjectives**: 〜くても. 高[たか]い → 高[たか]くても; いい → よくても
**な-adjectives and nouns**: 〜でも. 静[しず]かでも, 雨[あめ]でも, 子[こ]どもでも

items.jp: 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]っても、 お 祭[まつ]りに 行[い]く。
items.es: I'm going to the festival even if it rains.

items.jp: この ケーキは 高[たか]くても 買[か]いたい。
items.es: I want to buy this cake even if it's expensive.

items.jp: カゲは 寒[さむ]くても コートを 着[き]ない。
items.es: Kage won't wear a coat even when it's cold.
items.nota: Proud, even in the face of the cold.

items.jp: 明日[あした]は 休[やす]みでも、 早[はや]く 起[お]きる。
items.es: Even though tomorrow's a day off, I'm getting up early.

items.jp: 今[いま] 行[い]かなくても、 間[ま]に 合[あ]うよ。
items.es: Even if you don't go now, you'll make it in time.

bloques.md: A detail English speakers will appreciate: English distinguishes «even **if** it rains» (it might) from «even **though** it's raining» (it is). Japanese makes no such distinction with ても: both are 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]っても. Nor does ても have a tense of its own: it never goes into the past. The final verb sets the time: 昨日[きのう]は 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]っても 出[で]かけた, «yesterday I went out even though it was raining».

**ても is not のに.** Both can come out as «even though», but they don't think alike. のに, which you met when learning to link sentences, is about a **real** fact that clashes with expectations, and it brings annoyance or surprise: 雨[あめ]なのに、 カゲは 傘[かさ]を 持[も]って いない, «it's raining and Kage hasn't got an umbrella (how come?)». ても says the result **doesn't change** whatever happens, and it tends to look at possible situations: 雨[あめ]でも 行[い]く, «I'll go, rain or shine». If you're complaining about something that's already happened, のに; if you're standing firm against whatever may happen, ても.

By the way, now you can see where the permission you learned with 〜ても いい comes from: 食[た]べても いい is literally «even if you eat, it's fine». And 〜なくても いい, «even if you don't, it's fine»: there's no need. It wasn't a magic formula: it was ても all along.

secciones.titulo: No matter how much: いくら, どんなに and double ても

bloques.md: To say «no matter how much», ても teams up with **いくら** or **どんなに** at the start. The idea is pushed to the limit: not even in the most extreme case does the result change.

items.jp: ニャンは いくら 食[た]べても 太[ふと]らない。
items.es: Nyan doesn't put on weight no matter how much he eats.
items.nota: Or so he says.

items.jp: どんなに 練習[れんしゅう]しても、 カゲに 勝[か]てない。
items.es: No matter how much I practise, I can't beat Kage.

items.jp: 食[た]べても 食[た]べても、 お 腹[なか]が すく。
items.es: I eat and eat, and I'm still hungry.
items.nota: Repeating 〜ても twice gives the feeling of something that never ends.

secciones.titulo: It doesn't matter what: question word + ても

bloques.md:
Put a question word in front, and 〜ても says it **doesn't matter** what the answer is: the result is the same. What, who, where, when, how: anything goes.

In the lesson on questions you met 何[なん]でも (anything) and 誰[だれ]でも (anyone). Now you can see where they come from: they're 何[なに] and 誰[だれ] with the でも used after nouns, «even if it's what, even if it's who».

items.jp: タマは 何[なに]を 着[き]ても 似合[にあ]う。
items.es: Tama looks good in whatever she wears.

items.jp: 誰[だれ]に 聞[き]いても、 答[こた]えが 分[わ]からない。
items.es: No matter who I ask, nobody knows the answer.

items.jp: 富良野[ふらの]は いつ 行[い]っても きれいだ。
items.es: Furano is beautiful whenever you go.

items.jp: どこに 隠[かく]しても、 コタローが 見[み]つけて しまう。
items.es: Wherever you hide it, Kotarō always finds it.

bloques.md:
Special mention for **どうしても**, «whatever you do», which has become an expression in its own right, with two faces:

With an affirmative: «no matter what, at all costs». どうしても 雪[ゆき]まつりに 行[い]きたい, «I want to go to the snow festival whatever it takes».
With a negative: «there's no way». どうしても 納豆[なっとう]が 食[た]べられない, «I just can't bring myself to eat natto».

secciones.titulo: さえ: not even… and even

bloques.md:
**さえ** takes something and presents it as **the most extreme case**. With a negative: «not even that». With an affirmative: «even that». It's «even» said with your eyes wide open.

It goes after a noun and takes the place of が or を. With other particles, it comes after them: に さえ, と さえ. With a subject you'll often hear **で さえ**.

items.jp: カゲは ご 飯[はん]さえ 炊[た]けない。
items.es: Kage can't even cook rice.
items.nota: The most basic thing in Japanese cooking: if he can't do that, he can't do anything.

items.jp: 忙[いそが]しくて、 水[みず]を 飲[の]む 時間[じかん]さえ なかった。
items.es: I was so busy I didn't even have time for a drink of water.

items.jp: この 問題[もんだい]は 先生[せんせい]で さえ 分[わ]からなかった。
items.es: Not even the teacher could solve this problem.

items.jp: そんな ことは 子[こ]どもで さえ 知[し]って いる。
items.es: Even a child knows that.

bloques.md: So how is it different from も? In the lesson on は, も and が you saw that も with a negative also gives «not even»: 一口[ひとくち]も 食[た]べなかった, «I didn't eat a single bite». The difference is intensity: も is the ordinary way to say it; さえ stresses that it's **the bare minimum** or **the least expected thing**, and it sounds more emphatic, a little bookish. When in doubt, も never sounds odd; さえ, used all the time, sounds theatrical.
With verbs, さえ attaches to the stem and is rounded off with する: 見[み]さえ しない, «won't even look at it». 謝[あやま]りさえ しなかった, «didn't even apologise».

secciones.titulo: 〜さえ〜ば: as long as…

bloques.md: And now for the lovely twist. Put さえ together with the ば conditional, and the idea of «the minimum» flips around: it's no longer «not even the minimum», but **«the minimum is enough»**. It's English «as long as…», «if only…» or «all you need is…».

Noun + さえ + verb in ば: 時間[じかん]さえ あれば, «as long as I have time»
Verb stem + さえ + すれば: 飲[の]みさえ すれば, «as long as you take it»
い-adjective in く + さえ + あれば: 安[やす]くさえ あれば, «as long as it's cheap»

items.jp: おにぎりさえ あれば、 ニャンは 幸[しあわ]せだ。
items.es: As long as there are onigiri, Nyan is happy.

items.jp: 天気[てんき]さえ よければ、 明日[あした]は 羊蹄山[ようていざん]が 見[み]えるよ。
items.es: As long as the weather's good, you'll be able to see Mount Yōtei tomorrow.

items.jp: この 薬[くすり]を 飲[の]みさえ すれば、 すぐ 治[なお]りますよ。
items.es: All you need to do is take this medicine and you'll soon be better.

bloques.md: Notice it's the same さえ as before, seen from the other side. さえ always points to **the smallest extreme**. With a negative, not even that extreme is met (what a disaster). With ば, that extreme is enough (what a relief).

secciones.titulo: こそ: this one, precisely

bloques.md: **こそ** is a spotlight. It points at one word and says: «**this** one, and no other». It's English «precisely», «this very…», or the stressed «this year I **really** will…». Like さえ, it goes after the noun and takes the place of は, が or を.

items.jp: 今年[ことし]こそ さっぽろ 雪[ゆき]まつりに 行[い]きたい。
items.es: This year I really want to go to the Sapporo Snow Festival.
items.nota: こそ with a time word: «this time for sure», after several missed chances.

items.jp: 今度[こんど]こそ 負[ま]けないぞ！
items.es: This time I'm definitely not losing!
items.nota: Kage's favourite line.

items.jp: 好[す]きだからこそ、 厳[きび]しく 言[い]うんだ。
items.es: It's precisely because I care that I'm being tough on you.
items.nota: からこそ: «precisely because». It puts the spotlight on the reason.

bloques.md: And here's a set phrase you can start using straight away: **こちらこそ**. When someone says よろしく お 願[ねが]いします or ありがとう to you, you reply こちらこそ, «likewise», «no, thank **you**». こちら means «this side», that is, you; with こそ you're saying «no, it's me, precisely».

lineas.jp: いつも ありがとう ございます。
lineas.es: Thanks for always coming in.

lineas.jp: いえいえ、 こちらこそ！
lineas.es: Oh no, thank you!

bloques.md: こそ packs a punch, so don't scatter it everywhere: if everything is «this one precisely», nothing is. Save it for when you really want to single one thing out from all the rest. And don't mix up こそ and さえ: さえ goes to the **minimum** («not even that», «as long as that»); こそ goes to **the chosen one** («this one, for sure»).

secciones.titulo: Kage's rematch

lineas.jp: ニャン！ 今日[きょう]こそ 雪[ゆき]合戦[がっせん]で お 前[まえ]に 勝[か]つ！
lineas.es: Nyan! Today I'm finally beating you at snowball fighting!

lineas.jp: えー、 何回[なんかい] やっても 同[おな]じだよ。
lineas.es: Oh, come on, however many times you try, it'll end the same way.

lineas.jp: カゲは 負[ま]けても 負[ま]けても あきらめないね。
lineas.es: Kage loses and loses, but he never gives up, does he?

lineas.jp: うるさい。 手袋[てぶくろ]さえ あれば、 この 前[まえ]は 俺[おれ]が 勝[か]ってた。
lineas.es: Shut up. If I'd just had my gloves, I'd have won last time.

lineas.jp: じゃあ、 今日[きょう]は 手袋[てぶくろ]、 持[も]って きたよね？
lineas.es: So you've brought your gloves today, right?

lineas.jp: …ポケットに ある。 たぶん。
lineas.es: …They're in my pocket. Probably.

bloques.md: One short dialogue: こそ (today for sure), question word + ても (however many times), double ても (loses and loses) and さえ〜ば (if I'd just had my gloves). And, as ever, Kage with his excuse at the ready.

ejercicios.explica: The て-form, 食[た]べて, + も: «even if I eat».
The て-form of 行[い]く is irregular, 行[い]って; add も for 行[い]っても.
い-adjectives change い to くて, then add も: 高[たか]くても, «even if it's expensive».

ejercicios.pregunta: Noun + «even if»:
ejercicios.jp: 雨[あめ]＿、 お 祭[まつ]りに 行[い]く。
ejercicios.explica: With nouns and な-adjectives, 〜ても becomes でも: 雨[あめ]でも, «even if it rains».
The negative 書[か]かない, with ない → なくても: «even if you don't write».

ejercicios.pregunta: «It's raining, and Kage hasn't got an umbrella (how odd!).» What goes in the gap?
ejercicios.jp: 雨[あめ]＿、 カゲは 傘[かさ]を 持[も]って いない。
ejercicios.explica: It's a real fact that clashes with expectations, with surprise or annoyance: のに. でも would mean «even if it rains, it doesn't matter», and こそ means «precisely».

ejercicios.es: Tama looks good in whatever she wears.
ejercicios.explica: 何[なに]を 着[き]ても, «whatever she wears», comes before the result that doesn't change: 似合[にあ]う.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Kage can't even cook rice.»
ejercicios.jp: カゲは ご 飯[はん]＿ 炊[た]けない。
ejercicios.explica: さえ with a negative marks the bare minimum: if he can't do that, he can't do anything. こそ would mean «rice, precisely», which doesn't fit a negative.

ejercicios.es: As long as there are onigiri, Nyan is happy.
ejercicios.explica: さえ + ば: the minimum is enough. First the condition (おにぎりさえ あれば), then the result.

ejercicios.pregunta: Someone says よろしく お 願[ねが]いします when meeting you. How do you reply?
opciones: こちらこそ よろしく お 願[ねが]いします。
こちらさえ よろしく お 願[ねが]いします。
こちらでも よろしく お 願[ねが]いします。
ejercicios.explica: こちらこそ is the set reply: «likewise, it's me who…». こそ singles out «me, precisely». さえ and でも make no sense here.

ejercicios.pregunta: «This year I really want to go.»
ejercicios.jp: 今年[ことし]＿ 行[い]きたい。
ejercicios.explica: こそ shines the spotlight: this year, and no other, after letting it slip by before. さえ would be «not even this year» or «as long as it's this year», and ても doesn't go after a noun.

ejercicios.es: No matter how much I practise, I can't beat Kage.
piezas: 練習[れんしゅう]しても、
ejercicios.explica: どんなに opens the «no matter how much» and 〜ても closes it; then comes the result that doesn't change.

ejercicios.pregunta: «All you need to do is take this medicine and you'll get better.»
ejercicios.jp: この 薬[くすり]を 飲[の]み＿ すれば、 治[なお]ります。
ejercicios.explica: Verb stem + さえ + すれば: the minimum is enough. こそ isn't used like that with verbs, and 飲[の]みても doesn't exist (the form would be 飲[の]んでも).

lecciones.titulo: について, にとって and friends: expressions worth their weight in gold
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to give a talk about Hokkaido, say what Nyan means to Tama, explain that the price depends on the season, describe how it gets colder as you climb Mount Yōtei, ask someone to grab some milk while they're at it, and build new words with 〜さ, 〜 的[てき], 〜 化[か] and 〜 性[せい].

secciones.titulo: Prepositions in several pieces

bloques.md:
English has prepositions to spare: about, for, towards, according to… Japanese, which gets by with short particles, also has a handful of **set expressions** that work like big prepositions. Almost all of them are built the same way: the particle **に** + a verb frozen in the て-form.

について comes from 就[つ]く (to attach to), にとって from 取[と]る (to take), に 対[たい]して from 対[たい]する (to face), によって from よる (to rest on). You don't need to remember where they come from, but it helps with the meaning: について is «stuck to the topic», によって is «resting on».

They go after a noun and link that noun to the verb of the sentence:
北海道[ほっかいどう]に ついて 話[はな]す, «to talk about Hokkaido».

If instead of a verb you want to describe a **noun**, add **の** (or use the dictionary form of the frozen verb):
北海道[ほっかいどう]に ついての 本[ほん], «a book about Hokkaido».
子[こ]どもに 対[たい]する 愛情[あいじょう], «affection towards children».

secciones.titulo: について: about

bloques.md: **について** marks the **topic** that's being talked about, thought about, written about or asked about. It's the «about» of «talk about», «a book about».

items.jp: 明日[あした]、 北海道[ほっかいどう]に ついて 発表[はっぴょう]します。
items.es: Tomorrow I'm giving a presentation about Hokkaido.

items.jp: この 問題[もんだい]に ついて、 どう 思[おも]いますか。
items.es: What do you think about this problem?

items.jp: タマは 猫[ねこ]に ついての 本[ほん]を たくさん 持[も]って いる。
items.es: Tama has loads of books about cats.
items.nota: Before a noun: についての.

bloques.md: Watch out for English «about», which is a false friend with several faces. «I'll arrive at **about** five» isn't について: it's an approximate time, 五時[ごじ]ごろ. «There were **about** twenty people» isn't either: that's 二十人[にじゅうにん]ぐらい. について only covers the **topic** «about»: talk about, write about, know about. If you can swap «about» for «on the subject of», then it's について.
In speeches and very formal contexts you'll hear **につきまして**, the polite version: 今後[こんご]の 予定[よてい]に つきまして ご 説明[せつめい]します, «I shall now explain our schedule going forward».

secciones.titulo: にとって: for someone

bloques.md: **にとって** is «for X» in the sense of **«from X's point of view»**, «in X's eyes». It goes with judgements and evaluations: important, difficult, special, a problem, a treasure.

items.jp: ニャンに とって、 おにぎりは 宝物[たからもの]だ。
items.es: For Nyan, onigiri are treasure.

items.jp: わたしに とって、 タマは 一番[いちばん] 大切[たいせつ]な 友達[ともだち]です。
items.es: To me, Tama is my most important friend.

items.jp: 子[こ]どもに とって、 この 漢字[かんじ]は 難[むずか]しすぎる。
items.es: For a child, this kanji is too difficult.

bloques.md: English «for» is another dangerous all-rounder. にとって only covers the «for» of **opinion or evaluation** («for me, it's important»). It doesn't work for who receives something: «a present for Tama» is タマへの プレゼント or タマに あげる プレゼント. Nor for purpose: «I study for the exam» is 合格[ごうかく]する ために 勉強[べんきょう]する, as you saw in the lesson on ために and ように. If you can swap «for» for «in the eyes of», then it's にとって.

secciones.titulo: Towards someone, set against something

bloques.md:
**に 対[たい]して** has two uses, and both come from the idea of «facing»:

**1. Towards someone**: the direction of an attitude, a feeling or an action. Being kind to, rude to, complaining to.
**2. In contrast with**: «whereas». One thing is set against another to compare them.

items.jp: カゲは 先生[せんせい]に 対[たい]して 失礼[しつれい]な ことを 言[い]った。
items.es: Kage said something rude to the teacher.
items.nota: Direction of the attitude: towards the teacher.

items.jp: ポンさんは お 客[きゃく]さんに 対[たい]して、 いつも 丁寧[ていねい]だ。
items.es: Pon is always very courteous towards his customers.

items.jp: 兄[あに]が 静[しず]かなのに 対[たい]して、 弟[おとうと]は とても にぎやかだ。
items.es: Whereas the older brother is quiet, the younger one is really lively.
items.nota: Contrast: to join two sentences, put の in front: 静[しず]かなのに 対[たい]して.

bloques.md: Because it's more formal and «heavier» than a plain に, in everyday conversation it's used mainly when you want to stress someone's attitude towards another person. And before a noun you'll see **に 対[たい]する**: 先生[せんせい]に 対[たい]する 感謝[かんしゃ], «gratitude towards the teacher».

secciones.titulo: によって: depending on, according to, by

bloques.md: **によって** comes from よる, «to rest on, to be based on». Several uses grow out of it that look different but share the idea of «one thing resting on another»:
**1. Depending on**: the result changes according to X. It's the most useful one in conversation, and it nearly always comes with verbs like 違[ちが]う (to differ) or 変[か]わる (to change).

items.jp: 人[ひと]に よって、 好[す]きな 季節[きせつ]は 違[ちが]う。
items.es: People's favourite season differs from person to person.

items.jp: 季節[きせつ]に よって、 富良野[ふらの]の 景色[けしき]は 全然[ぜんぜん] 変[か]わる。
items.es: Furano's scenery changes completely depending on the season.

items.jp: 場合[ばあい]に よっては、 明日[あした]の 授業[じゅぎょう]は 休[やす]みに なるかもしれません。
items.es: Depending on how things go, there may be no class tomorrow.
items.nota: によっては: «in some cases», «possibly».

bloques.md: If someone asks you something and the answer is «it depends», the perfect reply is **場合[ばあい]に よります**, «it depends on the situation», or simply **人[ひと]に よります**, «it depends on the person».

**2. By, by means of, because of** (mainly in formal writing): the means or cause of something. **3. By whom** in the formal passive, instead of に. You'll see both a lot in the news and in books, as you'll find out in the lesson on written Japanese.

**4. According to a source**: **によると** (or によれば) introduces where a piece of information comes from, and usually finishes with そうだ or らしい, as you saw in the lesson on appearances.

items.jp: 台風[たいふう]に よって、 電車[でんしゃ]が 止[と]まった。
items.es: The trains stopped because of the typhoon.

items.jp: この 寺[てら]は 村[むら]の 人々[ひとびと]に よって 建[た]てられた。
items.es: This temple was built by the villagers.

items.jp: 天気[てんき] 予報[よほう]に よると、 明日[あした]は 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]るそうだ。
items.es: According to the forecast, it's going to snow tomorrow.

secciones.titulo: につれて and にしたがって: as…

bloques.md: **につれて** says that **two changes go hand in hand**: as one moves forward, so does the other. It's «as», «the more… the more». It goes after a dictionary-form verb or a noun that already means change, like 成長[せいちょう], «growth», or 変化[へんか], «change».

items.jp: 山[やま]を 登[のぼ]るに つれて、 寒[さむ]く なって きた。
items.es: As we climbed the mountain, it started getting colder.

items.jp: 秋[あき]が 深[ふか]まるに つれて、 紅葉[こうよう]が きれいに なる。
items.es: As autumn deepens, the leaves get more beautiful.

items.jp: 日本語[にほんご]が 上手[じょうず]に なるに つれて、 アニメが もっと 楽[たの]しく なった。
items.es: As my Japanese improved, anime became more and more fun.

bloques.md: **にしたがって** means the same in this use, with a slightly more formal or written feel: 北[きた]へ 行[い]くに したがって、 気温[きおん]が 下[さ]がる, «the further north you go, the lower the temperature». But したがう also has its own meaning, «to follow, to obey», and with that にしたがって means **«following»**: 先生[せんせい]の 指示[しじ]に したがって ください, «please follow the teacher's instructions».

につれて needs **change on both sides**, little by little. It doesn't work for a one-off action: 家[いえ]に 帰[かえ]るに つれて、 ご 飯[はん]を 食[た]べた makes no sense, because going home and having dinner don't grow together. For «when I get home…», use たら or とき. And if you want «the more…, the more…», you also have 〜ば〜ほど, from the lesson on ほど: 練習[れんしゅう]すれば するほど 上手[じょうず]に なる.

secciones.titulo: かわりに and ついでに

bloques.md: Two very practical words with a similar structure: they go after a noun with の, or after a verb.

bloques.titulo: かわりに: instead of, in exchange
bloques.md:
**Instead of, in place of**: noun + の 代[か]わりに, verb + 代[か]わりに.
先生[せんせい]の 代[か]わりに, «in place of the teacher».
出[で]かける 代[か]わりに, «instead of going out».

**In exchange**: one thing makes up for the other.
手伝[てつだ]う 代[か]わりに, «in return for helping you».

On its own at the start of a sentence, **その 代[か]わり** means «in return», «mind you».

items.jp: 今日[きょう]は フクロウ 先生[せんせい]の 代[か]わりに、 校長[こうちょう] 先生[せんせい]が 来[き]た。
items.es: Today the head teacher came in place of Fukuro-sensei.

items.jp: 雨[あめ]だから、 出[で]かける 代[か]わりに 家[いえ]で 映画[えいが]を 見[み]よう。
items.es: It's raining, so instead of going out let's watch a film at home.

items.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]を 手伝[てつだ]う 代[か]わりに、 ケーキを おごって ね。
items.es: I'll help with your homework, but in return you're buying me cake.
items.nota: That's how Nyan negotiates.

bloques.titulo: ついでに: while you're at it
bloques.md:
Taking advantage of doing one thing to do another.
Noun + の ついでに: 買[か]い 物[もの]の ついでに, «while I was out shopping».
Verb + ついでに: 駅[えき]に 行[い]く ついでに, «since you're going to the station anyway».

On its own, ついでに means «while you're at it», «on the way».

items.jp: 買[か]い 物[もの]の ついでに、 郵便局[ゆうびんきょく]に 寄[よ]った。
items.es: While I was out shopping, I popped into the post office.

items.jp: コンビニに 行[い]くなら、 ついでに 牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]も 買[か]って きて。
items.es: If you're going to the shop, grab some milk while you're at it.

items.jp: 札幌[さっぽろ]に 行[い]った ついでに、 小樽[おたる]まで 足[あし]を のばした。
items.es: Since I was in Sapporo anyway, I went on as far as Otaru.
items.nota: 足[あし]を のばす: «stretch your legs», meaning go a little further than planned.

bloques.md: ついでに is for small things you do **on the side**. If you tell someone タマに 会[あ]う ついでに…, you're saying that seeing her is the minor part, something you do «while you're at it». Tama might take offence, and rightly so. With people who matter, make the visit the main event.

secciones.titulo: Suffixes for building words

bloques.md: Japanese has suffixes that turn one word into another, just as English does with «-ness», «-ization» or «-ic». Knowing these four will let you understand hundreds of words you've never studied.

filas: Adjective → noun: the degree of something
高[たか]さ (height), 寒[さむ]さ (the cold), 優[やさ]しさ (kindness), 大切[たいせつ]さ (importance)
日本的[にほんてき] (very Japanese), 伝統的[でんとうてき] (traditional), 個人的[こじんてき]に (personally)
国際化[こくさいか] (internationalisation), 映画化[えいがか] (film adaptation), 自動化[じどうか] (automation)
安全性[あんぜんせい] (safety), 可能性[かのうせい] (possibility), 必要性[ひつようせい] (necessity)

bloques.md: **〜さ** attaches to い-adjectives (minus the い) and to many な-adjectives (minus the な). It measures or names the degree of a quality: 高[たか]さ is «height» (how tall something is), 重[おも]さ «weight». いい gives よさ, «the good thing about something»: この 町[まち]の よさ, «what's good about this town».

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 冬[ふゆ]の 寒[さむ]さに びっくりした。
items.es: I was shocked by how cold Hokkaido gets in winter.

items.jp: 羊蹄山[ようていざん]の 高[たか]さは どのくらいですか。
items.es: How high is Mount Yōtei?

items.jp: タマの 優[やさ]しさに 助[たす]けられた。
items.es: Tama's kindness saved me.

bloques.md: **〜 的[てき]** turns a noun into a な-adjective. Many of these words are educated, newspaper vocabulary, but some come up every day: 基本的[きほんてき]に (basically), 個人的[こじんてき]に (personally, speaking for myself). Among young people you'll even hear わたし 的[てき]には, «as for me», which is colloquial and a bit tongue-in-cheek: don't use it in an exam.

items.jp: この 旅館[りょかん]は とても 日本的[にほんてき]だ。
items.es: This inn is very Japanese.

items.jp: 個人的[こじんてき]には、 夏[なつ]より 冬[ふゆ]の 北海道[ほっかいどう]が 好[す]きです。
items.es: Personally, I prefer Hokkaido in winter to summer.

bloques.md: **〜 化[か]** names a process of change, and with する it becomes a verb: この 漫画[まんが]は 映画化[えいがか]される, «this manga is going to be made into a film». **〜 性[せい]** names a quality or nature: 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]る 可能性[かのうせい]が ある, «there's a possibility of snow».

These suffixes mostly attach to words of Chinese origin (two kanji, on-reading), not to native Japanese words or to verbs. You can't invent 食[た]べる 的[てき] or 猫化[ねこか] (though the second one would get a laugh). Use them to **recognise** words; before coining your own, check they actually exist.

secciones.titulo: Tama's presentation

lineas.jp: 今日[きょう]は 北海道[ほっかいどう]に ついて 発表[はっぴょう]します。
lineas.es: Today I'm going to talk about Hokkaido.

lineas.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]は 季節[きせつ]に よって、 景色[けしき]が 全然[ぜんぜん] 違[ちが]います。 夏[なつ]は ラベンダー、 冬[ふゆ]は 雪[ゆき]です。
lineas.es: In Hokkaido the scenery is completely different depending on the season. Lavender in summer, snow in winter.

lineas.jp: わたしに とって、 一番[いちばん] 大切[たいせつ]な 場所[ばしょ]です。
lineas.es: To me, it's the most important place in the world.

lineas.jp: 質問[しつもん]！ 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 食[た]べ 物[もの]に ついても 教[おし]えて ください！
lineas.es: Question! Tell us about the food in Hokkaido too!

lineas.jp: お 前[まえ]に とっては、 それが 一番[いちばん] 大事[だいじ]だな。
lineas.es: For you, that's what matters most, huh?

lineas.jp: では、 次[つぎ]の 授業[じゅぎょう]で、 発表[はっぴょう]の 代[か]わりに みんなで 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 料理[りょうり]を 作[つく]りましょう。
lineas.es: Well then, next lesson, instead of presentations, we'll all cook a Hokkaido dish together.

lineas.jp: やったー！ ついでに デザートも！
lineas.es: Yay! And dessert too, while we're at it!

ejercicios.pregunta: «I'm going to write an essay about Hokkaido.»
ejercicios.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]＿ 作文[さくぶん]を 書[か]く。
ejercicios.explica: It's the topic of the essay: について. にとって would be «in Hokkaido's eyes» and によって «depending on Hokkaido» or «by means of Hokkaido».

ejercicios.pregunta: «For Nyan, onigiri are treasure.»
ejercicios.jp: ニャン＿、 おにぎりは 宝物[たからもの]だ。
ejercicios.explica: It's an evaluation from Nyan's point of view: にとって. について would be «about Nyan», and に 対[たい]して «towards Nyan».

ejercicios.pregunta: «A book about cats.» What goes between について and the noun?
ejercicios.jp: 猫[ねこ]に ついて＿ 本[ほん]
ejercicios.explica: To describe a noun, these expressions take の: についての 本[ほん].

ejercicios.es: People's favourite season differs from person to person.
ejercicios.explica: によって, «depending on», comes first, and 違[ちが]う closes the sentence: the result varies with the person.

ejercicios.pregunta: Someone asks if Sapporo ramen is spicy. You want to say «it depends on the shop». What do you say?
opciones: 店[みせ]に よります。
店[みせ]に とります。
店[みせ]に ついてです。
ejercicios.explica: 〜に よります is «it depends on…». It comes from the verb よる, «to rest on». The other two mean nothing in this context.

ejercicios.pregunta: «As we climbed, it got colder.»
ejercicios.jp: 山[やま]を 登[のぼ]る＿、 寒[さむ]く なった。
ejercicios.explica: Two changes moving together: climbing and getting colder. That's につれて. 代[か]わりに would be «instead of climbing», and ついでに «while I was climbing anyway».

ejercicios.es: Today the head teacher came in place of our teacher.
piezas: 校長[こうちょう] 先生[せんせい]が
ejercicios.explica: Noun + の 代[か]わりに: «in place of the teacher». Then who came (が) and the verb.

ejercicios.pregunta: Your friend is going to the shop and you want her to bring back milk. Which word do you use?
ejercicios.jp: コンビニに 行[い]くなら、 ＿ 牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]も 買[か]って きて。
ejercicios.explica: ついでに: making the most of her trip to do another small thing. 代[か]わりに would mean buying milk instead of going to the shop.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Whereas the older brother is quiet, the younger one is very lively.»
ejercicios.jp: 兄[あに]が 静[しず]かなのに＿、 弟[おとうと]は にぎやかだ。
ejercicios.explica: A contrast between two things: のに 対[たい]して, «whereas». The others don't express comparison.
Drop the い and add さ: 高[たか]さ, «height», how tall something is.
いい uses its old form, よい, for everything except the dictionary form: よ + さ = よさ, «the good thing about something».

ejercicios.pregunta: Which suffix turns 可能[かのう] into «possibility»?
ejercicios.explica: 〜 性[せい] names a quality or nature, like English «-ity»: 可能性[かのうせい], «possibility».

ejercicios.pregunta: You want to say «This cake is for Tama» (you're giving it to her). Which sentence is correct?
opciones: これは タマへの ケーキです。
これは タマに とっての ケーキです。
これは タマに ついての ケーキです。
ejercicios.explica: For the recipient, への (or タマに あげる). にとって is only the «for» of opinion («for Tama, it's important»), and について would be a cake that's about Tama.

ejercicios.es: Since I was in Sapporo anyway, I went on as far as Otaru.
piezas: 足[あし]を のばした
ejercicios.explica: Verb + ついでに: making the most of one trip to do something else. 足[あし]を のばす is «to extend your outing» to somewhere further.

lecciones.titulo: どころか, なんて and ようがない: speaking with force
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to say that Nyan, far from losing weight, has put some on; scoff «me, get up early? No way!» with all the scorn in the world; exclaim «what a beautiful view!»; and admit that without the address there's no way to find Pon's shop.

secciones.titulo: Nuances with attitude

bloques.md:
So far you've learned to say things clearly. In this lesson you'll learn to say them **with force**: to exaggerate, to scoff, to be amazed and to give up. These are three tools that textbooks leave till late, but on the street, in manga and on TV you hear them all the time:

**どころか**: «far from it», «let alone». Reality goes way beyond what was expected.
**なんて**: «things like that!», «to think that…!», «what a…!». Scorn, surprise or exclamation.
**ようがない**: «there's no way to…». It's not that you don't know how: there simply is no way to do it.

secciones.titulo: どころか: far from…, let alone

bloques.md:
**どころか** takes an idea and says: «that? Not even close». What actually happens is **way beyond** it, usually in the opposite or a more extreme direction. It has two uses:

**1. Quite the opposite**: «far from X, the exact opposite happened».
**2. Not even**: «forget X, not even Y», dropping down to something even more basic.

Noun + どころか: 漢字[かんじ]どころか
Plain-form verb + どころか: やせる どころか
い-adjective + どころか: 楽[たの]しい どころか
な-adjective (no だ; sometimes with な) + どころか: 静[しず]か どころか

items.jp: ダイエットを 始[はじ]めたのに、 やせる どころか 二[に]キロ 太[ふと]った。
items.es: I started a diet, and far from losing weight, I've put on two kilos.
items.nota: Use 1: the exact opposite happened.

items.jp: 図書館[としょかん]は 静[しず]か どころか、 子[こ]どもたちが 走[はし]り 回[まわ]って いた。
items.es: The library was anything but quiet: there were kids running all over the place.

items.jp: カゲは 漢字[かんじ]どころか、 ひらがなも 書[か]けない。
items.es: Kage can't write hiragana, let alone kanji.
items.nota: Use 2: dropping down to something even more basic, with も.

items.jp: 忙[いそが]しくて、 旅行[りょこう]どころか 散歩[さんぽ]する 時間[じかん]も ない。
items.es: I'm so busy I don't even have time for a walk, let alone a trip.

bloques.md: It's also very natural as a reply, to correct what the other person assumed: 「 楽[たの]しかった？」「 楽[たの]しい どころか、 大変[たいへん]だったよ」, «Did you have fun?» «Fun? Far from it, it was a nightmare!». And on its own at the start of a sentence, **それどころか** means «on the contrary», «what's more»: それどころか、 もっと 悪[わる]く なった, «if anything, it's got worse».

A very handy relative: **〜どころじゃない** (or どころではない), «this is no time for…», «I'm in no state to…». It says the situation is so serious or so pressing that anything else is out of the question. It's the perfect phrase for exam week.

items.jp: 明日[あした]は 試験[しけん]だから、 遊[あそ]ぶ どころじゃない。
items.es: I've got an exam tomorrow, so this is no time for fun.

items.jp: 寒[さむ]すぎて、 景色[けしき]を 楽[たの]しむ どころじゃなかった。
items.es: It was so cold we were in no state to enjoy the view.

bloques.md: どころか isn't «instead of», which would be 代[か]わりに. 代[か]わりに swaps one thing for another, neutrally: «instead of going out, I stayed in». どころか says **the expectation falls hopelessly short**, and it always carries surprise or complaint: «go out? I couldn't even get out of bed!». If there's no strong contrast with what was expected, どころか doesn't belong.

secciones.titulo: なんて after: scorn and surprise

bloques.md: **なんて** after a word or a sentence points at it and pulls a face: scorn («that? pfft!»), surprise («to think that…!») or, more gently, playing it down («something like…»). It attaches directly to nouns, and to verbs and adjectives in the plain form.
**1. Scorn: «things like…», «the whole business of…».** It belittles whatever it points at, as if it weren't worth the bother.

items.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]なんて 大嫌[だいきら]い！
items.es: I absolutely hate homework!
items.nota: Not just «homework»: «that horrible thing called homework».

items.jp: 朝[あさ] 五時[ごじ]に 起[お]きるなんて、 無理[むり]だよ。
items.es: Get up at five in the morning? Not a chance.

items.jp: わたしなんて、 まだまだです。
items.es: Oh, I've still got a long way to go.
items.nota: Applied to yourself, なんて is modesty: «someone like me…». It's the standard reply to a compliment.

bloques.md: **2. Surprise: «to think that…!», «who'd have thought…!».** After a whole sentence, it says you find something hard to believe, for better or for worse.

items.jp: こんな ところで 会[あ]えるなんて！
items.es: Fancy running into you here!

items.jp: カゲが 謝[あやま]るなんて、 珍[めずら]しいね。
items.es: Kage apologising? Now there's something you don't see every day.

items.jp: たった 一日[いちにち]で 全部[ぜんぶ] 読[よ]んだなんて、 すごい！
items.es: You read the whole thing in one day? Amazing!

bloques.md: **3. Playing it down: «something like…».** In suggestions, なんて softens things, presenting the idea as just a thought, with no pressure: 週末[しゅうまつ]、 映画[えいが]なんて どう？, «how about a film or something this weekend?».

**Be careful putting なんて after a person.** カゲなんて 知[し]らない is «I'm done with Kage!», said with contempt, and 先生[せんせい]なんて… is disrespecting the teacher. Between friends, as a joke or in the heat of an argument, it happens; but said seriously it hurts, because なんて belittles what it points at. In more relaxed speech you'll also hear **なんか** doing the same job (わたしなんか, 宿題[しゅくだい]なんか), as you saw in the lesson on casual speech.

secciones.titulo: なんて before: what a…!

bloques.md: There's another なんて, which goes **before** an adjective or a described noun, and it's for exclaiming: **«what a…!», «how…!»**. It's a somewhat literary or theatrical form (originally なんと), and it usually ends in だろう or nothing at all. In ordinary conversation people prefer すごく or ほんとに, but in songs, manga and emotional moments you'll hear it.

items.jp: なんて きれいな 景色[けしき]だろう。
items.es: What a beautiful view!
items.nota: Before the adjective: an exclamation, with no scorn at all.

items.jp: なんて 優[やさ]しい 人[ひと]なんだ。
items.es: What a kind person!

bloques.md: The clue for telling them apart is **position**: なんて **after** something points at it (scorn, surprise, «something like»); なんて **before** an adjective lifts it up («what a…!»).

secciones.titulo: ようがない: there's no way to…

bloques.md: **よう** means «way, manner», and **ようがない** is «there's no way». It attaches to the verb stem (the ます form without ます) and says there **is no method** of doing something: not because you lack the skill, but because the situation doesn't allow it.

items.jp: 住所[じゅうしょ]が 分[わ]からないから、 ポンさんの 店[みせ]を 探[さが]しようが ない。
items.es: I don't know the address, so there's no way to look for Pon's shop.

items.jp: 電話[でんわ]番号[ばんごう]を 知[し]らないから、 連絡[れんらく]しようが ない。
items.es: I haven't got his number, so there's no way to get in touch.

items.jp: こんなに 壊[こわ]れたら、 直[なお]しようが ないね。
items.es: Broken like this, there's no fixing it.

items.jp: この 景色[けしき]は 言[い]いようが ないほど 美[うつく]しい。
items.es: This view is beautiful beyond words.

bloques.md: **ようがない isn't the same as the negative potential.** 読[よ]めない means «I can't read it», and it may be your fault (you don't know those kanji). 読[よ]みようが ない means «there's no way to read it»: for instance, because the ink has faded away. That's why ようがない is so handy for excuses: it's nobody's fault, there just **is no way**.

And here's a surprise: one of the most common phrases in Japanese comes from this. **しょうがない** (or しようがない) is literally «there's no way to do (anything)», and it means **«it can't be helped», «oh well»**. It's the phrase of resignation: the train's gone, it's raining, the ice cream's run out… しょうがない. It has a more formal cousin, 仕方[しかた]が ない, which means the same.

And its maximum-strength version, **どうしようもない**, is «there's absolutely nothing to be done». Said of a person, どうしようもない やつ is «a hopeless case».

secciones.titulo: Nyan's diet

lineas.jp: ニャン、 ダイエットは どう？
lineas.es: Nyan, how's the diet going?

lineas.jp: やせる どころか、 二[に]キロ 太[ふと]った…。
lineas.es: Far from losing weight, I've put on two kilos…

lineas.jp: ダイエット 中[ちゅう]に たい 焼[や]きを 五[いつ]つも 食[た]べるなんて、 信[しん]じられない。
lineas.es: Eating five taiyaki in the middle of a diet? Unbelievable.

lineas.jp: だって、 ポンさんの たい 焼[や]きは おいしいんだもん。 我慢[がまん]しようが ないよ。
lineas.es: But Pon's taiyaki are so good. There's just no way to resist.

lineas.jp: まあ、 しょうがないね。
lineas.es: Oh well, it can't be helped.

lineas.jp: お 前[まえ]は どうしようもないな。
lineas.es: You're a hopeless case.

lineas.jp: カゲなんて、 もう 知[し]らない！
lineas.es: Well, I'm done with you, Kage!

lineas.jp: …ほら、 なんて きれいな 夕焼[ゆうや]けだ。
lineas.es: …Look, what a beautiful sunset!

bloques.md: Kage changes the subject as best he can, and in doing so hands you both なんて from this lesson: Nyan's, **after** his name, in a huff; and his own, **before** the adjective, in wonder. Taiyaki, by the way, are little fish-shaped cakes filled with sweet red bean paste: the weak spot of any cat.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Far from losing weight, I put some on.»
ejercicios.jp: やせる＿ 太[ふと]った。
ejercicios.explica: The exact opposite of what was expected happened, with a complaint: どころか. 代[か]わりに would be a plain «instead of», without that strong contrast.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Kage can't even write hiragana, let alone kanji.»
ejercicios.jp: カゲは 漢字[かんじ]どころか、 ひらがな＿ 書[か]けない。
ejercicios.explica: With どころか in its «let alone» use, the most basic thing usually takes も: ひらがなも, «not even hiragana».

ejercicios.es: I don't even have time for a walk, let alone a trip.
piezas: 旅行[りょこう]どころか
ejercicios.explica: First the big thing, 旅行[りょこう]どころか; then the most basic one with も, and the negative at the end.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Get up at five? No way!» (scornfully)
ejercicios.jp: 五時[ごじ]に 起[お]きる＿、 無理[むり]だよ。
ejercicios.explica: なんて after the idea belittles it: «the whole business of getting up at five». どころか would need a second, more extreme part.

ejercicios.pregunta: Someone compliments your Japanese. What's a natural modest reply?
opciones: いえいえ、 わたしなんて まだまだです。
いえいえ、 わたしどころか まだまだです。
いえいえ、 わたしようが ないです。
ejercicios.explica: なんて applied to yourself is modesty: «someone like me still…». The other two make no sense.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which one is an exclamation of admiration, with no scorn?
opciones: なんて きれいな 景色[けしき]だろう。
景色[けしき]なんて どうでも いい。
景色[けしき]なんて 見[み]たくない。
ejercicios.explica: なんて **before** the adjective exclaims: «what a beautiful view!». After 景色[けしき], on the other hand, it scorns it: «who cares about the view», «I don't want to look at views».
The verb stem, 直[なお]し, + ようがない: «there's no way to fix it».

respuestas: れんらくしようがない
ejercicios.explica: The stem of する is し: 連絡[れんらく]し + ようがない, «there's no way to get in touch».

ejercicios.pregunta: The ink on the letter has faded away. What do you say?
opciones: これじゃ、 読[よ]みようが ない。
これじゃ、 読[よ]めなくて ごめん。
これじゃ、 読[よ]むなんて。
ejercicios.explica: It's not a lack of skill: the situation makes reading it impossible. That's ようがない. 読[よ]めない would sound as though the problem were you.

ejercicios.es: Oh well, it can't be helped.
ejercicios.explica: しょうがない is しようがない, «there's no way to do anything»: the phrase of resignation.

ejercicios.pregunta: «Fancy running into you here!»
ejercicios.jp: こんな ところで 会[あ]える＿！
ejercicios.explica: なんて after a whole sentence expresses surprise: something seems hard to believe. Here, a happy surprise.

ejercicios.es: I don't know the address, so there's no way to look for the shop.
ejercicios.explica: First the reason with から, then what you'd like to do, 店[みせ]を 探[さが]す, with ようがない: the situation makes it impossible.

lecciones.titulo: Written Japanese: である, において and company
lecciones.resumen: By the end you'll be able to read a news story, a sign or an article without being put off by that stiff Japanese with no です or ます, and you'll understand why written sentences are joined with a stem instead of with て.

secciones.titulo: Another Japanese: the one you read

bloques.md:
One day Nyan opens Pon's newspaper and gets a fright: not a single です, not a single ます, no よ, no ね. Everything ends in curt forms, words like である and において pop up, and sentences run on without one て-form. Is the newspaper angry?

No. Japanese simply has a **written** register, the one used in newspapers, textbooks, articles, reports and encyclopedias. That kind of Japanese isn't talking to anyone in particular, so it doesn't need to be polite to anyone: it uses the plain form, which in a text sounds not rude but **neutral and impersonal**.

English does the same, even if you don't notice: nobody down the pub says «it should be noted that» or «notwithstanding», but in an article they're perfectly at home. In this lesson you're not going to learn to write like that (that'll come), but to **recognise** it so you can read without fear.

lineas.jp: 先生[せんせい]、 この 新聞[しんぶん]、 です も ます も ありません。 怒[おこ]って いるんですか。
lineas.es: Sensei, this newspaper hasn't got any です or ます. Is it angry?

lineas.jp: いいえ、 怒[おこ]って いる わけでは ありませんよ。 新聞[しんぶん]は 誰[だれ]か 一人[ひとり]に 話[はな]して いる わけでは ないので、 普通[ふつう]の 形[かたち]で 書[か]くんです。
lineas.es: No, it's not that it's angry. A newspaper isn't talking to any one person, so it's written in the plain form.

bloques.md: Mind you, not everything written is in the plain form. Letters, emails, notices addressed to the reader and many blogs use です/ます, because they are talking to someone. Written plain form belongs to texts that **inform or argue** without addressing a particular person.

secciones.titulo: である: the だ of texts

bloques.md: The most recognisable mark of written Japanese is **である**, which takes the place of だ. It does the same job («to be» with nouns and な-adjectives), but it sounds solemn, like an essay or a book. You may know it without realising: Natsume Sōseki's most famous novel is called 吾輩[わがはい]は 猫[ねこ]で ある, «I Am a Cat», and the narrator is, indeed, a cat. Nyan approves.

filas: 学生[がくせい]で ある
学生[がくせい]じゃない
学生[がくせい]では ない
学生[がくせい]で あった
学生[がくせい]じゃなかった
学生[がくせい]では なかった
学生[がくせい]で あろう
学生[がくせい]なので ある

bloques.md: In texts, **じゃない** becomes **ではない**. じゃ is the spoken contraction of では, so in serious writing it looks sloppy, like writing «gonna» in a report. The same goes for the other contractions: ている, not てる; なければならない, not なきゃ; のだ or のである, not んだ.

Not every text uses である. Many newspapers write with だ, and keep である for opinion pieces, books and academic work, where the tone is more reflective. What matters is that both are plain form and neither addresses anyone in particular.

secciones.titulo: Joining sentences with the stem

bloques.md:
In conversation, you join two sentences with the て-form: 雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]って、 道[みち]が 凍[こお]った. In texts, though, you'll very often see something else: the verb **stem** (the ます form without ます) followed by a comma.

雪[ゆき]が 降[ふ]り、 道[みち]が 凍[こお]った. «It snowed, and the roads froze.»

It means the same as the て-form, but it's shorter and sounds more serious. Said aloud in a conversation, it would sound like you were reading the news.

**Verbs**: stem + 、 → 降[ふ]り、 行[い]き、 食[た]べ、 し、
**い-adjectives**: く + 、 → 広[ひろ]く、 寒[さむ]く、
**である**: であり、
**Negative**: ず + 、 → 降[ふ]らず、 (as you saw in the lesson on ないで and ずに)

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]は 広[ひろ]く、 自然[しぜん]が 豊[ゆた]かで ある。
items.es: Hokkaido is vast, and its nature is rich.
items.nota: 広[ひろ]く、 instead of 広[ひろ]くて.

items.jp: 札幌[さっぽろ]は 北海道[ほっかいどう]の 中心[ちゅうしん]で あり、 多[おお]くの 人[ひと]が 住[す]んで いる。
items.es: Sapporo is the heart of Hokkaido, and many people live there.
items.nota: であり、 instead of で.

items.jp: 雨[あめ]は 降[ふ]らず、 気温[きおん]も 下[さ]がらなかった。
items.es: It didn't rain, and temperatures didn't drop either.
items.nota: ず、 instead of なくて.

secciones.titulo: Paper connectors

bloques.md: Texts use their own set of connectors. They all exist in formal speech too (a presentation, a speech), but among friends they'd sound as if you were reading out a report.

filas: しかし、 だが、 が
そのため、 したがって

items.jp: 計画[けいかく]は 順調[じゅんちょう]で あった。 しかし、 大雪[おおゆき]の ため 中止[ちゅうし]と なった。
items.es: The plan was going smoothly. However, it was cancelled due to heavy snow.
items.nota: ため: «due to». And と なった, the written version of に なった.

items.jp: この 町[まち]は 温泉[おんせん]で 有名[ゆうめい]で ある。 また、 海[うみ]の 幸[さち]も 豊富[ほうふ]で ある。
items.es: This town is famous for its hot springs. Its seafood is also plentiful.

bloques.md: **また** has two faces: in conversation it means «again» (また 来[き]てね, «come again»), and in texts, at the start of a sentence, it means «also», «furthermore». Position tells you which: if it opens a sentence and is followed by a comma, it's almost certainly «furthermore».

secciones.titulo: において, による and other written expressions

bloques.md: Just like について, にとって and によって, texts have more に-expressions that conversation handles with a simple particle. These are the ones you'll meet most:

filas: 〜に おいて / 〜に おける
in, at (a place, a field, a moment)
caused by, due to, by means of
〜に 関[かん]して / 〜に 関[かん]する

bloques.md:
**において** is the solemn «in»: 会議[かいぎ]に おいて, «at the meeting»; 日本[にほん]に おける 教育[きょういく], «education in Japan». Before a noun it takes the form における, just as に 対[たい]して becomes に 対[たい]する.

**による** you already know from the lesson on によって: here it mostly appears attached to a noun, to say what caused something. It's the vocabulary of every weather report.

items.jp: 大雨[おおあめ]に よる 被害[ひがい]が 広[ひろ]がって いる。
items.es: Damage caused by torrential rain is spreading.

items.jp: 台風[たいふう]に より、 多[おお]くの 便[びん]が 欠航[けっこう]した。
items.es: Many flights were cancelled due to the typhoon.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]に おける 観光[かんこう]の 歴史[れきし]
items.es: The history of tourism in Hokkaido
items.nota: における + noun: typical of book and article titles.

items.jp: 彼[かれ]は 通訳[つうやく]と して 働[はたら]いて いる。
items.es: He works as an interpreter.

secciones.titulo: News and signs

bloques.md:
**Headlines** are a special case: they compress so much that they swallow particles and verbs. Three habits will help you crack them:

**1. Lots of Chinese-origin nouns**, one after another: 大雪[おおゆき] (heavy snow), 運休[うんきゅう] (service suspension), 影響[えいきょう] (effect).
**2. する-verbs without する**: 運休[うんきゅう] instead of 運休[うんきゅう]する.
**3. Present tense for past events**: the headline tells what happened in the present, just like English «Snow halts trains».

items.jp: 札幌[さっぽろ]で 大雪[おおゆき]、 電車[でんしゃ] 運休[うんきゅう]
items.es: Heavy snow in Sapporo: trains suspended

items.jp: 大雪[おおゆき]で 電車[でんしゃ] 止[と]まる
items.es: Snow brings trains to a halt
items.nota: 止[と]まる in the present, even though it's already happened: that's the headline convention.

bloques.md: **Signs** have a style of their own: kanji compounds and fixed formulas. These are the ones you'll see in any Japanese city:

filas: 立入[たちいり] 禁止[きんし]
関係者[かんけいしゃ] 以外[いがい] 立入[たちいり] 禁止[きんし]
撮影[さつえい] 禁止[きんし]
本日[ほんじつ] 休業[きゅうぎょう]
〜は ご 遠慮[えんりょ]ください

bloques.md: And in school or dormitory rules you'll spot a curious trick: a sentence ending in **こと** used as an instruction. 廊下[ろうか]を 走[はし]らない こと, «no running in the corridors». 十時[じゅうじ]までに 帰[かえ]る こと, «be back by ten». It's the impersonal way of giving written instructions, much like English signs saying «No running» or «Keep off the grass».

ご 遠慮[えんりょ]ください literally means «kindly show restraint», and although it sounds gentle, **it's a ban**. 携帯[けいたい] 電話[でんわ]の ご 使用[しよう]は ご 遠慮[えんりょ]ください isn't a suggestion: it means «no mobile phones», said with good manners. Japanese written for the public prefers to forbid politely rather than with a blunt 禁止[きんし], but the message is the same.

secciones.titulo: The same text, in two Japaneses

bloques.md: To finish, here's a short paragraph about Hokkaido in written Japanese, and the same content as Tama would tell it to her friends. Notice everything that changes: how sentences end, how they join, the connectors and even the vocabulary.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]は 日本[にほん]の 北[きた]に 位置[いち]する 大[おお]きな 島[しま]で ある。 冬[ふゆ]は 寒[さむ]さが 厳[きび]しく、 雪[ゆき]が 多[おお]い。 一方[いっぽう]、 夏[なつ]は 涼[すず]しく、 富良野[ふらの]の ラベンダー 畑[ばたけ]には 多[おお]くの 観光客[かんこうきゃく]が 訪[おとず]れる。
items.es: Hokkaido is a large island situated in the north of Japan. Winters are harsh, with heavy snowfall. Summers, by contrast, are cool, and the lavender fields of Furano attract large numbers of tourists.
items.nota: Written: である, stems like 厳[きび]しく、 and 涼[すず]しく、, the connector 一方[いっぽう] and educated verbs like 位置[いち]する and 訪[おとず]れる.

items.jp: 北海道[ほっかいどう]って、 日本[にほん]の 北[きた]に ある 大[おお]きい 島[しま]だよ。 冬[ふゆ]は すごく 寒[さむ]くて、 雪[ゆき]が いっぱい 降[ふ]るの。 でも 夏[なつ]は 涼[すず]しくて、 富良野[ふらの]の ラベンダー 畑[ばたけ]に 観光客[かんこうきゃく]が たくさん 来[く]るんだ。
items.es: Hokkaido's this big island up in the north of Japan. Winter's freezing and it snows loads. But summer's nice and cool, and tons of tourists come to see the lavender fields in Furano.
items.nota: Spoken: って, だよ, て-forms, でも, の and んだ at the end, いっぱい and たくさん.

bloques.md: You don't need to write like the first paragraph to enjoy Japan, but once you can read it, newspapers, temple noticeboards, museum panels and encyclopedias will open up to you. For a learner, that's like going from watching the world through a window to stepping out into the street.

ejercicios.pregunta: What's the written version of 学生[がくせい]だ?
opciones: 学生[がくせい]で ある
学生[がくせい]じゃない
ejercicios.explica: である takes the place of だ in texts: same job, solemn tone. です is polite, for talking to someone, not the impersonal style of a text.

ejercicios.pregunta: In a formal text, how is 問題[もんだい]だ negated?
opciones: 問題[もんだい]では ない
問題[もんだい]じゃない
問題[もんだい]で ないだ
ejercicios.explica: じゃ is the spoken contraction of では, and in serious writing it looks sloppy. In writing: では ない.

ejercicios.pregunta: Which connector belongs in a written text?
ejercicios.jp: 計画[けいかく]は 順調[じゅんちょう]で あった。 ＿、 大雪[おおゆき]の ため 中止[ちゅうし]と なった。
ejercicios.explica: しかし is the «however» of texts. でも and けど belong to conversation: in formal writing they're out of place.
In texts, the stem (the ます form without ます) replaces the て-form: 降[ふ]り、 instead of 降[ふ]って、.
い-adjectives join with く instead of くて: 広[ひろ]く、 自然[しぜん]が 豊[ゆた]かで ある.
である joins with であり、, the written version of で: 中心[ちゅうしん]で、 becomes 中心[ちゅうしん]で あり、.

ejercicios.pregunta: What does 会議[かいぎ]に おいて mean?
ejercicios.explica: において is the solemn «in, at» of texts: 会議[かいぎ]で, but in writing. «About the meeting» would be 会議[かいぎ]に ついて.

ejercicios.es: Hokkaido is a large island.
piezas: 北海道[ほっかいどう]は
ejercicios.explica: Topic with は, the adjective before 島[しま] and で ある at the end, instead of だ.

ejercicios.es: damage caused by torrential rain
ejercicios.explica: による before a noun says what caused something: the vocabulary of weather reports.

ejercicios.pregunta: You see the sign 立入[たちいり] 禁止[きんし]. What does it mean?
ejercicios.explica: 立入[たちいり] means «entering», and 禁止[きんし] «prohibited». Signs string kanji nouns together without particles.

ejercicios.pregunta: Headline: 大雪[おおゆき]で 電車[でんしゃ] 止[と]まる. When did it happen?
opciones: It's already happened: the trains stopped.
ejercicios.explica: Headlines report past events in the present, just like English «Snow halts trains».

ejercicios.pregunta: What's the written version of 行[い]かなきゃ いけない?
opciones: 行[い]かなければ ならない
ejercicios.explica: なきゃ and なくちゃ are spoken contractions, and 〜ないと is colloquial. In writing, the full form: なければ ならない.
